meaning: New Year (New Year’s Day; also the New Year holiday/season).
additional_notes: Often refers to January 1st (New Year’s Day), but it can also mean the New Year holiday period in general. Common in greetings like “Feliz Año Nuevo” (“Happy New Year”). Capitalization varies; it’s frequently capitalized in greetings or as a holiday name.
target_language_example: ¡Feliz Año Nuevo! ¿Qué vas a hacer en Año Nuevo?
native_language_example: Happy New Year! What are you going to do on New Year’s Day?

additional_notes: A common greeting used in the morning and early afternoon. Use it in both formal and informal situations (shops, at work, with strangers). Often said on its own, or followed by a name/title: “Buenos días, señora.”
target_language_example: Buenos días, ¿cómo está?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

meaning: The White House (U.S. president’s official residence).
additional_notes: Usually written with capitals when referring to the U.S. government/the White House. Literally means “white house,” so it can also refer to any house painted white in a normal context; capitals help clarify the political meaning.
target_language_example: La Casa Blanca anunció nuevas medidas hoy.
native_language_example: The White House announced new measures today.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise, shock, worry, or frustration. Often written with exclamation marks: ¡Dios mío! You may also hear the more religious-sounding variants "¡Dios mío!" and "¡Ay, Dios mío!". In more polite contexts, some people avoid it and use softer options like "¡Madre mía!" or "¡Dios!".
target_language_example: ¡Dios mío! Se me olvidó el pasaporte.
native_language_example: Oh my God! I forgot my passport.

additional_notes: Used to say you genuinely don’t know the answer or that something is uncertain. Often followed by an indirect question: “Dios sabe cuándo/dónde/por qué…”. Can sound a bit dramatic or emphatic; common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: ¿Cuándo llegará el paquete? Dios sabe.
native_language_example: When will the package arrive? God knows (who knows).

additional_notes: Standard Spanish abbreviation for "Estados Unidos". The double letters show the plural (Estados, Unidos). Often written with periods and a space: "EE. UU." You’ll see it in addresses, news, and formal writing; you can also say/write "Estados Unidos" or "EUA" (less common).
target_language_example: Vivo en EE. UU. desde 2020.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in the U.S. since 2020.

additional_notes: Proper name for the country. Often appears as “los Estados Unidos” and is commonly abbreviated as “EE. UU.” in writing. Use “estadounidense” for “American (from the U.S.).”
target_language_example: Vivo en los Estados Unidos desde 2018.
native_language_example: I have lived in the United States since 2018.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or gratitude that something good happened or something bad didn’t happen. Common in everyday speech; can be religious or just a set expression even for non-religious speakers. Often followed by a clause: “Gracias a Dios, …”
target_language_example: Gracias a Dios, llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank God, you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Refers to the island that includes England, Scotland, and Wales. It is not the same as the United Kingdom (Reino Unido), which also includes Northern Ireland. Used in geography, news, and formal contexts; often appears as "en Gran Bretaña" (in Great Britain).
target_language_example: Vivo en Gran Bretaña, pero trabajo a veces en Irlanda del Norte.
native_language_example: I live in Great Britain, but I sometimes work in Northern Ireland.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is surprising because it includes the speaker too (similar to “even I did it”). It can express pride, disbelief, or that something is very easy/obvious. Often followed by a verb: “Hasta yo lo sé” (“Even I know it”).
target_language_example: ¡Hasta yo lo puedo hacer!
native_language_example: Even I can do it!

additional_notes: A common noun with the definite article: *la reina* (queen). Capitalized (*La Reina*) it can also be a title or a proper name (e.g., a nickname, a business name, a place name). Gendered: *el rey* = the king. Plural: *las reinas* = the queens.
target_language_example: La reina vive en el palacio.
native_language_example: The queen lives in the palace.

additional_notes: Usually written lowercase as “la silla” when it means a chair. In Spanish, nouns have gender, so it takes the feminine article “la.” You’ll also hear “sentarse en la silla” (to sit on the chair) and “silla” for many kinds of chairs (dining chair, office chair, etc.). Capitalized “La Silla” can also be a proper name (e.g., a place or institution) depending on context.
target_language_example: Pon la mochila en la silla, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the backpack on the chair, please.

meaning: Las Vegas (a city in Nevada, USA).
additional_notes: A proper noun used as a place name. In Spanish it’s usually said the same as in English, often with the definite article: “Las Vegas.” You can use it after prepositions like en (in), a (to), de (from), or desde (from/since): “en Las Vegas,” “a Las Vegas,” “de Las Vegas.”
target_language_example: Vamos a Las Vegas el fin de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to Las Vegas this weekend.

meaning: “the cats.” Also a place name (Los Gatos, California).
additional_notes: Usually the plural noun phrase “los” (the) + “gatos” (cats). Capitalization matters: “los gatos” is just “the cats,” while “Los Gatos” is often used as a proper noun (e.g., the town in California). In Spanish, article + noun place names keep the article as part of the name.
target_language_example: Vivimos cerca de Los Gatos, pero en casa tenemos dos gatos.
native_language_example: We live near Los Gatos, but at home we have two cats.

additional_notes: "Muchos" is the masculine plural form of “mucho” and it agrees with the noun. "Niños" can mean “boys” specifically, or “children/kids” in general (mixed group). For an all-girls group you’d say "muchas niñas."
target_language_example: Muchos niños juegan en el parque.
native_language_example: Many children play in the park.

additional_notes: Proper noun used for the U.S. state or (often) New York City; context usually makes it clear. With cities you typically use "en" to say you are there ("Estoy en Nueva York") and "a" to say you’re going there ("Voy a Nueva York").
target_language_example: Voy a Nueva York la semana que viene.
native_language_example: I’m going to New York next week.

additional_notes: A proper noun (place name). It’s feminine, so you’ll often see it with feminine articles/adjectives: «Nueva Zelanda es bonita». In Spanish, «zelandés/zelandesa» means “New Zealander” (person), and «neozelandés/neozelandesa» is also common.
target_language_example: Quiero viajar a Nueva Zelanda el próximo año.
native_language_example: I want to travel to New Zealand next year.

additional_notes: Used for the Christmas gift-bringer in Spain and many Latin American countries. Often written with capitals (Papá Noel) and used with the article: "El Papá Noel". In some places people also say "Santa Claus" or "San Nicolás"; in Spain, "los Reyes Magos" are also a major gift-giving tradition.
target_language_example: Los niños están esperando a Papá Noel.
native_language_example: The children are waiting for Santa Claus.

additional_notes: Proper noun used for the country (Great Britain + Northern Ireland). Often appears with the article: "el Reino Unido". Not the same as "Inglaterra" (England), which is only one part of the UK.
target_language_example: Mi prima vive en el Reino Unido.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in the United Kingdom.

additional_notes: A respectful title used mainly in Catholic contexts to refer to the Pope. It’s usually written with capital letters as a proper title (Santo Padre), though you may also see it in lowercase in general text (santo padre). In everyday speech, many people simply say "el Papa".
target_language_example: El Santo Padre visitará el país el próximo mes.
native_language_example: The Holy Father will visit the country next month.

additional_notes: A formal royal style used to address or refer to a prince/princess or other high-ranking royalty. Capitalized in writing. Often appears as part of a longer title: “Su Alteza Real” (His/Her Royal Highness) or “Su Alteza Serenísima” (His/Her Serene Highness). The possessive changes depending on formality/grammar: “Su Alteza” (his/her/your), “Sus Altezas” (their/your plural).
target_language_example: Su Alteza, es un honor conocerle.
native_language_example: Your Highness, it is an honor to meet you.

additional_notes: A very formal way to refer to a king or queen. Use **Su Majestad** when addressing or speaking about the monarch; plural is **Sus Majestades** (“Their Majesties”). Often written with capital letters in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Su Majestad el Rey visitará la ciudad mañana.
native_language_example: His Majesty the King will visit the city tomorrow.

meaning: “Your Honor” (a formal way to address a judge).
additional_notes: Used in court or legal contexts when speaking to or about a judge. It’s very formal and typically capitalized in writing (Su Señoría). You can use it with verbs in the third person: “¿Qué desea Su Señoría?” In some countries you may also hear “Señoría” without “Su.”
target_language_example: Con el debido respeto, Su Señoría, solicito un receso.
native_language_example: With due respect, Your Honor, I request a recess.

additional_notes: A proper name used in Spanish (and many other languages) to refer to the planned language “Toki Pona.” It’s usually capitalized and treated like the name of a language (similar to “español” / “inglés”), e.g., with verbs like hablar, aprender, estudiar. You may also see: “en Toki Pona” (“in Toki Pona”).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo Toki Pona, pero todavía es difícil para mí.
native_language_example: I’m learning Toki Pona, but it’s still difficult for me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to God in religious contexts, usually after verbs like "rezar" (to pray) or "encomendar" (to entrust). It’s also part of common phrases like "gracias a Dios" (thank God) and "que Dios te bendiga" (may God bless you).
target_language_example: Rezo a Dios para que todo salga bien.
native_language_example: I pray to God that everything turns out well.

meaning: based on; made from; by means of.
additional_notes: Used to describe what something is mainly made from (ingredients/materials), what it relies on, or the method used to achieve something. Often followed by a noun: "una dieta a base de verduras" (a diet based on vegetables), "un producto a base de leche" (a milk-based product).
target_language_example: Está siguiendo una dieta a base de frutas y verduras.
native_language_example: He/She is following a diet based on fruits and vegetables.

additional_notes: Colloquial intensifier used in some regions to emphasize that something happened "a lot" or "in a great way." It often appears after a verb (e.g., divertirse, reírse, bailar, disfrutar) to mean you did it a ton / had a great time. Not standard in all Spanish-speaking countries; in many places you’d just say "muy bien" or "mucho" instead.
target_language_example: En la fiesta nos divertimos a base de bien.
native_language_example: At the party we had a really great time.

additional_notes: Common as a toast or call to start drinking. It uses the pattern “a + infinitive” (a + verb) meaning “let’s + verb” or “to + verb” as an encouragement (e.g., “¡A comer!” = “Let’s eat!”). Often said with “¡Vamos!” or “¡Salud!”
target_language_example: ¡A beber! Que hoy celebramos.
native_language_example: Let’s drink! Today we’re celebrating.

a buen entendedor, pocas palabras bastan

target_language_multi_word_term: a buen entendedor, pocas palabras bastan
meaning: A smart person understands with few words; no need to explain much.
additional_notes: A common proverb used when you expect someone to “get the point” quickly, often after a brief hint or indirect comment. It can sound a bit pointed or ironic, depending on tone (similar to “if you know, you know”). You can also hear shortened versions like “A buen entendedor…”
target_language_example: No hace falta que te lo explique todo: a buen entendedor, pocas palabras bastan.
native_language_example: I don’t need to explain everything: a smart person understands with few words.

a buen hambre no hay pan duro

target_language_multi_word_term: a buen hambre no hay pan duro
meaning: When you’re really hungry, you can’t be picky (any food is good enough).
additional_notes: A common proverb used to say that necessity (especially hunger) makes you accept what’s available, even if it’s not your favorite. Often said humorously or to justify eating something simple or not very tasty. Literally: “for good hunger, there is no hard bread.”
target_language_example: No me encanta lo que hay para cenar, pero a buen hambre no hay pan duro.
native_language_example: I’m not thrilled with what’s for dinner, but when you’re hungry you can’t be picky.

meaning: (to do something) the nice/easy/peaceful way; voluntarily (not by force).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the contrast "a buenas o a malas" (also "por las buenas o por las malas"), meaning someone will do something either willingly/nicely or by force. It’s fairly colloquial and often used in warnings or negotiations.
target_language_example: Más te vale venir a buenas, porque a malas no vas a querer.
native_language_example: You’d better come the easy way, because you won’t like it the hard way.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ir/andar/montar to say someone is traveling or riding on a horse. It can also be used more generally to mean “straddling” something (legs on both sides), depending on context.
target_language_example: Fuimos al pueblo a caballo.
native_language_example: We went to the town on horseback.

meaning: in exchange for; in return for.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a trade, compensation, or a condition: you get/do something and you give/do something else. It’s commonly followed by a noun or an infinitive (a verb in the “to ___” form): “a cambio de dinero” (in exchange for money), “a cambio de ayudarte” (in return for helping you). Similar to “a cambio” = “in exchange”.
target_language_example: Te ayudaré a cambio de que me ayudes mañana.
native_language_example: I’ll help you in exchange for you helping me tomorrow.

meaning: “heads or tails” (flipping a coin to decide).
additional_notes: Used when making a quick choice by tossing a coin. You can say it right before the flip or when proposing the method: “¿Lo decidimos a cara o cruz?” You may also hear “jugar a cara o cruz” (to play heads-or-tails).
target_language_example: Si no nos ponemos de acuerdo, lo decidimos a cara o cruz.
native_language_example: If we can’t agree, we’ll decide by flipping a coin (heads or tails).

additional_notes: Used to say who has responsibility for a task, area, or people. Common patterns: “estar a cargo de” (to be in charge of) and “tener a cargo” (to have under your care/responsibility). Often followed by “de” + noun/person: “a cargo de Juan” (under Juan’s responsibility).
target_language_example: María está a cargo del proyecto.
native_language_example: María is in charge of the project.

meaning: in charge of; under the responsibility/care of.
additional_notes: Used to say who is responsible for a task, project, or group (often in work/school contexts): "Estoy a cargo de..." It can also mean something is in someone’s care or custody: "Los niños están a cargo de su abuela." Often followed by a person or organization ("a cargo de Ana / del departamento").
target_language_example: El proyecto está a cargo de Marta.
native_language_example: Marta is in charge of the project.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is moving very fast, as if in a race. Often appears with verbs like ir, correr, salir, huir, or venir: “ir a carrera abierta”, “salir a carrera abierta”. Can be used literally (running, vehicles, horses) and sometimes metaphorically (doing something urgently).
target_language_example: Cuando oyó la alarma, salió a carrera abierta.
native_language_example: When he heard the alarm, he ran out at full speed.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs of movement (ir, volver, llegar, venir) to say you’re going to your home or someone’s home. Often no article is used: "Voy a casa" = "I’m going home." Contrast: "en casa" means "at home" (location), not destination.
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, vuelvo a casa.
native_language_example: After work, I go back home.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, followed by a noun or noun phrase (or an infinitive in some contexts): a causa de la lluvia (because of the rain). For a clause with a verb ("because + subject + verb"), Spanish usually uses "porque" instead. Often interchangeable with "debido a" in formal contexts.
target_language_example: El vuelo se retrasó a causa de la niebla.
native_language_example: The flight was delayed because of the fog.

additional_notes: Used to say something is set/reset back to 0, especially scores ("ganamos 3 a cero" = we won 3–0) and quantities ("poner el contador a cero" = reset the counter). Also used more generally with verbs like "empezar" or "volver" to mean starting over with nothing: "empezar de/a cero".
target_language_example: Ganamos tres a cero y luego pusieron el marcador a cero.
native_language_example: We won three to zero, and then they reset the scoreboard to zero.

meaning: blindly; without being able to see (or without enough information).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something without seeing (e.g., in the dark) or without knowing the details (guessing, acting without guidance): "a ciegas" = "blindly." Often appears with verbs like hacer, ir, elegir, votar, buscar, confiar. Also common as "a tientas y a ciegas" (by feel and blindly).
target_language_example: Elegimos el restaurante a ciegas y salió muy bien.
native_language_example: We chose the restaurant without knowing (anything about it) and it turned out really well.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is done carefully and seriously, paying attention to details (not rushed). Common with verbs like hacer, revisar, limpiar, estudiar, investigar: “hacer/revisar/limpiar algo a conciencia”.
target_language_example: Revisé el informe a conciencia antes de enviarlo.
native_language_example: I reviewed the report thoroughly before sending it.

meaning: as a result of; due to.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause of something (often in more formal or written Spanish). Common with nouns or noun phrases: "a consecuencia de la lluvia". For a more everyday option, you’ll often hear "por" or "debido a".
target_language_example: El vuelo se canceló a consecuencia de la tormenta.
native_language_example: The flight was canceled as a result of the storm.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the following thing in a sequence or immediately afterward. Common in instructions, presentations, and formal writing: “A continuación, …” = “Next, …”. It can also refer to something that comes later in a document: “a continuación” = “below/what follows”.
target_language_example: A continuación, vamos a ver un ejemplo.
native_language_example: Next, we’re going to see an example.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like hablar/conversar/confesar to mean speaking sincerely and without holding back feelings or truths: "hablar a corazón abierto". It can also be used in medicine to mean "open-heart" (e.g., "cirugía/operación a corazón abierto").
target_language_example: Hablamos a corazón abierto sobre nuestros problemas.
native_language_example: We talked openly/from the heart about our problems.

meaning: at the expense of; at the cost of (often with a negative consequence).
additional_notes: Used to say someone achieves something by causing a loss, harm, or disadvantage to someone/something else. Often followed by a noun (a costa de mi salud) or an infinitive phrase (a costa de trabajar mucho). Similar to "a expensas de" (more formal).
target_language_example: Consiguió el ascenso a costa de sus compañeros.
native_language_example: He got the promotion at the expense of his coworkers.

additional_notes: Used when you buy something now and pay it over time (often in installments) instead of paying in full immediately. Common with verbs like comprar/vender/pagar a crédito. Contrast: al contado (“in cash / paid in full”).
target_language_example: Compré la computadora a crédito.
native_language_example: I bought the computer on credit.

additional_notes: Used to say something can happen at any moment, without a fixed schedule. Common in everyday speech for availability, opening hours, or when something might occur. Similar to "en cualquier momento" (at any moment).
target_language_example: Puedes llamarme a cualquier hora.
native_language_example: You can call me anytime.

meaning: 'on account of' / 'because of'; also 'as an advance (payment)'.
additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) Cause/reason: "a cuenta de" + noun means "because of" or "due to" (similar to "por/por culpa de" depending on context). (2) Payment: "a cuenta" (often "a cuenta de" + amount/total) means a partial payment or deposit toward a total, like "as an advance" or "on account".
target_language_example: No pude ir a la reunión a cuenta de la lluvia, pero dejé 50 euros a cuenta del total.
native_language_example: I couldn’t go to the meeting because of the rain, but I left 50 euros as an advance toward the total.

additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used mainly with verbs like *pelear*, *luchar*, or *defenderse* to mean fighting without weapons or tools—typically in a very physical, hand-to-hand way. Similar to *a mano limpia* or *a puño limpio* (with fists).
target_language_example: Se defendió a cuerpo limpio cuando lo atacaron.
native_language_example: He defended himself bare-handed when they attacked him.

meaning: carrying (something) on your back; figuratively, bearing (a burden).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "llevar" or "cargar" to mean carrying something (often heavy) on your back or while supporting its weight. It can also be figurative: "llevar" + "a cuestas" = to carry a responsibility/problem. Common pattern: "llevar + [noun/pronoun] + a cuestas".
target_language_example: Lleva la mochila a cuestas todo el día.
native_language_example: He carries the backpack on his back all day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest opinion or admission, often as a mild correction or clarification. Common at the start of a sentence or set off by commas: "A decir verdad, ...". Similar in tone to "la verdad" or "para ser sincero/a".
target_language_example: A decir verdad, no me gusta mucho esta película.
native_language_example: To tell the truth, I don’t really like this movie.

additional_notes: Most common with verbs like ir/viajar: “ir a dedo” = “to hitchhike.” Literally it means “by (the) finger/thumb,” referring to sticking out your thumb to ask for a ride. It can also appear in other expressions like “elegir a dedo” (to handpick/select someone deliberately), but on its own it often refers to hitchhiking.
target_language_example: Fuimos a dedo hasta la ciudad.
native_language_example: We hitchhiked to the city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each day. Often placed after the verb: "Trabajo a diario". Similar to "diariamente" (more formal).
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio a diario.
native_language_example: I exercise daily / every day.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two people, things, or situations. It’s followed by a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase: “A diferencia de mi hermano…”. For comparing in terms of “different from,” you’ll also hear “diferente de” or “distinto de,” but “a diferencia de” emphasizes contrast.
target_language_example: A diferencia de ayer, hoy hace buen tiempo.
native_language_example: Unlike yesterday, the weather is nice today.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is done with money involved (especially as a bet or stake), often after verbs like jugar (to play) or apostar (to bet). It contrasts with doing something just for fun. It does not translate literally as “to money.”
target_language_example: No jugamos a dinero; es solo por diversión.
native_language_example: We’re not playing for money; it’s just for fun.

meaning: as much as you want; unlimited (also: at someone’s discretion).
additional_notes: Often used with food/drinks to mean there’s no set limit: “comida/bebidas a discreción” = “all you can eat/drink.” In more formal contexts it can mean “at the discretion of”: “a discreción del juez” = “at the judge’s discretion.”
target_language_example: En el buffet, puedes comer a discreción.
native_language_example: At the buffet, you can eat as much as you want.

additional_notes: Used to offer help or indicate something is available for someone to use. Common in polite/formal contexts: “Estoy a su disposición” (“I’m at your disposal”). Often appears with possessives (a tu/su/nuestra disposición) or in “poner (algo) a disposición (de alguien)” (“to make (something) available to someone”).
target_language_example: Estoy a tu disposición si necesitas ayuda.
native_language_example: I’m at your disposal / available if you need help.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done without being physically present (remote work/study, services done online or by phone). With verbs like trabajar/estudiar/atender: “remotely.” It can also mean “from a distance” (e.g., seeing or recognizing something far away).
target_language_example: Trabajo a distancia tres días a la semana.
native_language_example: I work remotely three days a week.

additional_notes: A fairly formal way to contrast two things or people, similar to “a diferencia de”. It’s used to highlight how one thing differs from another, often at the beginning of a sentence: “A distinción de X, …”.
target_language_example: A distinción de la mayoría, ella prefirió quedarse en casa.
native_language_example: Unlike most people, she preferred to stay at home.

additional_notes: Colloquial/regional expression (common in parts of Latin America) used to emphasize that there is a large quantity of something or that something is done intensely—almost “so much it hurts.” It doesn’t mean literal physical pain in most uses.
target_language_example: En la fiesta había comida a dolor.
native_language_example: At the party there was tons of food.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to a destination (movement toward a place). Common in questions: "¿A dónde vas?" In modern Spanish it’s usually written with an accent: "adónde" in indirect questions/exclamations ("No sé adónde ir"), but many learners will also see it as two words ("a dónde"). Contrast with "dónde" (location, no movement).
target_language_example: ¿A dónde vas después de clase?
native_language_example: Where are you going after class?

meaning: as of today; up to now.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current situation or what is true at the present moment, often in formal or neutral contexts. Similar to "hoy en día" (nowadays), but "a día de hoy" emphasizes "as things stand today" (as of now). Common in news, reports, and conversations about current status.
target_language_example: A día de hoy, todavía no tenemos una respuesta.
native_language_example: As of today, we still don’t have an answer.

additional_notes: Colloquial way to mean “on some days” (similar to “hay días que…” or “unos días…”). It often appears in the pattern “a días sí, a días no” (“every other day / off and on”).
target_language_example: A días me siento con energía y a días no.
native_language_example: Some days I feel energetic and some days I don’t.

meaning: as a duo; in a duet (two people together).
additional_notes: Used to say that two people perform or do something together (often in music or dance): cantar/tocar/bailar/actuar a dúo. Similar to “en dúo.”
target_language_example: Cantaron a dúo en el concierto.
native_language_example: They sang as a duo at the concert.

meaning: 'to them' (referring to a group of females).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., dar, decir, escribir, explicar) to mean “to them,” when “them” refers to women/girls or grammatically feminine plural nouns. Often appears before the verb (A ellas les gusta...) or after it (Les gusta a ellas...), and can be used for emphasis/clarity. Contrast: a ellos (to them, masculine/mixed group).
target_language_example: Les di las llaves a ellas.
native_language_example: I gave them the keys (to the women/girls).

a enemigo que huye, puente de plata

target_language_multi_word_term: a enemigo que huye, puente de plata
meaning: “Let a retreating enemy escape” (don’t corner them; give them an easy way out).
additional_notes: A traditional proverb. It suggests that when an opponent (literal or figurative: a rival, problem, conflict) is backing off, it’s smarter to let them go rather than keep fighting or block their exit—because cornering them can make the situation more dangerous or harder to resolve. Often used to recommend ending an argument, accepting someone’s retreat, or not pushing for total victory.
target_language_example: Ya se está echando para atrás; a enemigo que huye, puente de plata.
native_language_example: He’s already backing off; let a retreating enemy escape.

meaning: around; at about (a time or number).
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate time, number, or amount (not exact). It often goes before a time expression: "a eso de las 3" = "around 3 o’clock." Similar to "alrededor de" or "aproximadamente," but common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Llegamos a eso de las ocho.
native_language_example: We arrived around eight.

additional_notes: Most often used as "a espaldas de + person" meaning "behind someone’s back" (without them knowing). It can also describe something physically located behind someone ("a mis espaldas" = "behind me").
target_language_example: Hicieron el trato a espaldas de su jefe.
native_language_example: They made the deal behind their boss’s back.

additional_notes: Used to say that, given how much time has passed or how advanced the situation is, something is expected or should already be true. It often implies mild surprise, impatience, or obviousness. Common with present tense (A estas alturas ya lo sabes) or with "debería" (A estas alturas debería estar aquí).
target_language_example: A estas alturas, ya deberías haber terminado el informe.
native_language_example: By now, you should have finished the report.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current time, often implying it’s late, unexpected, or that something should have happened already. Common in questions and comments about someone arriving, calling, eating, etc. Similar idea to “at this hour / at this point” in English.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde estás? ¡A estas horas ya deberías estar en casa!
native_language_example: Where are you? At this hour you should already be home!

additional_notes: Used to exclude something from a general statement. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: “A excepción de Juan, todos vinieron.” Similar to “excepto” or “salvo,” but slightly more formal.
target_language_example: A excepción de los domingos, trabajo todos los días.
native_language_example: Except for Sundays, I work every day.

a falta de pan, buenas son tortas

target_language_multi_word_term: a falta de pan, buenas son tortas
meaning: If you can’t have what you want, a substitute will do.
additional_notes: A common proverb used when you accept something less ideal because the preferred option isn’t available (similar to “beggars can’t be choosers” or “something is better than nothing”). Literally: “for lack of bread, cakes are good.” Often said to be practical or resigned rather than enthusiastic.
target_language_example: No hay entradas para el concierto, pero podemos ver la película. A falta de pan, buenas son tortas.
native_language_example: There are no tickets for the concert, but we can watch the movie. If we can’t have what we want, a substitute will do.

additional_notes: Used to express support or agreement, usually with "estar" or "votar": "Estoy a favor de..." (I’m in favor of...), "Voté a favor" (I voted in favor). Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive: "a favor de la idea", "a favor de cambiarlo".
target_language_example: Estoy a favor de la propuesta.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of the proposal.

additional_notes: Used to express support or agreement with a person, idea, proposal, or action. Common with verbs like estar/ser (Estoy a favor de…), votar (Votaron a favor de…), and hablar (Habló a favor de…). Often contrasts with "en contra de" (against).
target_language_example: Estoy a favor de la nueva ley.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of the new law.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize what you’re saying, similar to “indeed!” or “certainly!” in English. It can appear at the beginning of a sentence or before a clause (often with "que": "A fe que..."). It sounds literary/old-fashioned in modern everyday Spanish, so you’re more likely to see it in books, historical speech, or very formal/expressive writing.
target_language_example: A fe, no lo sabía.
native_language_example: Indeed, I didn’t know.

additional_notes: Almost always used as **a fin de + infinitive**: *a fin de ahorrar* (“in order to save”). You’ll also see **a fin de que + subjunctive**: *a fin de que todos entiendan* (“so that everyone understands”). It’s fairly formal; in everyday speech people often use *para* instead.
target_language_example: Salimos temprano a fin de llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: We left early in order to arrive on time.

meaning: in the end; after all; when all is said and done.
additional_notes: Used to sum up or conclude after considering everything, often to justify a final point or decision. Similar to "al final" but slightly more like "after all" (emphasizing the final conclusion). Often appears at the start of a sentence: "A fin de cuentas, ...".
target_language_example: A fin de cuentas, lo más importante es la salud.
native_language_example: In the end, the most important thing is health.

meaning: at the end of; towards the end of (a time period).
additional_notes: Used to place an event near the end of a month, year, season, or other period of time. Often followed by a month or year: a finales de enero (towards the end of January), a finales de 2026 (towards the end of 2026). Contrast with a principios de (“at the beginning of”) and a mediados de (“in the middle of”).
target_language_example: Voy a viajar a finales de marzo.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel towards the end of March.

meaning: afloat; (figuratively) staying afloat / managing to cope.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar", "seguir", "mantener(se)", or "salir". Literally means floating on water (not sinking). Figuratively, it means keeping going despite difficulties, especially financially or emotionally: "mantenerse a flote" = to stay afloat. Common in everyday speech and writing.
target_language_example: Con tantos gastos, apenas podemos mantenernos a flote.
native_language_example: With so many expenses, we can barely stay afloat.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something completely or with a lot of detail (study, analyze, investigate, clean, etc.). Often appears after the verb: “estudiar a fondo”, “analizar a fondo”, “conocer a fondo”.
target_language_example: Necesito estudiar este tema a fondo antes del examen.
native_language_example: I need to study this topic thoroughly before the exam.

meaning: by/through (doing something repeatedly); by force of.
additional_notes: Used to express that a result happens thanks to repeated effort, habit, insistence, or endurance (often over time): "a fuerza de trabajar" = "by working (so much/so long)." It’s followed by an infinitive (a fuerza de estudiar) or a noun (a fuerza de golpes = by blows). Often implies persistence rather than literal physical force.
target_language_example: A fuerza de practicar todos los días, mejoró mucho su español.
native_language_example: By practicing every day, he/she improved his/her Spanish a lot.

meaning: "by means of" / "with" (using repeated hits/effort); often "by" (e.g., by force or by learning the hard way).
additional_notes: Used to say something is achieved through repeated blows, pressure, or repeated effort: "a golpe de martillo" (with hammer blows), "a golpe de insistir" (by insisting again and again). It can be literal (physical hits) or figurative (force, persistence, or experience: "a golpe de errores" = by making mistakes).
target_language_example: Aprendí español a golpe de práctica y muchos errores.
native_language_example: I learned Spanish through practice and lots of mistakes.

meaning: Desperate times call for desperate measures.
additional_notes: A proverb used to justify taking strong or drastic action when the situation is very serious. You can say it on its own as a comment, or before/after explaining the action you’re going to take.
target_language_example: Voy a vender el coche para pagar las deudas; a grandes males, grandes remedios.
native_language_example: I’m going to sell the car to pay the debts; desperate times call for desperate measures.

meaning: at the top of one’s lungs; shouting.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing/saying something by shouting (often because you’re angry, excited, or trying to be heard). Common with verbs like decir, hablar, llamar, pedir, and cantar: “decir algo a gritos” = “say something shouting.”
target_language_example: Me llamó a gritos desde la calle.
native_language_example: He/She called to me shouting from the street.

additional_notes: Used with estar/sentirse to say you feel comfortable or at ease ("Estoy a gusto aquí"). With gusto it can also mean you like or enjoy something ("Me da gusto" = "I’m glad/pleased"). In many contexts it’s close to "comfortable" rather than "with taste."
target_language_example: ¿Estás a gusto en tu nuevo trabajo?
native_language_example: Are you comfortable/at ease in your new job?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is being carried with their legs around another person’s neck, or that something is being lifted and transported on the shoulders. Common with verbs like "llevar" (to carry), "ir" (to go), and "sacar" (to take out), e.g., "llevar a un niño a hombros".
target_language_example: Mi padre me llevaba a hombros cuando era pequeño.
native_language_example: My dad used to carry me on his shoulders when I was little.

additional_notes: Very common slang in Mexico and some other regions. It expresses strong agreement or certainty and can sound a bit crude/strong depending on tone and context, so avoid it in formal situations. It can also mean “by force / whether you like it or not” in some contexts (e.g., “Lo hizo a huevo” = “He did it by force”).
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —¡A huevo!
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —For sure!

additional_notes: Used to say that two things match well, especially clothes, colors, shoes/bag, curtains/furniture, etc. Often used with "ir" or "estar": "va a juego con" / "está a juego con" (it matches/goes with).
target_language_example: Estos zapatos van a juego con el bolso.
native_language_example: These shoes match the bag.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the evidence you’re basing your opinion or conclusion on. It’s common in both spoken and written Spanish and is often followed by a noun phrase or by “lo que + verb” (what someone said/did).
target_language_example: A juzgar por su acento, es de Argentina.
native_language_example: Judging by his accent, he’s from Argentina.

meaning: "to the" / "at the" (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Formed by the preposition "a" + the feminine singular definite article "la". It’s very common after verbs of movement or direction (ir, venir, volver) and before destinations: "a la tienda". Unlike "a el" → "al", "a la" does NOT contract. It can also appear in "a la + adjective/noun" to mean "in the style of" (e.g., "a la francesa" = French-style).
target_language_example: Voy a la tienda.
native_language_example: I’m going to the store.

meaning: up to (the standard); at the level/height of.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to a required level or expectation: "estar a la altura" = "to be up to it / to meet the standard." It can also be physical/location-related meaning "at the height/level of" (e.g., a point on a street or on your body). Often followed by "de" when specifying what standard/level ("a la altura de").
target_language_example: No creo estar a la altura del trabajo, pero lo voy a intentar.
native_language_example: I don’t think I’m up to the job, but I’m going to try.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a traditional, non-modern way (methods, style, cooking, etc.). Often appears after the noun it describes (e.g., “estilo a la antigua”) or after a verb (“hacerlo a la antigua”). Similar to “a la vieja usanza.”
target_language_example: Prefiero cocinar a la antigua, con ingredientes simples y sin máquinas.
native_language_example: I prefer to cook the old-fashioned way, with simple ingredients and no machines.

meaning: in good faith; relying on someone’s honesty.
additional_notes: Formal (often legal/administrative). It refers to acting honestly and without intent to deceive, or trusting that others will act honestly. Very often you’ll also see the more common form "de buena fe" (e.g., "actuar de buena fe"). "A la buena fe" is frequently used with verbs like "apelar a la buena fe de (alguien)" (to appeal to someone’s good faith).
target_language_example: Apelamos a la buena fe de todos para cumplir las normas.
native_language_example: We appeal to everyone’s good faith to follow the rules.

meaning: at the head; in charge; leading (in first place).
additional_notes: Used for position and leadership. Literally “to the head,” but in English it’s usually “at the head (of)” or “in charge (of).” Common with verbs like estar/ir/ponerse and with de: “a la cabeza de” = “at the head of / leading.” It can mean physically at the front of a group or figuratively being the leader/top in something.
target_language_example: María está a la cabeza del equipo desde 2024.
native_language_example: María has been leading the team since 2024.

meaning: à la carte; ordered individually from a menu.
additional_notes: Used mainly in restaurants to say you’re choosing specific dishes rather than a set menu (menú del día / menú fijo). Often appears on menus as “platos a la carta.” In Spanish it’s a fixed expression borrowed from French, so it keeps the same idea even though it’s not literally Spanish word-by-word.
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a pedir a la carta, no el menú del día.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to order à la carte, not the set menu.

a la corta o a la larga

target_language_multi_word_term: a la corta o a la larga
meaning: Sooner or later; in the end.
additional_notes: Used to say that something will eventually happen, even if you don’t know when. Common in advice or predictions. You can also hear the shorter version “a la larga” (“in the long run”).
target_language_example: A la corta o a la larga, tendrás que hablar con ella.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, you’ll have to talk to her.

meaning: “on the count of …” (used with numbers: una/dos/tres).
additional_notes: Common in Spain in the pattern “A la de una, a la de dos, y a la de tres…”, similar to “One, two, three…” or “On three…”. It’s used to coordinate an action (jump, run, start, etc.). You’ll almost always see it followed by a number.
target_language_example: A la de tres, empezamos.
native_language_example: On three, we start.

additional_notes: Used literally for boats or objects moving with the current/wind, and figuratively for a person, plan, or situation that lacks direction or is out of control. Common with verbs like "estar" or "ir": "estar a la deriva" (to be adrift) and "ir a la deriva" (to drift along).
target_language_example: Desde que perdió el trabajo, se siente a la deriva.
native_language_example: Since he lost his job, he feels adrift.

additional_notes: Used when something happens because someone is forced to do it, or because there is no other option. Often appears with verbs like hacer, obligar, llevar, or tener que: “hacer algo a la fuerza” (to do something by force).
target_language_example: Lo hicieron firmar el contrato a la fuerza.
native_language_example: They made him sign the contract by force.

meaning: when it comes to; when (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the moment or situation of doing something, often meaning “when it’s time to…” or “when it comes to…”. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (a la hora de + infinitive): a la hora de elegir, a la hora de pagar. Not necessarily about a specific clock time; for that you’d use “a la(s)…” or “a la hora de + [time]” in some contexts (e.g., “a la hora de comer” = at mealtime).
target_language_example: A la hora de pagar, prefiero usar tarjeta.
native_language_example: When it comes time to pay, I prefer to use a card.

meaning: English-style; the British way (e.g., English breakfast, tea with milk).
additional_notes: Used to describe something done in the English/British style. It often appears after a noun ("desayuno a la inglesa") or after verbs like "tomar"/"preparar" ("tomar el té a la inglesa"). Contrast with "a la francesa" (French-style).
target_language_example: Quiero un desayuno a la inglesa, con huevos y tostadas.
native_language_example: I want an English-style breakfast, with eggs and toast.

meaning: in the long run; eventually (over time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about results or consequences that appear after a long time. Often paired with phrases like "a la corta o a la larga" (sooner or later). It’s common at the start of a sentence or after a comma to add a general conclusion.
target_language_example: A la larga, es mejor decir la verdad.
native_language_example: In the long run, it’s better to tell the truth.

meaning: to the flame / to the llama.
additional_notes: “A” usually means “to” (sometimes “at”). “La llama” can mean either “the flame” or “the llama” (the animal), so context matters. There’s no contraction here because Spanish only contracts “a + el” → “al” (but “a + la” stays “a la”).
target_language_example: No acerques la cara a la llama.
native_language_example: Don’t bring your face close to the flame.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason, context, or evidence that affects a decision or opinion. Common in formal and neutral writing/speech (news, reports, explanations). Often followed by a noun or phrase: “a la luz de los hechos / la evidencia / lo ocurrido”. Similar idea to “teniendo en cuenta” (taking into account).
target_language_example: A la luz de los nuevos datos, vamos a cambiar el plan.
native_language_example: In light of the new data, we’re going to change the plan.

meaning: handy; within easy reach; readily available.
additional_notes: Used to say something is close by and easy to use or access (similar to “at hand”). Often with verbs like tener (“to have”) or estar (“to be”). Can also describe a shop or service being convenient/nearby in some regions.
target_language_example: Ten tu pasaporte a la mano por si lo piden en el hotel.
native_language_example: Keep your passport handy in case they ask for it at the hotel.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish (especially Mexico). It means “maybe/it could happen” and is often used to suggest a possibility: “A la mejor viene” = “Maybe he/she will come.” It can also express hope: “A la mejor ganamos” = “Hopefully we’ll win.” Often interchangeable with “a lo mejor.”
target_language_example: A la mejor mañana no llueve.
native_language_example: Maybe it won’t rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: A strong, vulgar expression used to show anger, rejection, or frustration. Often heard in phrases like “¡Vete a la mierda!” (Go to hell / Fuck off) or “¡A la mierda!” (To hell with it). Not appropriate in polite situations; use softer options like “¡Déjalo!” (Forget it) or “¡Basta!” (Enough).
target_language_example: ¡Vete a la mierda! No me hables así.
native_language_example: Fuck off! Don’t talk to me like that.

additional_notes: Used to describe people, clothes, or things that are trendy or up-to-date. Often goes after the noun: "ropa a la moda" (fashionable clothes).
target_language_example: A ella le gusta vestir a la moda.
native_language_example: She likes to dress fashionably.

meaning: in a modern (stylish) way; in a modern style.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something according to current fashion/trends, especially about clothes, hair, decoration, or style. It agrees with feminine nouns (e.g., “ropa a la moderna”); with a masculine noun you often hear “a lo moderno” (e.g., “un peinado a lo moderno”).
target_language_example: Se cortó el pelo a la moderna para la fiesta.
native_language_example: She got her hair cut in a modern style for the party.

additional_notes: Colloquial/regional expression (more common in some Latin American areas). It means doing something in silence or without drawing attention—similar to "a la callada" or "en silencio". Not very common in standard Spanish, and it can sound odd in some countries.
target_language_example: Se fue a la muda, sin despedirse de nadie.
native_language_example: He left quietly, without saying goodbye to anyone.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done extremely well or without mistakes. Often goes with verbs like hacer, salir, funcionar, and quedar (when describing how something fits/looks).
target_language_example: La receta me salió a la perfección.
native_language_example: The recipe turned out perfectly for me.

meaning: in the shade; out of direct sunlight.
additional_notes: Used to talk about being under shade (from a tree, umbrella, building, etc.), often for comfort in hot weather. It can also be used figuratively to mean "in someone’s shadow" (less common for beginners).
target_language_example: Hace mucho calor; vamos a sentarnos a la sombra.
native_language_example: It’s very hot; let’s sit in the shade.

meaning: at the same time; at once.
additional_notes: Used to say two things happen simultaneously. Common with verbs like "hacer" (do), "hablar" (talk), "trabajar" (work), "estudiar" (study). Also appears in the pattern "a la vez que" = "at the same time as / while".
target_language_example: No puedo hablar y escribir a la vez.
native_language_example: I can't talk and write at the same time.

additional_notes: Used to say something can be seen ("Está a la vista") or is obvious ("La respuesta está a la vista"). In banking, "cuenta/depósito a la vista" means money available on demand (like a checking account), not tied up in a time deposit.
target_language_example: La entrada está a la vista, junto al parque.
native_language_example: The entrance is in sight, next to the park.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or evidence for a conclusion, similar to “given (the fact that) …” or “considering …”. Often followed by a noun or phrase (e.g., a la vista de los hechos). More formal than “por” or “porque”.
target_language_example: A la vista de los resultados, vamos a cambiar el plan.
native_language_example: Given the results, we’re going to change the plan.

a la vuelta de la esquina

target_language_multi_word_term: a la vuelta de la esquina
meaning: just around the corner; very nearby (or coming very soon).
additional_notes: Used literally for a place that’s close (often reachable by turning the next corner), and figuratively for something that will happen soon. Often followed by "de" + place: "a la vuelta de la esquina de mi casa" (around the corner from my house).
target_language_example: La farmacia está a la vuelta de la esquina.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is just around the corner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about effects, plans, or results over a long period of time. Often contrasts with "a corto plazo" (short-term). It can modify a whole statement ("A largo plazo, ...") or be used after a verb ("pensar a largo plazo").
target_language_example: A largo plazo, es mejor ahorrar un poco cada mes.
native_language_example: In the long term, it’s better to save a little each month.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. With specific clock times, Spanish often uses "a" + "las" (for hours other than 1). For 1 o’clock, use "a la una" (singular).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las cinco.
native_language_example: See you at five o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. In Spanish, times are usually introduced with "a" (at) + the definite article: "a la" for 1:00 and "a las" for all other hours (2–12). You can also add "de la mañana/tarde/noche" if needed (e.g., "a las diez de la noche").
target_language_example: La reunión es a las diez.
native_language_example: The meeting is at ten o’clock.

meaning: at the first opportunity; as soon as something starts.
additional_notes: Usually used in idiomatic phrases like “a las primeras (de cambio)” to mean “at the first chance/at the first sign (of trouble),” often implying someone gives up or reacts too quickly. It’s colloquial but not slang. Often followed by an action: “a las primeras, se fue / lo dejó / se enfadó.”
target_language_example: A las primeras de cambio, dejó el trabajo.
native_language_example: At the first opportunity (at the first sign of trouble), he/she quit the job.

meaning: 'in the (style/way) of' / 'like' (used before an adjective or noun).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a bigger phrase: **a lo + adjective/noun** to describe doing something in a certain style (similar to “in a … way” or “like …”). It’s most common with masculine **lo** (e.g., *a lo grande, a lo mexicano*). With feminine nouns you may also hear **a la** (e.g., *a la francesa*).
target_language_example: Se vistió a lo punk para la fiesta.
native_language_example: He dressed punk-style for the party.

meaning: in a big way; on a grand scale (often: lavishly).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something with a lot of effort, style, or expense—bigger than usual (e.g., celebrating, traveling, renovating). Often appears with verbs like celebrar, festejar, hacer, vivir, tirar la casa por la ventana. Not the same as "mucho" (a lot in quantity); it’s about doing something grandly.
target_language_example: Para su cumpleaños, lo celebraron a lo grande.
native_language_example: For his birthday, they celebrated in a big way.

additional_notes: Often used with "de": "a lo largo de" + a place, time period, or process. With places it means “along” (a line or route): "a lo largo de la calle" = along the street. With time it means “throughout/over the course of”: "a lo largo del año" = throughout the year. Usually not used by itself; learners will most often see and use "a lo largo de".
target_language_example: Viajamos a lo largo de la costa durante una semana.
native_language_example: We traveled along the coast for a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening or extending over an entire time period or the length of a place. Often followed by a noun: a lo largo del día (throughout the day), a lo largo del río (along the river). Note the contraction: de + el = del (a lo largo del año).
target_language_example: A lo largo de la semana, voy al gimnasio tres veces.
native_language_example: Throughout the week, I go to the gym three times.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you can see, hear, or notice from far away. Often goes with verbs like ver (to see) or oír (to hear): “Se ve/Se oye a lo lejos…”.
target_language_example: Se ve una montaña a lo lejos.
native_language_example: You can see a mountain in the distance.

additional_notes: Common way to express possibility/uncertainty. It’s often interchangeable with “quizás/quizá” or “tal vez.” It doesn’t mean “the best” here; it introduces a guess or suggestion.
target_language_example: A lo mejor mañana llueve, así que lleva un paraguas.
native_language_example: Maybe it will rain tomorrow, so bring an umbrella.

meaning: "Anyway, back to what I was saying" / "back to my point."
additional_notes: Used in conversation to return to the main topic after a digression or interruption. Often appears with connectors like "Bueno," "En fin," or "Pero" (e.g., "Pero, a lo que iba..."). It can introduce what you wanted to say next: "A lo que iba es que..."
target_language_example: Bueno, a lo que iba: ¿puedes enviarme el informe hoy?
native_language_example: Anyway, back to my point: can you send me the report today?

meaning: by brute force; in a rough, heavy-handed way.
additional_notes: Literally refers to doing something “with a jackhammer” (machamartillo). It’s commonly used figuratively to criticize a solution or approach that is too forceful, crude, or not thoughtful (instead of doing it carefully or with a better method).
target_language_example: Quieren arreglarlo todo a machamartillo, sin pensar en las consecuencias.
native_language_example: They want to fix everything by brute force, without thinking about the consequences.

meaning: as a last resort; worst case; if it comes to it.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you’ll do if the preferred option doesn’t work out. Often appears with “y si no…” or “si hace falta…” (e.g., “Y si no, a malas…”). It’s common in casual speech and can sound a bit colloquial.
target_language_example: Podemos ir en coche, y si no, a malas, vamos en autobús.
native_language_example: We can go by car, and if not—worst case—we’ll go by bus.

meaning: "At your service" / "You got it" (said when someone asks you to do something).
additional_notes: Common, especially in Spain, as a polite/colloquial reply after a request or instruction. It literally suggests “(here I am) to obey/serve,” like “at your command,” but it’s usually friendly rather than overly formal. Often used on its own as a complete response.
target_language_example: —¿Me pasas la sal? —A mandar.
native_language_example: —Can you pass me the salt? —Sure / You got it.

meaning: as a way of; by way of; in the form of.
additional_notes: Used to introduce something that serves as an example, substitute, or manner of doing something. Often followed by a noun: "a manera de ejemplo" (by way of example), "a manera de introducción" (as an introduction), "a manera de broma" (as a joke).
target_language_example: A manera de ejemplo, voy a mostrarte dos opciones.
native_language_example: By way of example, I’m going to show you two options.

additional_notes: Commonly means something is done manually (not by a machine), especially in phrases like "hecho a mano" (handmade). It can also mean "within reach/handy" in expressions like "tener algo a mano" (to have something at hand).
target_language_example: Lo hice a mano.
native_language_example: I did it by hand.

additional_notes: Used especially in news and legal contexts to describe a robbery/assault carried out while the attacker is armed (often with a gun, but it can be any weapon). Common with verbs like asaltar, atracar, and robar: “robo/asalto a mano armada.”
target_language_example: Lo asaltaron a mano armada cuando salía del banco.
native_language_example: They robbed him at gunpoint when he was leaving the bank.

meaning: with bare hands; by hand (without tools).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does something without tools, gloves, weapons, or tricks. It can also be used more figuratively to mean “fair and square / honestly,” especially when talking about winning or succeeding without cheating.
target_language_example: Ganó el torneo a mano limpia.
native_language_example: He won the tournament fair and square.

additional_notes: Idiom meaning that something is available, given, received, or done in large quantities. Common with verbs like dar, recibir, tener, haber, and ganar: “dar a manos llenas” (to give generously), “hay trabajo a manos llenas” (there’s plenty of work). It’s not usually used literally about hands.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay oportunidades a manos llenas.
native_language_example: In this city there are plenty of opportunities.

meaning: a lot; in large quantities (often: “a ton”).
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like "haber" or "tener" to mean there is/are or someone has plenty of something. It’s informal and emphatic. You’ll often hear it in phrases like "hay comida a mares" (there’s tons of food) or "tiene trabajo a mares" (he/she has loads of work).
target_language_example: En esta playa hay turistas a mares en verano.
native_language_example: There are tons of tourists on this beach in the summer.

additional_notes: Used informally to intensify an action or quantity. Often translates as “a lot/tons,” “like crazy,” or “like hell,” depending on context: “Trabajé a matar” (I worked like crazy), “Había gente a matar” (There were tons of people), “Me duele a matar” (It hurts like hell). It’s not usually meant literally.
target_language_example: Ayer trabajé a matar y terminé agotado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I worked like crazy and ended up exhausted.

meaning: to mediation; to a mediation process.
additional_notes: Used in more formal/legal contexts when talking about taking a dispute or problem to mediation. Common with verbs like “ir a mediación” (to go to mediation), “acudir a mediación” (to turn to mediation), or “someter(se) a mediación” (to submit to mediation). Not the same as English “a mediation” (one mediation event); here “a” means “to.”
target_language_example: Si no llegamos a un acuerdo, iremos a mediación.
native_language_example: If we don’t reach an agreement, we’ll go to mediation.

meaning: in the middle of; around the middle of (a time period).
additional_notes: Used with months, years, or longer periods to say something happens around the midpoint (not an exact date). Common patterns: "a mediados de + mes" (a mediados de enero = mid-January), "a mediados de + año" (a mediados de 2026 = mid-2026), "a mediados de + la semana" (midweek). Similar to "hacia mediados de" (toward mid-...).
target_language_example: Vamos a mudarnos a mediados de marzo.
native_language_example: We’re going to move in mid-March.

additional_notes: Most often used in the expression "a medida que" to mean "as" or "as/while" something changes over time: "A medida que pasa el tiempo..." It can also appear after a noun as "a medida" meaning "made to measure" or "custom-made" (e.g., "un traje a medida").
target_language_example: A medida que aprendes español, entiendes más.
native_language_example: As you learn Spanish, you understand more.

additional_notes: Used to show that one thing happens gradually or simultaneously as another thing happens or changes. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present or imperfect): “A medida que pasa el tiempo…” = “As time goes by…”. Similar in meaning to “conforme” or “a medida de que” is generally avoided; the standard form is “a medida que”.
target_language_example: A medida que aprendes más español, entiendes mejor las películas.
native_language_example: As you learn more Spanish, you understand movies better.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that must be met for something to happen (a negative exception). It’s usually followed by the subjunctive: “a menos que + subjunctive” (e.g., “a menos que llueva”). Similar to “except if / unless.”
target_language_example: Iremos al parque a menos que llueva.
native_language_example: We’ll go to the park unless it rains.

additional_notes: Common adverb phrase used to talk about how frequently something happens. It can go before or after the verb: “A menudo voy…” / “Voy a menudo…”. Similar in meaning to “frecuentemente” (more formal) and “muchas veces” (very common).
target_language_example: A menudo tomo café por la mañana.
native_language_example: I often drink coffee in the morning.

meaning: at the mercy of; dependent on (often in a vulnerable way).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is in a situation controlled by another person/force, or strongly affected by something (like weather, fate, a decision). Often followed by a noun: "a merced de la tormenta" (at the mercy of the storm), "a merced del jefe" (at the boss’s mercy). It’s fairly formal and common in writing.
target_language_example: Sin refugio, estábamos a merced del viento y la lluvia.
native_language_example: Without shelter, we were at the mercy of the wind and rain.

additional_notes: Used to say you will do something according to your own style, preferences, or method. Common after verbs like hacerlo (to do it), vivir (to live), or aprender (to learn): "Lo haré a mi manera." It can sound neutral or slightly assertive depending on tone.
target_language_example: Gracias por el consejo, pero lo haré a mi manera.
native_language_example: Thanks for the advice, but I’ll do it my way.

meaning: at full speed; very fast / extremely busy.
additional_notes: Literally “at a thousand per hour,” used as an exaggeration. It can describe physical speed (moving/driving very fast) or how busy someone is, especially with the verb phrase “estar a mil por hora” (to be super busy, going nonstop).
target_language_example: Estos días estoy a mil por hora con el trabajo.
native_language_example: These days I’m extremely busy with work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that serves as an example, a substitute, or a kind of informal “version” of something else (e.g., an explanation, a summary, a joke, an introduction). Common patterns: “a modo de + noun” (a modo de ejemplo = as an example; a modo de resumen = by way of a summary; a modo de broma = as a joke).
target_language_example: A modo de ejemplo, te voy a mostrar dos opciones.
native_language_example: As an example, I’m going to show you two options.

meaning: really intensely; to the max; (sometimes) “to death.”
additional_notes: Common in informal spoken Spanish to emphasize strong intensity or commitment (similar to “super” or “like crazy”): Me gusta a muerte = “I love it so much.” In some contexts it can keep its literal meaning “to death” (e.g., a golpes a muerte = “beaten to death”), so the tone depends on context.
target_language_example: Me encanta esta canción a muerte.
native_language_example: I love this song so much.

meaning: as much as possible; extremely (to the limit).
additional_notes: Used to intensify an adjective or an action, meaning something is done/experienced to the maximum degree ("to the limit"). Often translates naturally as “really/very” or “as much as possible,” depending on context. Common with adjectives (e.g., cansado, feliz) and with verbs (e.g., trabajar, correr).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado a más no poder.
native_language_example: I’m extremely tired / I’m tired to the limit.

meaning: no later than; at the latest.
additional_notes: Used to set a deadline or latest possible time/date. It often comes before a day/date/time: “a más tardar el lunes / a las 5 / mañana”. Common in formal and neutral contexts (messages, work, instructions).
target_language_example: Necesito el informe a más tardar el viernes a las 3.
native_language_example: I need the report no later than Friday at 3.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes somewhere or crosses something by swimming. Common with verbs like ir (to go), cruzar (to cross), and llegar (to arrive): ir a nado, cruzar a nado. It contrasts with other ways of traveling (en coche/by car, en barco/by boat).
target_language_example: Cruzamos el río a nado porque no había puente.
native_language_example: We crossed the river by swimming because there was no bridge.

additional_notes: Used when you estimate something visually instead of using exact measurements (e.g., distance, quantity, size). Often appears with verbs like calcular, medir, and estimar: "a ojo" / "a ojo de buen cubero" (very roughly).
target_language_example: Calculé la distancia a ojo, sin usar una regla.
native_language_example: I estimated the distance by eye, without using a ruler.

additional_notes: Used to describe being in a place with no light, or doing something without light. Common with verbs like estar/quedarse/dejar (e.g., quedarse a oscuras = to be left in the dark due to a power outage).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos a oscuras cuando se fue la luz.
native_language_example: We were left in the dark when the power went out.

meaning: on bread and water (with almost nothing else to eat).
additional_notes: Used to describe a very basic diet, often as a punishment ("castigar a pan y agua", "poner/dejar a pan y agua"). It can also be used more generally/figuratively to mean living with very little or being on a very tight budget.
target_language_example: Lo castigaron a pan y agua por una semana.
native_language_example: They punished him by putting him on bread and water for a week.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to indicate a starting point in time, date, age, quantity, or place: a partir de mañana (starting tomorrow), a partir del 1 de mayo (from May 1st), a partir de los 18 años (from age 18), a partir de 50 euros (from 50 euros). It can also mean 'based on' with information or evidence: a partir de los datos (based on the data).
target_language_example: A partir de mañana, abrimos a las 9.
native_language_example: Starting tomorrow, we open at 9.

meaning: on foot; walking (instead of using transport).
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial. Often used with verbs like ir/venir/andar: “ir a pata” = “to go on foot.” Literally, pata means an animal’s leg/paw, and in casual speech it can refer to a person’s leg/foot, which is why the expression sounds informal.
target_language_example: Me voy a pata porque no pasa el autobús.
native_language_example: I’m going on foot because the bus isn’t coming.

meaning: in kicks; kicking (often: "a lot," in an exaggerated way).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: "with kicks." Commonly used with verbs like "echar" or "sacar" to mean forcing someone out violently ("echar a patadas" = "kick out"). It can also be used figuratively to mean "in abundance/loads" (e.g., "hay trabajo a patadas" = "there’s tons of work"), which is informal and hyperbolic.
target_language_example: Lo echaron a patadas del bar.
native_language_example: They kicked him out of the bar.

additional_notes: Used to express contrast: something happens even though there is an obstacle or opposing fact. It is followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive: a pesar de la lluvia (despite the rain), a pesar de eso (despite that), a pesar de estar cansado/a (despite being tired). With a full clause, Spanish often uses "a pesar de que" + verb (often subjunctive): A pesar de que llueve, salgo.
target_language_example: A pesar de la lluvia, fuimos al parque.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, we went to the park.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast: one thing is true, but another happens anyway. It must be followed by a clause (subject + verb): “a pesar de que + verb…”. With the same meaning, you’ll also hear “aunque”. (Note: “a pesar de” without “que” is followed by a noun or infinitive: “a pesar del frío”, “a pesar de estar cansado”.)
target_language_example: A pesar de que estaba cansado, fue al trabajo.
native_language_example: Even though he was tired, he went to work.

additional_notes: Used to express contrast: something is true or happens even though there are problems, obstacles, or negative circumstances. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence. Close to "sin embargo" (however), but it specifically highlights that there were difficulties.
target_language_example: A pesar de todo, seguimos adelante.
native_language_example: Despite everything, we kept going.

additional_notes: Used to say you go somewhere by walking (not by car/bus, etc.). Often follows verbs like ir/venir/llegar: "Voy a pie" (I’m going on foot). Also common with "estar": "Estoy a pie" can mean you’re without a car/ride and need to walk or get a ride.
target_language_example: Voy al trabajo a pie.
native_language_example: I go to work on foot.

meaning: as you please; at your leisure; to your heart’s content.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something freely, without hurry or restrictions, often enjoying it. Common with verbs like dormir, comer, descansar, pasear: “Dormimos a placer” = “We slept as much as we wanted.” You may also hear “a tu placer / a su placer” (“at your pleasure”).
target_language_example: En vacaciones, dormimos a placer.
native_language_example: On vacation, we slept as much as we wanted.

meaning: in broad daylight; in full light.
additional_notes: Often used with "del día" ("a plena luz del día") to emphasize that something happens openly, in daylight, sometimes implying it’s surprising or shameless. Common with verbs like "ocurrir", "pasar", "robar", "atacar".
target_language_example: El robo ocurrió a plena luz del día.
native_language_example: The robbery happened in broad daylight.

additional_notes: Most common as a reaction question: “¿A poco?” It expresses surprise, disbelief, or that you didn’t expect what you just heard. It’s especially associated with Mexican Spanish. Don’t confuse it with “poco a poco” (“little by little”).
target_language_example: —Me gané la lotería. —¿A poco?
native_language_example: —I won the lottery. —Really?

meaning: a few steps away; within walking distance.
additional_notes: Used to say something is very close by. Often followed by "de" + place/thing: "a pocos pasos de la estación" (a few steps from the station). It’s common in directions and in ads (e.g., hotels, apartments).
target_language_example: El hotel está a pocos pasos de la playa.
native_language_example: The hotel is a few steps from the beach.

meaning: by dint of; by repeatedly (doing something); through (great effort).
additional_notes: Used to say that a result was achieved thanks to persistence or continuous effort, often with verbs like insistir (to insist), trabajar (to work), luchar (to fight), etc. It’s fairly formal/literary and common in writing and more careful speech. Often followed by an infinitive: “A poder de + infinitive …”.
target_language_example: A poder de insistir, consiguió una cita con el médico.
native_language_example: By dint of insisting, he/she got an appointment with the doctor.

meaning: 'to go get' / 'go for' (to pursue or fetch something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially "ir", also "salir", "venir") + "a por" + noun/infinitive to mean going in order to fetch something or pursue a goal. Very common in Spain; in much of Latin America people often say "por" or "a" instead. Example patterns: "Voy a por pan" (I’m going to get bread), "Vamos a por ellos" (Let’s go after them / Let’s go get them).
target_language_example: Voy a por un café y vuelvo.
native_language_example: I’m going to get a coffee and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done with urgency, stress, or without real choice: "hacer algo a presión". It’s also used in cooking contexts to mean "by pressure" (pressure-cooked), as in "olla a presión" (pressure cooker) or "cocinar a presión".
target_language_example: Tuve que tomar una decisión a presión.
native_language_example: I had to make a decision under pressure.

meaning: early (in the morning); first thing (in the day).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very early, often at the start of the workday or morning. Common with verbs like "ir," "llegar," "llamar," "salir," or "hacer" (e.g., "a primera hora de la mañana"). It’s similar to "a primera hora" = "first thing" and doesn’t necessarily mean exactly 1:00.
target_language_example: Te llamo a primera hora mañana.
native_language_example: I’ll call you first thing tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to describe a first impression before looking more closely. Often followed by a contrast like "pero" (but) to show that things changed after a closer look.
target_language_example: A primera vista, el apartamento parece perfecto, pero es muy ruidoso.
native_language_example: At first glance, the apartment seems perfect, but it’s very noisy.

additional_notes: Used with a month or with an understood reference to the current/next month: "a primeros de enero" = "at the beginning of January." It contrasts with "a mediados" (mid-month) and "a finales" (end of the month).
target_language_example: Te pago a primeros de febrero.
native_language_example: I’ll pay you at the beginning of February.

meaning: at the beginning of (a time period).
additional_notes: Used with months, years, seasons, or other time periods to indicate the early part of them. It’s often contrasted with a mediados de (“in the middle of”) and a finales de (“at the end of”). Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: A principios de mayo empezamos el curso.
native_language_example: At the beginning of May we start the course.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that bullets can’t penetrate (a vest, a car, glass). More generally, it can be used figuratively to mean “unbreakable” or “foolproof” (very hard to damage or defeat). Often follows the noun: “chaleco a prueba de balas.”
target_language_example: El coche del presidente es a prueba de balas.
native_language_example: The president’s car is bulletproof.

meaning: (Usually in set phrases) “behind doors,” i.e., in private / with no audience.
additional_notes: Most often appears as **a puerta cerrada** (“behind closed doors,” privately; or in sports/events, **without spectators**) and **a puertas cerradas** (plural, especially for matches). The opposite is **a puertas abiertas** (“open to the public”). On its own, **a puertas** is incomplete and typically needs **cerradas/abiertas** or context.
target_language_example: El partido se jugó a puertas cerradas.
native_language_example: The match was played behind closed doors (with no spectators).

additional_notes: Used to say something is ready or will happen very soon. Common patterns: "estar a punto de + infinitive" (to be about to do something): "Estoy a punto de salir." Also "a punto" can mean "ready" or "well-prepared": "La cena está a punto." It’s also used as "a punto de" meaning "on the verge of" (almost happening).
target_language_example: Estoy a punto de salir.
native_language_example: I'm about to leave.

meaning: about to (do something); on the verge of.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is going to happen very soon: “estar a punto de + infinitive.” You can also use it for something nearly ready (“La cena está a punto”). In negative form, “no estar a punto de” means “not about to / not going to (do something).”
target_language_example: Estoy a punto de salir, pero puedo esperar cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I’m about to leave, but I can wait five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to challenge someone or express confident doubt, often like a playful dare. It’s commonly followed by a verb phrase in the present tense: “A que no + verb…”. In many situations English would use “Bet you can’t…” or “I bet you won’t…”.
target_language_example: A que no te atreves a decírselo en la cara.
