You may also see the plural: artes modernas (modern arts) or arte moderno y contemporáneo (modern and contemporary art).
target_language_example: Me gusta el arte moderno, pero no lo entiendo siempre.
native_language_example: I like modern art, but I don’t always understand it.

meaning: short ribs (beef ribs cut crosswise into strips).
additional_notes: Common in Argentina/Uruguay/Chile. It’s a specific cut of beef ribs (often called "tira de asado" too) that’s popular for grilling at an asado (barbecue). In restaurants or butcher shops, you might see it listed as a cut of meat rather than as a general cooking method.
target_language_example: Para el asado compramos asado de tira y chorizos.
native_language_example: For the barbecue we bought short ribs and sausages.

additional_notes: Used to add another item (meaning “as well as”) or to compare two things (meaning “just like”). In lists it often pairs with y (“and”): “A así como B”. Also common when giving examples: “así como...” = “such as...”.
target_language_example: Me gusta el café, así como el té.
native_language_example: I like coffee, as well as tea.

meaning: just like that; for no good reason; out of the blue.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens without warning, without explanation, or without sufficient justification. Often appears with a negative (no) to stress that you can’t do something casually or without a reason: “No puedes irte así como así.” It can describe sudden actions, decisions, cancellations, etc.
target_language_example: No puedo cancelar la cita así como así.
native_language_example: I can’t cancel the appointment just like that.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective or adverb to emphasize the extent of something, often supported by a gesture indicating size/amount (e.g., holding your hands apart). Common pattern: “así de + adjective/adverb” = “this/that + adjective/adverb” or “so + adjective/adverb” (e.g., “así de fácil” = “that easy / so easy”). It can also appear in “así de + noun” in informal speech, but it’s most common with adjectives.
target_language_example: La prueba fue así de fácil.
native_language_example: The test was that easy.

additional_notes: Used to express acceptance or resignation when something can’t be changed (often after bad luck or an unfair situation). It can be sympathetic or a bit dismissive depending on tone. Often said as a standalone phrase; you may also hear “Así es la vida, ¿qué le vamos a hacer?” (“That’s life—what can we do?”).
target_language_example: Perdí el trabajo, pero así es la vida.
native_language_example: I lost my job, but that’s life.

meaning: “That’s better like this.” / “This way is better.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is better done in the current way or after a change. Often follows an adjustment or suggestion (e.g., moving something, changing a plan). You can also hear it as a short, approving comment: “Así, mejor.”
target_language_example: Pon la silla aquí; así mejor.
native_language_example: Put the chair here; this way is better.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or result (“therefore”), or to move the conversation forward (“so, then…”). Common in more formal or written Spanish; in casual speech you’ll often hear “así que” instead.
target_language_example: Así pues, no podemos ir hoy.
native_language_example: So, we can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to link a cause to its consequence (similar to English “so/therefore”). It often comes after a comma in writing: "..., así que ...". In conversation, it can also introduce a conclusion or follow-up question: "Así que..." = "So...".
target_language_example: No tenía dinero, así que me fui a casa.
native_language_example: I didn’t have any money, so I went home.

additional_notes: Used to express acceptance, agreement, or a wish that something happens. Common in formal or literary contexts, and also in set phrases like "Amén, así sea". It uses the subjunctive of "ser" (sea), and often refers to something just said ("Let it be that way").
target_language_example: —Ojalá todo salga bien. —Así sea.
native_language_example: —I hope everything goes well. —So be it / May it be so.

additional_notes: A medical emergency referring to a sudden problem with the heart (often a heart attack). In everyday Spanish you may also hear "infarto" or "infarto de miocardio". Common with verbs like "tener" (to have) or "sufrir" (to suffer).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo tuvo un ataque al corazón y lo llevaron al hospital.
native_language_example: My grandfather had a heart attack and they took him to the hospital.

additional_notes: Common medical/emergency term. Often used with the verb "tener" (to have): "Tuvo un ataque cardíaco" = "He/She had a heart attack." You may also hear "infarto" as a shorter synonym in many countries.
target_language_example: Llama al 911: mi padre está teniendo un ataque cardíaco.
native_language_example: Call 911: my dad is having a heart attack.

additional_notes: A common health/mental health term. It can describe a sudden episode of intense fear with physical symptoms (e.g., racing heart, shortness of breath). You’ll often see it with the verb "tener" (to have): "tener un ataque de pánico". In everyday speech, people may also say "me dio un ataque de pánico" (I had a panic attack / I got a panic attack).
target_language_example: Creo que tuve un ataque de pánico anoche.
native_language_example: I think I had a panic attack last night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or exception: one thing is true, but another thing happens/is true anyway. Common patterns: "aunque + indicative" for real/known facts (Aunque llueve, salgo) and "aunque + subjunctive" for uncertain/hypothetical situations (Aunque llueva, saldré = Even if it rains, I'll go out). Often placed at the beginning of the sentence, but it can also appear later (Salgo aunque llueve).
target_language_example: Aunque estoy cansado, voy a estudiar.
native_language_example: Although I’m tired, I’m going to study.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase for a toy airplane folded from paper. It’s usually used literally; you can also say “un avión de papel” or “hacer un avión de papel” (to make a paper airplane).
target_language_example: Hice un avión de papel y lo lancé por la clase.
native_language_example: I made a paper airplane and threw it across the classroom.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the start of the calendar year and is very common in greetings and holiday wishes. As a holiday, people often say (la) Nochevieja for New Year’s Eve and (el) Año Nuevo for New Year’s Day. In writing, you may see it capitalized (Año Nuevo) when referring to the holiday, but lowercase is also common in general use.
target_language_example: ¡Feliz Año Nuevo!
native_language_example: Happy New Year!

additional_notes: Used both literally (physically lowering your head) and figuratively to show submission, shame, or resignation (similar to “hang your head” or “bow your head” in English). You can also hear it in advice or commands (e.g., “¡Baja la cabeza!”).
target_language_example: Cuando el profesor lo regañó, bajó la cabeza y no dijo nada.
native_language_example: When the teacher scolded him, he lowered his head and didn’t say anything.

additional_notes: Used for things located beneath the surface (pipes, tunnels, roots) and also figuratively to mean buried (e.g., a body or treasure). It’s a common location phrase: estar bajo tierra (to be underground/buried), vivir bajo tierra (to live underground).
target_language_example: El tesoro estaba bajo tierra, cerca del árbol.
native_language_example: The treasure was underground, near the tree.

additional_notes: A literal phrase: ballena = “whale” and azul = “blue.” Used as the common name of the animal; in Spanish it’s usually written in lowercase unless it starts a sentence. In plural: ballenas azules.
target_language_example: La ballena azul es el animal más grande del mundo.
native_language_example: The blue whale is the largest animal in the world.

additional_notes: A raised area of sand in a river, lake, or sea (often near the coast) that can be shallow and sometimes visible at low tide. Common in travel, boating, and geography contexts. Also used in warnings because boats can run aground (encallar) on a banco de arena.
target_language_example: Cuidado: el barco puede encallar en ese banco de arena.
native_language_example: Careful: the boat can run aground on that sandbank.

additional_notes: Common in tech and office contexts. Often used with verbs like "crear" (to create), "guardar" (to store/save), "buscar" (to search), and "actualizar" (to update): "crear una base de datos", "buscar en la base de datos". Also commonly appears with the preposition "de": "base de datos de clientes" (customer database).
target_language_example: Tenemos que actualizar la base de datos de clientes.
native_language_example: We have to update the customer database.

additional_notes: Used when you choose to trust someone or assume they’re telling the truth (or didn’t do something wrong) even though you’re not completely sure. Common with verbs like "dar" (to give): "Darle a alguien el beneficio de la duda" = "to give someone the benefit of the doubt."
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de lo que pasó, pero voy a darte el beneficio de la duda.
native_language_example: I’m not sure what happened, but I’m going to give you the benefit of the doubt.

meaning: a weirdo; an odd person (someone seen as different).
additional_notes: Common in Spain and Latin America. It can be playful or mildly insulting depending on tone and context. Literally means “rare bug/creature,” but it’s used to label a person as unusual or not fitting in. You can also use it about yourself: “Soy un bicho raro.”
target_language_example: En el instituto me sentía como un bicho raro porque no me gustaban las mismas cosas que a los demás.
native_language_example: In high school I felt like a weirdo because I didn’t like the same things as everyone else.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for something they did. It can also describe something that is properly or skillfully made/done (e.g., un trabajo bien hecho = a job well done). With food, bien hecho means “well-done” (cooked thoroughly), especially for steak (carne bien hecha).
target_language_example: ¡Bien hecho! Terminaste el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: Well done! You finished the project on time.

meaning: “good for …” (used to praise or congratulate someone).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a person or pronoun: “¡Bien por ti!” = “Good for you!” You can also use it with someone’s action: “¡Bien por haber venido!” = “Good for coming!” It’s casual/neutral and often said with enthusiasm (¡Bien por …!).
target_language_example: ¡Bien por ti! Te lo mereces.
native_language_example: Good for you! You deserve it.

additional_notes: A conjunction used to introduce a contrast. It is typically followed by the subjunctive: “bien que + subjunctive” (e.g., bien que sea / tengas / vaya). Often interchangeable with “aunque,” but “bien que” is a bit more formal and usually clearly triggers the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Bien que esté cansado, voy a salir.
native_language_example: Although I’m tired, I’m going to go out.

meaning: own assets; separate property (often in a marriage/legal context).
additional_notes: Used to refer to property or assets that belong to a person personally, especially those that are not shared with a spouse (as opposed to bienes gananciales, jointly owned marital property). Common in legal, financial, and formal contexts like contracts, divorce, or inheritance. In everyday speech you might also hear simply bienes (assets/property) or propiedad propia (one’s own property).
target_language_example: Antes de casarse, firmaron un acuerdo para proteger sus bienes propios.
native_language_example: Before getting married, they signed an agreement to protect their separate property.

meaning: face down; lying on your stomach.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person or object with the front side facing downward (opposite of "boca arriba" = face up). Common with verbs like "estar", "poner(se)", and "caer" (e.g., "pon el libro boca abajo" = put the book face down).
target_language_example: El niño está boca abajo en la cama.
native_language_example: The child is lying face down on the bed.

meaning: 'face up' / 'on your back' (lying with your face toward the sky).
additional_notes: Used to describe a position (lying down) or how an object is placed, especially cards, photos, or a body. Often contrasts with "boca abajo" (face down).
target_language_example: Acuéstate boca arriba y relájate.
native_language_example: Lie on your back (face up) and relax.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the object a fortune-teller uses to “see the future.” It can also be used humorously to mean “I can’t predict the future,” often in phrases like: No tengo una bola de cristal (“I don’t have a crystal ball”).
target_language_example: No tengo una bola de cristal, pero creo que va a llover.
native_language_example: I don’t have a crystal ball, but I think it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: A neutral, formal term for a nuclear weapon. Often shortened to "la bomba" when the context is clear. In Spanish, "atómico/a" means "atomic" and agrees in gender/number (e.g., "arma atómica", "bombas atómicas").
target_language_example: La bomba atómica destruyó la ciudad en segundos.
native_language_example: The atomic bomb destroyed the city in seconds.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for a container where you throw away trash. Also said as "cubo de basura" (more common in Spain) or "basurero" in some regions. You may also see "tirar a la basura" = "to throw in the trash."
target_language_example: Tira eso en el bote de basura, por favor.
native_language_example: Throw that in the trash can, please.

meaning: rowing boat (a small boat moved with oars).
additional_notes: Used to describe a small boat propelled by rowing (with oars). In everyday Spanish you may also hear "bote de remos" or "bote de remos" to emphasize the oars, and "bote" can sometimes be translated as "boat" or "small boat" depending on context.
target_language_example: Alquilamos un bote de remo en el lago.
native_language_example: We rented a rowing boat on the lake.

meaning: a rowing boat (a boat you move with oars).
additional_notes: Used for a small boat propelled by oars. In everyday Spanish you may also hear "bote de remos" to contrast with a motorboat ("lancha" or "bote con motor"). Similar terms: "barca de remos" (rowboat), and the more general "bote" = small boat.
target_language_example: Alquilamos un bote de remos en el lago.
native_language_example: We rented a rowing boat on the lake.

additional_notes: Often used figuratively to mean someone’s key helper or second-in-command (not necessarily literally their right arm). You’ll commonly see it with a possessive: “mi/su brazo derecho.”
target_language_example: María es mi brazo derecho en el trabajo.
native_language_example: María is my right-hand person at work.

additional_notes: A common, polite phrase said before someone starts eating. You can say it to one person or a group. Often used with ¡Buen provecho! (more common in some countries).
target_language_example: ¡Buen apetito! La comida ya está lista.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal! The food is ready.

meaning: a kind heart; a good-hearted person.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is kind, generous, and well-intentioned. Often appears with the verb "tener": "Tiene buen corazón" (He/She has a kind heart). Can also be used with "ser": "Es de buen corazón" (He/She is good-hearted).
target_language_example: No te preocupes; Ana tiene buen corazón y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; Ana has a kind heart and always helps others.

meaning: “Good day” (a greeting; often like “good morning” or “hello”).
additional_notes: Used as a greeting, especially in Argentina, Uruguay, and other parts of Latin America. It’s common to say it when arriving somewhere (e.g., a shop, office) and can be used into the afternoon in some places. You may also hear the plural form “buenos días” (more standard across the Spanish-speaking world).
target_language_example: Buen día, ¿tiene mesa para dos?
native_language_example: Good day/Hello, do you have a table for two?

additional_notes: Often refers to someone’s sense of style (clothes, decoration, music, etc.) or to something being tasteful. In plural, "buenos gustos" can mean “good taste(s).” You can also use "de buen gusto" = “in good taste / tasteful,” and "tener buen gusto" = “to have good taste.”
target_language_example: Ese vestido es muy elegante; tienes muy buen gusto.
native_language_example: That dress is very elegant; you have very good taste.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s positive, cheerful mood (often with estar/tener). Common in phrases like “estar de buen humor” (to be in a good mood) and “tener buen humor” (to have a good sense of humor / to be good-humored, depending on context).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de buen humor porque es viernes.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a good mood because it’s Friday.

meaning: good judgment; a good eye (for noticing/choosing things).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is good at spotting details, picking good options, or judging quality (e.g., in fashion, art, deals, or people). Often followed by "para" + noun/infinitive: "Tiene buen ojo para la moda" / "para elegir".
target_language_example: Tienes buen ojo para elegir regalos.
native_language_example: You have a good eye for choosing gifts.

meaning: a good catch (a desirable potential romantic partner).
additional_notes: Often used when talking about someone as a desirable person to date or marry (because of their personality, job, money, etc.). It can sound a bit judgmental because it treats a person like an “option.” You’ll commonly see it with verbs like ser: “Es un buen partido.”
target_language_example: Dicen que Marta es un buen partido: es inteligente y tiene un buen trabajo.
native_language_example: They say Marta is a good catch: she’s smart and has a good job.

meaning: a good while; a long time (in a pleasant way).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like esperar (to wait), estar (to be), or pasar (to spend) to mean “for quite a while.” It suggests a considerable amount of time and can imply it was enjoyable or at least fine (depending on context). Common patterns: “un buen rato” = “a good while,” “hace un buen rato” = “a while ago.”
target_language_example: Te estuve esperando un buen rato.
native_language_example: I was waiting for you for quite a while.

meaning: a good guy; a nice person (usually a man).
additional_notes: Common in casual speech to describe someone as friendly, decent, or trustworthy. "Tipo" literally means "guy/type," so the phrase is fairly transparent. You can also say "una buena tipa" for a woman, but in many places "buen tipo" is mostly used for men.
target_language_example: Juan es un buen tipo; siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: Juan is a good guy; he always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for something they did well. You can also say “¡Buen trabajo!” as an exclamation. Note: “trabajo” can mean “work” or “job,” so in context it may also mean “a good job (position),” but the common phrasebook use is praise.
target_language_example: ¡Buen trabajo! Terminaste muy rápido.
native_language_example: Good job! You finished very quickly.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well when they’re leaving on a trip. You can say it when someone is about to depart or in a message before they travel. Often used with ¡Que tengas un buen viaje! (to one person) or ¡Que tengan un buen viaje! (to more than one person / formal).
target_language_example: ¡Buen viaje! Mándame un mensaje cuando llegues.
native_language_example: Have a good trip! Text me when you arrive.

meaning: a good deed; a kind act.
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something helpful or kind for someone. Common in expressions like “hacer una buena acción” (to do a good deed). Often implies a small act of kindness rather than a big, formal “action.”
target_language_example: Ayudar a tu vecino con las bolsas es una buena acción.
native_language_example: Helping your neighbor with the bags is a good deed.

additional_notes: Informal expression (very common in Latin America) used to praise something someone did or said, or to show approval/enthusiasm. Often said as a quick reaction on its own: "¡Buena esa!" You may also hear "¡Esa es buena!" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: —Aprobé el examen. —¡Buena esa!
native_language_example: —I passed the exam. —Nice one!

additional_notes: Used to talk about how people view a person, place, business, product, etc. Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have) or "gozar de" (to enjoy) and with "de" to say what it’s famous for ("buena fama de…").
target_language_example: Este restaurante tiene buena fama por su paella.
native_language_example: This restaurant has a good reputation for its paella.

additional_notes: Used in legal, business, and everyday contexts to mean acting honestly, without trying to deceive, and with sincere intentions. Common in phrases like "actuar de buena fe" (to act in good faith) and "de buena fe" (in good faith).
target_language_example: Firmamos el contrato de buena fe.
native_language_example: We signed the contract in good faith.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone (or a group) as kind, friendly, and decent. Often said with the verb "ser": "Es buena gente" = "He/She is a good person." It’s common and conversational, and it can refer to one person or several depending on context.
target_language_example: Juan es buena gente; siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: Juan is a good person; he always helps others.

meaning: “good hand”; also “a knack / good touch” (skill, especially with food, plants, or dealing with people).
additional_notes: Often used in phrases like “tener buena mano para…” (to have a knack for…) or “tener buena mano con…” (to be good with…). It can also be literal, like having a “good hand” in cards.
target_language_example: Mi abuela tiene buena mano para las plantas: siempre están verdes.
native_language_example: My grandma has a knack for plants: they’re always green.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck, especially before an exam, interview, trip, or competition. Often said on its own (“¡Buena suerte!”) or with “con” + noun (“Buena suerte con el examen”). You can also hear the longer form “¡Mucha suerte!” (“Lots of luck!”).
target_language_example: ¡Buena suerte con tu examen mañana!
native_language_example: Good luck with your exam tomorrow!

additional_notes: Literally “good life.” Used to talk about living well or enjoying comforts/pleasures. It can be neutral or slightly ironic depending on context (someone living luxuriously). Often appears with verbs like llevar (to lead/live) or darse (to treat oneself).
target_language_example: Desde que cambió de trabajo, lleva una buena vida.
native_language_example: Since he changed jobs, he’s been living the good life.

additional_notes: Used for a friendly, cooperative attitude (good intentions) or for being willing to do something. Common with verbs like tener/mostrar (“to have/show”) and with expressions like con buena voluntad (“with goodwill/willingly”). It can refer to a general friendly attitude (“goodwill”) or practical cooperation (“willingness”).
target_language_example: Agradezco tu buena voluntad para ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: I appreciate your willingness/goodwill to help me with the move.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting in the evening/night and also as a farewell when going to bed or leaving at night. Very common and polite. Usually said without “(las)”—just “Buenas noches.”
target_language_example: Buenas noches, ¿cómo estás?
native_language_example: Good evening, how are you?

additional_notes: A common phrase for announcing something positive. Often used with verbs like "tener" or "traer": "Tengo buenas noticias" (I have good news), "Te traigo buenas noticias" (I bring you good news). In Spanish, "noticias" is usually plural in this expression.
target_language_example: ¡Tengo buenas noticias! Nos aceptaron en el curso.
native_language_example: I have good news! They accepted us into the course.

additional_notes: Used as a polite greeting from midday until night (roughly after lunch through early evening). It can be used when arriving or when starting a conversation; in many places it can also work as a polite goodbye in the afternoon/evening. Often used on its own, or with a title like "Buenas tardes, señor/señora".
target_language_example: Buenas tardes, ¿cómo está usted?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to react to new information (often like “Good to know” in English). In everyday Spanish you’ll very often hear it with an object: “Bueno saberlo” (“Good to know that/it”) or “Es bueno saberlo” (more complete, a bit more formal).
target_language_example: —El museo abre los lunes. —Bueno saberlo, gracias.
native_language_example: —The museum is open on Mondays. —Good to know, thanks.

meaning: "Well, look..." / "Well, listen..." (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: In real conversation you’ll usually hear this as "Bueno, mira," with "mira" (the tú command form of "mirar"). It’s a common filler/discourse marker to start an explanation, change topic, or soften what comes next. It doesn’t always mean literally "look"—often it’s closer to "so" or "well" in English.
target_language_example: Bueno, mira, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: Well, look, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to describe a strong friendship. It can mean simply “good friends” (not romantic), but context matters—sometimes it can imply being very close. Singular: "buen amigo" / "buena amiga". You can also say "somos buenos amigos" (we’re good friends).
target_language_example: Somos buenos amigos desde la escuela.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends since school.

additional_notes: Standard, polite greeting used from the morning until around lunchtime/early afternoon. Often written with the accent: “días.” You can also use it to greet a group (it’s plural).
target_language_example: Buenos días, ¿cómo está?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to greet someone during the morning and often into early afternoon, depending on the country. It can be said when arriving and sometimes when leaving (like 'have a good day'). Often used with courtesy: "Buenos días, señor/señora" or "¡Muy buenos días!".
target_language_example: Buenos días, ¿cómo está?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about being polite and behaving appropriately (often taught at home or in school). Common with verbs like “tener” (to have), “mostrar” (to show), and “enseñar” (to teach): “tener buenos modales.”
target_language_example: En este restaurante hay que tener buenos modales.
native_language_example: In this restaurant you have to have good manners.

meaning: to look for (a person or animal).
additional_notes: Use "buscar a" when the direct object is a specific person (or a pet/animal treated as a person): "Busco a mi hermana." With things, places, or more general objects, you usually drop "a": "Busco mis llaves." It often implies going to find or pick someone up: "Voy a buscar a Juan" = "I’m going to go get Juan."
target_language_example: Voy a buscar a Ana a la estación.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick Ana up at the station.

meaning: to look for a job; to job hunt.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning you are searching for employment. Often used with “estar” to describe your current situation: “Estoy buscando trabajo” (I’m looking for a job). You can also specify the type of work: “buscar trabajo de…” (look for work as a…).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando trabajo en Madrid.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a job in Madrid.

meaning: to manage / get by; to find a way (to make a living).
additional_notes: Very common informal expression. It means being resourceful and solving practical problems on your own, often under pressure (finding work, money, a solution, etc.). You’ll often see it in commands like “Búscate la vida” (“Figure it out / You’re on your own”). Conjugates as a reflexive verb: me/te/se/nos/os buscan la vida.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, yo me busco la vida.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll manage / I’ll find a way.

additional_notes: Used for the voicemail service on a phone line. You’ll often see it with verbs like "dejar" (to leave) or "tener" (to have): "Dejé un mensaje en tu buzón de voz." Also commonly shortened to "buzón" in context.
target_language_example: Te dejé un mensaje en el buzón de voz.
native_language_example: I left you a message in your voicemail.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or is repeated yearly. Often paired with present tense for habits ("Viajamos cada año") or with future/past for repeated events across years ("Iremos cada año", "Íbamos cada año").
target_language_example: Visitamos a mis abuelos cada año en verano.
native_language_example: We visit my grandparents every year in the summer.

additional_notes: Used to mean “each one” in the sense of each person making their own choice or having their own preference. Often appears in expressions like “Cada cual a lo suyo” (everyone to their own thing / mind your own business) or “Cada cual con su tema” (to each their own). Also used with “su” to emphasize individuality: “Cada cual tiene su opinión” (Everyone has their own opinion).
target_language_example: Cada cual tiene su propia manera de hacer las cosas.
native_language_example: Everyone has their own way of doing things.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens daily or with increasing frequency. It can describe a routine ("every day") or a gradual change when used with comparisons like "cada día más" ("more and more every day").
target_language_example: Cada día voy al trabajo en metro.
native_language_example: Every day I go to work by subway.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens once per hour or repeats at hourly intervals. It can modify a verb (Cada hora reviso el correo.) or describe a schedule/dose/frequency (Toma este medicamento cada hora.).
target_language_example: El tren pasa cada hora.
native_language_example: The train comes every hour.

cada palo que aguante su vela

target_language_multi_word_term: cada palo que aguante su vela
meaning: Everyone should deal with their own problems (and take responsibility for themselves).
additional_notes: Common proverb/idiom used to say that each person should handle the consequences of their own actions, or that you won’t help someone fix what they caused. Often said when people are blaming others or expecting others to solve their situation. Literally it refers to each pole/stick holding up its own candle, but the real meaning is figurative.
target_language_example: Yo ya hice mi parte; cada palo que aguante su vela.
native_language_example: I already did my part; everyone should deal with their own problems.

meaning: each person; to each their own.
additional_notes: Commonly used to express that everyone has their own preferences or ways of doing things. Often appears as “Cada quien…” or “Cada quien con lo suyo.” Similar to “each to their own.”
target_language_example: A mí no me gusta, pero cada quien tiene sus gustos.
native_language_example: I don’t like it, but everyone has their own tastes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about individuals in a group one by one. Often followed by “de” + plural noun: “cada uno de mis amigos” (each of my friends). It can also be used alone as a pronoun: “Cada uno tiene su opinión” (Each one has their own opinion). Feminine form: “cada una.”
target_language_example: Cada uno de nosotros tiene una tarea.
native_language_example: Each one of us has a task.

additional_notes: Most often used to talk about something that happens on every occasion: “Cada vez que…” = “Every time that…”. It’s also common in the pattern “cada vez más/menos” to mean “more and more / less and less” (i.e., increasingly/decreasingly).
target_language_example: Cada vez que voy al supermercado, compro fruta.
native_language_example: Every time I go to the supermarket, I buy fruit.

additional_notes: Used to describe a trend or change that keeps growing over time. Often followed by an adjective/adverb ("cada vez más difícil") or by "gente/personas" ("cada vez más gente").
target_language_example: Cada vez es más difícil encontrar estacionamiento en el centro.
native_language_example: It’s getting harder and harder to find parking downtown.

additional_notes: A legal term meaning a prison sentence for life. Often used with verbs like "condenar a" (to sentence to) or "cumplir" (to serve): "condenado a cadena perpetua". Literally "perpetual chain," but in modern Spanish it refers to life imprisonment, not literal chains.
target_language_example: Lo condenaron a cadena perpetua por el crimen.
native_language_example: They sentenced him to life imprisonment for the crime.

meaning: to like someone; to get along well (with someone).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the impression a person makes on you. Common pattern: "Me cae bien" = "I like him/her" (literally “he/she falls well to me”). Negative: "Me cae mal" = "I don’t like him/her". Often used with people rather than things; for things you’d usually say "me gusta" (I like it).
target_language_example: Me cae bien tu hermano; es muy simpático.
native_language_example: I like your brother; he’s very nice.

meaning: to rub someone the wrong way; to dislike someone (first impression).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something gives a bad impression or annoys someone. Structure: “X me/te/le cae mal” = “I/you/he/she don’t like X” (often meaning “X rubs me/you/him/her the wrong way”). Opposite: “caer bien” (to like / to get along with). Not the same as “sentirse mal” (to feel sick/bad).
target_language_example: Me cae mal ese tipo; siempre está quejándose.
native_language_example: That guy rubs me the wrong way; he’s always complaining.

meaning: to get along well; to like each other.
additional_notes: Used for mutual/reciprocal liking (often after meeting or when talking about how two people get along). It’s typically used with plural reflexive/reciprocal pronouns: nos caemos bien (we like each other), se caen bien (they like each other). For one-way liking, Spanish usually uses caer bien (no -se): Me caes bien = “I like you / You seem nice.”
target_language_example: Nos caemos bien desde el primer día.
native_language_example: We’ve gotten along well since the first day.

meaning: coffee with milk (usually a milky coffee).
additional_notes: Common drink order in cafés. In Spain it often means espresso with steamed/hot milk; in Latin America it can also refer to brewed coffee with milk. You can order it “caliente” (hot) or “frío/helado” (cold/iced), and sometimes specify “con leche” vs. “solo” (black).
target_language_example: Para mí, un café con leche, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a coffee with milk, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a box/case that holds tools (literal meaning), and sometimes figuratively to mean a set of resources or methods (e.g., “a toolbox of skills”). Plural: "cajas de herramientas".
target_language_example: Necesito una caja de herramientas para arreglar la bicicleta.
native_language_example: I need a toolbox to fix the bike.

additional_notes: Most commonly used for an airplane’s device that records flight data and cockpit audio ("the black box"), especially in news and investigations. It can also mean a "black box" more generally: a device/system whose internal workings are unknown or not explained. Literally "black box" (caja = box, negra = black).
target_language_example: Los investigadores encontraron la caja negra del avión.
native_language_example: The investigators found the plane’s black box.

additional_notes: Used mainly in stores/supermarkets to refer to the machine where payments are processed. You’ll also hear related phrases like "en la caja" (at the checkout) and "cajero/cajera" (cashier).
target_language_example: Pagué en la caja registradora con tarjeta.
native_language_example: I paid at the cash register with a card.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an ATM where you withdraw cash with a bank card. In many places you’ll also hear just cajero. Plural: cajeros automáticos.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde hay un cajero automático cerca?
native_language_example: Where is there an ATM nearby?

additional_notes: Often used as a command: "¡Calla la boca!" / "¡Cállate la boca!" It’s usually rude or aggressive, similar to "Shut up!" In a softer, non-command use, it can mean “to keep quiet” or “to stop talking,” but beginners should treat it as strong language. Common variation: "callarse la boca" (to shut up / to keep your mouth shut).
target_language_example: ¡Cállate la boca y escucha un momento!
native_language_example: Shut up and listen for a moment!

meaning: to shut up; to keep your mouth shut.
additional_notes: A strong, often rude way to tell someone to stop talking. It can also be used reflexively about yourself ("me callé la boca" = "I shut up/I kept quiet"). In many situations, "cállate" or the more polite "cállate, por favor" / "guarda silencio" is safer.
target_language_example: ¡Cállate la boca y déjame hablar!
native_language_example: Shut up and let me talk!

meaning: dead end (street); dead end (no way forward).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “alley without an exit.” Used for a street that doesn’t go through, and also figuratively for a situation with no solution or progress. Common in signs: “Callejón sin salida.”
target_language_example: Seguimos caminando y era un callejón sin salida.
native_language_example: We kept walking, and it was a dead end.

additional_notes: Used when someone decides something different from what they previously thought or planned. Often follows a first decision: “Voy a salir… pero cambié de idea.” You can use it in different tenses (cambié, cambiaste, cambia, etc.) and also as an infinitive after another verb: “puedo cambiar de idea.”
target_language_example: Iba a ir al cine, pero cambié de idea.
native_language_example: I was going to go to the movies, but I changed my mind.

additional_notes: Used when someone decides something different from what they thought before. Often used with a person as the subject: "He cambiado de opinión" (I’ve changed my mind) or "¿Has cambiado de opinión?" (Have you changed your mind?).
target_language_example: Lo siento, he cambiado de opinión: no voy a ir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I changed my mind: I’m not going to go.

additional_notes: Common in news, science, and everyday discussion about the environment. Usually refers to long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns, often linked to global warming. Often used with verbs like combatir (to fight), frenar (to slow down), and causar (to cause).
target_language_example: El cambio climático está afectando a muchas especies en todo el mundo.
native_language_example: Climate change is affecting many species all over the world.

meaning: on the way to; heading to.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like ir/venir/estar (e.g., "Voy/Estoy camino de + place") to say you are heading toward a destination. The word "camino" literally means "path/road," so "camino de + place" is like "(on the) road to + place," but in everyday English it’s usually translated as "on my way to" or "heading to."
target_language_example: Voy camino de casa.
native_language_example: I’m on my way home.

additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning “field of battle.” Used for real war contexts and also figuratively to describe a place or situation with intense conflict (e.g., politics, work debates). Plural: campos de batalla.
target_language_example: El campo de batalla estaba lleno de humo.
native_language_example: The battlefield was full of smoke.

additional_notes: A serious, historical term (often associated with Nazi Germany and WWII), but it can also refer more generally to camps where large groups of people are detained. In Spanish you may also see the plural: "campos de concentración". Often used with "nazis": "campos de concentración nazis".
target_language_example: Durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial, millones de personas fueron enviadas a campos de concentración.
native_language_example: During World War II, millions of people were sent to concentration camps.

meaning: Side A (of a cassette, vinyl record, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to label the first side of physical media (especially cassette tapes and vinyl). It’s often paired with "cara B" (Side B). In everyday speech, you might also hear "lado A/lado B".
target_language_example: En la cara A está la canción más famosa.
native_language_example: On side A is the most famous song.

meaning: facing; in view of; with regard to (when thinking about or preparing for something).
additional_notes: A formal-ish prepositional phrase used to mean “looking toward” a situation or event, often when planning or considering what to do. It’s commonly followed by a noun (“cara a la reunión”) or an infinitive (“cara a mejorar”). Not to be confused with “cara a cara” (“face to face”).
target_language_example: Cara a la reunión de mañana, tenemos que preparar la presentación.
native_language_example: In view of tomorrow’s meeting, we have to prepare the presentation.

additional_notes: Used to say two people meet or talk directly, physically present (not online/over the phone). Often used with verbs like hablar, reunirse, verse, or estar: "hablar cara a cara". Also appears as "de cara a cara" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Prefiero hablar contigo cara a cara.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk to you face to face.

additional_notes: A science/physics term for the property of matter that can be positive or negative and causes electric forces. Common in school contexts and in phrases like "carga eléctrica positiva/negativa" and "unidad de carga eléctrica" (unit of electric charge).
target_language_example: El electrón tiene una carga eléctrica negativa.
native_language_example: The electron has a negative electric charge.

additional_notes: Common food term for meats like beef (carne de res), pork (cerdo), and lamb (cordero), often contrasted with "carne blanca" (white meat) like chicken. You’ll see it on menus and in dietary/health contexts (e.g., “reduce la carne roja”).
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de comer menos carne roja.
native_language_example: I’m trying to eat less red meat.

additional_notes: A written message expressing romantic love. You can also say "una carta de amor" (a love letter). Very close to English word-for-word: "carta" = letter, "de" = of, "amor" = love.
target_language_example: Le escribí una carta de amor.
native_language_example: I wrote him/her a love letter.

meaning: a sure thing; a safe bet.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an option or person that feels guaranteed to work out (the least risky choice). Literally it’s “safe card,” like a winning move you can rely on. Often used in everyday speech and in contexts like politics, sports, or planning.
target_language_example: Para ganar el partido, sacar a Marta fue nuestra carta segura.
native_language_example: To win the game, putting Marta in was our sure thing.

meaning: Chinese character (a symbol used in Chinese writing).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the written symbols of Chinese. The plural is often "caracteres chinos". Also used in computing/typography: e.g., "introducir caracteres chinos" (to enter Chinese characters).
target_language_example: No puedo leer este carácter chino.
native_language_example: I can’t read this Chinese character.

additional_notes: Literally “house of God.” Often used to refer to a church, especially in a religious context. In some regions it can also refer more generally to a place of worship. Capitalization varies; “Casa de Dios” may be part of an official church name.
target_language_example: Vamos a la casa de Dios el domingo.
native_language_example: We’re going to church on Sunday.

meaning: country house; farmhouse; cottage (in the countryside).
additional_notes: Refers to a house outside the city, typically used for weekends, vacations, or living in a rural area. In Spain it can be similar to a “country home” or “cottage”; in Latin America it may refer to a rural house or small farm home.
target_language_example: El fin de semana vamos a la casa de campo de mis abuelos.
native_language_example: This weekend we’re going to my grandparents’ country house.

additional_notes: Used to say that very few people (or practically no one) do something. It’s common with the verb in singular: "Casi nadie vino". You can also use it after prepositions: "No hablé con casi nadie".
target_language_example: En la reunión, casi nadie habló.
native_language_example: At the meeting, hardly anyone spoke.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to talk about how often something happens. It often goes before the main verb ("Casi nunca voy...") but can also come at the beginning for emphasis ("Casi nunca salgo...").
target_language_example: Casi nunca como comida rápida.
native_language_example: I almost never eat fast food.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very frequently, but not 100% of the time. It commonly goes before the verb ("Casi siempre voy...") or after it ("Voy casi siempre...").
target_language_example: Casi siempre desayuno en casa.
native_language_example: I almost always eat breakfast at home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or possible situation. It’s very common in formal signs and instructions: "En caso de incendio" (In case of fire). Also used in everyday speech before a clause: "En caso de que + subjunctive" (in case …), e.g., "En caso de que llueva". Without "en", "caso de" is less common by itself and often appears in set phrases like "en caso de".
target_language_example: En caso de emergencia, llama al 112.
native_language_example: In case of emergency, call 112.

meaning: a lost cause; a hopeless case.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is unlikely to improve or succeed. Often refers to a situation (“Es un caso perdido”) or a person when you think they won’t change (“Eres un caso perdido”). Not usually a medical “case” here—more like “hopeless.”
target_language_example: Lo intenté todo, pero este proyecto es un caso perdido.
native_language_example: I tried everything, but this project is a lost cause.

meaning: "in case" / "if" (used to talk about a possible situation).
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a condition or contingency, similar to "por si" or "si". Often followed by the subjunctive when referring to a possible or uncertain future situation: "Caso que llueva..." (= in case it rains). In some contexts you may also hear "en caso de (que)"; "en caso de" is usually followed by a noun or infinitive, while "en caso de que" is followed by a verb.
target_language_example: Caso que tengas dudas, llámame.
native_language_example: In case you have doubts, call me.

meaning: the vocative case (a grammatical form used to address someone directly).
additional_notes: A grammar term, not a phrase you normally use in everyday conversation. In Spanish, people often talk about “vocativo” to refer to direct address (e.g., “Juan,” “amigo,” “señor”), even though Spanish doesn’t have a distinct vocative case ending like some other languages. You might see it in textbooks, grammar explanations, or language classes.
target_language_example: En la frase «María, ven aquí», «María» funciona como vocativo (caso vocativo).
native_language_example: In the sentence “María, come here,” “María” functions as a vocative (vocative case).

additional_notes: A common bathroom item. Literally “brush of teeth,” but in English you say “toothbrush.” Often used with verbs like *usar* (to use), *comprar* (to buy), *necesitar* (to need), and *lavarse/cepillarse los dientes* (to brush one’s teeth).
target_language_example: No encuentro mi cepillo de dientes.
native_language_example: I can’t find my toothbrush.

additional_notes: As a preposition, it’s followed by a noun/pronoun: "cerca de la casa" (near the house), "cerca de mí" (near me). It’s also used for approximate amounts of time/quantity: "cerca de dos horas" (about two hours). Often similar to "near to" and "about" in English, depending on context.
target_language_example: Vivo cerca de la estación, a cerca de diez minutos a pie.
native_language_example: I live near the station, about a ten-minute walk away.

additional_notes: Common name for the animal that eats ants and termites. Literally “ant pig,” but it refers to an anteater (not a pig). In some regions you may also hear “oso hormiguero.”
target_language_example: Vimos un cerdo hormiguero en el zoológico.
native_language_example: We saw an anteater at the zoo.

additional_notes: A strong, insulting way to tell someone to be quiet. Literally means “to close the beak,” using pico (“beak”) to compare someone’s mouth to an animal’s. Commonly used as an imperative: “¡Cierra el pico!” Use with caution; in most situations, “cállate” (still rude) or “por favor, guarda silencio” (polite) are safer.
target_language_example: ¡Cierra el pico y déjame hablar!
native_language_example: Shut up and let me talk!

meaning: to close your mouth; (often) to shut up / be quiet.
additional_notes: Literally “to close the mouth.” It can be a neutral/physical action (“close your mouth”) or a strong command meaning “be quiet,” especially in the imperative: “¡Cierra la boca!” For a more polite option, use “Cierra la boca, por favor” or better “Por favor, cállate” (still direct) / “Por favor, guarda silencio” (more formal).
target_language_example: ¡Cierra la boca y escucha un momento!
native_language_example: Shut up and listen for a moment!

meaning: to be naive; to be easily fooled (“I wasn’t born yesterday”).
additional_notes: Literally “to suck your thumb/finger,” but it’s usually used in the negative to say you’re not naive: “No me chupo el dedo” = “I’m not that gullible.” You can also use it to say someone thinks others are naive: “¿Te crees que me chupo el dedo?” = “Do you think I’m stupid/that gullible?” Common in Spain and Latin America, and it sounds informal and slightly confrontational depending on tone.
target_language_example: ¿Te crees que me chupo el dedo? ¡Esa excusa no cuela!
native_language_example: Do you think I’m that gullible? That excuse doesn’t fly!

additional_notes: An idiomatic, colloquial way to say food is extremely tasty. Often used with "¡Para chuparse los dedos!" or "Está para chuparse los dedos." Literally it means “to suck your fingers,” but it’s usually meant as “finger-licking good.”
target_language_example: Este pastel está para chuparse los dedos.
native_language_example: This cake is finger-licking good.

additional_notes: Used for exact percentages (100%) and also to show strong agreement or certainty (like “totally” or “absolutely”). Often said as an emphatic reply: “¡Cien por ciento!” In math or formal contexts you may also see “el ciento por ciento.”
target_language_example: —¿Estás seguro de que quieres hacerlo? —Sí, cien por ciento.
native_language_example: —Are you sure you want to do it? —Yes, one hundred percent.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the genre of books, movies, TV shows, etc. Often appears as "película de ciencia ficción" (sci‑fi movie) or "novela de ciencia ficción" (sci‑fi novel). Common abbreviation: "ciencia ficción" → "sci‑fi" in English, but in Spanish you usually say the full phrase.
target_language_example: Me gustan las películas de ciencia ficción.
native_language_example: I like science fiction movies.

additional_notes: Used to talk about amounts (money, people, things). In Spanish, the comma and period are often reversed compared to English: 5,000 in English is usually written 5.000 in Spanish. With nouns, use plural: "cinco mil dólares", "cinco mil personas".
target_language_example: Tengo cinco mil dólares ahorrados.
native_language_example: I have five thousand dollars saved.

additional_notes: Commonly used for car safety. You’ll often hear it with verbs like ponerse/abrocharse (to put on/buckle up) and in commands: Ponte el cinturón de seguridad. It can also refer to a safety belt/harness in other contexts, but the most common meaning is the seat belt in a car.
target_language_example: Ponte el cinturón de seguridad, por favor.
native_language_example: Put on your seat belt, please.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree, confirm, or emphasize that something is obvious or certain. Often followed by a full clause (e.g., “claro que sí/no…”, “claro que puedo…”). In conversation it can sound more emphatic than just “claro.”
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Claro que sí.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: Used to give a strong, confident negative answer. Often responds to a yes/no question or to deny an assumption. Tone depends on context: it can be neutral or sound a bit emphatic/defensive if said sharply. Related: “¡Claro que sí!” = “Of course!”
target_language_example: —¿Vas a venir mañana? —Claro que no, tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course not, I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to agree enthusiastically or confirm something strongly. Very common in conversation; you can also say just “claro” as a shorter “sure/clearly.” Often responds to a question or request.
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —¡Claro que sí!
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course!

additional_notes: Refers to the social/economic group between the working class and the wealthy/upper class. Often used when talking about income, lifestyle, taxes, politics, and cost of living. Usually used with an article: "la clase media" (the middle class).
target_language_example: La clase media está preocupada por el costo de la vida.
native_language_example: The middle class is worried about the cost of living.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for a car powered by electricity (an EV). In Spain, “coche” is the usual word for “car”; in much of Latin America, “carro” or “auto” is more common. You may also hear “vehículo eléctrico” (more formal) or the abbreviation “EV” in technical contexts.
target_language_example: Quiero comprar un coche eléctrico para ahorrar en gasolina.
native_language_example: I want to buy an electric car to save on gas.

meaning: to pick up the phone; to answer the phone.
additional_notes: Used for physically picking up the handset or for answering when the phone rings. In much of Latin America, many speakers avoid "coger" because it can be a vulgar slang verb meaning "to have sex"; instead they often say "contestar el teléfono" or "agarrar el teléfono". In Spain, "coger" is common and neutral in this context.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes coger el teléfono? Está sonando.
native_language_example: Can you answer the phone? It’s ringing.

additional_notes: Common phrase for unhealthy, highly processed food (fast food, chips, candy, soda, etc.). It’s usually used in a negative/critical way. Also said as “comida chatarra” in many countries.
target_language_example: Intento no comer comida basura durante la semana.
native_language_example: I try not to eat junk food during the week.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about quick, inexpensive food from places like McDonald’s, Burger King, or a local burger/pizza place. Also used with verbs like comer (to eat) or pedir (to order): "comer comida rápida", "pedir comida rápida". Literally means "quick food."
target_language_example: No quiero comida rápida hoy; prefiero algo más saludable.
native_language_example: I don’t want fast food today; I’d rather have something healthier.

meaning: As if you own the place; very comfortably/confidently (often without permission).
additional_notes: Colloquial idiom used when someone moves around or behaves in a place as if it were their own—too familiar or overly comfortable, sometimes seen as rude or presumptuous. Often used with verbs like "andar" or "entrar" (e.g., "andar como Pedro por su casa").
target_language_example: Entró en la oficina y empezó a usar mi ordenador como Pedro por su casa.
native_language_example: He walked into the office and started using my computer as if he owned the place.

meaning: “so to speak”; “like, say,” (used to rephrase or give an example).
additional_notes: Used as a spoken filler to clarify what you mean, soften a statement, or introduce an approximation or example. Common in conversation: “Es, como decir, …” = “It’s, so to speak, …”. Not the same as the question “¿cómo decir…?” (“how do you say…?”).
target_language_example: Es, como decir, el jefe del grupo.
native_language_example: He’s, so to speak, the leader of the group.

meaning: (look) exactly alike; like two peas in a pod.
additional_notes: Used to say two people (often siblings) look extremely similar. It can describe appearance, and sometimes very similar behavior. Literally “like two drops of water,” which is a natural Spanish comparison.
target_language_example: Los gemelos son como dos gotas de agua.
native_language_example: The twins look exactly alike.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done the correct/appropriate way, often implying it should be done carefully or according to rules or good manners. Common with verbs like hacer (to do), estar (to be), tratar (to treat), vestir (to dress), and comportarse (to behave). Can also be used to criticize: No lo hiciste como es debido (“You didn’t do it properly”).
target_language_example: Hay que hacer el trabajo como es debido.
native_language_example: You have to do the job properly.

meaning: Out of place; uncomfortable in an unfamiliar situation.
additional_notes: An idiomatic comparison used to describe someone who feels awkward, uneasy, or doesn’t fit in (for example, in a new group or environment). It’s often used with verbs like "estar" or "sentirse": "Me siento/estoy como gallina en corral ajeno". Similar idea: "como pez fuera del agua" (“like a fish out of water”).
target_language_example: En la reunión con tanta gente desconocida, me sentía como gallina en corral ajeno.
native_language_example: At the meeting with so many strangers, I felt out of place.

additional_notes: Uses the formal usted form (guste, from gustar). Common in customer service or polite conversation to let someone choose: “Como guste” = “Whatever you prefer.” You can also hear “como gustes” (informal tú) or “como guste(n)” depending on who is being addressed.
target_language_example: ¿En mesa o para llevar? — Como guste.
native_language_example: For here or to go? — However you prefer.

como la copa de un pino

target_language_multi_word_term: como la copa de un pino
meaning: huge; very obvious (often about something negative).
additional_notes: Colloquial idiom used to intensify a noun, especially something seen as clearly wrong or very big (e.g., un error, una mentira, una injusticia). It usually comes after the noun: “un error como la copa de un pino.” Literally “like the top of a pine tree,” but it means “a massive/obvious one,” similar to “as big as a house.”
target_language_example: Eso es un error como la copa de un pino.
native_language_example: That’s a huge mistake.

meaning: like the roses themselves; like the very roses.
additional_notes: A poetic/emphatic comparison (simile). "Las propias" adds emphasis, similar to "the very" in English. It’s often used to highlight beauty, redness, freshness, or delicacy by comparing something directly to roses.
target_language_example: Sus mejillas estaban rojas, como las propias rosas.
native_language_example: Her cheeks were red, like the roses themselves.

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit or maximum amount (time, quantity, price, etc.). Often placed after the number/amount it limits. Similar to "como máximo".
target_language_example: Tardaré una hora como mucho.
native_language_example: It will take me an hour at most.

meaning: at the latest; no later than.
additional_notes: Used to give a latest possible time or deadline. It often follows a time expression: "a las 5, como muy tarde" (5 o’clock at the latest). Also common with "para" + time: "para mañana, como muy tarde" (by tomorrow at the latest).
target_language_example: Te lo envío mañana, como muy tarde.
native_language_example: I’ll send it to you tomorrow at the latest.

additional_notes: Used to express a minimum requirement or lower bound (quantity, time, effort, etc.). Often placed before a number or amount: “como mínimo, 10 minutos.” Similar to “por lo menos.”
target_language_example: Necesito como mínimo dos días para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: I need at least two days to finish the project.

meaning: Like new; as good as new.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that looks or works as if it were new (often after being repaired, cleaned, or not used much). It can also be used about a person feeling refreshed after resting. Usually follows the noun: “un teléfono como nuevo.”
target_language_example: Después de arreglarlo, mi coche quedó como nuevo.
native_language_example: After fixing it, my car was like new.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is happening to an extreme degree, more than ever in the past. Often appears after a verb (trabajar, estudiar, llover, etc.). Sometimes you’ll also hear it with a comparison word: “más que nunca” (“more than ever”).
target_language_example: Estoy trabajando como nunca para terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m working like never before to finish the project on time.

meaning: “enough to” / “to the point of” (usually before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express that something is sufficient to cause a result or reach a situation. It’s often followed by an infinitive: “como para + infinitive” (e.g., “como para entenderlo”). Common in both speech and writing. Note: not the same as “cómo” (with accent) used in questions.
target_language_example: Hace mucho frío, como para quedarse en casa.
native_language_example: It’s very cold—cold enough to stay at home.

additional_notes: Common idiom used with verbs like estar or sentirse to say someone feels perfectly at ease in a situation or place: “Me siento como pez en el agua aquí.” It can also describe being naturally good at something (because you feel so comfortable doing it).
target_language_example: En mi nuevo trabajo me siento como pez en el agua.
native_language_example: In my new job I feel very comfortable (in my element).

additional_notes: Used to point out evidence or make something obvious to the listener. Often followed by an explanation: “Como puedes ver, …” You can also hear it with accents: “Como puedes ver” or “Como puedes ver,” and in more formal contexts you might use “Como puede ver” (usted).
target_language_example: Como puedes ver, hoy hace mucho frío.
native_language_example: As you can see, it’s very cold today.

meaning: “however you want / as you like”; also “anyway” (in some contexts).
additional_notes: Often used to give someone freedom of choice: "Hazlo como quieras" = “Do it however you want.” It can also mean “anyway / in any case” when dismissing an option or moving on: "Como quiera, ya es tarde" = “Anyway, it’s already late.”
target_language_example: Hazlo como quieras; a mí me da igual.
native_language_example: Do it however you want; I don’t mind.

meaning: since/because (formal); also “however / in any case” depending on context.
additional_notes: This is a fairly formal connector, common in writing. It often appears as one word: “comoquiera que”. Most often it introduces a reason (“since/because…”). In other contexts it can be concessive or general (“however / in any case…”), so the best translation depends on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Como quiera que no tengo tiempo, me voy.
native_language_example: Since I don’t have time, I’m leaving.

meaning: “however you want” / “whatever you prefer” (also: “fine, suit yourself”).
additional_notes: Used to let someone choose the way to do something: “Do it however you want.” Depending on tone, it can sound neutral and flexible, or slightly annoyed/dismissive (“Fine, suit yourself”). Uses the present subjunctive of querer: quieras (tú).
target_language_example: Podemos ir en coche o en metro, como quieras.
native_language_example: We can go by car or by subway—whatever you prefer.

additional_notes: Used to express a consequence of something mentioned before. Often followed by “de” when you name the cause: “como resultado de…” (“as a result of…”). Common in writing and formal speech, but also fine in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Hubo mucho tráfico; como resultado, llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: There was a lot of traffic; as a result, we arrived late.

meaning: “as a result of” / “as a consequence of.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause or reason for something. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive: como resultado de la lluvia (as a result of the rain), como resultado de no estudiar (as a result of not studying). Similar to “a causa de” and “debido a,” and it’s common in more formal or neutral writing/speech.
target_language_example: Como resultado de la tormenta, no hubo clases hoy.
native_language_example: As a result of the storm, there were no classes today.

additional_notes: Often used to dismiss details or show indifference (similar to “whatever”), or to move on in the conversation (“anyway”). It can sound rude if said with a sharp tone. Also used in phrases like "como sea, ..." = "anyway, ..." and "como sea" = "either way" depending on context.
target_language_example: Como sea, ya es tarde. Vámonos.
native_language_example: Anyway, it’s already late. Let’s go.

meaning: “as if” / “like” (introduces an unreal or hypothetical comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined or unreal situation. It’s very commonly followed by the imperfect subjunctive: como si fuera / tuviera / pudiera (“as if I/he were / had / could”). In casual speech you may hear indicative sometimes, but the standard beginner pattern is: como si + imperfect subjunctive.
target_language_example: Me habla como si fuera mi jefe.
native_language_example: He talks to me as if he were my boss.

meaning: “so to speak”; “as if we could say” (used to clarify or soften what you’re saying).
additional_notes: Used when you’re giving an approximate description, comparing something, or saying something in a less direct way—similar to “kind of,” “let’s say,” or “so to speak” in English. Often introduces an explanation or a rephrasing: “como si dijéramos, X…”. The verb is in the imperfect subjunctive (dijéramos), and in conversation you’ll also hear “como si dijera(s)” or “como si dijéramos.”
target_language_example: Es, como si dijéramos, el motor del equipo.
native_language_example: It’s, so to speak, the engine of the team.

meaning: “as if nothing happened” / “like it’s no big deal.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone acts normally or doesn’t show concern after something surprising, embarrassing, or serious. Often implies indifference or pretending nothing happened. You can also use it after a clause: “como si nada hubiera pasado” (“as if nothing had happened”).
target_language_example: Se cayó delante de todos y siguió caminando como si nada.
native_language_example: He fell in front of everyone and kept walking as if nothing happened.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens the usual way or as expected. Common in casual conversation, and it can be neutral or slightly ironic depending on tone. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Todo está igual, como siempre.
native_language_example: Everything is the same, as always.

additional_notes: Used after saying something surprising or hard to believe to emphasize that you mean it literally (there’s no hidden meaning). Often appears as “Tal como suena” (“exactly as it sounds”). In writing, you may also see it as “como suena” or “como suena,” depending on context.
target_language_example: —¿De verdad te pagaron por viajar? —Sí, como suena.
native_language_example: —Did they really pay you to travel? —Yes, just like it sounds.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something in its role, category, or exact sense (“as such”), often to clarify a distinction. Common in more formal explanations or writing. It can also mean “in itself” when emphasizing the thing itself rather than its effects or consequences.
target_language_example: No tengo nada en contra del trabajo como tal, sino del horario.
native_language_example: I have nothing against the job as such, but rather the schedule.

meaning: “How are you?” (very informal spelling of “¿Cómo estás?”).
additional_notes: Common in texting/chat and casual speech as a shortened form of “¿Cómo estás?”. In standard writing you should use accents and punctuation: “¿Cómo estás?”. You can reply with “Bien, ¿y tú?” (Good, and you?).
target_language_example:
—Ey, ¿como tas?
—Bien, ¿y tú?
native_language_example:
—Hey, how are you?
—Good, and you?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize speed (how quickly someone moves or how quickly something happens). Often appears with verbs like correr (to run), ir (to go), salir (to leave), and pasar (to pass by).
target_language_example: Salió como un rayo cuando oyó su nombre.
native_language_example: He left like lightning when he heard his name.

meaning: all together; united as one (in agreement or action).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a group acts or reacts in total unity, at the same time, or with the same opinion. Often appears with verbs like levantarse (to rise), apoyar (to support), responder (to respond), votar (to vote), or protestar (to protest). It’s a fixed expression; you can also hear the feminine form “como una sola mujer,” though “como un solo hombre” is common as a generic phrase.
target_language_example: El público se levantó como un solo hombre y aplaudió.
native_language_example: The audience stood up all together and applauded.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "estar" or "volverse" to describe someone behaving in an irrational or eccentric way. It’s colloquial and can be insulting, so use it carefully (mainly with friends or humor). Often appears as "estar como una cabra".
target_language_example: Mi hermano está como una cabra: quiere ir en bici en plena tormenta.
native_language_example: My brother is crazy: he wants to ride his bike right in the middle of a storm.

meaning: like an arrow; very fast/straight (often: “like a shot”).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to emphasize speed or directness. Common with “ir,” “salir,” or “pasar” (e.g., “ir como una flecha” = to go very fast).
target_language_example: Cuando empezó la carrera, salió como una flecha.
native_language_example: When the race started, he took off like a shot.

additional_notes: Common in Latin America. In Spain, people more often say “ordenador portátil” or simply “portátil”. You can also say “una laptop” in many places. Used with gender: “la computadora portátil”.
target_language_example: Necesito mi computadora portátil para la clase.
native_language_example: I need my laptop for class.

meaning: “with God”; (as a goodbye) “God be with you.”
additional_notes: Literally means “with God.” It can be used as a religious/formal-sounding goodbye or blessing, similar to “go with God” or “God be with you.” You may also see it in set phrases like “Que vayas con Dios” (“May you go with God”).
target_language_example: Adiós, y que vayas con Dios.
native_language_example: Goodbye, and may God be with you.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a loving/caring way, or as a warm closing in messages (like signing a note or card). Similar closings include "Con cariño" and "Con mucho amor" (stronger).
target_language_example: Te lo preparo con amor.
native_language_example: I’ll make it for you with love.

meaning: charged to; billed to; debited from (an account/budget).
additional_notes: Used in formal or business contexts to say that an expense will be paid using a particular account, budget, card, or person/entity’s funds. Often followed by a noun or account name: “con cargo a la cuenta…”, “con cargo a la tarjeta…”, “con cargo al presupuesto…”. Similar idea to “a cargo de” (at the expense of / paid by), but “con cargo a” is especially common in accounting and invoicing language.
target_language_example: El importe se cargará con cargo a la tarjeta que indiques.
native_language_example: The amount will be charged to the card you specify.

additional_notes: Used to show warmth, care, or fondness. Common in messages and sign-offs (similar to “with love” / “warmly”), and also to describe how you do something (e.g., say something kindly, prepare something with care).
target_language_example: Te lo digo con cariño: creo que deberías descansar.
native_language_example: I’m telling you this with affection: I think you should rest.

additional_notes: A polite, formal phrase used to introduce disagreement, criticism, or correction while showing respect (often in conversations, meetings, or written arguments). It can sometimes sound a bit sharp or ironic depending on tone.
target_language_example: Con el debido respeto, creo que esa decisión no es la mejor opción.
native_language_example: With all due respect, I think that decision isn’t the best option.

meaning: in order to; for the purpose of.
additional_notes: A formal connector used to express purpose. It is followed by an infinitive (con el fin de + verb), and it’s common in writing, announcements, and official speech. In everyday conversation, people often use “para” instead.
target_language_example: Con el fin de reducir el ruido, cerramos las ventanas.
native_language_example: In order to reduce the noise, we closed the windows.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens gradually or changes as time passes. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence as a time reference (Con el tiempo, ...). In some contexts it can be close to “eventually.”
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, vas a hablar español mejor.
native_language_example: Over time, you’re going to speak Spanish better.

meaning: with enthusiasm; really wanting to (do something).
additional_notes: Often used after a verb to say you do something eagerly/with energy: "estudiar con ganas" (study hard/with enthusiasm). With "tener" it expresses strong desire: "tener ganas de + infinitive" = to feel like/want to do something (e.g., "Tengo ganas de comer"). It can also describe effort/intensity, similar to "hard" or "properly" in context.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a estudiar con ganas porque tengo ganas de aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to study hard/with enthusiasm because I really want to pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to accept a request politely (like “sure, gladly”) or to respond to thanks, similar to “you’re welcome”/“my pleasure.” Common in many Spanish-speaking countries; in Spain you may also hear “de nada” or “encantado/a.”
target_language_example: —Gracias por tu ayuda. —Con gusto.
native_language_example: —Thanks for your help. —My pleasure.

meaning: desperate; under intense pressure (often because of money or time).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning you’re in a very difficult situation with no room to breathe—e.g., because of debt, deadlines, or urgent problems. Also common as "tener la soga al cuello" (to be in that situation).
target_language_example: Con tantas deudas, estoy con la soga al cuello.
native_language_example: With so many debts, I’m desperate / under a lot of pressure.

additional_notes: Often used in set expressions about surviving or dying. Common patterns: “pagar con la vida” (to pay with your life), “salir con la vida” (to get out alive), “escapar con vida” is more common than “con la vida.” The article “la” usually refers to a specific life (someone’s life), not “life” in general.
target_language_example: Pagó con la vida su error.
native_language_example: He paid for his mistake with his life.

meaning: with your hands crossed/folded; (figuratively) doing nothing.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone standing or waiting with their hands crossed (often in front of the body). It can also be used figuratively to mean “not taking action” or “just standing by.” A more common variant is “con los brazos cruzados” (“with arms crossed”), especially for the figurative meaning.
target_language_example: No puedo quedarme con las manos cruzadas mientras ellos necesitan ayuda.
native_language_example: I can't just stand by and do nothing while they need help.

con las manos en la masa

target_language_multi_word_term: con las manos en la masa
additional_notes: Idiom used when someone is discovered doing something (usually something wrong) at that exact moment. Literally “with (your) hands in the dough,” like being caught while making something—so you can’t deny it. Often used with verbs like "pillar" or "sorprender": "Lo pillaron con las manos en la masa."
target_language_example: La policía lo encontró con las manos en la masa, robando en la tienda.
native_language_example: The police found him red-handed, stealing in the store.

additional_notes: Used when someone arrives or goes somewhere without carrying or bringing anything (often a gift, food, or something requested). It can be literal (not holding anything) or idiomatic (showing up without a contribution).
target_language_example: No quiero ir a la fiesta con las manos vacías.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go to the party empty-handed.

additional_notes: Used to describe drinks (especially coffee or tea) that include milk. Common in cafés when ordering: "Un café con leche, por favor." You can swap in other items: "té con leche" (tea with milk).
target_language_example: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with milk, please.

meaning: with (your) arms crossed; doing nothing / not helping.
additional_notes: Literally describes having your arms crossed. Often used figuratively to criticize someone for staying passive and not taking action: "No te quedes con los brazos cruzados" = “Don’t just stand there / don’t do nothing.”
target_language_example: No te quedes con los brazos cruzados; ven a ayudarme.
native_language_example: Don’t just stand there with your arms crossed; come help me.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as an intensifier meaning “by far,” especially with superlatives or comparisons: “con mucho, el mejor/la mejor” (“by far the best”). It can also mean “with a lot of” before a noun: “con mucho esfuerzo” (“with a lot of effort”). Often appears set off by commas: “con mucho, ...”
target_language_example: Este es, con mucho, el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This is by far the best restaurant in the city.
