additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to say someone/something can be trusted (often with "ser" or "no ser"). Common with people, businesses, or products: "No es de fiar" = "He/It can’t be trusted." Related idea: "fiar" can mean "to trust" or "to sell on credit," but "de fiar" is about reliability/trustworthiness.
target_language_example: No creo que sea de fiar.
native_language_example: I don’t think he’s trustworthy.

additional_notes: Commonly used with nouns to describe something that is behind or underlying something else (e.g., "ruido de fondo" = background noise, "música de fondo" = background music). Also used in expressions like "a fondo" / "de fondo" to mean doing something thoroughly or in depth (the exact phrasing varies by region and context).
target_language_example: Puse música de fondo mientras estudiaba.
native_language_example: I put on background music while I studied.

meaning: “in a … way/manner” (used to describe how something is done).
additional_notes: Usually followed by an adjective or adverbial phrase: de forma rápida (quickly), de forma diferente (differently), de forma clara (clearly), de forma sencilla (in a simple way). It’s a common, slightly formal alternative to “de manera”.
target_language_example: Necesito que lo expliques de forma sencilla.
native_language_example: I need you to explain it in a simple way.

additional_notes: Often used to describe direction or position (similar to “straight ahead / in front”). It can also describe speaking or facing directly (“face-to-face,” “head-on”): “de frente a” = “facing / opposite.” Common with verbs like ir, mirar, ponerse, estar.
target_language_example: Sigue de frente y gira a la izquierda en la esquina.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and turn left at the corner.

meaning: in formal wear; dressed up (in one’s finest).
additional_notes: Used to describe clothing or how someone is dressed for a special, formal occasion. Common with verbs like "ir" or "vestirse" ("ir de gala" = to go dressed formally) and after a noun: "vestido de gala" (evening gown/formal dress), "traje de gala" (formal suit/ceremonial uniform).
target_language_example: Para la boda, todos iremos de gala.
native_language_example: For the wedding, we’ll all be dressed in formal wear.

meaning: person to person; as equals (speaking frankly).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a direct, honest conversation, emphasizing sincerity and equality ("no formalities" / "let’s be real"). Often appears with verbs like hablar (to talk), decir (to say), or tratar (to treat): “Hablemos de gente a gente…”.
target_language_example: De gente a gente, necesito que me digas la verdad.
native_language_example: Person to person, I need you to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens abruptly or unexpectedly. Often used with verbs like "pasar" (to happen), "llegar" (to arrive), "cambiar" (to change), or with "de golpe y porrazo" for extra emphasis. Closely related in meaning to "de repente" and "de pronto."
target_language_example: De golpe, se fue la luz.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, the power went out.

additional_notes: Colloquial expression used to emphasize that something happens unexpectedly and quickly (often with a sense of surprise or a sudden change). It’s commonly placed at the beginning of the sentence followed by a comma. Similar to: "de repente", "de pronto", "de buenas a primeras".
target_language_example: De golpe y porrazo, se fue sin decir nada.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, he left without saying anything.

additional_notes: Used to say something costs nothing or is included at no extra cost (often in offers, tickets, apps, trials, etc.). Common in expressions like "entrada de gracia" (free admission) or "periodo/mes de gracia" (grace period/free trial period).
target_language_example: La primera clase es de gracia.
native_language_example: The first class is free.

meaning: willingly or by force; whether you like it or not.
additional_notes: A fixed, fairly formal/old-fashioned expression meaning something will happen voluntarily or, if necessary, by force. Often used to emphasize that someone has no real choice (sometimes with a threatening tone).
target_language_example: De grado o por fuerza, tendrás que devolver el dinero.
native_language_example: Whether you like it or not, you’ll have to return the money.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is working a shift and responsible/available (common for doctors, nurses, police, security, etc.). Often with estar: "Estoy de guardia". Also used for services that are open/available after hours: "farmacia de guardia" (pharmacy on duty).
target_language_example: El médico está de guardia esta noche.
native_language_example: The doctor is on call tonight.

additional_notes: Used to add emphasis, correct a misunderstanding, or introduce information that supports what you just said. Common in both speech and writing. Often placed at the start of a sentence (De hecho, ...), but it can also appear mid-sentence.
target_language_example: De hecho, no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe what something is made of: "una puerta de hierro" (an iron door). In common figurative phrases it means "iron/strong" in character or willpower, e.g., "voluntad de hierro" (iron will) or "salud de hierro" (very robust health).
target_language_example: Tiene una voluntad de hierro.
native_language_example: He/She has an iron will.

meaning: very rarely; once in a blue moon.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say something happens only occasionally or at long intervals. It’s common in everyday speech (especially in Spain). You can use it after the verb or at the end of the sentence: “Viene de higos a brevas.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos de higos a brevas, pero siempre lo pasamos bien.
native_language_example: We see each other once in a blue moon, but we always have a good time.

meaning: "man to man"; speaking frankly and directly (one-on-one).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a serious, honest, direct conversation between two people, often in private. It emphasizes sincerity and “no nonsense.” It’s gendered in wording (hombre), so it can sound old-fashioned or masculine, but it may still be used even if the speakers aren’t both men.
target_language_example: Hablemos de hombre a hombre: no puedo seguir así.
native_language_example: Let’s talk man to man: I can’t keep going like this.

additional_notes: Used to stress that two people (or groups) are dealing with each other with the same status and respect—no hierarchy or superiority. Common with verbs like hablar (to talk), tratar (to treat/deal with), and negociar (to negotiate): hablar/tratar/negociar de igual a igual.
target_language_example: Quiero hablar contigo de igual a igual.
native_language_example: I want to talk to you as an equal.

additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to say something happens without delay. It often goes after the verb ("Vuelvo de inmediato"), but can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis ("De inmediato, llamé...").
target_language_example: Te llamo de inmediato.
native_language_example: I’ll call you right away.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: de + la. Common for possession/relationships ("la puerta de la casa" = "the door of the house"), origin ("vengo de la escuela" = "I come from the school"), and describing something ("un vaso de la cocina" = "a glass from the kitchen"). Compare: de + el → del (not *de el*).
target_language_example: La llave es de la casa.
native_language_example: The key is for the house.

additional_notes: Used in restaurants, bars, and shops to describe something that is a house specialty or made in-house (e.g., salsa, wine, dessert). It often implies “our own” or “homemade,” depending on context. Common pattern: "[noun] de la casa" ("vino de la casa", "salsa de la casa").
target_language_example: ¿Tienen vino de la casa?
native_language_example: Do you have house wine?

meaning: hand in hand; together (in close connection).
additional_notes: Most literally means “of the hand,” and is commonly used as "ir de la mano" (“to go hand in hand”), meaning two things happen together or are closely linked. It can be physical (“walking hand in hand”) or figurative (“one thing goes with another”).
target_language_example: La educación y la salud van de la mano.
native_language_example: Education and health go hand in hand.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is done similarly to something else, or to add a similar point (like “likewise”). Often followed by “que” + a clause (e.g., “de la misma manera que…” = “in the same way that…”).
target_language_example: De la misma manera que tú, yo quiero aprender español.
native_language_example: In the same way as you, I want to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens unexpectedly, without warning or an obvious cause. Often with verbs like aparecer (to appear), salir (to come out), and surgir (to arise). It can also describe someone starting from nothing (e.g., crear algo de la nada = create something from nothing), but most commonly it’s about something surprising happening.
target_language_example: De la nada, empezó a llover muy fuerte.
native_language_example: Out of nowhere, it started raining really hard.

de la noche a la mañana

target_language_multi_word_term: de la noche a la mañana
meaning: overnight; suddenly (from one day to the next).
additional_notes: Used to say something changes very quickly and unexpectedly, without a gradual process. Often used with verbs like cambiar (to change), pasar (to happen), or volverse (to become): “cambiar de la noche a la mañana.” It’s an idiomatic expression, not meant literally.
target_language_example: Todo cambió de la noche a la mañana.
native_language_example: Everything changed overnight.

meaning: from the earth/ground; of the land.
additional_notes: Used to indicate origin or source (e.g., something that comes from the ground) or that something belongs to the land/earth. Common in phrases like "productos de la tierra" (local/land-grown products) and "delante de la tierra" isn’t typical—note the article changes: "de la" (feminine singular: la tierra) and sometimes contracts to "del" with masculine nouns (not here).
target_language_example: Estos tomates son de la tierra.
native_language_example: These tomatoes are from the land (locally grown).

additional_notes: Used to describe position or movement to the side (ponerse de lado = turn sideways/lie on your side). Also used figuratively to mean “aside” or “left out” (dejar de lado = set aside/leave out). Often follows the verb: mirar de lado (look sideways), estar de lado (be to the side).
target_language_example: Deja el teléfono de lado y presta atención.
native_language_example: Put your phone aside and pay attention.

meaning: from end to end; all the way along (something long).
additional_notes: Used to say something extends the full length of a long object or place (a street, hallway, beach, river, etc.). It can describe location or movement along that whole length. It’s not very common in everyday conversation; more common alternatives are “de punta a punta” or “de un extremo a otro.”
target_language_example: Había banderas de largo a largo de la avenida.
native_language_example: There were flags from end to end along the avenue.

meaning: (informal) darn / stupid / annoying (used to complain or emphasize).
additional_notes: A colloquial expression added after a noun (or sometimes a situation) to show irritation, frustration, or emphasis—similar to “this darn/stupid/annoying …”. Often translates better by tone than literally (literally: “of the noses”). It can sound rude depending on context.
target_language_example: No encuentro las llaves de las narices.
native_language_example: I can’t find these darn keys.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is a perfect, typical, or “textbook” example of it. Often appears in phrases like “un error de libro” (a textbook mistake) or “una definición de libro” (a textbook definition).
target_language_example: Eso fue un error de libro.
native_language_example: That was a textbook mistake.

meaning: across the plains; from one flat area to another.
additional_notes: A descriptive (often literary) way to talk about traveling over flat land (el llano/la llanura). In everyday speech you’re more likely to hear something like “por el llano” or “por la llanura.” The word “llano” can also mean “plain/straightforward” in other contexts (e.g., “hablar llano” = to speak plainly), but in this phrase it usually refers to terrain.
target_language_example: Caminamos de llano en llano hasta llegar al río.
native_language_example: We walked across the plains until we reached the river.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the alternative outcome if something doesn’t happen (often a warning about a consequence). It’s commonly set off with a comma: “..., de lo contrario, ...”. Similar to “si no” (“if not”), but “de lo contrario” often sounds a bit more formal and emphasizes the consequence.
target_language_example: Tienes que estudiar; de lo contrario, no aprobarás el examen.
native_language_example: You have to study; otherwise, you won’t pass the exam.

meaning: one of the best; among the best.
additional_notes: Used to praise something as top quality or a favorite. Often appears with verbs like ser/estar ("Es de lo mejor"), or after nouns ("una película de lo mejor"). The "lo" turns "mejor" into an abstract idea: "the best (thing)".
target_language_example: Este restaurante es de lo mejor que hay en la ciudad.
native_language_example: This restaurant is one of the best there is in the city.

additional_notes: Used to intensify an adjective: “Es de lo más interesante” = “It’s really interesting / one of the most interesting.” It often follows the verb (ser/estar/fue) and agrees in gender/number with the adjective that comes after: “de lo más divertido/divertida/divertidos/divertidas.”
target_language_example: La película fue de lo más entretenida.
native_language_example: The movie was really entertaining.

additional_notes: Most often used after comparatives like más/menos/mejor/peor to mean “than”: *más de lo que…* = “more than…”. It can also mean “of what/that which” when referring back to something: *hablar de lo que pasó* = “to talk about what happened.”
target_language_example: Tengo más trabajo de lo que pensaba.
native_language_example: I have more work than I thought.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to emphasize that something is extremely difficult, intense, impressive, or unreasonable. Common in everyday speech: "un calor de locos" (crazy heat), "un tráfico de locos" (insane traffic). Literally means "of crazy people," but it functions like "insane/crazy" in English.
target_language_example: Hace un calor de locos hoy.
native_language_example: It’s insanely hot today.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as luxurious or high-end: "un hotel de lujo" (a luxury hotel). In casual speech it can also mean something is really good: "¡De lujo!" = “Awesome!”/“Great!”.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos en un hotel de lujo.
native_language_example: We stayed in a luxury hotel.

meaning: in mourning; wearing mourning (after someone dies).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar/ir/vestir: "estar de luto" (to be in mourning), "ir de luto" (to be dressed in mourning), "vestir de luto" (to wear mourning clothes). Traditionally it implies black clothing, but it can also refer more generally to the mourning period.
target_language_example: Desde que murió su abuela, está de luto.
native_language_example: Since his grandmother died, he’s in mourning.

meaning: very early in the morning; at dawn (often: in the middle of the night).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the earliest hours of the day, typically after midnight and before sunrise (e.g., 2–6 a.m.). Common with verbs like salir (to go out/leave), volver (to come back), llegar (to arrive), and levantarse (to get up). It often implies it’s unusually early/late: staying out or waking up at an inconvenient hour.
target_language_example: Llegué a casa de madrugada.
native_language_example: I got home in the early hours of the morning.

meaning: getting worse and worse; from bad to worse.
additional_notes: Used to say a situation is deteriorating over time. Often goes with verbs like "ir" or "poner(se)": "todo va de mal en peor" (everything is going from bad to worse), "la situación se pone de mal en peor" (the situation gets worse and worse).
target_language_example: Desde que empezó la semana, todo ha ido de mal en peor.
native_language_example: Since the week started, everything has gone from bad to worse.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something without wanting to, often with annoyance or lack of enthusiasm. Common with verbs like aceptar (to accept), ir (to go), hacer (to do), or trabajar (to work). Similar to "a regañadientes" (more like "grudgingly").
target_language_example: Fue a la reunión de mala gana.
native_language_example: He went to the meeting reluctantly.

meaning: unlucky; having bad luck (also: in a bad mood).
additional_notes: Informal. Commonly used to say something happened because of bad luck (often with estar: "estar de malas" = to be having bad luck / to be in a bad mood). It can also describe a streak of misfortune: "Ando de malas". Not a literal translation into a fixed English phrase.
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de malas: perdí el autobús y se me cayó el café.
native_language_example: Today I’m unlucky: I missed the bus and I dropped my coffee.

meaning: from hand to hand; passed from person to person.
additional_notes: Used when something physically (a book, money, a note) or figuratively (news, a rumor) is passed along among several people, often without staying long with any one person.
target_language_example: El libro pasó de mano en mano durante la clase.
native_language_example: The book was passed from hand to hand during class.

additional_notes: Used to say something went very well or that you’re doing very well. Common after verbs like "estar" or "salir" (e.g., "Está de maravilla", "Salió de maravilla"). It can also describe something as excellent ("un plan de maravilla"), though that use is less common than the adverbial one.
target_language_example: ¡La fiesta salió de maravilla!
native_language_example: The party turned out great!

additional_notes: Used to say something is going very well or that you feel great. Common with verbs like "estar" (to be) and "ir" (to go): "Estoy de maravillas" = "I’m feeling great," "Me va de maravillas" = "It’s going great for me." It’s upbeat and conversational, and you can also use it to describe how something works or turned out: "Funciona de maravillas" = "It works wonderfully."
target_language_example: Todo salió de maravillas.
native_language_example: Everything turned out wonderfully.

meaning: in the morning; morning (used to describe something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the time period in the morning (often after a preposition like por: por la mañana = in the morning), or to describe something as happening/being scheduled for the morning (e.g., el turno de mañana = the morning shift). Don’t confuse with mañana by itself, which can mean “tomorrow” or “morning” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tengo clase de mañana, así que me levanto temprano.
native_language_example: I have a morning class, so I get up early.

meaning: out of the corner of (one’s) eye; with a sideways/suspicious glance.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like mirar/ver ("to look/see") to mean you’re not looking directly, often because you’re suspicious, annoyed, or trying not to be obvious. Common pattern: "mirar a alguien/algo de medio ojo".
target_language_example: Lo miró de medio ojo y siguió caminando.
native_language_example: She looked at him out of the corner of her eye and kept walking.

additional_notes: Used to say you know or can say/do something without looking at notes or reading. Common with verbs like saber, aprender, recitar: “saber algo de memoria” (to know something by heart). Don’t confuse with “en memoria de” (“in memory of”).
target_language_example: Me sé el poema de memoria.
native_language_example: I know the poem by heart.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is not real or is pretend: "un arma de mentira" (a fake gun), "una sonrisa de mentira" (a fake smile). It can mean either "fake" (an imitation) or "pretend" (for play), depending on context. Opposite: "de verdad" (real).
target_language_example: Es un anillo de mentira; no es de oro.
native_language_example: It’s a fake ring; it’s not gold.

meaning: “of my life.” (often: “ever” / “in my life” for emphasis)
additional_notes: Literally “of my life.” It’s commonly used after a superlative or with emotion to emphasize that something is the most/least you’ve experienced or that it has never happened to you before. Often appears in phrases like “el mejor/peor ___ de mi vida” (“the best/worst ___ of my life”) or “nunca/jamás en/de mi vida” (“never in my life”).
target_language_example: Es el mejor viaje de mi vida.
native_language_example: It’s the best trip of my life.

additional_notes: Literally means “of fear.” Commonly used after a noun or with ser/estar to describe something that causes fear (una película de miedo = a scary movie). In informal speech it can also mean something is impressively good (¡Está de miedo! = It’s awesome!). Context and tone usually make the meaning clear.
target_language_example: La película estuvo de miedo, pero me encantó.
native_language_example: The movie was scary, but I loved it.

additional_notes: A strong, insulting phrase used after a noun to say something is terrible or worthless: "un trabajo de mierda" (a shitty job), "este clima de mierda" (this shitty weather). It’s common in casual speech but very offensive/vulgar—avoid in polite situations. It doesn’t change for gender/number because it’s a fixed phrase with "de".
target_language_example: Este servicio es de mierda.
native_language_example: This service is shitty.

meaning: by a miracle; barely; luckily (at the last moment).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened with great luck, difficulty, or just in time (often after almost not happening). Common with verbs like llegar (to arrive), salvarse (to get away), and aprobar (to pass). Often translated naturally as “just barely” or “only by luck,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Llegué de milagro; el tren estaba a punto de salir.
native_language_example: I made it just barely; the train was about to leave.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is currently popular or trendy: "ropa de moda" (fashionable clothes). With "estar" it means "to be in fashion": "Eso está de moda" (That’s in fashion). Not usually translated word-for-word as "of fashion" in natural English.
target_language_example: Ese color está de moda este año.
native_language_example: That color is in style this year.

meaning: "so" / "so that" (as a result; in order that).
additional_notes: Used to connect two clauses. With the indicative, it often means “so/therefore” (result): "No tenía dinero, de modo que me fui." With the subjunctive, it often means “so that” (purpose), similar to "para que": "Habla más despacio, de modo que todos entiendan."
target_language_example: Estaba lloviendo, de modo que nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: It was raining, so we stayed at home.

additional_notes: Common way to say something is true temporarily or only at the present time. Often used to soften plans or decisions: “De momento, no voy a salir” (I’m not going out for now). Similar to “por ahora” and “por el momento.”
target_language_example: De momento, no tengo tiempo, pero mañana sí.
native_language_example: For now, I don’t have time, but tomorrow I do.

meaning: an intensifier meaning “terribly/very” (e.g., “dead tired”), or “to die for/stunning” depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally “of death,” but it’s usually used idiomatically after a noun or adjective to emphasize how extreme something is: cansado de muerte (dead tired), un susto de muerte (a terrible fright), aburrido de muerte (bored to death). With positive things, it can mean “to die for / amazing”: un vestido de muerte (a stunning dress). Common in everyday speech and informal writing.
target_language_example: Estoy cansado de muerte.
native_language_example: I’m dead tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something is more than needed or not necessary. Common with verbs like "tener" (to have) and "ser" (to be): "Tengo comida de más" (I have extra food), "Eso está de más" (That’s unnecessary / besides the point). You can also hear "De más" meaning "extra" on its own when talking about quantities.
target_language_example: No hace falta traer postre; ya tenemos comida de más.
native_language_example: No need to bring dessert; we already have extra food.

de mírame y no me toques

target_language_multi_word_term: de mírame y no me toques
meaning: so delicate/fragile that it’s basically “look but don’t touch”.
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase used after verbs like "ser" or "estar" to describe something (or sometimes someone) that is very fragile, finicky, or ‘for show’—as if it can’t be handled without damage. Often implies it breaks easily or needs extreme care.
target_language_example: Ese adorno es de mírame y no me toques; se rompe con nada.
native_language_example: That ornament is a “look but don’t touch” kind of thing; it breaks at the slightest thing.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or adjective to say something is true since birth or because someone was born that way. Common in phrases like “ciudadano/a de nacimiento” (citizen by birth), “sordo/a de nacimiento” (deaf from birth), and “mexicano/a de nacimiento” (Mexican by birth).
target_language_example: Soy mexicano de nacimiento, pero vivo en Estados Unidos.
native_language_example: I’m Mexican by birth, but I live in the United States.

additional_notes: Common reply after someone says "gracias." It’s polite and very frequent in everyday Spanish. Literally it’s like "of nothing," so it can also feel like "it was nothing" or "don’t mention it."
target_language_example: —Gracias por tu ayuda. —De nada.
native_language_example: —Thanks for your help. —You’re welcome.

meaning: really; extremely (often to emphasize something good or bad).
additional_notes: Colloquial intensifier used after an adjective or adverb: "(adjective/adverb) de narices". It adds strong emphasis, like "really" / "super" / "a heck of a" in English. Depending on context it can be positive ("genial de narices") or negative ("feo de narices", "caro de narices").
target_language_example: Hace un frío de narices hoy.
native_language_example: It’s really cold today.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as necessary/essential. Very common in the set phrase "de primera necesidad" (“basic necessities”), especially with things like food, water, medicine, and other essential supplies.
target_language_example: Tras el huracán, repartieron agua y otros artículos de primera necesidad.
native_language_example: After the hurricane, they handed out water and other basic necessities.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse, deny, or say something is impossible. Similar in strength to “absolutely not,” but the meaning is negative (it does NOT mean “absolutely”). Often used alone as an emphatic response: “—¿Vienes? —De ninguna manera.”
target_language_example: —¿Me prestas tu coche? —De ninguna manera.
native_language_example: “Can you lend me your car?” “No way.”

additional_notes: A strong, emphatic way to say “no” or “absolutely not.” Common in refusals and disagreements. Similar in strength to “en absoluto” or “para nada.” In writing or formal speech, it can sound firm but not slangy.
target_language_example: —¿Vas a aceptar ese trato? —De ningún modo.
native_language_example: —Are you going to accept that deal? —No way.

additional_notes: Used to talk about when something happens (time of day). Often contrasts with "de día" (during the day). It’s a set phrase; you don’t usually say *en noche* for this meaning. In some contexts it can also describe something done at night as a habit (e.g., "Trabajo de noche" = "I work nights").
target_language_example: No me gusta conducir de noche.
native_language_example: I don't like driving at night.

additional_notes: Common in Spain in casual conversation, often after a question about how something is going: “¿Qué tal?” — “Bien, de normal.” It means things are normal/typical (nothing special). Also used to talk about a usual habit or routine: “Me levanto temprano de normal.” Similar idea: “como siempre”.
target_language_example: Todo bien, de normal.
native_language_example: Everything’s fine, as usual.

additional_notes: Used to describe a bossy, top-down way of acting or leading—giving orders without discussion. It often goes with nouns like actitud, estilo, política, or manera (e.g., actitud de ordeno y mando). In more formal contexts you may also see por ordeno y mando in official/military wording (“by order and command”).
target_language_example: No me gusta su actitud de ordeno y mando; aquí trabajamos en equipo.
native_language_example: I don’t like his order-and-command attitude; we work as a team here.

additional_notes: Used to describe something’s colors (a flag, team uniform, decoration, crest, etc.). In Spanish, "oro" can mean the metal gold, but in color descriptions it often means a golden/yellow color. The pattern "de + color + y + color" is common for describing color combinations.
target_language_example: El uniforme del equipo es de oro y azul.
native_language_example: The team’s uniform is gold and blue.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen differently if a condition isn’t met, or to suggest an alternative way of doing something. Very common in warnings and instructions (often like “or else”). Similar phrases: “si no” (if not), “de lo contrario” (otherwise/on the contrary, more formal).
target_language_example: Apúrate, de otro modo llegaremos tarde.
native_language_example: Hurry up, otherwise we’ll arrive late.

meaning: by ear; from what you’ve heard (not from direct experience).
additional_notes: Used to say you know something because you heard it (not because you saw/experienced it). Common with verbs like saber/conocer ("Sé de oído que…") or with musical contexts ("tocar de oído" = play by ear).
target_language_example: No lo conozco personalmente; lo sé de oído.
native_language_example: I don’t know him personally; I only know of him from what I’ve heard.

de padre y muy señor mío

target_language_multi_word_term: de padre y muy señor mío
meaning: an old-fashioned, very formal way of addressing someone in a letter (like “Dear Sir”).
additional_notes: This is a traditional/archaic epistolary formula associated with very formal letters. Today it’s often mentioned jokingly or critically to describe a stiff, old-fashioned style of writing or speaking (very proper, overly formal). It’s not commonly used as an actual greeting in modern everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Eso de «de padre y muy señor mío» suena a carta antigua; hoy con «Estimado/a…» basta.
native_language_example: That “Dear Sir” kind of wording sounds like an old letter; today “Dear…” is enough.

additional_notes: Used to indicate who sends something (a message, greeting, gift, invitation) or who something comes from. Very common in polite speech: "De parte de Juan" = "From Juan" / "On Juan’s behalf." Often appears alone as a short phrase when giving a message or handing something over.
target_language_example: Tengo un mensaje de parte de Ana.
native_language_example: I have a message from Ana.

meaning: while I’m at it; on the way / passing by.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something incidentally, because you’re already going somewhere or doing something else. Very common with verbs like "aprovechar" (to take advantage), and with phrases like "de paso" at the start or end of a sentence. Literal sense is "as a passing thing / in passing," but the natural English is usually "while I’m at it" or "since I’m going by."
target_language_example: Voy al supermercado y, de paso, compro pan.
native_language_example: I’m going to the supermarket and, while I’m at it, I’ll buy bread.

additional_notes: Literally “of sin.” Used to describe something as a guilty pleasure, especially rich food or desserts: “un postre de pecado,” “este chocolate es de pecado.” It often comes after the noun, or after “ser/estar” (to be).
target_language_example: Este pastel de chocolate es de pecado.
native_language_example: This chocolate cake is sinful (so indulgent / to die for).

meaning: like in a movie; amazing; unbelievable.
additional_notes: Used to describe something as spectacular, dramatic, or hard to believe—like something you’d see in a film. Often follows a noun ("una vista de película") or is used after a situation ("Fue de película").
target_language_example: La vista desde la montaña era de película.
native_language_example: The view from the mountain was like in a movie.

meaning: in profile; from the side (side view).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone/something seen from the side (not facing forward). Common in photo/video contexts with verbs like ponerse (to turn), salir (to come out/appear in a photo), or quedar (to look/turn out): “ponte de perfil” = “turn sideways.”
target_language_example: Ponte de perfil para la foto, por favor.
native_language_example: Turn to the side for the photo, please.

additional_notes: Informal expression meaning something is ideal or works very well. Often used with verbs like "venir" or "quedar": "Me viene de perlas" = "That’s perfect for me" / "It suits me perfectly." It literally means "of pearls," but the idiomatic meaning is "perfectly."
target_language_example: Me viene de perlas que me ayudes hoy.
native_language_example: It’s perfect for me that you help me today.

additional_notes: Common colloquial expression used after a noun to emphasize that something is really bad or unpleasant. Very often used with time or weather phrases like "un día de perros" (a horrible day) or "un tiempo de perros" (awful weather). Literally it means "of dogs," but the idiomatic meaning is "terrible/awful."
target_language_example: Hace un día de perros: llueve y hace mucho frío.
native_language_example: It’s a terrible day: it’s raining and it’s very cold.

meaning: person to person; from one person to another (directly).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize direct, personal contact or communication (often without intermediaries). It can imply handling something one-on-one, sometimes face-to-face, as opposed to something impersonal or done through a company/system.
target_language_example: Prefiero hablarlo de persona a persona, sin intermediarios.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk about it person to person, without intermediaries.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something has real importance or influence (not literally “made of weight”). Common collocations: “razón de peso” (a compelling reason), “argumento de peso” (a strong argument), “cargo de peso” (a high-responsibility position), “una figura de peso” (an influential person).
target_language_example: Necesitamos una razón de peso para cambiar el plan.
native_language_example: We need a compelling reason to change the plan.

additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like estar/ponerse/quedarse: “Estoy de pie” (I’m standing). It can also mean “upright” (not fallen over): “El vaso sigue de pie” (the glass is still standing). In “ir/venir de pie,” it can mean you’re standing (not seated) while traveling, especially on public transport.
target_language_example: Estoy de pie porque no hay sillas.
native_language_example: I’m standing up because there are no chairs.

meaning: made of stone; (figuratively) frozen in shock.
additional_notes: Literal use describes the material something is made from (often after a noun: una casa de piedra). Figuratively, it’s common in the expression “quedarse de piedra” = “to be stunned / to be left speechless,” meaning you don’t react because you’re so surprised.
target_language_example: Cuando me lo dijo, me quedé de piedra.
native_language_example: When they told me, I was stunned.

additional_notes: Used to describe being in an upright position (not sitting or lying down). Common with verbs like "estar" ("estar de pie/de pies"), "ponerse" (to stand up), and "quedarse" (to remain standing). Also used to talk about doing something by walking rather than using a vehicle ("ir de pies").
target_language_example: Tuvimos que esperar de pies porque no había sillas.
native_language_example: We had to wait standing because there were no chairs.

meaning: from head to toe; completely (all over).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that covers your whole body or all parts of something (often with verbs like "estar," "cubrir," or "mojar"/"manchar"). Literal meaning: "from feet to head"; in English the natural order is "head to toe."
target_language_example: Estaba mojado de pies a cabeza después de la lluvia.
native_language_example: He was soaked from head to toe after the rain.

meaning: by right; automatically (as a full legal entitlement).
additional_notes: Formal/legal phrase meaning someone has something "as a matter of right" (not by permission or favor). It often appears in documents and official contexts, e.g., "ser de pleno derecho" (to be full/fully entitled) or "miembro de pleno derecho" (full member).
target_language_example: Los ciudadanos son miembros de pleno derecho de la Unión.
native_language_example: Citizens are full members of the Union by right.

meaning: not talkative; a person of few words.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who speaks very little or is reserved. Often follows forms of "ser" (e.g., "Es de pocas palabras"). Similar in meaning to "callado/a" (quiet) or "reservado/a" (reserved), but focuses on speaking briefly rather than being shy.
target_language_example: Mi padre es de pocas palabras, pero siempre escucha con atención.
native_language_example: My dad is a man of few words, but he always listens attentively.

additional_notes: Used to give an imprecise location ("around there") or, in some contexts, an imprecise time/amount ("around/about"). Often goes with verbs like estar, vivir, quedar, pasar, and andar. Example: "Vivo de por ahí" = "I live somewhere around there" (not an exact address).
target_language_example: Creo que mi bolso está de por ahí, cerca de la puerta.
native_language_example: I think my bag is somewhere around there, near the door.

meaning: in the middle; involved; in between (as an obstacle or factor).
additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is involved in a situation (“Hay dinero de por medio” = money is involved), or that something is in the way/in between (“No te metas; no tienes nada que ver, no hay nada de por medio”). Often appears with verbs like haber (hay), estar, tener, or meterse/ponerse.
target_language_example: No puedo ir; tengo trabajo de por medio.
native_language_example: I can’t go; I have work in the way / I have work going on.

meaning: in itself; as it is; by itself.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true inherently, without any extra reasons or changes (similar to “in itself / as it is”). It’s also used to mean something happens or exists without help (“by itself”). Very common with emphasis: “ya de por sí” = “already (as it is)”.
target_language_example: El trabajo es difícil de por sí, y con tanta presión, peor.
native_language_example: The job is difficult in itself, and with so much pressure, even worse.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts forever or for the rest of someone’s life. Often follows a noun (e.g., "amigo de por vida") or is used with verbs like "ser"/"quedar" ("ser de por vida" = to be for life; "quedar de por vida" = to remain for life). It can be literal (a sentence, a condition) or figurative (a friendship).
target_language_example: Son amigos de por vida.
native_language_example: They are friends for life.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that is very accurate or made for accurate work. Common with objects like instruments, tools, and parts: “instrumento de precisión”, “herramienta de precisión”, “reloj de precisión”.
target_language_example: Necesitamos un instrumento de precisión para medir esto.
native_language_example: We need a precision instrument to measure this.

additional_notes: Used to describe something (or someone) as excellent or high quality. It often goes after the noun: “un hotel de primera” = “a first-class hotel.” In sports (especially in Spain), it can also mean “in the first division” (La Primera).
target_language_example: Este restaurante es de primera.
native_language_example: This restaurant is first-class.

additional_notes: Used mainly in Spain when talking about a multi-course meal (often: "de primero" / "de segundo" / "de postre"). It answers what you’re having for the first course: "De primero, sopa." You can also see it on menus or in cafeterias to label the first dish.
target_language_example: De primero voy a tomar una ensalada.
native_language_example: For the first course I’m going to have a salad.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done quickly or that someone is rushing. Very common with verbs like ir/venir/salir/hacer (e.g., ir de prisa = to be in a hurry). Similar meaning to “rápido” (quickly) and “con prisa” (in a hurry).
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo que irme de prisa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to leave in a hurry.

additional_notes: Common in everyday Spanish to describe something unexpected that happens quickly. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence or before the verb: "De pronto, ..." / "Me llamó de pronto". Similar meaning to "de repente" and "de golpe" (also "suddenly").
target_language_example: De pronto empezó a llover.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started to rain.

meaning: trial / test; for testing (a demo version).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something temporary or experimental: "versión de prueba" (trial version), "periodo de prueba" (trial period/probation), "cuenta de prueba" (test account). Also used to mean "sample" in some contexts (e.g., a test/sample question: "pregunta de prueba").
target_language_example: Descargué la versión de prueba antes de comprar el programa.
native_language_example: I downloaded the trial version before buying the program.

meaning: outwardly; in public (as opposed to privately).
additional_notes: Used to contrast public appearance with what happens “behind closed doors.” Often paired with “de puertas para adentro” (privately/at home). It can describe behavior, rules, or a relationship that looks one way to others but is different in private.
target_language_example: De puertas para afuera, parecen una pareja perfecta, pero en casa discuten mucho.
native_language_example: Outwardly, they seem like a perfect couple, but at home they argue a lot.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "ponerse" or "estar." Common meanings: (1) "de punta" = on tiptoe: "caminar/ponerse de punta". (2) "ponerse de punta" = to stand on end (e.g., hair, spikes, bristles), often from fear or excitement. The exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Se me puso el pelo de punta al oír ese ruido.
native_language_example: My hair stood on end when I heard that noise.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done or known in its entirety, thoroughly (like reading something all the way through or knowing someone very well). Literally "from tip to end," but the natural English equivalent is "from start to finish" / "from beginning to end".
target_language_example: Leí el informe de punta a cabo.
native_language_example: I read the report from start to finish.

meaning: from one end to the other; end to end (throughout).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize covering the whole length or extent of something (a street, a beach, a country, etc.). It can also mean doing something completely from beginning to end (e.g., reading a book).
target_language_example: Recorrimos el país de punta a punta en dos semanas.
native_language_example: We traveled across the country from end to end in two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to describe walking or standing with your heels raised (quietly or carefully). Often used with verbs like "andar" (to walk), "ponerse" (to stand/get), or "caminar" (to walk): "andar de puntillas", "ponerse de puntillas". Can also be used figuratively to mean doing something very delicately or cautiously (e.g., approaching a topic carefully).
target_language_example: Entró en la habitación de puntillas para no despertar al bebé.
native_language_example: He/She came into the room on tiptoe so as not to wake the baby.

additional_notes: Used to describe clothing or fabric: "un suéter de punto" (a knit sweater), "una falda de punto" (a knit skirt). Often appears as "tejido de punto" = "knit fabric/knitwear." Not the same as "en punto" (exactly on the hour).
target_language_example: Me compré un suéter de punto para el invierno.
native_language_example: I bought a knit sweater for the winter.

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar slang (common in Spain). Used to say something is excellent: "Está/estuvo de puta madre" = "It’s/was awesome." Avoid in polite situations, at work, or with people you don’t know well. It can occasionally be used sarcastically depending on tone.
target_language_example: La fiesta estuvo de puta madre.
native_language_example: The party was freaking awesome.

meaning: in (someone’s) own handwriting; handwritten (by the person themselves).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something was written personally by someone (not typed, not dictated, not written by another person). Often appears with possessives: “de mi/tu/su puño y letra” (in my/your/their own handwriting). Common with words like “carta” (letter), “nota” (note), “firma” (signature), or “escrito” (writing).
target_language_example: Necesito una nota de tu puño y letra para autorizarlo.
native_language_example: I need a note in your own handwriting to authorize it.

meaning: easy to remove and put back; temporary; not permanent.
additional_notes: Used as an adjective phrase after a noun, especially for things that can be taken off/on or changed quickly (e.g., un collar de quita y pon, una funda de quita y pon). By extension, it can describe something not fixed or stable (e.g., un trabajo de quita y pon). Literally “of take off and put on.”
target_language_example: Compré una funda de quita y pon para el sofá.
native_language_example: I bought a removable cover for the sofa.

additional_notes: Used to say an animal (especially a dog or cat) is a specific breed and often implies pedigree/purebred. With people, it can be used figuratively to mean “a natural/born” something (e.g., "un líder de raza"), but this can sound old-fashioned or sensitive depending on context—use with care. Often appears after the noun: "perro de raza".
target_language_example: Buscamos un perro de raza, pero también consideramos adoptar uno mestizo.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a purebred dog, but we’re also considering adopting a mixed-breed one.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something intended for delivering goods/food (e.g., "servicio de reparto" = delivery service, "repartidor/a" = delivery person). Common in phrases like "a domicilio y de reparto" (eat-in/at home and delivery), or "pedido de reparto" (delivery order).
target_language_example: Quiero una pizza para llevar o de reparto.
native_language_example: I want a pizza to take away or for delivery.

additional_notes: Used to describe something happening unexpectedly or quickly. Very common in everyday speech and works in many positions: at the start (De repente, empezó a llover.) or mid-sentence (Empezó a llover de repente.). Not the same as "de vez en cuando" (from time to time).
target_language_example: De repente, se fue la luz.
native_language_example: Suddenly, the power went out.

meaning: spare; replacement (extra one in case the main one fails).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean an extra or backup item: “una llave de repuesto” (a spare key), “una rueda de repuesto” (a spare tire). Also used for replacement parts: “piezas de repuesto” (spare parts).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una llave de repuesto?
native_language_example: Do you have a spare key?

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something kept for emergencies or just in case: “una llave de reserva” (a spare key), “una batería de reserva” (a backup battery), “un plan de reserva” (a backup plan). Often interchangeable with “de repuesto” for physical spare parts.
target_language_example: Siempre llevo una batería de reserva por si se me acaba la del móvil.
native_language_example: I always carry a backup battery in case my phone’s runs out.

additional_notes: Somewhat formal and less common in everyday conversation than "a causa de", "debido a", or "por". It introduces the cause of something, often an event or situation that happened earlier.
target_language_example: De resultas de la tormenta, se canceló el vuelo.
native_language_example: As a result of the storm, the flight was canceled.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s position (kneeling), often with verbs like estar/ponerse/caer: “estar de rodillas” (to be kneeling), “ponerse de rodillas” (to kneel down), “caer de rodillas” (to fall to your knees). Can be literal (kneeling) or figurative in emotional/dramatic contexts (e.g., begging).
target_language_example: Se puso de rodillas para atarse los zapatos.
native_language_example: He/She knelt down to tie his/her shoes.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something privately or without others knowing. Common with verbs like "hacer" (to do), "decir" (to say), or "hablar" (to talk): "hacer algo de secreto" = to do something secretly. You may also hear the more common form "en secreto" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Lo hicieron de secreto para que nadie se enterara.
native_language_example: They did it in secret so that nobody would find out.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that isn’t new (second-hand) or is low quality/less prestigious. Often used in shopping contexts: "ropa de segunda" (second-hand clothes), "un coche de segunda" (a used car). For "used car" you’ll also commonly hear "coche de segunda mano".
target_language_example: Compré una chaqueta de segunda en esa tienda.
native_language_example: I bought a second-hand jacket in that shop.

additional_notes: Used to describe items that have had a previous owner (clothes, cars, furniture, etc.). Common in shopping contexts. Often appears after the noun: "ropa de segunda mano" (second-hand clothes), "un coche de segunda mano" (a used car).
target_language_example: Compré un coche de segunda mano porque era más barato.
native_language_example: I bought a used car because it was cheaper.

additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase meaning you are confident about something. Often placed before the verb or at the end of the sentence. It’s similar to “seguro” meaning “sure,” but “de seguro” sounds a bit more formal/literary. In some contexts it can also mean “probably,” depending on tone and region.
target_language_example: De seguro mañana lloverá.
native_language_example: Surely it will rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with jobs or roles to say someone is currently working: "Estoy de servicio" (I’m on duty). Also used to describe items meant for doing work or serving a function, especially vehicles or equipment: "coche de servicio" (service vehicle). Depending on context it can also mean "for serving" (e.g., utensils).
target_language_example: El médico está de servicio esta noche.
native_language_example: The doctor is on duty tonight.

meaning: more than enough; extra; left over.
additional_notes: Used to say something is sufficient in excess ("de sobra") or that there is something extra/left over ("queda de sobra"). Often follows what it describes: "Tengo dinero de sobra" (I have more than enough money). You can also use it as an adverb meaning "amply" or "plenty": "Lo sé de sobra" (I know it perfectly well).
target_language_example: Con lo que ganamos, tenemos dinero de sobra para el viaje.
native_language_example: With what we earn, we have more than enough money for the trip.

meaning: from sunrise to sunset; all day long.
additional_notes: An idiomatic way to emphasize a very long day (often of hard work), especially in contexts like farming or outdoor work. Common with verbs like "trabajar" (to work): "trabajar de sol a sol."
target_language_example: En la cosecha, trabajamos de sol a sol.
native_language_example: During the harvest, we work from sunrise to sunset.

additional_notes: Used to mean two people speaking privately, without anyone else present. It often appears with verbs like hablar, tratar, or discutir: “hablar de solo a solo” = “to talk in private / one-on-one.” Similar to “a solas” or “en privado.”
target_language_example: Necesito hablar contigo de solo a solo.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you in private (one-on-one).

meaning: in itself; by itself; on its own.
additional_notes: Somewhat formal. Used to say something is true or has a quality inherently, without needing anything else. Often appears in phrases like “de suyo es…” (in itself it is…) or “no es malo de suyo” (it’s not bad in itself).
target_language_example: La idea no es mala de suyo, pero hay que explicarla mejor.
native_language_example: The idea isn’t bad in itself, but it needs to be explained better.

meaning: every now and then; once in a while.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens infrequently or only occasionally. Similar to "de vez en cuando" or "de cuando en cuando". Despite containing "tarde" (afternoon/late), it’s not about the time of day; it means "from time to time."
target_language_example: Vamos al cine de tarde en tarde.
native_language_example: We go to the movies once in a while.

meaning: seasonal; in season (available only at certain times of the year).
additional_notes: Common with food, products, or tourism. With fruit/vegetables it means they are in season (often fresher and cheaper): “fruta/verdura de temporada”. With places or work it can mean seasonal (only during a particular season): “trabajo de temporada”, “hotel de temporada”.
target_language_example: Prefiero comprar frutas de temporada porque son más frescas.
native_language_example: I prefer to buy seasonal fruit because it’s fresher.

additional_notes: Used to say something is of poor quality or not very good, often in a complaining or dismissive tone. It can describe things (un hotel de tercera, una comida de tercera) and sometimes people’s behavior or work, though that can sound insulting. Common contrast: de primera (top-quality) and de segunda (second-rate).
target_language_example: Este hotel es de tercera: la habitación está sucia y no hay agua caliente.
native_language_example: This hotel is third-rate: the room is dirty and there’s no hot water.

meaning: (something/someone) for as long as you can remember; lifelong; the usual/always.
additional_notes: Used to say something has always been that way (a long-time habit, a traditional thing, or someone you’ve known forever). It often describes people (un amigo de toda la vida), places/things (un bar de toda la vida = a long-established, traditional bar), or routines (lo de toda la vida = the usual).
target_language_example: Es mi amigo de toda la vida.
native_language_example: He’s my lifelong friend / a friend I’ve known forever.

additional_notes: Used to move on from a point, show that something doesn’t change the decision/result, or soften disagreement. Common in conversation. Often placed at the start or end of a sentence (also said as "de todas maneras").
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo, pero de todas formas voy a ayudarte.
native_language_example: I don’t have time, but anyway I’m going to help you.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen or is true regardless of what was just said (changing plans, obstacles, or new information). Very common in conversation; also appears as "de todas formas" with the same meaning. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: No tengo mucho tiempo, pero iré de todas maneras.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time, but I’ll go anyway.

meaning: With all my heart; wholeheartedly; sincerely.
additional_notes: Used to express genuine sincerity, gratitude, congratulations, apologies, or wishes. Often appears with verbs like "agradecer" (to thank), "felicitar" (to congratulate), "pedir perdón" (to apologize), and "desear" (to wish). It can refer to the speaker’s feelings ("te lo digo de todo corazón") or modify an action ("te agradezco de todo corazón").
target_language_example: Te lo agradezco de todo corazón.
native_language_example: I thank you with all my heart.

de todo hay en la viña del Señor

target_language_multi_word_term: de todo hay en la viña del Señor
meaning: “There are all kinds of people/things” (it takes all sorts).
additional_notes: A common proverb used to react to something surprising, odd, or unexpected, meaning that in life you find every type of person or situation. It’s often said in a mildly humorous or resigned tone. Sometimes shortened to “de todo hay”. The religious imagery (“the Lord’s vineyard”) is idiomatic and doesn’t necessarily mean the speaker is being religious.
target_language_example: ¿Viste lo que hizo? Bueno, de todo hay en la viña del Señor.
native_language_example: Did you see what he did? Well, there are all kinds of people.

additional_notes: Formal/emphatic phrase used to strengthen an adjective or judgment (similar to “utterly” / “totally”). Often appears as: “de todo punto + adjective” (e.g., de todo punto imposible). You may also see it as “en todo punto” with a very similar meaning. Not used much in casual everyday conversation.
target_language_example: La propuesta es de todo punto inaceptable.
native_language_example: The proposal is completely unacceptable.

additional_notes: Used to move on or conclude despite what was just said (similar to “anyway”). It can also mean “regardless” when you’re saying something won’t change the outcome. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: De todos modos, mañana tengo que ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: Anyway, tomorrow I have to go to work.

additional_notes: An idiom used to emphasize that something (or someone) is important, weighty, or “proper/real,” not superficial. It often follows a noun: *un problema de tomo y lomo* (a serious problem), *un libro de tomo y lomo* (a substantial book), *un delincuente de tomo y lomo* (a real/hardened criminal).
target_language_example: Lo de ayer fue un escándalo de tomo y lomo.
native_language_example: What happened yesterday was a full-blown scandal.

additional_notes: Informal idiom used to criticize someone or something as cheap, poorly made, or not worth much attention. Often used after a noun (e.g., “un restaurante de tres al cuarto”).
target_language_example: No quiero un teléfono de tres al cuarto; necesito uno que funcione bien.
native_language_example: I don’t want a second-rate phone; I need one that works well.

additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone that is temporarily passing through a place, not staying there. Common in travel/transport contexts (e.g., passengers or luggage) and in road/traffic contexts meaning “traffic-related” (e.g., multa de tránsito = traffic ticket). Often follows a noun: estar de tránsito = to be in transit.
target_language_example: Estuve de tránsito en Madrid solo unas horas.
native_language_example: I was in transit in Madrid for only a few hours.

meaning: overnight; from one day to the next (suddenly).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something changing very quickly or unexpectedly, often implying “all of a sudden” or “it doesn’t happen instantly.” Common with verbs like cambiar (to change), desaparecer (to disappear), and aprender (to learn).
target_language_example: No puedes aprender español de un día para otro.
native_language_example: You can’t learn Spanish overnight.

meaning: all at once; suddenly; in one go (sometimes: with one hit).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens immediately or in a single action, often without pauses or gradually. With verbs like "hacer," "terminar," "beber," it means "in one go / all at once" (e.g., do/finish/drink something without stopping). In more physical contexts, it can mean "with one blow/strike" (e.g., break something with a single hit).
target_language_example: Se bebió el vaso de agua de un golpe.
native_language_example: He drank the glass of water in one go.

meaning: from one side/place to another; back and forth.
additional_notes: Used to describe moving repeatedly between places or directions (often with a sense of restlessness or being busy), similar to “back and forth” or “from place to place.” You can use it with verbs like ir, venir, caminar, correr, andar, or mover(se).
target_language_example: Estuve caminando de un lado para otro toda la tarde.
native_language_example: I was walking back and forth all afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen or be done somehow, even if you don’t know exactly how. Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Also appears as "de una manera u otra" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: De un modo u otro, vamos a terminar este proyecto hoy.
native_language_example: One way or another, we’re going to finish this project today.

meaning: at any moment; suddenly; from one moment to the next.
additional_notes: Used to say something can happen very soon, without warning, or unexpectedly. Often used with future tense or phrases like "puede"/"podría" (can/could).
target_language_example: Puede llover de un momento a otro, así que lleva un paraguas.
native_language_example: It could start raining at any moment, so bring an umbrella.

de un tiempo a esta parte

target_language_multi_word_term: de un tiempo a esta parte
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been happening from a point in the (usually recent) past up to the present. Often appears with the present tense or present perfect (e.g., "he notado", "ha cambiado"). It’s a fairly common, neutral expression.
target_language_example: De un tiempo a esta parte, he notado que duermo peor.
native_language_example: For some time now, I’ve noticed that I’m sleeping worse.

meaning: for some time now; lately; in recent months/years (up to now).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been happening or has changed starting at an unspecified point in the past and continuing until the present. It’s similar to “desde hace un tiempo” or “últimamente.” Often used with the present perfect (“he notado…”) or with the present (“estoy…”).
target_language_example: De un tiempo para acá, he notado que me canso más rápido.
native_language_example: For some time now, I’ve noticed that I get tired more quickly.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something continuously, without breaks (e.g., reading, drinking, working, traveling). It can also imply doing it quickly. Similar to "de una vez" in some contexts, but "de un tirón" emphasizes no pauses.
target_language_example: Me leí el libro de un tirón.
native_language_example: I read the book in one go.

additional_notes: Very common in informal speech. It often means doing something without delay: “Voy de una” = “I’m going right now.” In some places it’s also used as an enthusiastic “Sure!/Absolutely!/Let’s do it!”: “¡De una!”
target_language_example: Voy de una a tu casa.
native_language_example: I’m going to your place right away.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) literally, to say something is intact or assembled as a single unit ("en una sola pieza"); (2) figuratively with verbs like "quedarse" or "dejar" to mean someone is left stunned, speechless, or very surprised ("quedarse/dejar a alguien de una pieza").
target_language_example: Me quedé de una pieza cuando me dijo que se iba mañana.
native_language_example: I was stunned when he/she told me they were leaving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to push for something to be done immediately or definitively, often showing impatience or emphasis. Common in commands and requests: "Hazlo de una vez" = "Do it already" / "Do it once and for all." It can also mean "at one time" in some contexts (less common for beginners).
target_language_example: Dímelo de una vez.
native_language_example: Tell me already. / Tell me once and for all.

meaning: "once and for all"; permanently, for good.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you want something decided, solved, clarified, or finished definitively so it won’t happen again. Often used with verbs like resolver, terminar, aclarar, decidir, or dejar (de).
target_language_example: Tenemos que resolver este problema de una vez para siempre.
native_language_example: We have to solve this problem once and for all.

meaning: "once and for all"; finally, for good.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you want something to be decided, done, or stopped permanently (often with impatience or determination). Common with commands or requests: "Dímelo de una vez por todas" (Tell me once and for all).
target_language_example: Resuélvelo de una vez por todas y dejemos de discutir.
native_language_example: Settle it once and for all and let’s stop arguing.

meaning: very rarely; once in a blue moon.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say something happens only occasionally. It often goes with verbs like ver(se) (to see each other), ir (to go), pasar (to happen), or visitar (to visit): “Nos vemos de uvas a peras.” It’s more colloquial than formal, and you can also hear “muy de uvas a peras” to emphasize the rarity.
target_language_example: Desde que cambié de trabajo, salgo con mis amigos de uvas a peras.
native_language_example: Since I changed jobs, I go out with my friends once in a blue moon.

meaning: in a bad mood; irritable (usually in “estar/ponerse de uñas”).
additional_notes: Common colloquial expression meaning someone is cranky, touchy, or ready to snap. It’s most often used with “estar” (to be) or “ponerse” (to get/become): “Estoy de uñas”, “Se puso de uñas”.
target_language_example: No le digas nada ahora: está de uñas.
native_language_example: Don’t tell him/her anything right now: he/she’s in a bad mood.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe it ("something valuable"). Often appears in phrases like "objetos de valor" (valuables) or "cosas de valor". You can also use it more generally to mean something is worth having/keeping.
target_language_example: No dejes objetos de valor en el coche.
native_language_example: Don’t leave valuables in the car.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is genuine or serious, or to express surprise/disbelief (similar to “really?”). Often placed after what it emphasizes (e.g., “Es de verdad”), but it can also start a question (“¿De verdad?”).
target_language_example: ¿De verdad no sabes dónde está?
native_language_example: Do you really not know where it is?

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something meant to be worn or intended for a more formal, “dress” occasion. Common with clothing and accessories: ropa de vestir (dress clothes), zapatos de vestir (dress shoes), camisa de vestir (dress shirt).
target_language_example: Necesito zapatos de vestir para la boda.
native_language_example: I need dress shoes for the wedding.

meaning: every now and then; from time to time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally (not regularly). It often goes at the beginning or end of a sentence. Similar to: "a veces" (sometimes), but "de vez en cuando" usually suggests less frequent.
target_language_example: De vez en cuando salgo a caminar después de cenar.
native_language_example: Every now and then I go for a walk after dinner.

meaning: traveling; on a trip (away from home).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar, ir, andar, or to say someone is away because they’re traveling. Often followed by the destination: “Estoy de viaje por México / a México.” Can also describe something meant for travel (especially with items/containers): “tamaño de viaje” = travel size.
target_language_example: No puedo verte hoy porque estoy de viaje en Madrid.
native_language_example: I can’t see you today because I’m traveling in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (or in phrases like "es muy de viejo") to say something is typical of older people or seems old-fashioned. It can be neutral or teasing depending on tone. Similar ideas: "de antes" (from before/old-timey), "anticuado" (old-fashioned).
target_language_example: Eso de acostarte a las nueve es muy de viejo.
native_language_example: Going to bed at nine is such an old-person thing.

meaning: “of will” (used in phrases about willpower or willingness).
additional_notes: This is a prepositional phrase that usually comes after a noun, forming common expressions like: **fuerza de voluntad** (“willpower”), **acto de voluntad** (“act of will”), **falta de voluntad** (“lack of willingness”). On its own, **de voluntad** typically sounds incomplete—you normally say what kind of thing it is (e.g., *fuerza*, *acto*, *falta*).
target_language_example: Necesito fuerza de voluntad para dejar de fumar.
native_language_example: I need willpower to quit smoking.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone/something has returned: "Estoy de vuelta" = "I’m back." Also used with verbs like "volver" (to return) for emphasis: "Volví de vuelta" (very common in speech, but redundant). Can also mean "again" in the sense of doing something back/returning an action: "Te llamo de vuelta" = "I’ll call you back."
target_language_example: Ya estoy de vuelta en casa.
native_language_example: I’m back home now.

meaning: period (from a particular time in the past); vintage/period-style.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is from a certain historical period or made in an old-fashioned style. Common with things like furniture, clothing, cars, and buildings (e.g., "muebles de época", "vestido de época"). Often implies an antique, classic, or historically authentic look.
target_language_example: Compró un sofá de época para el salón.
native_language_example: He bought a period (vintage-style) sofa for the living room.

additional_notes: Used for something that happens or is decided very recently, often unexpectedly. Common with nouns like "noticia" (breaking news), "cambio" (last-minute change), "decisión" (last-minute decision), or "imprevisto" (last-minute surprise).
target_language_example: Hubo un cambio de última hora y salimos más tarde.
native_language_example: There was a last-minute change and we left later.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a position lower than something else. It’s a common prepositional phrase that’s followed by a noun/pronoun (e.g., debajo de la mesa, debajo de mí). Often interchangeable with "bajo" in simple location phrases, but "debajo de" is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: El gato está debajo de la mesa.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

additional_notes: Commonly used as a modal verb: **deber + infinitive** (e.g., *Debo estudiar* = “I have to study” / “I should study”). In the noun form, it often appears as **el deber** (“duty”). Sometimes **deber de + infinitive** can suggest probability in some contexts (e.g., “must be”), though many speakers also use **deber** for this.
target_language_example: Debo irme ahora.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: to have to eat; should eat.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "deber" + infinitive to talk about obligation or advice. Depending on context, it can mean a strong obligation ("have to") or a recommendation ("should"). Very common with other verbs too: "deber estudiar" (should study). For advice, you’ll often hear the conditional: "Deberías comer" (You should eat).
target_language_example: Debo comer algo antes de salir.
native_language_example: I have to eat something before leaving.

meaning: 'must' / 'to probably' (used to express likelihood or a conclusion).
additional_notes: Often followed by an infinitive: "deber de + infinitive". In many contexts it means "must" in the sense of "it must be..." (a guess based on evidence): "Debe de estar en casa" = "He/She must be at home" (probably). In everyday speech, many people also use "deber" without "de" for the same idea, though some grammar guides distinguish: "deber" = obligation (must/should) vs. "deber de" = probability (must/probably).
target_language_example: Debe de ser tarde ya.
native_language_example: It must be late already.

additional_notes: Used to express probability or a logical conclusion (supposition), not obligation. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Debe de ser + noun/adjective". In everyday speech many people drop the "de" ("debe ser"), but in careful usage "deber de" is the form for guesses, while "deber" (without "de") can indicate obligation.
target_language_example: Debe de ser tarde ya; vámonos.
native_language_example: It must be late already; let’s go.

meaning: “should say / ought to say” or “must say.”
additional_notes: Used with a conjugated form of deber + infinitive decir to express obligation, recommendation, or a polite/softened statement (often like “I must say…”). Common forms: debo decir (I must say), deberías decir (you should say), debemos decir (we should say).
target_language_example: Debo decir que tu idea es muy buena.
native_language_example: I must say that your idea is very good.

meaning: to have to / should enter (go in).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "deber" + infinitive ("entrar") to express obligation, necessity, or what is advisable. In conversation it’s usually conjugated (e.g., "debes entrar" = you should/must enter; "debo entrar" = I have to go in).
target_language_example: Para continuar, debes entrar tu contraseña.
native_language_example: To continue, you must enter your password.

meaning: to have to wait; to need/must to wait.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "deber" (to have to/should) + an infinitive ("esperar" = to wait). In real sentences you usually conjugate "deber": "debo esperar" (I have to wait), "debes esperar" (you have to wait), "debe esperar" (you must wait—formal/you/he/she). "Esperar" can also mean "to hope" or "to expect," but in this phrase it normally means "to wait."
target_language_example: Debe esperar aquí hasta que lo llamen.
native_language_example: You must wait here until they call you.

meaning: "to have to be" / "must be" (often: "must be" as a guess).
additional_notes: Used with a conjugated form of **deber** + **estar** to talk about (1) obligation/requirement: *Debes estar aquí a las ocho* (“You have to be here at 8”), or (2) probability/assumption (very common): *Debe estar en casa* (“He/She must be at home”). With probability, English often uses “must” or “is probably.”
target_language_example: Debe estar en casa ahora.
native_language_example: He/She must be at home now.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "deber" + infinitive to talk about obligation or strong advice. You usually conjugate "deber": "Debo fumar" (I have to/should smoke), "Debes fumar" (you have to/should smoke), "Debe fumar" (he/she/you formal has to/should smoke). For the opposite idea, use the negative: "No debes fumar" (You shouldn’t smoke / You mustn’t smoke).
target_language_example: No debes fumar aquí.
native_language_example: You mustn’t smoke here.

meaning: to have to win; should win (be expected to win).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "deber" + infinitive ("ganar") to express obligation ("must win") or strong expectation ("is supposed to win"). In conversation you’ll often see it conjugated: "debo ganar" (I have to win), "debes ganar" (you have to win), "debe ganar" (he/she/it has to win).
target_language_example: Para clasificar, debemos ganar este partido.
native_language_example: To qualify, we have to win this match.

meaning: “there must be / there should be” (expressing obligation or strong probability).
additional_notes: This is the pattern **deber + haber + (noun)**, but in real sentences you almost always conjugate **deber**: **debe haber** (there must be), **debería haber** (there should be / there ought to be), **debía haber** (there was supposed to be). It’s used to say something is necessary, expected, or very likely. In some places you may also see **debe de haber** with a similar meaning (“there must be / there’s probably”).
target_language_example: Debe haber un error.
native_language_example: There must be a mistake.

additional_notes: This is a common structure for making a guess about the past: **deber + haber + past participle**. In conversation you’ll usually see it conjugated (not in the infinitive): **debe haber pasado** (he/she/it must have happened), **deben haber pasado** (they must have happened), **debí haber pasado** (I must have passed). With **pasar**, the meaning depends on context: **pasar** = to happen, or to pass (an exam, time, etc.).
target_language_example: Debe haber pasado algo; no contesta el teléfono.
native_language_example: Something must have happened; he/she isn’t answering the phone.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "deber" + infinitive (here, "hablar") to express obligation or advice. It usually appears conjugated: "Debo hablar" (I have to talk), "Debes hablar" (you should talk), "Debe hablar" (he/she/you formal should talk). For softer advice, Spanish often uses the conditional: "Deberías hablar" (You should talk).
target_language_example: Deberías hablar con tu jefe sobre el problema.
native_language_example: You should talk to your boss about the problem.

additional_notes: Use deber + infinitive to talk about obligations or what you think is the right thing to do. Conjugate only deber (debo, debes, debe, debemos, deben) and keep the next verb in the infinitive: debo hacer, debes hacer, etc. For stronger obligation, Spanish often uses "tener que"; "deber" can also sound like advice or expectation depending on context.
target_language_example: Debo hacer la tarea hoy.
native_language_example: I have to do the homework today.

meaning: to have to go; should go.
additional_notes: Uses the verb deber + infinitive to talk about obligation, necessity, or strong recommendation. In context it’s usually conjugated (debo/debes/debe/debemos/deben ir). Often means “should go” (advice) or “must go” (obligation), depending on tone and situation.
target_language_example: Debo irme ahora; mañana trabajo temprano.
native_language_example: I have to go now; tomorrow I work early.

meaning: to have to leave; should leave.
additional_notes: Uses deber + infinitive to express obligation or a strong recommendation. With irse (reflexive), it means leaving (going away), often implying departing from a place. Conjugate deber for the subject: Debo irme (I have to leave), Debes irte (you have to leave), Debe irse (he/she/you formal has to leave). In conversation, irse is often shortened with pronouns: irme, irte, irse, irnos, iros, irse.
