additional_notes: Commonly used as a slightly formal or euphemistic way to say someone is pregnant, especially in the phrase “estar en estado” or “estar en estado de gestación.” By itself, “en estado” can also mean “in a (certain) state/condition,” but in everyday conversation it most often refers to pregnancy when talking about a person.
target_language_example: Dicen que Marta está en estado.
native_language_example: They say Marta is pregnant.

additional_notes: Means “more than is necessary/healthy/allowed.” Often used with verbs like beber (to drink), comer (to eat), gastar (to spend), trabajar (to work), or with quantities: en exceso de + number (more than…). Similar to “demasiado,” but “en exceso” sounds a bit more formal and is common in warnings/labels (e.g., about alcohol, sugar, speed).
target_language_example: No es bueno comer en exceso.
native_language_example: It’s not good to eat too much.

meaning: falsely; by mistake (e.g., a false alarm).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened incorrectly or without a real cause. Very common with alarms and automatic systems: “sonar/activarse/saltar en falso” (to go off by mistake). Also used in sports: “salida en falso” (false start).
target_language_example: La alarma sonó en falso.
native_language_example: The alarm went off by mistake (it was a false alarm).

additional_notes: Used to conclude, change topic, or sum up what you just said (similar to “anyway” or “well”). It can also mean “in the end/finally,” though in everyday speech it’s often a discourse filler. Not the same as “en fin” in French (which more often means “well, anyway”).
target_language_example: En fin, ¿vamos al cine o no?
native_language_example: Anyway, are we going to the movies or not?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically fit or in good condition. Often with the verb "estar": "estar en forma" = "to be in shape." You can also use it more generally for being ready/in good form (e.g., for an activity), but the most common meaning is physical fitness.
target_language_example: Quiero estar en forma antes del verano.
native_language_example: I want to be in shape before summer.

meaning: "in front of"; sometimes "opposite" (a place across from another).
additional_notes: Used to describe a position directly ahead of something: "en frente de la casa" (in front of the house). It can also mean "across from" when talking about locations: "Está en frente del banco" (It’s opposite the bank). You may also see it written as one word: "enfrente de". A common alternative is "frente a".
target_language_example: La farmacia está en frente de la estación.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is across from the station.

meaning: "by virtue of" / "because of" (often legal or formal).
additional_notes: Used in formal, administrative, or legal Spanish to indicate that something happens or is valid due to a law, rule, document, authority, or reason. Similar to "en virtud de" or "por" in many contexts. It’s not very common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: En fuerza de la ley, el contrato queda rescindido.
native_language_example: By virtue of the law, the contract is terminated.

meaning: in office; currently serving (especially temporarily, as a caretaker).
additional_notes: Used mainly with roles like "presidente", "gobierno", "alcalde", or "director" to say someone is still performing the duties of the position (often until a replacement is chosen). Common collocations: "gobierno en funciones" (caretaker government), "presidente en funciones" (acting president).
target_language_example: El gobierno sigue en funciones hasta que se forme el nuevo gabinete.
native_language_example: The government remains in office until the new cabinet is formed.

additional_notes: Used to show that something changes or is decided according to a factor or condition. Very common in both everyday Spanish and formal writing. Often followed by a noun or clause ("en función de lo que..."). Similar to "según" in many cases, but a bit more formal/technical.
target_language_example: El precio cambia en función de la temporada.
native_language_example: The price changes depending on the season.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something as a whole or most of the time (a general tendency, not a specific case). Often written with an accent: “en general”. You can also say “por lo general” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: En general, me gusta el café, pero hoy prefiero té.
native_language_example: In general, I like coffee, but today I prefer tea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something on a large scale or in a bold/ambitious way ("hacerlo en grande"). It’s also used for images or text shown enlarged, like a photo displayed bigger ("ver la foto en grande").
target_language_example: Vamos a celebrarlo en grande este fin de semana.
native_language_example: Let’s celebrate in a big way this weekend.

meaning: on guard; ready and alert (also: in a fighting/defensive stance).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is being watchful or cautious (often after a warning), or literally taking a defensive posture in boxing/fencing. Common with verbs like estar/ponerse: "Estoy en guardia" (I’m on guard), "Ponte en guardia" (Be on guard).
target_language_example: Ponte en guardia: creo que alguien nos está siguiendo.
native_language_example: Be on guard—I think someone is following us.

additional_notes: Used to say something is being risked or depends on the outcome ("at stake"), or that something is currently happening/active ("in play"), especially in sports or games. Often appears with verbs like "estar" or "poner": "está en juego" (is at stake/in play), "poner en juego" (to put into play / to put at stake).
target_language_example: Hay mucho en juego, así que tenemos que decidir bien.
native_language_example: There’s a lot at stake, so we have to decide carefully.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically in bed (resting, sleeping, sick) or that something happens while you’re in bed. Also commonly used with the verb "estar": "Estoy en la cama" (I’m in bed).
target_language_example: Hoy me quedo en la cama porque estoy enfermo.
native_language_example: Today I’m staying in bed because I’m sick.

additional_notes: Used to contrast theory with reality: what really happens or what works in real life. Often appears with "pero" or after a theoretical statement (e.g., "En teoría..., pero en la práctica..."). Also common meaning: "effectively" (what something amounts to in reality).
target_language_example: En teoría es fácil, pero en la práctica es más complicado.
native_language_example: In theory it’s easy, but in practice it’s more complicated.

en la punta de la lengua

target_language_multi_word_term: en la punta de la lengua
meaning: “on the tip of my tongue” (you can almost remember/say it).
additional_notes: Used when you can’t quite remember a word, name, or idea but you feel it’s about to come to you. Often said with forms of "tener": "Lo tengo en la punta de la lengua" (I’ve got it on the tip of my tongue). Also common: "Está en la punta de la lengua" (It’s on the tip of my tongue).
target_language_example: Lo tengo en la punta de la lengua, pero ahora no me sale el nombre.
native_language_example: It’s on the tip of my tongue, but the name isn’t coming to me right now.

additional_notes: Used when you rewrite notes or a draft in a clearer, more presentable version. Very common with verbs like "pasar en limpio" (to copy out neatly / make a clean copy) and "poner en limpio" (to write up neatly / finalize in writing).
target_language_example: Cuando termines el borrador, pásalo en limpio y me lo mandas.
native_language_example: When you finish the draft, write it up neatly and send it to me.

additional_notes: Used to describe something literally burning (a building, a car, a forest). It can also be used figuratively to mean something is very intense or out of control (e.g., a situation or social media). Common verb: "estar" → "Está en llamas" (It’s on fire).
target_language_example: ¡La cocina está en llamas! Llama a los bomberos.
native_language_example: The kitchen is on fire! Call the firefighters.

meaning: in what’s to come; in the future.
additional_notes: Somewhat literary/formal. It refers to future events or the time ahead. A more common everyday alternative is “en el futuro” or “de aquí en adelante.” You may also see the very similar phrase “en lo que está por venir” (“in what is yet to come”).
target_language_example: En lo por venir, tendremos que tomar decisiones difíciles.
native_language_example: In the future / in what’s to come, we’ll have to make difficult decisions.

additional_notes: Often used in formal or written Spanish (especially legal/administrative texts) to mean “starting at this point and continuing in the future.” It can also introduce a new way of referring to something: “en lo sucesivo, ‘la Empresa’…” = “hereafter, ‘the Company’…”.
target_language_example: En lo sucesivo, las comunicaciones se enviarán por correo electrónico.
native_language_example: From now on, communications will be sent by email.

meaning: in deep trouble; in a very difficult/dangerous situation.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression typically used with verbs like estar or verse (e.g., estar/verse en los cuernos del toro). It suggests being in a critical, risky situation with no easy way out—similar to “in hot water” or “between a rock and a hard place.” Not to be confused with coger el toro por los cuernos (“to take the bull by the horns”), which means to face a problem directly.
target_language_example: Con tantas deudas, estamos en los cuernos del toro.
native_language_example: With so many debts, we’re in deep trouble.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a replacement or alternative: one thing is done/chosen rather than another. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun or an infinitive (verb in the -ar/-er/-ir form): "en lugar de café" / "en lugar de ir". Often interchangeable with "en vez de" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Voy a tomar té en lugar de café.
native_language_example: I’m going to have tea instead of coffee.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “online” (on the internet), especially with services, shopping, classes, etc.: "comprar en línea". It can also literally mean “in line” (waiting in a queue), often said as "hacer fila" or "estar en la fila" depending on the country. Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Puedes comprar los boletos en línea.
native_language_example: You can buy the tickets online.

additional_notes: Used for things that are moving (a vehicle), functioning (a machine), or already started/in progress (a plan or project). Often with verbs like estar/poner (estar en marcha = to be running/underway; poner en marcha = to start/launch/put into operation).
target_language_example: El proyecto ya está en marcha.
native_language_example: The project is already underway.

meaning: in large numbers; en masse; as a group.
additional_notes: Used to say that many people/things do something together or at the same time. Common with verbs like salir (to leave/go out), llegar (to arrive), comprar (to buy), and asistir (to attend). It also has a more specific meaning of “in bulk” when talking about buying/producing large quantities.
target_language_example: La gente salió en masa a la calle.
native_language_example: People went out into the street in large numbers.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a physical location (in the center of something) or a position between two things/people. Also commonly used in time or situations meaning “in the middle of (doing something)” (often as “en medio de + noun/infinitive”).
target_language_example: Estoy en medio de una reunión, te llamo luego.
native_language_example: I’m in the middle of a meeting; I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Common in casual spoken Spanish to mean something will happen very quickly. Often used with verbs like "volver" (to come back) or "estar" (to be): "Vuelvo en nada" = "I’ll be right back."
target_language_example: No te preocupes, vuelvo en nada.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll be right back.

meaning: on behalf of; in the name of.
additional_notes: Used to say you act or speak representing someone else ("on behalf of") or invoking a person/authority/cause ("in the name of"). Common in formal contexts (speeches, letters, announcements). Often followed by a person, group, or institution: en nombre de mi familia / en nombre del equipo / en nombre de la empresa.
target_language_example: Hablo en nombre de todos: muchas gracias por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I speak on behalf of everyone: thank you very much for your help.

additional_notes: Used to say a place (a building, street, station, etc.) is being worked on or renovated. Often appears on signs: “Disculpen las molestias, estamos en obras.” You can use it after a noun: “El hotel está en obras” (the hotel is being renovated).
target_language_example: La calle está en obras, así que tendremos que dar la vuelta.
native_language_example: The street is under construction, so we’ll have to go around.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say something happens from time to time. Often used at the beginning of a sentence or before the verb: “En ocasiones, voy…” / “En ocasiones voy…”. Similar to “a veces” (sometimes), but slightly more formal.
target_language_example: En ocasiones salgo a caminar después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Sometimes I go for a walk after work.

additional_notes: Often used to say something is arranged, tidy, correct, or that there’s no problem. Common in questions like “¿Todo en orden?” (“Everything okay?”). It can also describe objects being orderly: “Todo está en orden” (“Everything is in order”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo está en orden.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is okay.

meaning: in order to; for the purpose of.
additional_notes: Formal prepositional phrase used to express purpose or aim. In everyday conversation, Spanish more often uses "para" or "a fin de" with the same idea. It is followed by an infinitive ("en orden a + infinitive") or by a noun phrase ("en orden a + noun").
target_language_example: Tomamos medidas en orden a reducir los gastos.
native_language_example: We took measures in order to reduce expenses.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is in a different location from here or from the place being discussed. Often used with verbs like estar (to be) or vivir (to live): "Está en otra parte" (It’s elsewhere).
target_language_example: Si no encuentras las llaves aquí, tal vez estén en otra parte.
native_language_example: If you can’t find the keys here, maybe they’re somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used to rephrase or clarify what was just said (similar to “that is” / “I mean”). Very common in both speech and writing. It often comes after a statement and can be followed by a comma: “En otras palabras, …”
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo hoy; en otras palabras, no puedo ir.
native_language_example: I don’t have time today; in other words, I can’t go.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone is in a different location, or to suggest moving/looking elsewhere. Common with verbs like estar (to be), ir (to go), buscar (to look for), or vivir (to live).
target_language_example: La reunión es en otro lugar.
native_language_example: The meeting is somewhere else.

meaning: in another time; in the past (formerly).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an earlier period, often contrasting past vs. present. It can mean “once/upon a time” or “back then,” depending on context. Similar to "antes" or "en el pasado".
target_language_example: En otro tiempo, esta calle era muy tranquila.
native_language_example: In the past, this street was very quiet.

additional_notes: Used to contrast a paper/printed version with a digital or online version (e.g., un documento en papel vs. un documento digital). It can also mean “in theory” or “according to what’s written,” similar to English “on paper” (En papel suena bien, pero...).
target_language_example: Prefiero tener el contrato en papel, no solo en digital.
native_language_example: I prefer to have the contract on paper, not only digitally.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or done only to some extent (not completely). Common in opinions and explanations: “En parte tienes razón” (you’re partly right). You can also use it to split an answer: “En parte sí, en parte no” (partly yes, partly no).
target_language_example: En parte tienes razón, pero no del todo.
native_language_example: You’re partly right, but not completely.

meaning: in parts; in portions; in installments.
additional_notes: Used to say something is divided into separate parts or done little by little. Common with payments ("pagar en partes" = pay in installments) or splitting something up ("dividir en partes" = divide into parts).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo pagar en partes?
native_language_example: Can I pay in installments?

additional_notes: Used to single out one person/thing from a group or to add emphasis. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence. Common with phrases like “(algo) en particular” = “(something) in particular.”
target_language_example: Me gusta la comida italiana, en particular la pasta.
native_language_example: I like Italian food, especially pasta.

additional_notes: Used to talk about calm/quiet situations or not being bothered: "Déjame en paz" (Leave me alone). Also appears in the phrase "Descansar en paz" (Rest in peace). Often follows verbs like dejar (to leave), vivir (to live), or estar (to be).
target_language_example: Déjame en paz, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, please.

additional_notes: Used with estar (or other verbs like correr) to say someone or something is in danger. Common in warnings and emergencies: “¡Estamos en peligro!” You can also hear “en peligro de + infinitive” (in danger of doing something).
target_language_example: El niño está en peligro; llama a emergencias.
native_language_example: The child is in danger; call emergency services.

additional_notes: Colloquial and somewhat vulgar way to say someone is nude, especially common in Spain. Use with close friends, not in formal settings; in polite speech prefer “desnudo/a”. Similar slang: “en bolas” (more common in some Latin American countries), “en cueros”.
target_language_example: ¡No abras la puerta, que estoy en pelotas!
native_language_example: Don’t open the door—I’m naked!

meaning: in small size; in a smaller version.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something reduced in size/scale (a small version, miniature, or scaled-down format). Common with verbs like ver (to see), imprimir (to print), hacer (to make), or nouns like formato/tamaño. Often contrasts with en grande (“large / full-size”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes imprimirlo en pequeño, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you print it in a small size, please?

additional_notes: Used to say you will do something face-to-face (not online/over the phone) or that someone will handle something themselves. Often used with verbs like ver (to see), hablar (to talk), conocer (to meet), ir (to go), and entregar (to hand in/deliver).
target_language_example: Prefiero hablar contigo en persona.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk to you in person.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “standing” (not sitting/lying): Estar de/en pie. It can also mean “on foot” (walking, not by vehicle): Ir/venir/andar a pie (more common) or en pie in some contexts. Used for people or things that are upright/still functioning: El edificio sigue en pie (“still standing”).
target_language_example: Estoy de pie porque no hay sillas.
native_language_example: I’m standing because there are no chairs.

meaning: (Spain, informal) “like…”, “kind of…”, “in a … way” (a filler to introduce an attitude, style, or quote).
additional_notes: Very common in casual speech in Spain, especially among younger speakers. Used to soften what you say (“en plan tranquilo” = “kind of relaxed”), to describe someone’s vibe/style (“en plan serio” = “in a serious way”), or to introduce what someone said/thought, similar to English “and I was like…”. Not used in formal situations.
target_language_example: Y yo en plan: «¿Perdona? ¿Qué has dicho?»
native_language_example: And I was like, “Excuse me? What did you say?”

meaning: in a few words; in short.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a brief summary or simplified explanation. Common in both speaking and writing. Often followed by a summary: "En pocas palabras, ...".
target_language_example: En pocas palabras, no puedo ir mañana.
native_language_example: In short, I can’t go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen shortly. Often heard as part of the fuller expression "en poco tiempo" (in a short time), and it can be interchangeable with "pronto" or "en breve" depending on the context.
target_language_example: En poco te llamo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you soon.

additional_notes: Informal (mostly Spain). You’ll also commonly hear it in the plural: "en porretas". Used with verbs like "estar" or "quedarse" to say someone is (or ends up) naked, often in a humorous or embarrassing situation.
target_language_example: Entró sin llamar y yo estaba en porreta.
native_language_example: He came in without knocking and I was naked.

meaning: first (of all); in the first place.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point in a list or argument (often followed by "en segundo lugar" = secondly, "por último" = lastly). Common in both speech and writing. It can also mean "in the first place" when giving a reason or correction (e.g., "En primer lugar, eso no es cierto").
target_language_example: En primer lugar, quiero darte las gracias por venir.
native_language_example: First of all, I want to thank you for coming.

additional_notes: Commonly means “in principle” (in theory, generally speaking). In everyday speech it can also mean “at first/initially,” especially when you’re about to add a change or exception (often followed by “pero…”).
target_language_example: En principio, podemos ir mañana, pero depende del tiempo.
native_language_example: In principle, we can go tomorrow, but it depends on the weather.

additional_notes: Used to say something should be done or discussed without other people present. Often appears with verbs like hablar (to talk), decir (to tell), and conversar (to chat): "Hablemos en privado" (Let’s talk in private). It can also describe something not meant to be public: "una conversación en privado" (a private conversation).
target_language_example: ¿Podemos hablar en privado un momento?
native_language_example: Can we talk in private for a moment?

meaning: about to happen; just around the corner (imminent).
additional_notes: Used mostly with forms of "estar" ("estar en puertas") to say something is very close to happening or arriving: an event, a trip, a change, etc. Common in Spain and understood widely; a close English equivalent is "right around the corner."
target_language_example: La Navidad ya está en puertas.
native_language_example: Christmas is just around the corner.

meaning: exactly (at a specific time); on the dot.
additional_notes: Used with clock times to mean 'exactly' with no extra minutes. Common with 'a las': 'a las tres en punto' = 'at three o’clock sharp.' It can also be said alone after a time: 'Son las tres en punto.'
target_language_example: La reunión empieza a las ocho en punto.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at eight o’clock sharp.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens where other people can see or hear it. Often contrasts with "en privado" (in private). Common with verbs like hablar (to speak), discutir (to argue), mostrar (to show), and besar (to kiss).
target_language_example: No me gusta discutir en público.
native_language_example: I don't like arguing in public.

additional_notes: Used to correct, clarify, or add emphasis—often like English “actually” or “in fact.” Common in conversation to introduce a contrast with what was just said or what someone believes: “En realidad, no…” It can also simply mean “really/truly,” depending on context.
target_language_example: En realidad, no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a brief summary or main point, often at the end of an explanation. Common in speaking and writing; you can also use it like “in short.”
target_language_example: En resumen, necesitamos más tiempo para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: In summary, we need more time to finish the project.

meaning: (to make someone) look ridiculous; to embarrass someone.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like poner/dejar (a alguien) en ridículo (“to make someone look ridiculous”) and sometimes quedar en ridículo (“to end up looking ridiculous / to make a fool of oneself”). Often used with delante de + people (“in front of”).
target_language_example: No me pongas en ridículo delante de mis amigos.
native_language_example: Don’t embarrass me in front of my friends.

additional_notes: Used to describe stopping or changing something suddenly (often with verbs like "parar," "frenar," "cortar," or "interrumpir"). It can also mean doing or saying something "dryly" or "bluntly" (with little emotion or explanation).
target_language_example: El coche frenó en seco y todos nos asustamos.
native_language_example: The car braked abruptly and we all got scared.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is done privately, without other people knowing. It often goes with verbs like "hacer" (to do), "hablar" (to talk), "reunirse" (to meet), or "guardar" (to keep). Similar to "a escondidas" (secretly/on the sly), but "en secreto" is more neutral.
target_language_example: Se reunieron en secreto para planear la sorpresa.
native_language_example: They met in secret to plan the surprise.

meaning: right away; immediately; as soon as.
additional_notes: Common in everyday Spanish to say you’ll do something now or very soon. Often used as a reply meaning “I’ll be right there / I’m coming right away.” It’s similar in meaning to “enseguida” (often written as one word) and to “de inmediato,” though “en seguida” can sometimes sound like “in a moment” depending on context.
target_language_example: Voy en seguida, espérame un momento.
native_language_example: I’m coming right away—wait for me a moment.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true, not a joke, or to show surprise or disbelief. Common in both statements and questions (often with ¿En serio?).
target_language_example: ¿En serio? No sabía nada de eso.
native_language_example: Seriously? I didn’t know anything about that.

additional_notes: An adverbial phrase used to describe how something is done: without talking or making noise. Often used with verbs like caminar, esperar, escuchar, quedarse. Similar to “en voz baja” (in a low voice), but “en silencio” means no talking at all.
target_language_example: Esperamos en silencio mientras empezaba la reunión.
native_language_example: We waited in silence while the meeting started.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is true for most of a group or in most cases. It’s common with plural nouns or groups (e.g., "las personas", "los estudiantes") and also with general situations. Similar to "la mayoría de" ("most of"), but "en su mayoría" often sounds more like an overall summary: "They are mostly..."
target_language_example: Los asistentes eran en su mayoría estudiantes.
native_language_example: The attendees were mostly students.

meaning: in their right mind; thinking clearly and reasonably.
additional_notes: Used to say that a reasonable person would (or would not) do something. Very common in negative phrases like “Nadie en su sano juicio…” (“No one in their right mind…”). It can refer to any person; the possessive changes to match: en mi/tu/su/nuestro/vuestro sano juicio.
target_language_example: Nadie en su sano juicio pagaría tanto por eso.
native_language_example: No one in their right mind would pay that much for that.

meaning: in his/her/their life; ever (usually in negative sentences).
additional_notes: Literally means “in his/her/their life.” Very common with negatives to mean “never ever / not ever,” especially with "nunca" or "jamás" for emphasis: "No he visto eso en mi vida" = “I’ve never seen that in my life.” The pronoun changes depending on who you’re talking about: "en mi vida" (in my life), "en tu vida" (in your life), "en su vida" (in his/her/their life or formal your life).
target_language_example: No he oído eso en mi vida.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard that in my life.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened while dreaming, or to contrast dream vs. reality. Often appears with verbs like "ver" (to see), "soñar" (to dream), "aparecer" (to appear), or "pasar" (to happen): "Lo vi en sueños" (I saw it/him/her in a dream). It can also be used more generally like "en sueños" = "in (my) dreams".
target_language_example: Anoche vi a mi abuela en sueños.
native_language_example: Last night I saw my grandmother in a dream.

meaning: in their right mind; thinking clearly.
additional_notes: Used with forms of "estar" (often in the negative) to say someone isn’t acting rationally: "No está en sus cabales." The possessive changes with the person: "en mis/tus/sus/nuestros cabales." You also hear "volver a sus cabales" / "recobrar sus cabales" = "to come to one’s senses."
target_language_example: ¿Estás en tus cabales? No puedes gastar tanto dinero.
native_language_example: Are you in your right mind? You can’t spend that much money.

additional_notes: Used mainly in more formal Spanish. Most often it introduces a condition or time frame: (1) "en tanto (que)" = "as long as" (condition) or "while" (at the same time). (2) It can also mean "insofar as" when talking about the extent to which something is true. In everyday speech, learners will often hear "mientras" (while) and "siempre que" or "mientras" (as long as) instead.
target_language_example: Puedes quedarte aquí en tanto termines tu tarea.
native_language_example: You can stay here as long as you finish your homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what should happen or what is supposed to be true in an ideal or expected situation, often implying that reality may be different. Commonly paired with contrast words like "pero" (but) or "aunque" (although).
target_language_example: En teoría, el tren sale a las ocho, pero casi siempre llega tarde.
native_language_example: In theory, the train leaves at eight, but it almost always arrives late.

meaning: “in times (of)…” / “during a time/era” (often used like “back in the days”).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time, often with “de” + a noun (en tiempos de crisis = in times of crisis) or with a qualifier (en tiempos modernos = in modern times). It can also introduce a past period with a nostalgic tone: en tiempos de mi abuela = in my grandmother’s days. Often interchangeable with “en la época de…”.
target_language_example: En tiempos de crisis, es importante ahorrar.
native_language_example: In times of crisis, it’s important to save money.

meaning: on land; ashore; on the ground.
additional_notes: Used to contrast with being in the air or at sea (e.g., viajar por aire/por mar vs. estar en tierra), and also to mean something/someone is down on the ground (often after falling). In some contexts it can imply being “grounded” (unable to fly) when talking about flights or aircraft.
target_language_example: Después del vuelo, por fin estuvimos en tierra.
native_language_example: After the flight, we were finally on land.

meaning: completely; across the board; on all counts.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something applies in every aspect (not just partly). Often follows a verb like ser/estar or a judgment: "está mal en toda la línea" (= it’s wrong in every way). It’s fairly formal/neutral and common in opinions, evaluations, and reviews.
target_language_example: Tu propuesta es excelente en toda la línea.
native_language_example: Your proposal is excellent across the board.

meaning: in any case; anyway; at least (if not).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion, correction, or fallback plan. Often similar to “anyway” when changing direction in conversation, or “at least” when something isn’t ideal but still true: “No puedo ir; en todo caso, te llamo.” It’s fairly neutral and common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No estoy seguro, pero en todo caso podemos preguntar en información.
native_language_example: I’m not sure, but in any case we can ask at the information desk.

additional_notes: Literally “on/in everything that is uncovered.” Often used for parts of the body not covered by clothing (skin that’s exposed), or any area that isn’t covered (e.g., uncovered surfaces). “Lo descubierto” turns the adjective descubierto (“uncovered/exposed”) into a noun phrase meaning “what is uncovered.”
target_language_example: Ponte protector solar en todo lo descubierto.
native_language_example: Put sunscreen on all exposed skin.

additional_notes: Means something is true continuously or throughout a period of time. Common in instructions and rules: "Mantenga su boleto en todo momento" (keep your ticket with you at all times). It can sound a bit formal compared with simply "siempre," but both are common.
target_language_example: Debes llevar tu identificación contigo en todo momento.
native_language_example: You must carry your ID with you at all times.

meaning: in every way; in all respects (completely).
additional_notes: An emphatic expression meaning “totally/without reservation.” It’s used to stress that something applies to every aspect of a situation or that you support/agree with someone fully. Common with verbs like confiar (to trust), apoyar (to support), estar de acuerdo (to agree), responder (to vouch).
target_language_example: Confío en ti en todo y por todo.
native_language_example: I trust you completely, in every way.

additional_notes: Often appears as **en torno a** + noun/pronoun. For location it means 'around/surrounding': *en torno a la plaza* ('around the square'). For an approximate quantity it means 'about/around': *en torno a 20 minutos* ('around 20 minutes'). Similar to **alrededor de**. Common in more formal speech/writing.
target_language_example: Hay varios restaurantes en torno a la plaza.
native_language_example: There are several restaurants around the square.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something surrounding a place/person ("around") or to give an approximate number or time ("about/roughly"). Often followed by a noun, number, or time expression. Common near-synonyms: "alrededor de" (around/about) and "en torno de" (less common).
target_language_example: Llegaremos en torno a las ocho y habrá en torno a veinte personas.
native_language_example: We’ll arrive around eight o’clock and there will be about twenty people.

additional_notes: Used to give a grand total after adding everything up (time, money, people, items). Common in everyday speech and writing. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: “En total, …” / “… en total.”
target_language_example: Pagamos 45 euros en total.
native_language_example: We paid 45 euros in total.

en un abrir y cerrar de ojos

target_language_multi_word_term: en un abrir y cerrar de ojos
meaning: in the blink of an eye; very quickly.
additional_notes: An idiomatic way to say something happens extremely fast. It’s common in spoken and written Spanish. Often used with verbs like pasar (to happen), ocurrir (to happen), or terminar (to finish): “Pasó en un abrir y cerrar de ojos.”
target_language_example: El verano pasó en un abrir y cerrar de ojos.
native_language_example: Summer went by in the blink of an eye.

meaning: in no time; very quickly (in a jiffy).
additional_notes: Common idiomatic expression (especially in spoken Spanish) to emphasize that something happens very fast. It doesn’t literally refer to the numbers; it just means “quickly.” You’ll also hear the shorter variant “en dos por tres.”
target_language_example: Dame cinco minutos y lo termino en un dos por tres.
native_language_example: Give me five minutes and I’ll finish it in no time.

meaning: at a given moment; at some point (in time).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific moment (sometimes not exactly specified) when something happens or becomes true. Common in explanations and storytelling: it can mean “at that point” in a sequence of events. Not the same as “en un momento” (“in a moment”/“in a second”), which often refers to the near future.
target_language_example: En un momento dado, me di cuenta de que estaba en el lugar equivocado.
native_language_example: At a certain point, I realized I was in the wrong place.

meaning: in a moment; in no time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very quickly or almost instantly. It’s a more literary/less common option than "en un momento" or "en un instante".
target_language_example: Vuelvo en un pensamiento.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a moment.

additional_notes: Formal/Latin American phrasing (common in Argentina/Uruguay) meaning something is taken or agreed to “as a whole” or “in full.” Often used in fixed expressions like “en un todo de acuerdo” (in full agreement) or “cumplir en un todo” (to comply completely). Not common in casual everyday Spanish; “totalmente” or “por completo” are more general alternatives.
target_language_example: Estoy en un todo de acuerdo con tu propuesta.
native_language_example: I completely agree with your proposal.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a brief summary or the main point, often after a longer explanation. It can be followed by a single word or a short phrase. Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: En una palabra, la película fue increíble.
native_language_example: In a word, the movie was incredible.

additional_notes: Used to say that an effort, attempt, search, or wait did not produce the desired result. Common with verbs like intentar (to try), buscar (to look for), esperar (to wait), and esforzarse (to make an effort).
target_language_example: Lo intenté muchas veces, pero fue en vano.
native_language_example: I tried many times, but it was in vain.

additional_notes: This is a regional/nonstandard way to say “sometimes” in Spanish. In most places and in standard Spanish, you should use “a veces” instead. You may hear “en veces” in casual speech in some regions, but it can sound incorrect in formal writing or outside those areas.
target_language_example: En veces voy al gimnasio por la mañana, pero a veces no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: Sometimes I go to the gym in the morning, but sometimes I don’t have time.

meaning: awake; not sleeping (often: staying up all night).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" or "pasar" to say you’re awake, often because you can’t sleep or you stayed up on purpose. Common in phrases like "estar en vela" (to be awake) and "pasar la noche en vela" (to spend the night awake).
target_language_example: Anoche estuve en vela pensando en el examen.
native_language_example: Last night I was awake thinking about the exam.

meaning: for sale; on sale (available to buy).
additional_notes: Used to say something is being sold (a product, house, car, etc.). Often seen on signs and listings: "Se vende" = “For sale”; "Está en venta" = “It’s for sale.” Can also appear with "poner"/"poner en venta" (“to put up for sale”).
target_language_example: Esta casa está en venta.
native_language_example: This house is for sale.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true or sincere, similar to “really” or “actually.” It can sound a bit formal or serious in everyday speech; common alternatives include “de verdad” or “la verdad.”
target_language_example: En verdad, no sé qué pasó.
native_language_example: Honestly/Really, I don’t know what happened.

additional_notes: Used to say one option/action replaces another. It’s commonly followed by a noun or an infinitive (verb in the “to …” form): en vez de café; en vez de ir. Also very similar to "en lugar de".
target_language_example: Voy a tomar té en vez de café.
native_language_example: I’m going to have tea instead of coffee.

meaning: alive; in one’s lifetime (while still alive).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is still alive, or that something happened/will happen before someone dies. Common with words like "aún" (still) and expressions like "en vida de" (during the lifetime of) or "ver" (to see) in phrases like "No lo veré en vida" (I won’t see it in my lifetime).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo aún está en vida.
native_language_example: My grandfather is still alive.

additional_notes: Used mostly in legal/official contexts to say a law, rule, contract, or policy is currently valid and applies. Often appears with verbs like "entrar en vigor" (to come into effect) and "seguir/estar en vigor" (to remain/be in effect).
target_language_example: La nueva ley entra en vigor el 1 de enero.
native_language_example: The new law comes into effect on January 1.

meaning: by virtue of; under (a law/rule); due to.
additional_notes: Formal phrase meaning “based on” or “under the authority of” something (often a law, rule, contract, or right). It can also mean “because of” in formal contexts. Common pattern: en virtud de + noun (en virtud de la ley, en virtud del contrato).
target_language_example: En virtud de la ley, tienes derecho a recibir una copia del contrato.
native_language_example: Under the law, you have the right to receive a copy of the contract.

additional_notes: A formal connector meaning “considering” or “because of,” used to introduce a reason or circumstance. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive phrase (commonly: “en vista de que” + clause = “given that…”). Similar to “debido a” or “a causa de,” but a bit more formal.
target_language_example: En vista de la lluvia, vamos a quedarnos en casa.
native_language_example: Given the rain, we’re going to stay at home.

meaning: live (not recorded); in person; live broadcast.
additional_notes: Used for events happening in real time: TV/radio/streaming ("en vivo" = live), concerts/shows (can imply "in person"), or social media ("transmisión en vivo" = live stream). Often contrasts with "grabado/a" (recorded).
target_language_example: El concierto es en vivo y empieza a las ocho.
native_language_example: The concert is live (in person) and starts at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spoken so other people can hear it (not silently/in your head). Common with verbs like leer (to read), decir (to say), hablar (to speak), repetir (to repeat): "leer en voz alta" = "to read aloud."
target_language_example: ¿Puedes leerlo en voz alta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you read it out loud, please?

meaning: in a low voice; quietly (in a whisper).
additional_notes: Used to describe speaking softly so others don’t hear. Often used with verbs like hablar (to speak), decir (to say), or pedir (to ask). Similar to “en secreto” (secretly), but this one focuses on volume, not secrecy.
target_language_example: Por favor, habla en voz baja; el bebé está durmiendo.
native_language_example: Please speak quietly; the baby is sleeping.

meaning: to love; to really like (literally: “to delight/enchants”).
additional_notes: Very common with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les encanta + singular noun or infinitive; me/te/le/nos/les encantan + plural noun. It means something is pleasing to someone (similar to “gustar”), so the thing you like is the grammatical subject: “Me encanta esta canción” = “I love this song.”
target_language_example: Me encanta el café.
native_language_example: I love coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say that one thing is physically on top of another or higher than it. Very common with objects and places: "El libro está encima de la mesa" (on the table). It can often be translated literally as "on top of"; sometimes you’d use simply "on" in English. For "over" in the sense of covering (e.g., "over my head"), Spanish may use "sobre" in some contexts, but "encima de" is a safe, common choice for physical position.
target_language_example: Las llaves están encima de la mesa.
native_language_example: The keys are on top of the table.

additional_notes: Used to talk about energy produced through nuclear reactions, especially as a source of electricity (often in contexts like policy, the environment, or science). You may also see it with related words like "central nuclear" (nuclear power plant) or "energía atómica" (atomic/nuclear energy, less common).
target_language_example: La energía nuclear produce mucha electricidad, pero genera residuos radiactivos.
native_language_example: Nuclear energy produces a lot of electricity, but it generates radioactive waste.

meaning: solar energy; energy from the sun.
additional_notes: Common in everyday and news contexts when talking about renewable energy, solar panels, or electricity generation. Often used with verbs like usar (to use), producir (to produce), or generar (to generate).
target_language_example: En mi casa usamos energía solar para calentar el agua.
native_language_example: At my house we use solar energy to heat the water.

additional_notes: Used to indicate location relative to something else. It commonly means “across from/opposite” (e.g., a building on the other side of the street). It can also mean “in front of” in some contexts, but “delante de” is the more standard way to say “in front of.” Often followed by a noun or place: “enfrente de la casa / del banco.”
target_language_example: La farmacia está enfrente del banco.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is across from the bank.

meaning: to enter (a place); to start to be in (a state/situation); to get into (a topic/argument).
additional_notes: Common preposition after "entrar". Use it for physically going into somewhere: "entrar en la casa" (enter the house). It’s also used figuratively: "entrar en pánico" (panic), "entrar en vigor" (come into effect), "entrar en detalles" (go into details), "entrar en una discusión" (get into an argument). For vehicles/large areas, Spanish often uses "entrar a" instead (e.g., "entrar al coche"), but "entrar en" is especially common with enclosed places and with many fixed expressions.
target_language_example: Cuando sonó la alarma, entraron en pánico.
native_language_example: When the alarm went off, they panicked.

meaning: between us; just between you and me (confidentially).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you want to keep private or say in confidence. It’s a shortened, slightly formal-sounding variant of "entre nosotros/entre nosotras". Often appears at the start of a sentence: "Entre nos, ..."
target_language_example: Entre nos, creo que van a despedir al jefe.
native_language_example: Just between us, I think they’re going to fire the boss.

meaning: “between us” (said by/among women) or “just between the two of us.”
additional_notes: Used to signal confidentiality or a private comment among female speakers (or a mixed group speaking as women). It’s the feminine plural form; compare: “entre nosotros” (men or mixed group) and “entre tú y yo” (between you and me). Often used as a quick aside before sharing a secret or opinion.
target_language_example: Entre nosotras, creo que él no va a venir.
native_language_example: Between us, I don’t think he’s going to come.

meaning: “between us” / “between you and me” (just among us).
additional_notes: Used to say something is private or confidential, or to share an opinion discreetly (“off the record”). Often followed by a comma: “Entre nosotros, …”. Similar to “entre tú y yo,” but “entre nosotros” can include more than two people.
target_language_example: Entre nosotros, creo que el jefe se va a ir pronto.
native_language_example: Between us, I think the boss is going to leave soon.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that a list is not complete (similar to “etc.”). It agrees in gender/number: entre otros (masc./mixed plural), entre otras (fem. plural). Often appears after several examples: “Madrid, Barcelona, entre otras ciudades…”.
target_language_example: Me gustan el café, el té y el chocolate caliente, entre otras bebidas.
native_language_example: I like coffee, tea, and hot chocolate, among other drinks.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is imprisoned or confined in a jail/prison. Often appears after verbs like estar, ir, terminar, or acabar (e.g., estar/terminar entre rejas). It can also be used more loosely to mean “behind a fence/grating,” but the most common meaning is “in jail.”
target_language_example: Después del juicio, terminó entre rejas.
native_language_example: After the trial, he ended up behind bars.

additional_notes: Used to describe interaction or relationship within a group (not involving the speaker). Often appears with verbs like hablar (to talk), discutir (to argue), mirar(se) (to look at each other), and pelear (to fight). Can also mean “to themselves” when each person is acting inwardly/independently (e.g., pensar entre sí).
target_language_example: Los niños hablaban entre sí mientras esperaban el autobús.
native_language_example: The kids were talking among themselves while they waited for the bus.

additional_notes: Used in shipping/logistics to say something will be delivered by air (faster, usually more expensive). Also commonly said as “envío aéreo” (air shipment) or “por vía aérea” (by air).
target_language_example: Si lo necesitas pronto, podemos hacer la entrega aérea.
native_language_example: If you need it soon, we can do air delivery.

meaning: "common era" (CE), the years counted from the traditional year of Jesus’s birth (roughly the same as AD).
additional_notes: Used mainly in history/archaeology/science to give a year without religious wording (CE instead of AD). It often appears in dates like “año 2024 de la era común” or abbreviated “EC” after a year. The opposite is “antes de la era común” (AEC), equivalent to BCE.
target_language_example: Roma cayó en el año 476 de la era común.
native_language_example: Rome fell in the year 476 CE.

meaning: the Christian Era; the Common Era (CE).
additional_notes: Used in dates and historical contexts to refer to years counted from the traditionally accepted birth of Jesus (equivalent to “CE” in English, and often contrasted with “antes de la era cristiana” = “BCE/BC”). You may also see “d. C.” (después de Cristo) used similarly in Spanish.
target_language_example: El Imperio romano se dividió en el siglo IV de la era cristiana.
native_language_example: The Roman Empire was divided in the 4th century of the Common Era.

additional_notes: Set phrase used to begin stories and fairy tales. Literally 'it was one time' (imperfect tense of ser: era). Commonly followed by a description of the character or setting: 'Era una vez un rey…'
target_language_example: Era una vez una princesa que vivía en un castillo.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a princess who lived in a castle.

meaning: that is (to say); in other words.
additional_notes: Used to clarify, restate, or explain what you just said. Often written with commas: ", es decir,". In speech it’s similar to “I mean” when you’re explaining, but it’s a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Vivo en Barcelona, es decir, en el noreste de España.
native_language_example: I live in Barcelona, that is (to say), in the northeast of Spain.

meaning: “That’s how it is” / “It is what it is.”
additional_notes: Common phrase used to show resignation or acceptance when something can’t be changed (often after bad news or an inconvenience). Tone can be matter-of-fact or slightly blunt. You’ll also hear it as “y es lo que hay” (“and that’s just how it is”).
target_language_example: No quedan entradas; es lo que hay.
native_language_example: There are no tickets left; it is what it is.

meaning: what’s more; moreover; in fact (to add emphasis or extra information).
additional_notes: Used as a connector to add a stronger point or an additional detail, often at the start of a sentence: “Es más, …”. It can also be used alone to emphasize/correct what was just said, similar to “in fact” or “actually.”
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo; es más, ni siquiera he empezado.
native_language_example: I don’t have time; what’s more, I haven’t even started.

meaning: 'it’s just that…' / 'the thing is…' (used to introduce an explanation or reason).
additional_notes: Very common in conversation to explain, justify, or soften what you’re about to say (often like giving an excuse). It can start a sentence by itself: “Es que…” = “It’s just that…”. In answers it can feel like “because…”, but it’s more like setting up an explanation than giving a direct cause.
target_language_example: —¿Por qué no vienes? —Es que tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: —Why aren’t you coming? —It’s just that I have to work.

meaning: “it’s a lot” / “it’s tons (of it)” (there’s a lot).
additional_notes: Common, informal-ish everyday way to say something is a lot or many. Used with singular “es” because it refers to “un montón” (“a pile/a lot”) as one amount. Often followed by “de” + noun: “Es un montón de trabajo” (“It’s a lot of work”). You can also use it as an intensifier: “Me gusta un montón” (“I like it a lot”).
target_language_example: Es un montón de dinero, no puedo pagarlo.
native_language_example: It’s a lot of money; I can’t pay it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or check information. With a statement, it means “it’s true that…”: “Es verdad que no vienes.” With rising intonation (or in questions), it means “Is it true that…?”: “¿Es verdad que no vienes?” Often followed by the subjunctive in the next clause when expressing doubt/denial (e.g., “No es verdad que venga”).
target_language_example: ¿Es verdad que mañana no hay clase?
native_language_example: Is it true that there’s no class tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a separate issue, a different case, or not the point being discussed. Often followed by a noun (e.g., “Esa es otra cosa”) or used on its own in conversation. “Esa” refers to something previously mentioned (that/that one), and “otra” means “another.”
target_language_example: Podemos ir mañana; lo del dinero, esa es otra.
native_language_example: We can go tomorrow; the money thing, that’s another matter.

additional_notes: Common in places like malls, subway/metro stations, and airports. It’s a feminine noun phrase, so you’ll often see it with feminine articles/adjectives: “la escalera mecánica”, “una escalera mecánica”. Not to be confused with “ascensor” (elevator).
target_language_example: La escalera mecánica está al lado del ascensor.
native_language_example: The escalator is next to the elevator.

additional_notes: A common way to refer to a school or institute where you learn foreign languages. Often used with a specific language: "escuela de idiomas de inglés" (English language school). In many places you may also see "Escuela Oficial de Idiomas" (EOI), a public adult language school in Spain.
target_language_example: Estoy buscando una escuela de idiomas para aprender francés.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a language school to learn French.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you mean exactly that person/thing already mentioned or pointed at. It agrees in gender and number: ese mismo (masc. sing.), esa misma (fem. sing.), esos mismos (masc. pl.), esas mismas (fem. pl.). Often used for confirmation or identification (like “that one exactly”).
target_language_example: ¿Ves ese coche? Ese mismo es el mío.
native_language_example: Do you see that car? That very one is mine.

additional_notes: Used literally for the weakest link in a chain, and very commonly figuratively for the person/part of a group, team, or process that is most vulnerable or likely to fail. Often appears with a possessive: “el eslabón más débil de…” (the weakest link in/of…).
target_language_example: En este proyecto, la comunicación es el eslabón más débil del equipo.
native_language_example: In this project, communication is the team’s weakest link.

meaning: “to believe that” / “to think so” (usually said as **eso creo** = “I think so”).
additional_notes: **Eso creer** is not a natural standalone phrase in Spanish; it sounds incomplete. In real speech you’ll most often hear **eso creo** (“I think so / that’s what I think”). If you want an infinitive construction, you’d usually say **creer eso** (“to believe that/it”).
target_language_example: —¿Vendrá mañana? —Eso creo.
native_language_example: —Will he/she come tomorrow? —I think so.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something is correct (“That’s right”) or to say something is finished/complete (“That’s it”). It can also be used to encourage someone while they’re doing something, like a coach or teacher: “Eso es, sigue así” (“That’s it, keep going like that”). Literally it’s “that is,” but in conversation it usually functions like an English confirmation.
target_language_example: —¿La salida es por aquí? —Sí, eso es.
native_language_example: —Is the exit this way? —Yes, that’s right.

additional_notes: Used to say there is nothing more to add, explain, or do. Common at the end of a list or explanation. Also used to confirm something is complete (e.g., after finishing an order or instructions). Sometimes you’ll hear the shorter “Eso es.” for “That’s it.”
target_language_example: Eso es todo por hoy, gracias.
native_language_example: That’s all for today, thanks.

additional_notes: **“Eso esperar”** by itself is not a natural/grammatical phrase in Spanish. What learners often mean is **“Eso espero”** (literally “That, I hope”), used to express that you hope something will happen or be true. Note: **esperar** can mean “to wait” or “to hope,” and it’s a common false friend with English **“to expect.”**
target_language_example: —¿Vas a llegar a tiempo? —Eso espero.
native_language_example: —Are you going to arrive on time? —I hope so.

additional_notes: Used to agree strongly with what someone just said (“Exactly!”). It can also mean “that very thing” to specify something precisely: “Quiero eso mismo” = “I want that exact thing.” Often said on its own as a short confirmation.
target_language_example: —¿Entonces nos vemos a las ocho? —Eso mismo.
native_language_example: —So we’ll meet at eight? —Exactly.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific thing or idea, often something already known or just mentioned. Common in spoken Spanish before a clause: “Eso que dices…” (“That thing you’re saying…”). Also used to refer back to something with an explanation: “Eso que no viniste…” (“The fact that you didn’t come…”).
target_language_example: Eso que dijiste ayer me hizo pensar.
native_language_example: What you said yesterday made me think.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or emphasize certainty about what was just said. Often follows a statement ("…, eso seguro") or can stand alone as a short reply. Common in conversation; you may also hear "¡Eso sí!" or "Seguro" depending on region/context.
target_language_example: Mañana va a llover, eso seguro.
native_language_example: It’s going to rain tomorrow, that’s for sure.

meaning: "that is" (but this is not a normal Spanish phrase; you usually say "eso es").
additional_notes: "Eso" means "that" (an idea/thing). "Ser" is the infinitive "to be," but after "eso" you normally need a conjugated form: "eso es" (that is), "eso era" (that was), "eso será" (that will be). You might only see "eso ser" in notes, word lists, or when talking *about* Spanish grammar rather than in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: En español, no se dice "eso ser"; se dice "eso es".
native_language_example: In Spanish, you don’t say “eso ser”; you say “eso es.”

additional_notes: Used to add an important limitation, correction, or contrast to what was just said—similar to “that said” or “mind you.” It can also emphasize a positive point after a negative one (or vice versa). Often followed by a comma: “Eso sí, …”.
target_language_example: Podemos ir en coche; eso sí, salimos temprano.
native_language_example: We can go by car; that said, we’re leaving early.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "esos" (those, near the listener / not near the speaker) + the number "cinco". It must match a plural masculine noun (or a mixed-gender group). For feminine nouns, use "esas cinco". Often used when the noun is understood from context: "esos cinco (libros)" = those five (books).
target_language_example: ¿Ves esos cinco edificios? Son muy antiguos.
native_language_example: Do you see those five buildings? They’re very old.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the part of the sky/atmosphere above a country or area that is controlled or regulated for aircraft. Common in news, travel, and aviation contexts (e.g., airspace closures, restrictions, violations).
target_language_example: El espacio aéreo está cerrado por la tormenta.
native_language_example: The airspace is closed because of the storm.

meaning: 'to wait (for)'; also 'to hope' or 'to expect' depending on context.
additional_notes:
Common meanings:
- To wait (for someone/something): "Esperar a alguien" (very common in Spain) or "esperar por alguien" (common in many parts of Latin America).
- To hope: "Espero que..." + subjunctive (e.g., "Espero que vengas").
- To expect: can mean you think something will happen (context usually makes this clear).
Not usually used with "para" to mean "wait for".
target_language_example: Te espero en la entrada.
native_language_example: I’ll wait for you at the entrance.

meaning: to wait for (someone/something); to wait to do something.
additional_notes: Use **esperar a + noun/pronoun** to mean “to wait for”: *Espero a mi amigo.* With an infinitive, use **esperar a + infinitive** to mean “to wait to (do something)” or “wait until you can”: *Espera a entrar.* (Often **esperar** is also used without **a** before a noun: *Espero el autobús* is common in many places, but **esperar a** is very common especially with people.)
target_language_example: Tengo que esperar a María en la entrada.
native_language_example: I have to wait for María at the entrance.

meaning: to expect that / to hope for that.
additional_notes: In everyday Spanish, "esperar" can mean "to expect," "to hope," or "to wait (for)." With "eso" (“that”), it often means reacting to something surprising: "No esperaba eso" = “I didn’t expect that.” If you mean “wait for that (thing),” Spanish usually adds "por": "esperar por eso" or just "esperar eso" in some regions.
target_language_example: No esperaba eso de ti.
native_language_example: I didn’t expect that from you.

additional_notes: Most often used as a reply with a subject: “Espero que no” = “I hope not.” It follows the pattern “esperar que + subjunctive” (e.g., “Espero que no llueva” = “I hope it doesn’t rain”).
target_language_example: —¿Va a llover? —Espero que no.
native_language_example: —Is it going to rain? —I hope not.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or events happening later today after it gets dark. It can refer to the evening or the night, depending on context. Often used with the near future: "Esta noche voy a...".
target_language_example: Esta noche vamos al cine.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current/next attempt or occasion, often contrasting with another time (e.g., last time). It’s common with verbs like "hacer" and "ser": "Esta vez voy a hacerlo bien" (This time I’m going to do it well), "Esta vez es diferente" (This time it’s different).
target_language_example: Esta vez no voy a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: This time I’m not going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a station on an urban underground/metro system. In many Spanish-speaking places, "metro" is the common word for the subway; in some regions you may also hear "subte" (e.g., Argentina) or "subterráneo". You can also say "la estación" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la estación de metro más cercana?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest метро/subway station?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you catch or arrive by train. Often appears with common travel phrases like “¿Dónde está la estación de tren?” (Where is the train station?) or “Voy a la estación de tren” (I’m going to the train station). In some countries you may also hear “estación ferroviaria” as a more formal synonym.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la estación de tren más cercana?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest train station?

additional_notes: Used for temporary states, feelings, conditions, and locations: Estoy cansado (I’m tired), Está en Madrid (He/She is in Madrid). Often contrasted with ser (more permanent identity/characteristics). Common present forms: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están.
target_language_example: Estoy en casa, pero mañana estaré en la oficina.
native_language_example: I’m at home, but tomorrow I’ll be at the office.

meaning: to be about to (do something); to be on the verge of.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is going to happen very soon: "estar a punto de + infinitive". Conjugate "estar" to match the subject (estoy/estás/está/estamos/están). Often implies the action is imminent (seconds/minutes).
target_language_example: Estoy a punto de salir, pero todavía no tengo las llaves.
native_language_example: I’m about to leave, but I still don’t have the keys.

meaning: to be down; to be downstairs/below.
additional_notes: Used to indicate location at a lower level (downstairs, below, down there). It can also mean being "down" emotionally (sad/low), especially with context. Often appears with a place: "Estoy abajo" (I’m downstairs/down there) or "Está abajo en la cocina" (He/She is downstairs in the kitchen).
target_language_example: Estoy abajo, en la entrada.
native_language_example: I’m downstairs, at the entrance.

meaning: to taste good; (also) to be attractive (“hot”).
additional_notes: Use **estar** (temporary state) rather than **ser**. Most common for **food/drinks**: *La sopa está buena* (“The soup tastes good”). When used about a **person**, it usually means they are physically attractive and is more colloquial: *Él/ella está bueno/a*. It agrees in gender/number: **está bueno/a**, **están buenos/as**. For health, Spanish more often says **estar bien** than *estar bueno*.
target_language_example: La tortilla está buena, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: The omelet tastes good, right?

meaning: Not correct Spanish; you usually mean “estar buscando” (“to be looking for”).
additional_notes: After “estar” (to be), Spanish normally uses the gerund (-ando/-iendo) to talk about an action in progress. So instead of *estar buscar*, say **estar buscando + noun**: *Estoy buscando mi teléfono.* You can also use **buscar** alone for a general action: *Busco trabajo* (“I’m looking for work”).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando mis llaves.
native_language_example: I’m looking for my keys.

additional_notes: Used mainly for things (food, drinks, objects): *La sopa está caliente* = “The soup is hot.” For talking about how you feel (you’re hot because of the weather), Spanish usually uses **tener calor** (*Tengo calor*). If you say **Estoy caliente** about a person (or yourself), it often has a sexual meaning (“I’m horny/aroused”), so use with care.
target_language_example: La sopa está caliente, cuidado.
native_language_example: The soup is hot—careful.

additional_notes: Used for physical or figurative proximity. It’s commonly followed by **de** + a place/thing/person: **estar cerca de** = “to be close to.” You can also use it without an object when it’s understood: **Está cerca.** Note: **estar cerca de + infinitive** can mean “to be about to” do something (e.g., **Estoy cerca de salir** = “I’m close to leaving”).
target_language_example: Mi casa está cerca del parque.
native_language_example: My house is near the park.

meaning: to be clear; to be obvious.
additional_notes: Used to say something is evident or understood. Often appears as a statement ("Está claro") or with a clause: "Está claro que..." = "It’s clear that...". Also used to agree/emphasize: "¡Está claro!" = "Of course!/Clearly!".
target_language_example: Está claro que no quiere venir.
native_language_example: It’s clear that he/she doesn’t want to come.

additional_notes: Used with a person to say you are accompanying them or in their company: "Estoy con Ana" = "I’m with Ana." In some contexts it can also imply being in a romantic relationship/seeing someone ("Está con alguien" = "He/She is with someone"), but often the context makes this clear.
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; estoy con mi familia.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m with my family.

meaning: to be with you (with you, in your company).
additional_notes: Uses the verb estar to talk about being physically with someone or in someone’s company at a moment or for a period of time. Often used to express support (“I’m with you”) or presence (“I’ll be with you soon”). Not the same as being together romantically; for that, Spanish more often uses “estar con alguien” or “salir con alguien,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: estoy contigo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m with you.

meaning: to agree; to be in agreement.
additional_notes: Used to express agreement with a person, idea, or plan. Common patterns: "Estoy de acuerdo" (I agree), "Estoy de acuerdo contigo" (I agree with you), and "estar de acuerdo en + noun" (to agree on/about something). Can also be used in questions: "¿Estás de acuerdo?" (Do you agree?).
target_language_example: Estoy de acuerdo contigo: es una buena idea.
native_language_example: I agree with you: it’s a good idea.

meaning: to be joking; to be kidding.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not serious or that something is meant as a joke. Often used in questions like “¿Estás de broma?” (“Are you kidding?”). Similar in meaning to “estar bromeando” and “estar de coña” (more informal).
target_language_example: ¿Estás de broma? No puedo creerlo.
native_language_example: Are you kidding? I can’t believe it.

additional_notes: Used with "estar" to describe a temporary physical position (standing), often contrasted with "estar sentado/a" (to be seated) or "estar acostado/a" (to be lying down). "De pie" literally means "on (one’s) feet."
target_language_example: Estoy de pie porque no hay sillas.
native_language_example: I’m standing up because there are no chairs.

meaning: to be back; to have returned.
additional_notes: Used after someone returns to a place (home, work, a city, etc.). Very common with time expressions: "Estoy de vuelta en cinco minutos" (I’ll be back in five minutes). Also works as "volver" in meaning, but with "estar" it emphasizes the state of being back now.
target_language_example: Hola, ya estoy de vuelta en casa.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m back home now.

meaning: to be behind (someone/something); to be after/in pursuit of.
additional_notes: Used for physical position (someone/something is behind another thing) and also for pursuing or looking for something/someone. In the physical sense it’s often interchangeable with "estar atrás de". It’s also used figuratively to mean someone is responsible for something (e.g., "estar detrás de un plan" = to be behind a plan).
target_language_example: El baño está detrás de la cocina.
native_language_example: The bathroom is behind the kitchen.

meaning: 'to be in' / 'to be at' (a place or situation).
additional_notes: Used with locations and situations: estar en casa (to be at home), estar en Madrid (to be in Madrid), estar en clase (to be in class). Spanish uses estar (not ser) for where someone/something is located and for temporary states. The preposition en can translate as in/at/on depending on context.
target_language_example: Estoy en casa ahora.
native_language_example: I’m at home now.

meaning: to be in bed (often because you’re sick).
additional_notes: Used for being physically in bed, commonly implying you’re ill or resting ("Estoy en cama con gripe"). It can also simply mean you’re in bed (e.g., already went to bed). In some contexts it can imply “to be bedridden” (unable to get out of bed).
target_language_example: No puedo ir a trabajar; estoy en cama con fiebre.
native_language_example: I can’t go to work; I’m in bed with a fever.

additional_notes: Used to express opposition to an idea, plan, or action. It’s often followed by "de" + a noun/infinitive ("estar en contra de algo / de hacer algo") or used in contrast with "estar a favor" (to be in favor).
target_language_example: Estoy en contra de subir los impuestos.
native_language_example: I’m against raising taxes.

additional_notes: Used to express opposition to an idea, plan, rule, or action. It’s commonly followed by a noun or an infinitive: estar en contra de la ley (against the law) / estar en contra de prohibir algo (against banning something). For people, it means being opposed to them or their side. Related: estar a favor de (to be in favor of).
target_language_example: Estoy en contra de esa propuesta.
native_language_example: I’m against that proposal.

meaning: to be working on it; to be on it.
additional_notes: Used to say you are currently dealing with a task or trying to solve something. Common replies: “Estoy en ello” (I’m working on it / I’m on it) and “Ya estoy en ello” (I’m already on it). It often implies progress is in motion but not finished yet.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, ya estoy en ello.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m already on it.

additional_notes: Uses "estar" (a temporary state), not "ser." "Enfermo" changes for gender/number: "estar enferma" (female), "estar enfermos/enfermas" (plural). Common with "de" + illness: "Estoy enfermo de gripe" (I’m sick with the flu).
target_language_example: No voy a trabajar hoy porque estoy enfermo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to work today because I’m sick.

additional_notes: Formed with estar + the gerund (esperando) to describe an action in progress: someone is currently waiting. Often followed by por + a noun/pronoun (estar esperando por el autobús) or an implied object (Te estoy esperando = I'm waiting for you). In some regions (especially Spain), "esperar" is used without "por" (Estoy esperando el autobús).
target_language_example: Estoy esperando por el autobús.
native_language_example: I'm waiting for the bus.

meaning: to be out; to be outside; (informal) to be not included / out of the loop.
additional_notes: Often used literally for location (outside or away from a place): "Estoy fuera" = "I’m outside / I’m out." It can also mean something isn’t available (e.g., an item is out of stock) or that someone is excluded/doesn’t know what’s going on (informal). If you mean "to be out of" a container/position, Spanish usually uses "estar fuera de" + noun ("Estoy fuera de la oficina" = "I’m out of the office").
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; estoy fuera de la oficina.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m out of the office.

meaning: to be talking / to be speaking (right now).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase "estar" + the gerund "hablando" (present progressive), used to emphasize an action in progress at the moment. It often appears with a subject ("Estoy hablando") or with "de" to introduce a topic ("Estamos hablando de...").
target_language_example: Ahora mismo estoy hablando con mi hermana.
native_language_example: Right now I’m talking with my sister.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase (likely a mistake).
additional_notes: Spanish doesn’t use *estar* + infinitive like this. Beginners sometimes mix up *estar* (to be) and *hacer* (to do/make). Depending on what you mean, you probably want: **estar haciendo** (to be doing / to be in the middle of doing something), **estar hecho/a** (to be made/done), or just **hacer** (to do/make).
target_language_example: *“Estar hacer”* no se usa; se dice **estar haciendo** (por ejemplo: *Estoy haciendo la tarea*).
native_language_example: “Estar hacer” isn’t used; you say **estar haciendo** (for example: “I’m doing my homework”).

meaning: to be fed up (sick and tired).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re annoyed because you’ve had too much of something. Very common in everyday speech. Often followed by “de” + noun or infinitive: “Estoy harto de este ruido” (I’m fed up with this noise), “Estoy harto de esperar” (I’m sick of waiting). Agree gender/number: “harto” (masc.), “harta” (fem.), “hartos/hartas” (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy harto de esperar; vámonos.
native_language_example: I’m sick of waiting; let’s go.

additional_notes: Uses **estar** (state/situation) + **juntos** (together). It can mean being in the same place at the same time, or being together as a couple (dating/in a relationship); context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Me gusta estar juntos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I like being together on weekends.

meaning: to be free; to be available.
additional_notes: Often used to talk about availability (time) or whether something/someone is unoccupied. For people: "¿Estás libre?" = "Are you free?" (to meet/call). For places/objects: "Está libre" = "It’s free/available" (e.g., a seat, room, table).
target_language_example: ¿Estás libre esta tarde para tomar un café?
native_language_example: Are you free this afternoon to have a coffee?

meaning: to be ready; (in some contexts) to be smart/clever.
additional_notes: Most commonly means “to be ready” (for something or to do something): “Estoy listo/a” = “I’m ready.” You can add what you’re ready for with “para” + noun/infinitive: “listo/a para salir” (ready to leave). It changes for gender/number: listo (m.), lista (f.), listos/listas (pl.). In some regions it can also mean “smart/clever,” but “ser listo” is more commonly used for that general trait.
target_language_example: ¿Estás listo para salir?
native_language_example: Are you ready to go out?

meaning: to be full; to be filled up.
additional_notes: Used for a temporary state (with estar), often about stomachs, containers, rooms, or schedules. Common patterns: “estar lleno de + noun” (to be full of) and “estar lleno/a” agrees with what is full (lleno for masculine, llena for feminine).
target_language_example: El restaurante está lleno.
native_language_example: The restaurant is full.

meaning: to be busy; to be occupied (not available).
additional_notes: Uses "estar" because it describes a temporary state. Often followed by "con" + noun or "en" + activity: "Estoy ocupado con el trabajo" (I’m busy with work), "Estoy ocupado en una reunión" (I’m busy/in a meeting). You can also say "ocupado/a" to agree with the person’s gender: "Estoy ocupado" (male speaker), "Estoy ocupada" (female speaker). Also used for things/lines meaning "in use": "El baño está ocupado" (The bathroom is occupied).
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora estoy ocupado. ¿Puedes llamarme más tarde?
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m busy right now. Can you call me later?
