additional_notes: Used to express a temporary or current feeling of pride, often with "de" + noun/pronoun or "de" + infinitive: "estar orgulloso de ti" (be proud of you), "estar orgulloso de ser..." (be proud to be...). Agree the adjective with the subject: "orgulloso" (masc. sing.), "orgullosa" (fem. sing.), "orgullosos/orgullosas" (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy orgullosa de ti.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you.

meaning: 'to be about to' (do something); also 'to be in the mood/condition for' something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with an infinitive: "estar para + infinitive" = very close to doing something (similar to "about to"). It can also be used with a noun to mean you’re not in the mood or not in good condition for something: "No estoy para bromas" (I’m not up for jokes).
target_language_example: Estoy para salir, pero todavía no tengo las llaves.
native_language_example: I'm about to leave, but I still don’t have the keys.

meaning: to be about to (do something); to be in favor of (something).
additional_notes:
Two very common uses:
1) "estar por" + infinitive = "to be about to" / "on the verge of" doing something (often something that is close to happening, or that you feel like doing): "Estoy por salir".
2) "estar por" + noun/infinitive = "to be for" / "in favor of" an idea or option: "Estoy por la idea" / "Estoy por ir en tren".
Context usually makes the meaning clear. In speech, it’s often used like "I’m leaning toward..." when choosing between options.
target_language_example: Estoy por llamar a mi mamá, pero no sé si tiene tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m about to call my mom, but I don’t know if she has time.

additional_notes: Used to express certainty. Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive ("Estoy seguro de eso" = "I’m sure of that"; "Estoy seguro de que..." = "I’m sure that..."). Uses "estar" (a temporary state/feeling), not "ser".
target_language_example: Estoy seguro de que va a llover.
native_language_example: I’m sure it’s going to rain.

meaning: to be without; to not have (something) available.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone is lacking something at the moment. Common with everyday needs: estar sin dinero (without money), estar sin trabajo (without a job), estar sin batería (phone has no battery), estar sin hambre (not hungry). It often implies a temporary situation.
target_language_example: Hoy estoy sin dinero, así que no puedo salir.
native_language_example: Today I’m without money, so I can’t go out.

meaning: “the latter” / “this last one” (the second of two previously mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to the second of two items/people just mentioned. It agrees in gender and number with the noun: este último (masc. sing.), esta última (fem. sing.), estos últimos (masc. pl.), estas últimas (fem. pl.). Often contrasted with “el primero / la primera” (the former/first).
target_language_example: Entre té y café, prefiero este último.
native_language_example: Between tea and coffee, I prefer the latter.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone lives in general (habits, diet, work-life balance, activities, values). Very common in health, fitness, and social topics. Often appears with verbs like llevar (to lead) and cambiar (to change): "llevar un estilo de vida saludable" (to lead a healthy lifestyle).
target_language_example: Quiero llevar un estilo de vida más saludable.
native_language_example: I want to lead a healthier lifestyle.

additional_notes: Used to announce or state pregnancy. It’s from the adjective “embarazada” (pregnant) with “estar” (“to be,” for a temporary/physical state). Common false friend: it does NOT mean “I’m embarrassed” (that would be “estoy avergonzada” or “me da vergüenza”). A man would say “voy a ser padre” (“I’m going to be a father”) or “mi pareja está embarazada” (“my partner is pregnant”).
target_language_example: Estoy embarazada de tres meses.
native_language_example: I’m three months pregnant.

additional_notes: Common phrase for the bright streak you see in the sky when a meteor enters the atmosphere. Often used with verbs like ver (to see) and pedir un deseo (to make a wish): "¡Pide un deseo!" It can also be used figuratively to mean a “flash in the pan” / someone or something famous for a very short time (una estrella fugaz).
target_language_example: Anoche vimos una estrella fugaz y pedimos un deseo.
native_language_example: Last night we saw a shooting star and made a wish.

meaning: to study Law (as a university major/degree).
additional_notes: In Spanish, when referring to the university subject/degree, you often capitalize it: Derecho (Law). With the verb estudiar, it commonly means you are pursuing that field of study (majoring in it), not just studying for a single law class.
target_language_example: Mi hermana quiere estudiar Derecho en Madrid.
native_language_example: My sister wants to study Law in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to agree to a plan (“OK”), to reassure someone (“It’s alright”), or to say something is acceptable. Literal meaning is “it is well,” but in everyday Spanish it usually means “OK/fine.” Tone matters: said firmly, it can also mean “Alright, that’s enough / OK, stop.”
target_language_example: —¿Nos vemos a las siete? —Está bien.
native_language_example: —Shall we meet at seven? —OK.

additional_notes: Used to say something is incorrect, unacceptable, or in a bad condition. From estar (temporary state) + mal (bad/badly). Common in moral judgments (Eso está mal = That’s wrong) and when something isn’t working well (El ordenador está mal = The computer is not working right).
target_language_example: Eso está mal. No debes mentir.
native_language_example: That’s wrong. You shouldn’t lie.

meaning: "are you okay?/are you well?" or "you’re okay/fine."
additional_notes: Uses the tú form of estar (estás). Often said as a question (¿Estás bien?) to check on someone’s physical or emotional state, especially after something happens. As a statement, it can reassure someone (Estás bien = You’re fine/okay). For a more formal version, use ¿Está bien? (usted).
target_language_example: ¿Estás bien? Te ves cansado.
native_language_example: Are you okay? You look tired.

additional_notes: Common in polite requests, especially in Mexico: "Favor de + infinitive" = "Please + verb". You’ll often see it on signs and in formal/service contexts (instructions, announcements). Similar to "por favor," but "favor de" sounds more directive/official.
target_language_example: Favor de esperar en la sala.
native_language_example: Please wait in the waiting room.

additional_notes: Common on forms and when giving personal information. Often appears with “Tu/Su fecha de nacimiento” (your date of birth) and in the format day/month/year in many Spanish-speaking countries.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu fecha de nacimiento?
native_language_example: What is your date of birth?

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting used in December. Capitalization varies (often written “Feliz Navidad”). You can also use it in longer wishes, e.g., “¡Feliz Navidad y próspero Año Nuevo!”
target_language_example: ¡Feliz Navidad, Marta!
native_language_example: Merry Christmas, Marta!

meaning: "Happy year" (used as part of New Year’s greetings).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the full greeting "¡Feliz año nuevo!" (Happy New Year!). You may also see "Feliz año" on its own on cards/messages, but in conversation people usually add "nuevo". Often said with "¡Próspero año nuevo!" (Prosperous New Year!).
target_language_example: ¡Feliz año nuevo! Que tengas un gran año.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! Have a great year.

additional_notes: A common greeting used around New Year’s Eve and New Year’s Day. You can say it to friends, family, coworkers, or strangers; it’s neutral and widely appropriate. Also often written without accents in casual text (feliz ano nuevo), but the correct spelling is “año.”
target_language_example: ¡Feliz año nuevo! Que tengas un gran año.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! Have a great year.

additional_notes: Standard birthday greeting. You can say it by itself, or add the person's name (e.g., "¡Feliz cumpleaños, Ana!"). Often used with "¡Que tengas un buen cumpleaños!" (Have a good birthday!).
target_language_example: ¡Feliz cumpleaños, Carlos! ¿Cuántos años cumples hoy?
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Carlos! How old are you turning today?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a party celebrating someone’s birthday. You’ll often hear it with possessives (mi/tu/su fiesta de cumpleaños) or with "de" + a person’s name (la fiesta de cumpleaños de Ana).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a la fiesta de cumpleaños de Carlos el sábado?
native_language_example: Are you going to Carlos’s birthday party on Saturday?

additional_notes: Literally “end of (the) week.” Used for Saturday and Sunday as a unit. Common with the preposition "el" to mean "on the weekend" (e.g., "el fin de semana"). You can also say "este fin de semana" (this weekend) and "el fin de semana pasado" (last weekend).
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do this weekend?

additional_notes: Literally “end of the world.” Used both for the literal idea (apocalypse) and figuratively to mean something is extremely far away or very remote (like “in the middle of nowhere”). Often appears with verbs like estar/quedar: “Está/queda en el fin del mundo.”
target_language_example: Ese pueblo queda en el fin del mundo.
native_language_example: That town is in the middle of nowhere (really far away).

additional_notes: Used to talk about the ending of a story, movie, book, or situation when things turn out well. Often used with verbs like "tener" (to have) or "terminar" (to end): "tiene un final feliz" / "termina con un final feliz". You can also say "con final feliz" (“with a happy ending”).
target_language_example: La película tiene un final feliz.
native_language_example: The movie has a happy ending.

meaning: cherry blossom (flower of a cherry tree).
additional_notes: Literally “cherry tree flower.” Used to talk about the blossoms themselves (often associated with spring). You may also hear the plural: “flores de cerezo.”
target_language_example: En primavera, las flores de cerezo son muy bonitas.
native_language_example: In spring, cherry blossoms are very pretty.

meaning: way of speaking; manner of talking.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person's speech style, expression, accent, or the way they phrase things. Often appears with possessives (mi/tu/su forma de hablar) or to comment on how something sounds (No me gusta tu forma de hablar).
target_language_example: Me gusta tu forma de hablar; eres muy claro.
native_language_example: I like the way you speak; you’re very clear.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how a person, group, or society lives (habits, customs, daily routines). It can also refer to a living organism as a "life form" in scientific contexts, but beginners will most often see it meaning "way of life." Often used with possessives: "mi/tu/su forma de vida" or in general statements: "una forma de vida saludable."
target_language_example: Caminar todos los días es parte de mi forma de vida.
native_language_example: Walking every day is part of my way of life.

meaning: to be part of; to belong to (a group/whole).
additional_notes: Usually used with "de": "formar parte de" + organization, team, family, project, etc. It’s slightly formal/neutral and common in writing and speech. Often interchangeable with "ser parte de" (more direct). Conjugate "formar" as needed: "formo parte", "forma parte", "formaban parte", etc.
target_language_example: María forma parte del equipo de ventas.
native_language_example: María is part of the sales team.

meaning: in front of; facing; compared to (as opposed to).
additional_notes: Used mainly as a preposition. For physical location it means "in front of" or "opposite/facing" (often interchangeable with "delante de"). In more abstract contexts it can mean "compared to" or "in contrast to" (similar to "en comparación con" or "en contraste con").
target_language_example: El banco está frente a la farmacia, frente a la plaza.
native_language_example: The bank is in front of the pharmacy, facing the plaza.

meaning: to rub your hands (often: in anticipation/satisfaction).
additional_notes: Literally “to rub (one’s) hands.” Used both physically (to warm your hands) and figuratively to show excitement, satisfaction, or anticipation—often because you expect something good for you (sometimes with a slightly mischievous/greedy tone).
target_language_example: Se estaba frotando las manos porque pensaba que iba a ganar mucho dinero.
native_language_example: He was rubbing his hands because he thought he was going to make a lot of money.

meaning: To frown; to furrow your brow.
additional_notes: Used to describe the facial expression you make when you’re angry, worried, confused, or concentrating. Often appears with verbs like "estar"/"ponerse" (to become) or "hacer" (to make): "frunció el ceño" (he/she frowned).
target_language_example: Cuando escuchó la noticia, frunció el ceño.
native_language_example: When he/she heard the news, he/she frowned.

additional_notes: In everyday Spanish, fruto seco often refers to nuts (like almonds, walnuts, pistachios), especially in snacks: frutos secos. It can also mean “dried fruit” in some contexts, but “dried fruit” is more specifically fruta deshidratada (or fruta seca in some regions).
target_language_example: Soy alérgico a los frutos secos.
native_language_example: I’m allergic to nuts.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: fuegos artificiales (“fireworks”). Common when talking about celebrations (New Year’s, festivals). In Spanish you also hear the synonym “pirotecnia” (more general: fireworks/pyrotechnics).
target_language_example: En Año Nuevo hubo fuegos artificiales en la plaza.
native_language_example: On New Year’s there were fireworks in the plaza.

meaning: crossfire; being caught in the middle of a conflict.
additional_notes: Used both literally (shooting coming from two sides) and figuratively (getting involved in or affected by an argument, dispute, or controversy). Often appears with verbs like "estar" or "quedar" (to be/get caught): "estar/quedar en medio del fuego cruzado".
target_language_example: El niño quedó en medio del fuego cruzado durante la discusión de sus padres.
native_language_example: The child got caught in the crossfire during his parents’ argument.

meaning: 'outside of' / 'out of' (not in; not included in).
additional_notes: Used to talk about being physically outside a place (fuera de la casa) or being excluded from something (fuera de la lista). It can also mean “out of” in the sense of lacking something (fuera de dinero = out of money). Often followed by a noun; contrast with dentro de (“inside of”).
target_language_example: El perro está fuera de la casa.
native_language_example: The dog is outside the house.

additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, action, or behavior that is no longer being managed or contained. Often follows a form of "estar" (e.g., "está fuera de control"). It can refer to people, emotions, events, prices, etc.
target_language_example: La situación está fuera de control.
native_language_example: The situation is out of control.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t fit the situation or is inappropriate (a comment, joke, behavior, or even an object). Often appears with verbs like "estar" ("Está fuera de lugar") or to describe something directly: "un comentario fuera de lugar".
target_language_example: Tu comentario estuvo fuera de lugar.
native_language_example: Your comment was out of place / inappropriate.

additional_notes: Used on signs or to describe machines, services, or people that are temporarily unavailable (e.g., elevators, bathrooms, phones, buses, ATMs). Common in public places: “Baño fuera de servicio.” For people, it can mean someone is off duty (e.g., a worker), but for “off duty” you’ll also hear “fuera de turno” or “no está de servicio.”
target_language_example: El ascensor está fuera de servicio, así que tenemos que usar las escaleras.
native_language_example: The elevator is out of service, so we have to use the stairs.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a country’s military air branch. Often used with a possessive or country name: “la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos”, “nuestra fuerza aérea”. Capitalization varies; it’s often lowercase in general use, but may be capitalized in official names.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo sirvió en la fuerza aérea.
native_language_example: My grandfather served in the air force.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the mental strength to resist temptations or keep doing something difficult. Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have), "necesitar" (to need), and "faltar" (to lack): "Tengo fuerza de voluntad", "Necesito fuerza de voluntad", "Me falta fuerza de voluntad".
target_language_example: Me falta fuerza de voluntad para dejar de comer dulces.
native_language_example: I lack willpower to stop eating sweets.

additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to the sport played mainly in the U.S. (with helmets and an oval ball), to distinguish it from fútbol (soccer). Often appears in sports contexts and with the verb jugar (to play): jugar al fútbol americano.
target_language_example: En la universidad, juego al fútbol americano los sábados.
native_language_example: In college, I play American football on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for sunglasses. Often used with verbs like llevar (to wear), ponerse (to put on), and olvidarse de (to forget). You can also say "las gafas de sol" (the sunglasses) or "unas gafas de sol" (a pair of sunglasses).
target_language_example: No olvides tus gafas de sol; hace mucho sol hoy.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your sunglasses; it’s very sunny today.

additional_notes: A place where artworks are exhibited (and often sold). You can also say just "galería" when the context is clearly about art. Not to be confused with "museo" (museum), which usually focuses on exhibiting rather than selling.
target_language_example: Vamos a una galería de arte este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to an art gallery this weekend.

meaning: to buy time; to gain time.
additional_notes: Used when you do something to delay a decision or event so you have more time to prepare or think. Very common in everyday speech. Literally “to win time,” but in English the natural phrase is usually “to buy time.”
target_language_example: Necesitamos ganar tiempo antes de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: We need to buy time before making a decision.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone supports themselves financially, usually through work. Often followed by "como" + job ("Me gano la vida como..."), or with "ganarse la vida" + gerund to emphasize the activity ("se gana la vida vendiendo...").
target_language_example: Me gano la vida como profesor, pero los fines de semana trabajo en una cafetería.
native_language_example: I make a living as a teacher, but on weekends I work in a café.

additional_notes: Literally “Persian female cat.” Use gata for a female cat and gato for a male cat; for the breed in general you can also say “gato persa.” In Spanish, breed adjectives usually come after the noun: “gato/gata persa.”
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene una gata persa muy tranquila.
native_language_example: My sister has a very calm Persian cat.

additional_notes: A common way to name cat breeds in Spanish: "gato" + the adjective for the breed/origin. The adjective agrees with "gato" (masculine singular): persa. For a female cat you can also say "gata persa".
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene un gato persa muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: My sister has a very calm Persian cat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a twin sister who is identical (not fraternal). In everyday Spanish you’ll more often hear "gemela idéntica" or simply "gemela" when context is clear. For mixed gender or male twins, use "gemelo idéntico".
target_language_example: Mi hermana es mi gemela idéntica; todo el mundo nos confunde.
native_language_example: My sister is my identical twin; everyone mixes us up.

additional_notes: Used to specify that someone is one of two twins who look the same because they come from the same fertilized egg (as opposed to a fraternal twin, "gemelo fraterno"). In everyday Spanish, people also commonly say "gemelo/a" or "gemelo/a idéntico/a" to match the person’s gender.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es mi gemelo idéntico, pero yo soy un minuto mayor.
native_language_example: My brother is my identical twin, but I’m one minute older.

meaning: “thanks to” (because of, due to — usually with a positive result).
additional_notes: Used to give credit or explain a cause. It’s often followed by a person/thing (“Gracias a ti…”) or an event (“Gracias a la lluvia…”). Can also be used ironically to blame someone/something, depending on tone.
target_language_example: Gracias a tu ayuda, terminé el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thanks to your help, I finished the project on time.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or gratitude that something good happened or something bad didn’t happen. You can use it in religious or non-religious contexts (often just meaning “luckily/thankfully”). Commonly placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: “Gracias a Dios, …” or “…, gracias a Dios.”
target_language_example: Gracias a Dios, llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank God you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a big store that sells many different types of products (clothes, home goods, cosmetics, etc.). Plural: "grandes almacenes". Commonly used with "ir a" (to go to) or "comprar en" (to shop at).
target_language_example: Voy al gran almacén a comprar un regalo.
native_language_example: I’m going to the department store to buy a gift.

additional_notes: Literally “great thing,” but it’s commonly used sarcastically or to downplay something: “No es gran cosa” = “It’s not a big deal / It’s nothing special.” Also appears in exclamations like “¡Gran cosa!” meaning “Big deal!” (sarcastic).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, no es gran cosa.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s no big deal.

meaning: a small contribution; doing your part (even if it’s small).
additional_notes: Literally “grain of sand.” Most often used in the phrase “poner/ aportar su grano de arena” to mean contributing a little to help a bigger cause or project. Common in everyday speech and can be used in work, community, or personal contexts.
target_language_example: Todos podemos poner nuestro grano de arena para cuidar el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: We can all do our part to take care of the environment.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the historical form of Greek used in ancient Greece (e.g., in classics, history, or language classes). As an adjective phrase, it agrees in gender/number with the noun: el griego antiguo, la lengua griega antigua, textos griegos antiguos.
target_language_example: Estoy estudiando griego antiguo en la universidad.
native_language_example: I'm studying Ancient Greek at university.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the contemporary Greek language, as opposed to Ancient Greek (griego antiguo). As an adjective + noun phrase, it agrees in gender and number if modified (e.g., cultura griega moderna = modern Greek culture).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo griego moderno en la universidad.
native_language_example: I’m learning modern Greek at the university.

additional_notes: A person whose job is to protect a place or control access (e.g., a building, store, event). Often used with definite articles: "el/la guardia de seguridad". You may also hear the shorter "guardia" when it’s clear from context. Plural: "guardias de seguridad".
target_language_example: El guardia de seguridad está en la entrada del edificio.
native_language_example: The security guard is at the entrance of the building.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an internal war within one country (factions or regions fighting each other), often in historical or political contexts. Usually appears with a country or dates (e.g., "la Guerra Civil española").
target_language_example: La guerra civil terminó hace décadas, pero todavía se habla de sus consecuencias.
native_language_example: The civil war ended decades ago, but people still talk about its consequences.

additional_notes: A neutral, formal term used in news, history, and politics. It can refer to a hypothetical scenario or a specific conflict involving nuclear weapons. Often used with verbs like "haber" (to be/there is), "evitar" (to avoid), "temer" (to fear), or "amenazar con" (to threaten with).
target_language_example: Mucha gente teme una guerra nuclear.
native_language_example: Many people fear a nuclear war.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: guitarra (guitar) + eléctrica (electric). Use it to specify an electric (not acoustic) guitar. In Spanish, adjectives usually come after the noun. You can also say: una guitarra eléctrica (an electric guitar), la guitarra eléctrica (the electric guitar).
target_language_example: Quiero comprar una guitarra eléctrica.
native_language_example: I want to buy an electric guitar.

additional_notes: Spanish uses an indirect-object structure: the thing you like is the subject, and the person is shown with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les). Common forms: “me gusta” + singular thing or infinitive (“Me gusta bailar”); “me gustan” + plural things (“Me gustan los libros”). You can add emphasis/clarity with “a mí/a ti/a él/a ella/a nosotros…” (e.g., “A mí me gusta…”).
target_language_example: Me gustan las películas de terror.
native_language_example: I like horror movies.

meaning: “to have” (as an auxiliary), or “to exist / there to be” (impersonal).
additional_notes: Haber is usually not used for possession (that’s typically tener). It’s mainly used (1) as an auxiliary to form the present perfect and other compound tenses: he/has/ha/hemos/han + past participle (He comido = I have eaten), and (2) in impersonal expressions of existence, especially hay = “there is/there are” (Hay un problema = There is a problem).
target_language_example: Tiene que haber una solución.
native_language_example: There has to be a solution.

meaning: Not grammatical in Spanish; you can’t use *haber* + infinitive like this.
additional_notes: To form the perfect tense in Spanish (e.g., “to have said”), use *haber* + past participle: *haber dicho* (e.g., *he dicho* = “I have said / I said”). If you mean “to have to say,” a more correct (and formal) structure is *haber de decir* (less common than *tener que decir*).
target_language_example: He dicho la verdad.
native_language_example: I have said the truth. / I told the truth.

additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive of the verb "estar" (formed with "haber" + past participle "estado"). It’s used after another verb (often a modal like "deber", "poder", "querer") to talk about a state in the past that happened before the main verb’s time. Example pattern: "puede/debe + haber estado + (adjective/place)".
target_language_example: Debo haber estado cansado ayer.
native_language_example: I must have been tired yesterday.

additional_notes: Periphrasis used to express an action that started in the past and continued for some time up to another past moment (or up to now, depending on context). Structure: "haber" (conjugated) + "estado" + gerund. Common with time expressions like "durante" and "por" (e.g., "durante dos horas", "por mucho tiempo"). Example conjugations: "he/has/ha/hemos/han estado esperando" (present perfect), "había/habías/había... estado esperando" (past perfect).
target_language_example: He estado esperando el autobús durante media hora.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for the bus for half an hour.

additional_notes:
This isn’t a fixed phrase; it’s two common verbs that beginners often mix up.

- Use **haber** in the impersonal form **hay** to say something *exists* or *there is/are*: **Hay una tienda aquí.**
- Use **estar** to say where someone/something *is located* or in a *temporary condition/state*: **La tienda está aquí.** / **Está abierta.**
- They can also combine in real sentences when **haber** is an auxiliary: **he estado** = “I have been” (haber + past participle of estar).
target_language_example: En mi barrio hay un supermercado, pero hoy no está abierto.
native_language_example: In my neighborhood there is a supermarket, but today it isn’t open.

additional_notes: Uses the infinitive of "haber" + the past participle "hecho" to express an action completed before another action. Common after prepositions like "después de" (after) or "por" (for), and after verbs like "sentir" (to be sorry), "lamentar" (to regret), or "alegrarse de" (to be glad) to talk about something you did earlier.
target_language_example: Después de haber hecho la tarea, salimos.
native_language_example: After having done the homework, we went out.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "haber" + past participle (llegado) to talk about an arrival that has already happened, often with a connection to the present. In Spain it’s very common for recent past actions; in much of Latin America people often use the simple past instead ("llegué").
target_language_example: Ya hemos llegado a casa.
native_language_example: We’ve already arrived home.

meaning: "to have heard" (to have previously heard something).
additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive: "haber" + past participle ("oído"). It’s used to talk about an action completed before another moment, often after another verb: "Me alegro de haber oído eso" (I’m glad to have heard that), "Dice haber oído un ruido" (He says he has heard a noise), or with modal verbs: "Debes haber oído la noticia" (You must have heard the news). "Oír" means to hear (not necessarily to listen).
target_language_example: Me alegro de haber oído la verdad.
native_language_example: I’m glad to have heard the truth.

meaning: to be time (available); to be enough time.
additional_notes: Used with forms of "haber" (almost always "hay") to say that there is time to do something: "Hay tiempo para + infinitive" (There’s time to...). Often appears in negatives too: "No hay tiempo" (There isn’t time).
target_language_example: Todavía hay tiempo para desayunar.
native_language_example: There’s still time to have breakfast.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase (likely a mistake).
additional_notes:
In Spanish, you generally don’t say *haber venir*. Depending on what you mean, you may be looking for:
- **haber de venir** = “to have to come / be supposed to come” (more formal/less common; *haber de* + infinitive expresses obligation or expectation).
- **a ver venir** (often in **dejar (a alguien) ver venir**) = “to see it coming / let someone see it coming.”
If you share the sentence you saw, it’s easier to choose the correct expression.
target_language_example: He de venir mañana temprano.
native_language_example: I’m supposed to come tomorrow early / I have to come tomorrow early.

additional_notes: Formed with the infinitive "haber" + past participle ("visto"). It’s used to talk about an action that happened before another action, often after another verb or a preposition like "de" (e.g., "después de", "antes de", "me alegro de").
target_language_example: Me alegro de haber visto tu mensaje a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m glad to have seen your message in time.

additional_notes: From the verb "hablar" (to speak). "Habla" is used for él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). It’s common in questions like "¿Habla inglés?" (Do you speak English? / Does he/she speak English?) or statements like "Ella habla inglés." For "you" informal, use "hablas inglés".
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿habla inglés?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English?

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman whose first language is the one being talked about. For a man, use “hablante nativo.” Plural: “hablantes nativos/nativas.” You’ll also hear “persona nativa” or “nativo/a,” but “hablante nativo/a” is clear and common in language-learning contexts.
target_language_example: Ella es hablante nativa de español.
native_language_example: She is a native Spanish speaker.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who learned a language from childhood (their first language). Often appears with “de” + language: “hablante nativo de español/inglés”. Also common with gender/number agreement: “hablante nativa”, “hablantes nativos/nativas”.
target_language_example: Busco un hablante nativo de inglés para practicar conversación.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a native English speaker to practice conversation.

meaning: to talk with; to speak to.
additional_notes: Used with a person (or group) to say you are talking to/with them: "hablar con + persona". Often interchangeable with "hablar con" = "to speak to" in English. Don’t confuse it with "hablar de" / "hablar sobre" (“to talk about”).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con mi jefe mañana.
native_language_example: I need to talk to my boss tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun for “with”: consigo is used with él/ella/usted (and sometimes uno). With other persons, it changes: hablar conmigo (I), hablar contigo (you), hablar con nosotros/nosotras (we), hablar con vosotros/vosotras (you all), hablar con ellos/ellas/ustedes (they/you all). Often used for “talking to yourself” or “having an inner dialogue.”
target_language_example: A veces hablo conmigo cuando estoy nervioso.
native_language_example: Sometimes I talk to myself when I’m nervous.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re discussing. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun or an infinitive: hablar de algo (talk about something), hablar de ti (talk about you), hablar de viajar (talk about traveling).
target_language_example: ¿Podemos hablar de eso más tarde?
native_language_example: Can we talk about that later?

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase ("hablar" = to speak) used after other verbs (like "quiero" or "puedo") or as a general statement. Use "Hablo español" for "I speak Spanish" and "¿Hablas español?" for "Do you speak Spanish?".
target_language_example: ¿Hablas español?
native_language_example: Do you speak Spanish?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "hablar" (to speak) + a language. You can change the language: "hablar español", "hablar francés", etc. Common questions: "¿Hablas inglés?" (Do you speak English?) and "¿Puedes hablar inglés?" (Can you speak English?).
target_language_example: ¿Hablas inglés?
native_language_example: Do you speak English?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular tú form: (¿)Hablas…? = “Do you speak…?” It can be a question with rising intonation, often written with opening/closing question marks: ¿Hablas inglés? Use the formal version with usted: ¿Habla inglés? You can add por favor to be polite.
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿hablas inglés?
native_language_example: Sorry, do you speak English?

additional_notes: A classic story-opening phrase in Spanish, especially in fairy tales and children’s stories. It uses the imperfect tense of haber (“había”) to set the scene in the past, similar to English “Once upon a time…”.
target_language_example: Había una vez una princesa que vivía en un castillo.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a princess who lived in a castle.

meaning: years ago; for years (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses "hace" + time period to say how long ago something happened ("Hace años" = "Years ago"). With present tense, it can also mean something has been true for a long time: "Vivo aquí desde hace años" = "I’ve lived here for years."
target_language_example: Hace años que no veo a Marta.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen Marta in years.

additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary or missing. Often followed by an infinitive: “Hace falta + infinitive” = “It’s necessary to…”. With an indirect object: “Me/Te/Le/Nos/Os/Les hace falta…” = “I/you/he/she/we/you all/they need…”. Also common: “No hace falta” = “There’s no need / It’s not necessary.”
target_language_example: Hace falta comprar leche.
native_language_example: We need to buy milk.

meaning: 'a long time ago' / 'for a long time' / 'it's been a long time'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about time distance. Often appears with the present tense to mean “ago”: "Vivo aquí desde hace mucho" (I’ve lived here for a long time). With "que" + present tense it means “it’s been a long time since…”: "Hace mucho que no te veo" (I haven’t seen you in a long time). It can also be a short answer meaning “a long time ago”: "¿Cuándo fue? —Hace mucho."
target_language_example: Hace mucho que no voy al cine.
native_language_example: I haven't gone to the movies in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened not long ago (relative to now or another reference point). Common with the past: "Llegué hace poco" (I arrived recently). You can also use it with "que" for emphasis: "Hace poco que vivo aquí" (I’ve only been living here a short time).
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace poco.
native_language_example: I started this job recently.

meaning: 'a long time ago' / 'for a long time'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about time in the past relative to now. With the simple past, it often means “(X) ago” (Hace tiempo vi esa película = I saw that movie a long time ago). It can also mean “for a long time” in expressions like “desde hace tiempo” (for a long time) and “hace tiempo que + verb” (it’s been a long time since...).
target_language_example: Hace tiempo que no te veo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in a long time.

meaning: to leak (let water in); (figuratively) to fall apart / fail.
additional_notes: Most literal use: a boat, roof, pipe, etc. that has a leak and is letting water in (or through). Also used figuratively for a plan, argument, or project that has serious flaws ("isn’t holding up"). Common in Spain and Latin America.
target_language_example: El barco empezó a hacer agua durante la tormenta.
native_language_example: The boat started leaking during the storm.

meaning: 'some years ago' / 'a few years ago' (said about time passed).
additional_notes: Used mainly as part of expressions like "Hace algunos años..." to mean that a certain amount of time has passed since something happened. It literally uses "hacer" in the time expression "hace" (it’s been). You can also hear "hace unos años" as a very common variant.
target_language_example: Hace algunos años vivía en Madrid.
native_language_example: A few years ago I lived in Madrid.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the reflexive form when talking about making friends for yourself: "hacer(se) amigos". You’ll often hear "hacer amigos" in general statements, and "hacer amigos"/"hacerte amigos" when speaking directly to someone. Also very common: "hacer amigos nuevos" (make new friends).
target_language_example: Me mudé a una nueva ciudad y quiero hacer amigos.
native_language_example: I moved to a new city and I want to make friends.

meaning: to be years since; (most commonly) “years ago”.
additional_notes: Used in the time expression with an impersonal form of *hacer* (usually **hace**): **hace años** = “years ago.” It’s also used with *que* to mean “it’s been years since…”: **Hace años que no lo veo.** Don’t translate it word-for-word as “make years.”
target_language_example: Eso fue hace años.
native_language_example: That was years ago.

meaning: to do (something) well; to do the right thing.
additional_notes: Often used with an object: "hacer algo bien" = "to do something well." It can also mean "to be a good idea" / "to do well to" when followed by "en": "Haces bien en + infinitive" = "You’re right to..." / "It’s a good idea to..." (more idiomatic than a literal translation).
target_language_example: Haces bien en estudiar un poco cada día.
native_language_example: You’re right to study a little every day.

meaning: “to be right to” / “to do well to” (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to give advice or say someone made a wise choice. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (hacer bien en + verb): Hiciste bien en llamarme. In the present/conditional it often means “should/ought to”: Haces bien en estudiar más. You can also use it with objects: Haces bien en no decir nada (“You’re right not to say anything”).
target_language_example: Haces bien en llevar una chaqueta; hace frío.
native_language_example: You’re right to bring a jacket; it’s cold.

meaning: to be nice weather; to have good weather (said about the weather).
additional_notes: Used with the impersonal verb "hacer" to talk about weather in general (no subject: you don’t say *el tiempo hace*). Often appears in set phrases like "Hace buen tiempo" (The weather is nice) or in the past/future: "Hizo buen tiempo" / "Hará buen tiempo". Related: "hacer mal tiempo" (bad weather).
target_language_example: Hoy hace buen tiempo, así que vamos a pasear.
native_language_example: The weather is nice today, so we’re going for a walk.

meaning: to validate/redeem (a ticket, coupon, etc.); to make good on/fulfill (a promise, check, etc.).
additional_notes: Often used with an object: hacer bueno el billete/el cupón/el cheque/la promesa. In travel contexts it can mean “to validate” a ticket; in more general contexts it can mean “to honor” or “to make good on” something so it counts or becomes effective.
target_language_example: Tienes que hacer bueno el billete antes de subir al tren.
native_language_example: You have to validate the ticket before getting on the train.

meaning: to be hot (weather); it’s hot out.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the temperature/weather. It literally means “to make heat,” but in Spanish you use the verb hacer (not estar) for weather expressions: Hace calor (It’s hot). In the past/future: Hacía calor (It was hot), Hará calor (It will be hot).
target_language_example: En verano hace mucho calor aquí.
native_language_example: In summer it’s very hot here.

meaning: to pay attention (to); to listen to; to obey.
additional_notes: Commonly used with "a" + person/thing: "hacer caso a alguien/a algo". Often appears in the negative: "No me hagas caso" = "Don’t pay attention to me" / "Ignore me." Also used when telling someone to obey or follow advice: "Hazme caso" = "Listen to me."
target_language_example: Hazle caso al médico y toma la medicina.
native_language_example: Listen to the doctor and take the medicine.

additional_notes: In real use you almost always conjugate it as **hace + time period**: **Hace cinco días** = “five days ago” (literally “it makes five days,” but the meaning is “ago”). You can replace *cinco días* with other time expressions: *hace dos semanas, hace un año*. With **desde hace + time period**, it means “for/since”: *Vivo aquí desde hace cinco días* = “I’ve been living here for five days.”
target_language_example: Hace cinco días llegué a Madrid.
native_language_example: I arrived in Madrid five days ago.

meaning: to click (with a mouse or on a screen).
additional_notes: Common in computer/phone instructions. You can also hear "dar clic" in some countries. Often followed by "en/sobre" + a button/link: "Haz clic en Aceptar" (Click on OK).
target_language_example: Haz clic en el botón de “Enviar”.
native_language_example: Click on the “Send” button.

meaning: to wait in line; to queue up.
additional_notes: Used when people form a line to wait for something (tickets, checkout, services). In many places you can also hear the synonym “hacer fila.” Often followed by “para” + infinitive or noun: “hacer cola para comprar…” / “hacer cola para el bus.”
target_language_example: Tuvimos que hacer cola para entrar al museo.
native_language_example: We had to wait in line to enter the museum.

meaning: to hurt; to cause harm (physically or emotionally).
additional_notes: Often used for physical injury (Me hice daño = I hurt myself) and for causing pain to someone else (No quiero hacerte daño = I don’t want to hurt you). Can also describe something that is bad for you: Fumar hace daño = Smoking is harmful. With an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) it shows who is hurt.
target_language_example: Me duele la rodilla; me hice daño jugando al fútbol.
native_language_example: My knee hurts; I hurt myself playing soccer.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about earning money or making a profit. Often used about work or business (e.g., a job, a company, an idea). In everyday speech you may also hear “ganar dinero” (to earn money).
target_language_example: Quiero hacer dinero con este negocio.
native_language_example: I want to make money with this business.

additional_notes: Used in time expressions with **hacer** (almost always as **hace**): **Hace dos días** = “two days ago.” You can also say **Hace dos días que + verb** (“It’s been two days since…”). Not the same as **en dos días** (“in two days,” in the future).
target_language_example: Hace dos días vi a Marta en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I saw Marta at the supermarket two days ago.

additional_notes: Spanish uses the verb "hacer" in the impersonal expression "hace + time period" to say how long ago something happened. It’s almost always used as "hace" (present tense): "hace dos horas" = two hours ago. You can change the number: "hace una hora" (an hour ago), "hace tres días" (three days ago).
target_language_example: Salí de casa hace dos horas.
native_language_example: I left home two hours ago.

additional_notes: In time expressions, Spanish uses an impersonal form of **hacer** (almost always **hace**) to talk about how much time has passed: **Hace + time period** = “(It was) … ago” or “It’s been …”. You’ll usually see it as **Hace dos meses** (not *Hacer dos meses* in a normal sentence).
target_language_example: Hace dos meses empecé este trabajo.
native_language_example: I started this job two months ago.

additional_notes: Spanish uses "hacer" (most often in the form "hace") to talk about how much time has passed since something happened. In practice you’ll almost always say "hace dos semanas" = "two weeks ago." You can also use "Hace dos semanas que..." = "It’s been two weeks since..."
target_language_example: Llegué a Madrid hace dos semanas.
native_language_example: I arrived in Madrid two weeks ago.

meaning: to make love; to have sex (euphemistic).
additional_notes: A common, relatively gentle way to say “to have sex.” It can sound romantic, but in many contexts it simply means “to have sex.” Used with the verb hacer (yo hago, tú haces, etc.). Example: hacer el amor con alguien = “to make love with/to someone.”
target_language_example: Ellos hicieron el amor anoche.
native_language_example: They made love last night.

meaning: to make a fool of yourself; to embarrass yourself.
additional_notes: Used when someone does something that looks silly or causes embarrassment, often in public. Common with reflexive pronouns to specify who is embarrassed: “hacer el ridículo” / “hacer el ridículo delante de…” (in front of…). You can also hear “no hagas el ridículo” (“don’t make a fool of yourself”).
target_language_example: No quiero hacer el ridículo delante de mis amigos.
native_language_example: I don’t want to make a fool of myself in front of my friends.

meaning: to act silly; to fool around; to play dumb.
additional_notes: Common, informal expression meaning you’re behaving foolishly or wasting time instead of being serious. It can be playful (“Stop messing around”) or mildly critical (“Don’t be an idiot”). Often used with "estar" to describe someone’s behavior at the moment: "Estás haciendo el tonto."
target_language_example: Deja de hacer el tonto y ven a ayudarme.
native_language_example: Stop fooling around and come help me.

additional_notes: Used when one person or situation causes another person to wait. Very common in complaints/apologies. Usually takes an indirect object: “hacer esperar a alguien” (to keep someone waiting). In the reflexive form “hacerse esperar,” it means “to be late / keep people waiting on purpose” (often jokingly or slightly critical).
target_language_example: Perdón por hacerte esperar; había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: Sorry for making you wait; there was a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is needed or missing. Common patterns: (1) "Me/Te/Le hace falta + noun" = "I/you/he/she need(s) + noun" (literally, "it makes a lack to me/you..."). (2) "Hace falta + infinitive" = "It’s necessary to + verb" (e.g., "Hace falta estudiar"). Often interchangeable with "necesitar" in everyday speech, but the grammar is different (it agrees with what’s needed: "Hace falta una silla" / "Hacen falta dos sillas").
target_language_example: Me hace falta un bolígrafo.
native_language_example: I need a pen.

additional_notes: Common in Latin America. It means to have a party or go out partying. Often used with "hacer fiesta + en" (place) or "por" (reason): "hacer fiesta en mi casa" (party at my house), "hacer fiesta por tu cumpleaños" (party for your birthday). In Spain, learners may hear "ir de fiesta" or "salir de fiesta" more often for "to go partying."
target_language_example: Vamos a hacer fiesta en mi casa el sábado.
native_language_example: We’re going to party at my house on Saturday.

meaning: to face; to deal with (a difficult situation).
additional_notes: Used for confronting problems, challenges, or responsibilities. Often followed by “a” + noun/infinitive: “hacer frente a un problema / a la situación / a pagar…”. It can also mean “to stand up to” someone in a conflict.
target_language_example: Tenemos que hacer frente a este problema cuanto antes.
native_language_example: We have to deal with this problem as soon as possible.

meaning: to be cold (weather); to be chilly.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the temperature, not how a person feels. It’s an impersonal expression: you say "Hace frío" (It’s cold), not *"es frío" for the weather. To say a person feels cold, use "tener frío" (e.g., "Tengo frío").
target_language_example: Hace frío hoy, así que ponte una chaqueta.
native_language_example: It’s cold today, so put on a jacket.

meaning: to be funny; to amuse; to find (something) funny.
additional_notes: Used to talk about humor or amusement. Most often: "Me hace gracia" = "It makes me laugh / I find it funny." Can also mean "to amuse someone" ("Le hago gracia") or, in some contexts, "to like" in a light way (often about a person/thing that seems charming: "Me hace gracia"). Not the same as "hacer una gracia" (to do a favor/act of kindness).
target_language_example: Me hace gracia cómo lo dice.
native_language_example: I find the way he/she says it funny.

meaning: to make history; to go down in history.
additional_notes: Used when someone/something achieves something historic or groundbreaking. It can be literal (a record or first-ever event) or more general (an achievement people will remember). Often used in news and sports. Be careful: it doesn’t mean “to study history” (that’s “estudiar historia”) or “to tell a story” (that’s “contar una historia”).
target_language_example: La atleta hizo historia al ganar tres medallas de oro.
native_language_example: The athlete made history by winning three gold medals.

meaning: to look forward to (something); to be excited about (something).
additional_notes: Used to express that something makes you feel excited, happy, or eager in anticipation. The thing you’re looking forward to is usually introduced with “me/te/le/nos/les”: “Me hace ilusión…” (I’m excited about…). Common patterns: “Me hace ilusión + infinitive” (Me hace ilusión verte = I’m looking forward to seeing you) or “Me hace ilusión que + subjunctive” (Me hace ilusión que vengas = I’m happy/excited that you’re coming). Not the same as “tener ilusión” (to have hope/enthusiasm).
target_language_example: Me hace ilusión verte este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m looking forward to seeing you this weekend.

meaning: to match; to go well together.
additional_notes: Used to say that things look good together (colors, clothes, shoes and a bag, furniture, etc.). Often appears as "hacer juego con" + something: "Esta camisa hace juego con tus pantalones". In some regions you may also hear "combinar" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Estos zapatos hacen juego con el vestido.
native_language_example: These shoes match the dress.

additional_notes: Common daily routine phrase: you tidy the sheets/blankets and arrange the bed after getting up. In some contexts it can also mean “to prepare the bed” (for sleeping), but most often it’s “make the bed.” Used with the verb hacer (yo hago, tú haces, etc.).
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer la cama antes de salir.
native_language_example: I have to make the bed before leaving.

additional_notes: Used for getting your luggage ready before a trip. Often appears as "hacer las maletas" when talking about packing more than one bag, or in general. Common with "para" + destination/purpose: "hacer la maleta para el viaje". Similar phrase: "preparar la maleta" (to get the suitcase ready).
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer la maleta para mañana.
native_language_example: I have to pack for tomorrow.

meaning: to live/lead a (certain kind of) life.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s lifestyle or routine, often with an adjective: hacer una vida tranquila/normal/sana (“to live a calm/normal/healthy life”). It also appears in expressions like hacerle la vida imposible a alguien (“to make someone’s life impossible”). In some regions, it can be a euphemism for doing sex work, depending on context.
target_language_example: Desde que se mudaron al pueblo, hacen una vida más tranquila.
native_language_example: Since they moved to the town, they live a calmer life.

meaning: to pack (your bags); to pack up.
additional_notes: Used when preparing luggage to travel or when leaving a place (e.g., moving out). Often said with verbs like "tener que" (have to) or "ir a" (be going to): "Tengo que hacer las maletas" / "Voy a hacer las maletas".
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer las maletas porque mañana salimos temprano.
native_language_example: I have to pack my bags because we’re leaving early tomorrow.

meaning: to make up; to reconcile (after an argument).
additional_notes: Used when people stop being angry and return to friendly terms after a fight or disagreement. Often used with "con": "hacer las paces con alguien" = "make up with someone." You’ll also hear it in the reflexive form "hacerse las paces" (less common).
target_language_example: Después de la discusión, hicimos las paces y fuimos a cenar juntos.
native_language_example: After the argument, we made up and went to dinner together.

additional_notes: Uses the verb hacer + infinitive to express causing someone to do something. Often followed by an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les (e.g., Me hiciste llorar = You made me cry). In the past tense, hacer changes: hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicieron.
target_language_example: Esa película me hizo llorar.
native_language_example: That movie made me cry.

additional_notes: Used to talk about behaving ethically or making the best moral choice in a situation. It’s a common, neutral phrase (not slang). You can change the tense as needed: "Hice lo correcto" (I did the right thing), "Haz lo correcto" (Do the right thing).
target_language_example: Sé que es difícil, pero tienes que hacer lo correcto.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but you have to do the right thing.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather/temperature, not that a person ‘makes’ cold. Spanish often uses hacer + temperature words: hace frío (it’s cold), hace calor (it’s hot). You can change the intensity with mucho (very/a lot), or with other adverbs like bastante (quite) or tan (so).
target_language_example: En invierno hace mucho frío aquí.
native_language_example: In winter it’s very cold here.

meaning: to make a lot of noise.
additional_notes: Common with people, parties, pets, traffic, or machines. Conjugate "hacer" to match the subject (hago, hace, hacen, etc.). You can also say "hacer ruido" (make noise) or "hacer demasiado ruido" (make too much noise).
target_language_example: Los vecinos hacen mucho ruido por la noche.
native_language_example: The neighbors make a lot of noise at night.

meaning: “a long time ago” / “it’s been a long time.”
additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say that a lot of time has passed. Very common in phrases like: “Hace mucho tiempo que…” (It’s been a long time since…), “Hace mucho tiempo” (a long time ago), and in questions like “¿Hace mucho tiempo?” (Was it a long time ago?). Often uses the verb “hacer” in the third-person singular: “hace.”
target_language_example: Hace mucho tiempo que no te veo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in a long time.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long ago something happened or how long it has been since an event. It’s often used as **hace muchos años** (present tense), and it can be followed by **que** + a verb to introduce what happened: **Hace muchos años que no lo veo** (“I haven’t seen him in many years”).
target_language_example: Hace muchos años que no visito a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: I haven’t visited my grandparents in many years.

meaning: to make (someone) pay; to make (someone) pay for something.
additional_notes: Used when one person causes another to pay money or suffer consequences. Common patterns: "hacer pagar algo a alguien" (make someone pay for something) and "hacerle pagar a alguien" (make someone pay). In the second pattern, an indirect object pronoun is often used (me/te/le/nos/les). Depending on context it can be literal (money) or figurative (revenge: "hacer pagar" = make them pay for what they did).
target_language_example: El jefe me hizo pagar los daños.
native_language_example: The boss made me pay for the damages.

meaning: to break/smash into pieces; to tear to pieces.
additional_notes: Used for physically breaking something (a glass, a phone) or tearing something (paper, clothing) into pieces. In some contexts it can also be figurative (e.g., “hacer pedazos a alguien” = to destroy someone emotionally or defeat them badly). Often appears as “hacerlo pedazos” (to smash it to pieces).
target_language_example: Se me cayó el vaso y se hizo pedazos.
native_language_example: The glass fell from my hands and shattered into pieces.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to say “to urinate,” especially with children or in casual conversation. Also said as “hacer pipí.” In many places you’ll also hear “ir al baño” (“to go to the bathroom”) as a more neutral/polite option.
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo que hacer pis.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to pee.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about asking in general ("I like to ask questions"), or in a situation like class, work, or an interview. In Spanish you often use hacer (to do/make) + preguntas rather than a single verb. You can also say preguntar (to ask), but hacer preguntas emphasizes the activity of asking multiple questions.
target_language_example: Si no entiendes, puedes hacer preguntas.
native_language_example: If you don’t understand, you can ask questions.

meaning: to make (something) come true; to make (something) a reality.
additional_notes: Used for achieving a dream, plan, or goal. Very common with nouns like sueño (dream), deseo (wish), and proyecto (project). You can say it transitively (Hicieron realidad el sueño) or with a pronoun for emphasis (Hacerlo realidad = make it come true).
target_language_example: Con mucho esfuerzo, hizo realidad su sueño de viajar por el mundo.
native_language_example: With a lot of effort, she/he made her/his dream of traveling the world come true.

additional_notes: Used for any kind of noise (talking loudly, music, machines, etc.). Often appears in requests or complaints: "No hagas ruido" (Don’t make noise), "Hay mucho ruido" (There’s a lot of noise).
target_language_example: Por favor, no hagas ruido; el bebé está durmiendo.
native_language_example: Please, don’t make noise; the baby is sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with impersonal "hacer" to talk about weather conditions: "Hace sol" = "It’s sunny." Often contrasts with other weather phrases like "Hace frío" (It’s cold) or "Hace calor" (It’s hot). You can add time expressions: "Hoy hace sol" (Today it’s sunny), "Mañana hará sol" (Tomorrow it’ll be sunny).
target_language_example: Hoy hace sol, vamos al parque.
native_language_example: It’s sunny today; let’s go to the park.

meaning: to make (something) ring/sound; to ring (e.g., a bell, alarm, phone).
additional_notes: Used with an object: hacer sonar + noun (el timbre, la alarma, el teléfono, una canción). It means you cause the sound to happen (often by pressing/playing). Similar to "tocar" (to play an instrument) or "sonar" (to sound on its own), but "hacer sonar" emphasizes making it sound.
target_language_example: Hizo sonar el timbre dos veces.
native_language_example: He/She rang the doorbell twice.

additional_notes: Common in many Spanish-speaking regions (especially Latin America) to mean “do homework.” In Spain, you’ll often hear "hacer los deberes" instead. You can also say "hacer la tarea" (the homework) or "hacer tarea" (homework in general).
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer tarea después de cenar.
native_language_example: I have to do homework after dinner.

meaning: to do everything possible; to do your best.
additional_notes: Used to say you will make the maximum effort to achieve something. Common in promises/apologies: "Haré todo lo posible" (I’ll do everything I can). Often followed by "para" + infinitive: "Haremos todo lo posible para llegar a tiempo" (We’ll do everything possible to arrive on time).
target_language_example: Haré todo lo posible para ayudarte hoy.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to help you today.

meaning: to cheat (e.g., on a test, in a game).
additional_notes: Used for cheating in games, exams, sports, or situations where someone breaks the rules to gain an unfair advantage. Often appears with "en" + activity: "hacer trampa en un examen" (cheat on an exam). You can also say "No hagas trampa" (“Don’t cheat”).
target_language_example: No hagas trampa en el examen.
native_language_example: Don’t cheat on the exam.

meaning: to be three months ago (in the expression “hace tres meses”).
additional_notes: Spanish often uses “hace + time period” to talk about how long ago something happened: “Hace tres meses” = “Three months ago.” You’ll usually see it as “hace tres meses” (with “hace” meaning “ago”), often with a verb in the present: “Llegué hace tres meses” = “I arrived three months ago.” You can also use “hace tres meses que + verb” to mean “it’s been three months since…”.
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace tres meses.
native_language_example: I started this job three months ago.

meaning: '(it’s been) three weeks' / 'three weeks ago' (to say how long ago something happened).
additional_notes: This is usually used conjugated as **hace tres semanas** (present) to mean “three weeks ago / it’s been three weeks.” It often appears in patterns like **Hace tres semanas que + verb** (“It’s been three weeks since...”) or **Va a hacer tres semanas que...** (“It’s going to be three weeks since...”). Here **hacer** doesn’t mean “to do/make,” but works like “ago / it’s been.”
target_language_example: Hace tres semanas que no lo veo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him in three weeks.

meaning: to tear to pieces; to shred (something).
additional_notes: Means breaking or ripping something into many small pieces (paper, cloth, etc.). It can also be used figuratively to mean ruining/destroying something (plans, hopes). Often used with an object: "Hizo trizas la carta". Similar to "hacer pedazos".
target_language_example: Hizo trizas la carta antes de tirarla a la basura.
native_language_example: He tore the letter to pieces before throwing it in the trash.

meaning: to work a few hours (often extra hours).
additional_notes: Uses hacer + a time amount (unas horas = “a few hours”) to talk about putting in some work time. Very common in work contexts, and often implies extra hours beyond your normal schedule, especially when you add extra: hacer unas horas extra. You can specify where: hacer unas horas en el bar.
target_language_example: Hoy no puedo salir; tengo que hacer unas horas en el trabajo.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I have to work a few hours at work.

additional_notes: This is the time expression used to say how long ago something happened. In real sentences it’s almost always conjugated as “hace unos días” (literally “it’s been a few days”). You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence: “Hace unos días…” / “…hace unos días.”
target_language_example: Te escribí hace unos días.
native_language_example: I wrote to you a few days ago.

meaning: to be windy (for the wind to blow).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather. It literally means “to make wind,” but in English you normally say “it’s windy” or “the wind is blowing.” Often used in the impersonal form: “Hace viento.”
target_language_example: Hoy hace viento, así que lleva una chaqueta.
native_language_example: It’s windy today, so bring a jacket.

meaning: “to do it with” (often: “to have sex with”).
additional_notes: “Hacerlo” literally means “to do it,” but very commonly works as a euphemism for sex. With “con + person,” it often means “to have sex with (someone).” You can also use it more generally to mean “to do it with (something/someone)” depending on context.
target_language_example: No quiero hacerlo con él.
native_language_example: I don’t want to do it with him. (Often: I don’t want to have sex with him.)

additional_notes: Reflexive form of "hacer" (to do/make). Very commonly used to express a change or transformation: "hacerse + noun/adjective" = "to become" (Se hizo médico / Se hizo famoso / Se hizo viejo). It can also mean "to pretend" in set phrases like "hacerse el/la + adjective" (e.g., hacerse el tonto = to play dumb).
target_language_example: Se hizo médico a los 30 años.
native_language_example: He became a doctor at 30.

meaning: to take charge of; to take responsibility for (something/someone).
additional_notes: Often used with "de" ("hacerse cargo de") to mean taking responsibility, dealing with a situation, or taking care of a person/thing. It can imply stepping in to manage or handle something: "Me hago cargo" can mean "I’ll take care of it / I’ll handle it."
target_language_example: Cuando mi mamá se fue, me hice cargo de mi hermano menor.
native_language_example: When my mom left, I took responsibility for my younger brother.

meaning: to get dark; for night to fall.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the time of day changing naturally as evening arrives. Often used with an indirect object to say it got dark on someone: "Se me hizo de noche" = "It got dark on me" (I was out later than expected). Similar ideas: "se hace tarde" (it’s getting late), "anochecer" (to get dark).
target_language_example: Se nos hizo de noche en el camino y ya no vimos bien.
native_language_example: It got dark on us on the way and we couldn’t see well anymore.

meaning: to play dumb; to pretend not to understand.
additional_notes: Used when someone acts like they don’t know or didn’t notice something (often on purpose to avoid responsibility). Common in conversation and can sound accusatory depending on tone. Conjugates like a reflexive verb: me hago el tonto, se hace el tonto, etc.
target_language_example: No te hagas el tonto: sabes perfectamente lo que pasó.
native_language_example: Don’t play dumb—you know perfectly well what happened.

meaning: to get your hopes up (often unrealistically).
additional_notes: Used when someone starts believing something good will happen, sometimes without much evidence. Often appears in the negative: “No te hagas ilusiones” = “Don’t get your hopes up.” Can also be used with “con”: “Se hizo ilusiones con la idea de…” (He/She got carried away / got hopeful about the idea of…).
target_language_example: No te hagas ilusiones: no creo que nos den el trabajo hoy.
native_language_example: Don’t get your hopes up: I don’t think they’ll give us the job today.

meaning: to pretend to be (someone/something); to pass oneself off as.
additional_notes: Used when someone claims a false identity (often to deceive). It’s reflexive (hacerse), and it’s followed by a noun phrase: hacerse pasar por + un médico/mi hermano/la policía. In the past: se hizo pasar por…, and in the present: se hace pasar por….
target_language_example: Se hizo pasar por médico para entrar al hospital.
native_language_example: He pretended to be a doctor to get into the hospital.

meaning: to pee (yourself); to need to pee badly.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to talk about urinating, especially for kids or in casual situations. Literally "to make oneself pee." Use it for accidents ("I peed myself") or urgency ("I really need to pee"). In more neutral/formal contexts, people may say "orinar" or "hacer pipí".
target_language_example: ¡Me estoy haciendo pis! ¿Dónde está el baño?
native_language_example: I really need to pee! Where is the bathroom?

meaning: to make yourself liked; to win people’s affection.
additional_notes: Often used to talk about someone behaving in a sweet/charming way so others will like them, or about earning affection over time. It can be reflexive about yourself (Me hago querer) or about someone/something (Ese perro se hace querer = “That dog is easy to love / wins you over”). In some contexts it can sound a bit teasing or slightly ironic, depending on tone.
target_language_example: Con su forma de ser, se hace querer por todos.
native_language_example: With his/her way of being, he/she makes everyone like him/her.

meaning: to get late; to be getting late.
additional_notes: Impersonal expression with "se": the subject is the time (it’s getting late), not a person. Commonly used to say you should leave or hurry up. Often appears as "Se hace tarde" (It’s getting late) or "Se nos hace tarde" (It’s getting late for us / We’re running late).
target_language_example: Se hace tarde; mejor nos vamos ya.
native_language_example: It’s getting late; we’d better leave now.

meaning: to be torn to shreds; to fall apart (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used for things that rip or break into many pieces: "La ropa se hizo trizas". It’s also common figuratively for someone being emotionally devastated: "Me hice trizas" (= I was shattered). Often appears with a reflexive pronoun (se/me/te/nos).
target_language_example: Con el viento fuerte, la bandera se hizo trizas.
native_language_example: With the strong wind, the flag was torn to shreds.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or direction downward. Common with verbs like ir (to go), mirar (to look), caer (to fall), and bajar (to go down). It refers to direction rather than a fixed location (contrast: 'abajo' = 'downstairs/down below').
target_language_example: Mira hacia abajo antes de cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: Look down before crossing the street.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction in the speaker’s direction (closer to where “here” is). Often heard in speech; in some regions people may also say “para acá.” It contrasts with “hacia allá” (toward there).
target_language_example: Ven hacia acá, por favor.
native_language_example: Come this way, please.

meaning: toward here; this way (in this direction).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward the speaker’s location. Often paired with verbs of movement like venir, caminar, correr: “Ven hacia aquí.” In everyday speech, “ven aquí” is more common and direct; “hacia aquí” emphasizes direction (toward here) rather than just the destination (here).
target_language_example: Ven hacia aquí, por favor.
native_language_example: Come this way, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about direction or movement toward a higher position. Often appears after verbs like mirar (to look), levantar (to lift/raise), subir (to go up), or mover (to move). Can also refer to location/placement (e.g., pointing upward).
target_language_example: Mira hacia arriba: hay un pájaro en el árbol.
native_language_example: Look up: there’s a bird in the tree.

meaning: 'back' / 'backward(s)' (toward the rear or toward the past).
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or direction opposite of forward: Ir/andar/moverse hacia atrás (to go/walk/move backward). Also used for looking or thinking about the past: mirar hacia atrás (to look back). Often interchangeable with "para atrás" in everyday speech, though "hacia atrás" can sound a bit more neutral/formal for direction.
target_language_example: Da un paso hacia atrás, por favor.
native_language_example: Take a step back, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction toward the speaker or the side that is closer/nearer in the situation. Common in giving directions or instructions, often with verbs like venir (to come), girar (to turn), mirar (to look), or mover (to move).
target_language_example: Ven hacia este lado, por favor.
native_language_example: Come this way, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that has happened or has been true from the past up to the present. Very common with the present perfect ("he/has"), e.g., "Hasta ahora he estudiado...". It can also be used at the end of a statement to mean "so far" ("Todo bien hasta ahora").
target_language_example: Hasta ahora, todo ha salido bien.
native_language_example: So far, everything has gone well.

meaning: up to there; that’s as far as (it goes).
additional_notes: Used to mark a limit or boundary (in distance, amount, or what you’re willing to accept). Often implies “no more than that” or “stop there.” In conversation it can mean “I agree/understand up to that point, but not beyond.”
target_language_example: Te ayudo hasta ahí, pero lo demás tienes que hacerlo tú.
native_language_example: I’ll help you up to that point, but you have to do the rest yourself.

meaning: 'up to here' / 'until now' / 'that’s as far as (we go)' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly used to mark a limit in place (Hasta aquí llega el autobús = the bus goes up to here), time (Hasta aquí, todo bien = up to now, everything’s fine), or to stop/finish something (Hasta aquí la reunión = the meeting ends here). In conversation it can also mean “that’s it” or “enough” when you want to end a situation.
target_language_example: Hasta aquí hemos llegado; mañana seguimos.
native_language_example: This is as far as we’ve gotten; we’ll continue tomorrow.

meaning: to a certain extent; up to a point.
additional_notes: Used to partially agree or to say something is true only in part. Often followed by a clarification (e.g., “..., pero...” / “..., aunque...”).
target_language_example: Estoy de acuerdo contigo hasta cierto punto, pero creo que también hay otros factores.
native_language_example: I agree with you up to a point, but I think there are other factors too.

additional_notes: Used as a casual goodbye meaning you’ll see the person later (often later the same day). It’s short for longer goodbyes like “hasta después” (until later) or “hasta luego” (see you later). Not typically used for a specific appointment time—more for a general “later.”
target_language_example: Tengo que irme; hasta después.
native_language_example: I have to go; see you later.

meaning: “as far as” / “up to where” (limit or extent).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a limit in space, time, degree, or knowledge. Common patterns: (1) physical limit: “hasta donde + verb” = “as far as + verb” (often with movement verbs like llegar, caminar). (2) knowledge/uncertainty: “hasta donde yo sé/recuerdo/entiendo” = “as far as I know/remember/understand.” Often appears with “llegar”: “hasta donde llega…” = “as far as … reaches/goes.”
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, la tienda cierra a las ocho.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the store closes at eight.

meaning: (vulgar) “up to my neck” / totally fed up / swamped.
additional_notes: Very informal and crude (literally “up to the ass”). Common in Spain. Often used as **estar hasta el culo de + noun** to mean being overwhelmed by something (“swamped with”) or fed up with it. Without **de**, it can also mean extremely drunk in some contexts.
target_language_example: Estoy hasta el culo de trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m swamped with work.

meaning: to the core; through and through.
additional_notes: Literally “to the marrow.” Used to emphasize that something is deep or essential (often about identity, beliefs, or feelings): *mexicano hasta el tuétano* (“Mexican to the core”), *feminista hasta el tuétano* (“feminist through and through”). It typically comes after the adjective/noun it intensifies.
target_language_example: Soy mexicano hasta el tuétano.
native_language_example: I’m Mexican to the core.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen from now up to a specific time already mentioned or understood. Often used as a casual sign-off meaning you’ll meet or talk again at that time (e.g., “Nos vemos mañana. Hasta entonces.”).
target_language_example: La reunión es el jueves; hasta entonces, seguimos en contacto.
native_language_example: The meeting is on Thursday; until then, we’ll stay in touch.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen or last up to the evening, or as a casual farewell meaning you’ll see someone later tonight. Often shortened to just "hasta la noche" or "hasta esta noche" depending on context.
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; trabajo hasta la noche.
native_language_example: I can’t talk now; I work until tonight.

additional_notes: A common goodbye said when you expect to see the person again. Literally means “until the next (time)”; “la próxima” is short for “la próxima vez” (“the next time”). Often used by itself as a friendly farewell.
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. ¡Hasta la próxima!
native_language_example: Well, I’m leaving. See you next time!

meaning: fucking fed up; at your limit.
additional_notes: Very vulgar Mexican slang (uses a crude word for "penis"). Often used with estar or tener: "Estoy hasta la verga" / "Me tienes hasta la verga" to show you’re extremely annoyed or done with a situation/person. In some contexts it can also mean "extremely drunk/high" or "totally exhausted," depending on what you’re talking about. Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ya estoy hasta la verga de este tráfico.
native_language_example: I’m so fucking sick of this traffic.

additional_notes: Informal idiom meaning “to the max.” Most often used for places or containers that are totally full ("El bar está hasta las trancas" = the bar is packed). It can also describe someone being very drunk in some contexts ("Está hasta las trancas"), but the “packed/full” meaning is the most common.
target_language_example: El metro iba hasta las trancas y no pudimos subir.
