native_language_example: The subway was completely packed and we couldn’t get on.

meaning: to the core; to the bone (completely, deeply).
additional_notes: An idiomatic intensifier meaning something affects you very deeply or completely. Common with emotions (e.g., hate, love, fear) or physical states (e.g., being soaked or cold): "odiar/amar hasta los tuétanos", "estar empapado hasta los tuétanos". Literally refers to bone marrow ("tuétano").
target_language_example: Estoy empapado hasta los tuétanos.
native_language_example: I’m soaked to the bone.

additional_notes: A very common, friendly way to say goodbye. It implies you’ll see the person again (later today or another time). It can be used in both casual and polite situations. Similar alternatives: "nos vemos" (more casual) and "hasta pronto" (see you soon).
target_language_example: Tengo que irme. ¡Hasta luego!
native_language_example: I have to go. See you later!

additional_notes: Common way to say goodbye when you expect to see the person the next day. It can also be used more literally to mean “until tomorrow” (e.g., waiting until tomorrow to do something). Often said as a standalone farewell.
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. ¡Hasta mañana!
native_language_example: Alright, I’m leaving. See you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used to say something will continue or remain true for an unspecified time, and will change only when a new update/announcement is given. Common in notices, emails, schedules, and official messages. Often used with suspensions or closures: "cerrado/suspendido hasta nuevo aviso".
target_language_example: La tienda estará cerrada hasta nuevo aviso.
native_language_example: The store will be closed until further notice.

meaning: “until” (introduces when something ends or will happen).
additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to a point in time: + present tense for habitual/general situations ("Trabajo hasta que oscurece"), and often + subjunctive when talking about the future/unknown ("Espera hasta que llegue"). Can also be used with "no" to mean “not until” ("No me fui hasta que terminó").
target_language_example: No vamos a comer hasta que llegues.
native_language_example: We’re not going to eat until you arrive.

meaning: “to such an extent that…” / “so much so that…”
additional_notes: Used to show degree or intensity and introduce a result clause with que. Similar in meaning to “tanto que,” but a bit more explicit/formal. Often followed by a verb in the indicative describing the consequence.
target_language_example: Estaba cansado hasta tal punto que se quedó dormido en el autobús.
native_language_example: He was so tired that he fell asleep on the bus.

additional_notes: Used to show surprise or emphasis that the person addressed is included too (often with a tone like “you of all people”). Although "hasta" often means “until,” in this expression it means “even.” Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: ¡No puedo creerlo, hasta tú llegaste tarde!
native_language_example: I can’t believe it—even you arrived late!

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity in an impersonal way (not tied to a specific person). It’s typically followed by an infinitive: "Hay que + infinitive". Common in advice, rules, and instructions. You can change the tense: "había que" (had to), "habrá que" (will have to).
target_language_example: Hay que llegar temprano.
native_language_example: You have to arrive early.

meaning: 'Let there be peace.' / 'May there be peace.'
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of "haber" (haya) to express a wish or appeal. Common in calls to calm down, end an argument, or promote reconciliation (sometimes with a formal or solemn tone). Often appears as "Que haya paz" (May there be peace) or "Haya paz" as a standalone phrase.
target_language_example: Ya basta de discutir; haya paz.
native_language_example: Enough arguing; let there be peace.

additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom to choose, or sometimes to show frustration/indifference (“Fine, do what you want”). Informal with friends/family; in formal situations you might say “haga lo que quiera” (usted). Literally: “do what you want.”
target_language_example: Si no te gusta mi idea, haz lo que quieras.
native_language_example: If you don’t like my idea, do whatever you want.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or point out something that is present, shown, or about to be mentioned. Common in writing, announcements, and formal speech; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear “aquí está(n)” instead. Can also appear as “He aquí que…” meaning “Here is/are that…” or “And then…”.
target_language_example: He aquí las llaves que buscabas.
native_language_example: Here are the keys you were looking for.

additional_notes: Used to describe items crafted manually rather than mass-produced. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: hecho a mano (masc. singular), hecha a mano (fem. singular), hechos a mano (masc. plural), hechas a mano (fem. plural). Common in shopping/markets and product descriptions.
target_language_example: Este bolso está hecho a mano en México.
native_language_example: This bag is handmade in Mexico.

meaning: a very offensive insult (roughly: “bitch” / “daughter of a bitch”).
additional_notes: Strong profanity. Used to insult a woman (feminine: hija). The masculine form is "hijo de puta". Can also be used as a harsh exclamation about a situation (“¡Hija de puta!”), but it’s still very vulgar—avoid in polite contexts. In some regions it can be used jokingly among close friends, but it’s risky and easily taken as aggressive.
target_language_example: ¡Esa hija de puta me robó la cartera!
native_language_example: That bitch stole my wallet!

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no sisters or brothers. It’s feminine; for a male, say "hijo único". Often used with "ser": "Soy hija única" (I’m an only child—female speaker).
target_language_example: Soy hija única, así que no tengo hermanos.
native_language_example: I’m an only daughter, so I don’t have any siblings.

meaning: “son of a bitch”; a very strong insult (also used jokingly among friends in some contexts).
additional_notes: A highly offensive phrase; avoid in polite conversation. Used to insult someone you’re angry with, similar in strength to “son of a bitch” in English. It can sometimes be used playfully between close friends, but it’s risky and can easily cause offense. For a milder alternative, you might hear “qué mala persona” (“what a bad person”) or “imbécil” (“idiot,” still insulting).
target_language_example: ¡Ese tipo es un hijo de perra!
native_language_example: That guy is a son of a bitch!

meaning: "son of a bitch" (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Highly offensive vulgar profanity. Used to insult someone directly (often: "¡Hijo de puta!") or refer to someone angrily ("Ese hijo de puta..."). In some contexts it can be used jokingly among close friends, but it’s risky and not appropriate in polite conversation. Literal meaning is "son of a prostitute," but in practice it functions like the English insult.
target_language_example: ¡Eres un hijo de puta!
native_language_example: You're a son of a bitch!

meaning: “my son” (often used as a warm form of address).
additional_notes: Literally “son of mine.” Used to address a boy/young man, or sometimes an adult, especially by a parent or older person. It can sound affectionate or patronizing depending on tone and context. In religious or formal-sounding contexts, it can also be used like “my child.”
target_language_example: Ven aquí, hijo mío, tengo que hablar contigo.
native_language_example: Come here, my son, I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the only child in their family. It can refer to a boy or a child in general; for a girl you can also say “hija única.” Often used with “ser”: “Soy hijo único/a.”
target_language_example: Soy hijo único, así que no tengo hermanos.
native_language_example: I’m an only child, so I don’t have any siblings.

additional_notes: Used for the floss you use to clean between your teeth. In some places you may also hear "seda dental" with the same meaning. Often used with the verb "usar" or "pasar": "¿Usas/pasas hilo dental?"
target_language_example: Uso hilo dental todas las noches.
native_language_example: I use dental floss every night.

additional_notes: Refers to a country’s official patriotic song, often played at sports events, ceremonies, or official occasions. Used with the definite article: "el himno nacional" (the national anthem).
target_language_example: En el estadio, todos cantaron el himno nacional.
native_language_example: In the stadium, everyone sang the national anthem.

additional_notes: A common way to refer to someone who works in business or commerce. It’s literally “man of business,” but in modern usage you may also see more gender-neutral alternatives like “persona de negocios” or “empresario” depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi tío es un hombre de negocios y viaja mucho por trabajo.
native_language_example: My uncle is a businessman and travels a lot for work.

meaning: “man of the world”; a worldly, sophisticated man.
additional_notes: Used to describe a man with lots of life experience, often from travel, social circles, or culture (someone “worldly” and polished). It can sound a bit formal or old-fashioned. Literally “man of the world.”
target_language_example: Dicen que mi tío es un hombre del mundo: ha vivido en varios países y habla tres idiomas.
native_language_example: They say my uncle is a man of the world: he’s lived in several countries and speaks three languages.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the mythical creature (a person who turns into a wolf). It’s masculine; the feminine form is "mujer lobo" (less common). Often used with the definite article: "el hombre lobo".
target_language_example: Dicen que en ese bosque vive un hombre lobo.
native_language_example: They say that a werewolf lives in that forest.

additional_notes: A literal phrase meaning a male person who has died. Common in news stories, horror/crime contexts, or when telling a story. For “a dead person” in general, Spanish often uses “un muerto / una muerta” or “una persona muerta”.
target_language_example: Encontraron a un hombre muerto en el parque.
native_language_example: They found a dead man in the park.

meaning: the moment of truth; the decisive moment.
additional_notes: Used when the important moment has arrived—when you have to act, decide, or find out the real result (e.g., an exam, a performance, a test, or a confrontation). Often appears with verbs like "llegar" or "ser": "Llegó la hora de la verdad" / "Es la hora de la verdad". Similar to English "moment of truth."
target_language_example: Mañana es la hora de la verdad: tengo el examen final.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is the moment of truth: I have the final exam.

additional_notes: Used mainly in work contexts to talk about working beyond your scheduled hours. Often used in the plural: “horas extra”. Related phrase: “hacer horas extra” = “to work overtime.”
target_language_example: Esta semana hice dos horas extra en la oficina.
native_language_example: This week I worked two hours of overtime at the office.

additional_notes: Used for the busiest time of day (especially for traffic and public transport), typically in the morning and late afternoon. Commonly appears with prepositions like "en hora punta" (during rush hour) or "a la hora punta" (at peak time).
target_language_example: Evita conducir en hora punta porque hay mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: Avoid driving during rush hour because there’s a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Often used to mean "nowadays/these days" rather than literally "today." It’s common in Spain and Latin America; you can also say "hoy en día" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Hoy día es difícil encontrar tiempo libre.
native_language_example: Nowadays it’s hard to find free time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the present time in general (modern life), often comparing with the past. It’s similar to "actualmente" or "en la actualidad" and does not mean "today" specifically (that would be "hoy").
target_language_example: Hoy en día, mucha gente trabaja desde casa.
native_language_example: Nowadays, many people work from home.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something will happen or should be done today (not another day). Often implies urgency or immediacy: “today, right now.” You can also use “ahora mismo” for “right now,” but “hoy mismo” specifically includes “today.”
target_language_example: Tengo que hacerlo hoy mismo.
native_language_example: I have to do it today (right away).

additional_notes: Fixed expression used to emphasize that something is obvious, expected, or already understood. It’s fairly formal and common in writing or careful speech. Often followed by "que": "Huelga decir que...". It uses the verb "holgar" (to be unnecessary), so it doesn’t relate to "huelga" meaning "strike" (work stoppage).
target_language_example: Huelga decir que tienes que llevar tu pasaporte.
native_language_example: Needless to say, you have to bring your passport.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a fingerprint (e.g., for ID, phones, police). In tech/privacy contexts it can also mean your “digital footprint” (the trace you leave online). Context usually makes it clear; for “fingerprint” you may also hear “huella dactilar.”
target_language_example: Para desbloquear el móvil, usa tu huella digital.
native_language_example: To unlock the phone, use your fingerprint.

meaning: boiled egg (cooked in its shell in water).
additional_notes: Usually refers to an egg boiled whole in its shell. You’ll also hear “huevo duro” (hard-boiled egg) and “huevo pasado por agua” (soft-boiled egg). In menus and everyday speech, it’s a common ingredient in salads and sandwiches.
target_language_example: Para el desayuno, quiero un huevo cocido y una tostada.
native_language_example: For breakfast, I want a boiled egg and a piece of toast.

additional_notes: Used for transportation tickets and travel plans. Common in phrases like “billete/boleto de ida y vuelta” (round-trip ticket). Contrast with “solo ida” or “de ida” (one-way). Literally means “going and returning.”
target_language_example: Quiero un billete de ida y vuelta a Madrid, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a round-trip ticket to Madrid, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a language that is not your native language (or not the main language of the place you’re in). Often used in school/work contexts: "clase de idioma extranjero" (foreign language class), "aprender un idioma extranjero" (to learn a foreign language). You may also hear "lengua extranjera" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo un idioma extranjero para el trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language for work.

meaning: “same with me” / “me too” (same situation for me).
additional_notes: Used to say that what someone just said also applies to you (similar to “a mí también” or “yo también”). It can also appear in requests meaning “the same with me” (e.g., do the same thing for/to me). Often you’ll also hear “igual que yo” (“same as me”) or “igual para mí” (“same for me”), depending on context.
target_language_example: —No tengo tiempo hoy. —Igual conmigo.
native_language_example: —I don’t have time today. —Same with me.

meaning: to not care at all (to not give a damn).
additional_notes: Very vulgar/strong slang. Used to say something matters zero to you: "No me importa un carajo" = "I don’t give a damn." Avoid in polite situations; consider softer options like "no me importa" (I don’t care) or "me da igual" (it’s all the same to me). Uses the verb "importar" (to matter), often with an indirect object: "me/te/le importa un carajo".
target_language_example: No me importa un carajo lo que digan.
native_language_example: I don’t give a damn what they say.

additional_notes: Common in news, safety warnings, and talking about emergencies. Often used with verbs like haber (There is/are), provocar (to cause), controlar (to control), and extinguir (to put out). Related terms: bomberos (firefighters), humo (smoke), evacuación (evacuation).
target_language_example: Hay un incendio forestal cerca del pueblo, así que tenemos que evacuar.
native_language_example: There’s a wildfire near the town, so we have to evacuate.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is true or will happen no matter what the other factor is. It’s followed by a noun, pronoun, or an infinitive clause: "independientemente de la edad" (regardless of age), "independientemente de si vienes" (regardless of whether you come). Often interchangeable with "sin importar" or "a pesar de" depending on context (but "a pesar de" emphasizes contrast: "despite").
target_language_example: Independientemente de lo que decidas, te apoyaré.
native_language_example: Regardless of what you decide, I’ll support you.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about instruments in general. It’s often used with an article (un/una, el/la) and can be plural (instrumentos musicales). Example questions: “¿Tocas algún instrumento musical?” (Do you play any musical instrument?).
target_language_example: Mi hermano toca un instrumento musical en la banda.
native_language_example: My brother plays a musical instrument in the band.

additional_notes: Very common irregular verb. Often used with **a** + place: *ir a la tienda* (to go to the store). Also used with **a** + infinitive for the near future: *voy a estudiar* (“I’m going to study”). Some key forms: *voy* (I go), *vas* (you go), *va* (he/she goes), *vamos* (we go), *van* (they go).
target_language_example: Voy a casa.
native_language_example: I’m going home.

meaning: 'to be going to' (do something); also 'to go to' (a place).
additional_notes: Very common structure. For plans/near future, use **ir a + infinitive** (conjugate *ir*, then *a*, then the verb in infinitive): *voy a comer* = “I’m going to eat.” For destinations, use **ir a + place**: *voy a Madrid* = “I’m going to Madrid.” With **el**, *a + el* contracts to **al**: *Voy al supermercado*.
target_language_example: Mañana voy a trabajar.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to work.

meaning: to go and get (someone/something); to go pick up.
additional_notes: Used when you physically go somewhere in order to collect or retrieve someone or something (often from a place). Common with a direct object: "Voy a buscar a mi hermano" (I’m going to pick up my brother) / "Voy a buscar el paquete" (I’m going to get the package). With people, Spanish often uses "a" before the person: "buscar a + person".
target_language_example: Voy a buscar a los niños a la escuela.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up the kids from school.

meaning: to go to Mass (a Catholic church service).
additional_notes: Used for attending the Catholic religious service called “la misa.” Conjugate “ir” to match the subject (voy/vas/va/van a misa). You can specify when (los domingos, hoy) or where (a misa en la iglesia de San José).
target_language_example: Mis abuelos van a misa todos los domingos.
native_language_example: My grandparents go to Mass every Sunday.

meaning: to be going to be; will be (future).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what something will be like in the future, often as part of the near-future structure "ir a + infinitive". Here, "ser" is used to describe identity or characteristics (who/what something is), not location. Very common when predicting or announcing plans: "va a ser + adjective/noun".
target_language_example: Mañana va a ser un día largo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is going to be a long day.

meaning: to go ahead; to move forward; to continue.
additional_notes: Used to give permission or encouragement to proceed (similar to "go ahead"), or to talk about progressing/moving forward. Common in commands: "¡Adelante!" (Go ahead!/Come in!). With "con": "ir adelante con" = to go ahead with (a plan/idea).
target_language_example: Si estás listo, puedes ir adelante con el proyecto.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, you can go ahead with the project.

meaning: To get to the point; to be direct.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone (or yourself) to stop giving extra details and say the main idea. Often appears as an imperative: "Ve al grano" (informal tú) or "Vaya al grano" (formal usted). Literal meaning is "to go to the grain," but it’s an idiom.
target_language_example: Dejemos las historias y vayamos al grano: ¿cuánto cuesta?
native_language_example: Let’s skip the stories and get to the point: how much does it cost?

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to a place that’s away from the speaker. Often contrasts with "ir aquí"/"venir aquí" depending on perspective. In everyday Spanish, people more commonly say "ir allí" or simply "ir a + place" ("ir a Madrid"). "Allá" can also emphasize distance: "por allá" = "over there / around that area".
target_language_example: Mañana voy allá con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going there with my friends.

meaning: to go up; to move upward.
additional_notes: Used to indicate upward movement or direction (opposite of "ir abajo"). You may hear it in simple directions (games, navigation), and in contexts like values/prices going up. In everyday Spanish, "subir" or "ir hacia arriba" is often more natural than "ir arriba" in many situations.
target_language_example: Para llegar al mirador, tienes que ir arriba por esas escaleras.
native_language_example: To get to the lookout point, you have to go up those stairs.

additional_notes: Used to say you accompany someone or something is included/paired with something else. Conjugate ir (voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van) and keep con + person/thing: "Voy con mi amigo" (I’m going with my friend). Also used for match/compatibility in clothes or items: "Esta camisa va con estos pantalones" (This shirt goes with these pants).
target_language_example: ¿Vas con nosotros al cine?
native_language_example: Are you going with us to the movies?

meaning: 'to go as' (dressed up as); also 'to be about' (a topic).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) Costumes/roles: "ir de + noun" = to dress up/go as (for a party, Halloween, etc.). Example: "Voy de pirata".
2) Topic/subject: "¿De qué va...?" (from "ir de") = What is it about? / What’s it about?
Sometimes "ir de" can also mean 'to act/pretend like' (e.g., "Va de experto" = He acts like an expert), but this can sound a bit critical depending on context.
target_language_example: Este año voy de vampiro para Halloween.
native_language_example: This year I’m going as a vampire for Halloween.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about going out to shop (often for clothes or errands). Uses the verb ir (to go) + de compras (“shopping”). You can add where/when: ir de compras al centro, ir de compras mañana. Also common: voy de compras (I’m going shopping).
target_language_example: El sábado voy a ir de compras con mi hermana.
native_language_example: On Saturday I’m going to go shopping with my sister.

meaning: to go hand in hand; to be closely connected.
additional_notes: Used to say two things happen together or are strongly related. Literally it can mean walking while holding hands, but very often it’s figurative: “X goes hand in hand with Y.” Common pattern: «X va de la mano de Y».
target_language_example: La práctica constante va de la mano del progreso.
native_language_example: Constant practice goes hand in hand with progress.

meaning: to go too far (to cross a limit).
additional_notes: Used when someone exceeds an acceptable limit—physically (going farther than intended) or, more often, socially/emotionally (a joke, comment, or action becomes inappropriate or hurtful). Conjugate "ir" to match the subject (fui/vas/va/etc.), and you can also say "te pasaste" in many situations.
target_language_example: Creo que el chiste fue gracioso, pero ya fue demasiado lejos.
native_language_example: I think the joke was funny, but it went too far.

meaning: to go toward; to head toward.
additional_notes: Used to express movement in the direction of a place, person, or thing. It’s followed by a destination or direction (often a noun/pronoun): ir hacia la puerta (toward the door), ir hacia ti (toward you). Similar to "ir a" (to go to), but "hacia" emphasizes direction rather than arrival.
target_language_example: Voy hacia la estación de tren.
native_language_example: I'm heading toward the train station.

meaning: to be late; to arrive late.
additional_notes: Used to talk about being late for something (an event, class, work, an appointment). It’s often used with “a” + noun: “ir tarde a clase / al trabajo”. Very commonly said as “Voy tarde” (I’m late) or “Vamos tarde” (We’re late).
target_language_example: Perdón, voy tarde a la reunión.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late to the meeting.

meaning: to come and go; to go back and forth.
additional_notes: Used to talk about repeated movement between places, frequent trips, or a constant flow of people/things. It can be literal (physically moving) or more general (ongoing changes or activity). Often appears with expressions like "todo el día" (all day) or "entre" (between).
target_language_example: He estado yendo y viniendo entre casa y el trabajo todo el día.
native_language_example: I’ve been going back and forth between home and work all day.

meaning: to go now; to leave now/already.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "ir" (to go) plus "ya" (now/already) to express urgency or that it’s time to leave. Common in sentences like "Tengo que ir ya" (I have to go now) or "Me voy ya" (I’m leaving now). As a direct command, Spanish more often uses "¡Vete ya!" (Go/Leave now!) rather than "¡Ir ya!".
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que ir ya.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: to be doing well; to be going well for someone.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how things are going for a person (work, life, school, etc.). It uses an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les) to show who it’s going well for: me va bien (I’m doing well), te va bien (you’re doing well), le va bien (he/she is doing well), nos va bien (we’re doing well), les va bien (they’re doing well). Often used in questions like “¿Cómo te va?” / “¿Te va bien?”.
target_language_example: A mi hermana le va bien en el trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister is doing well at work.

additional_notes: Reflexive form of **ir** (“to go”). **Irse** emphasizes departing from a place or situation (often translated as “to leave”). Very common with **de** + place: **irse de casa** (to leave home), **irse de aquí** (to get out of here/leave here). Often used with **tener que**: **tengo que irme** (I have to leave).
target_language_example: Tengo que irme ahora.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: to leave for / to go to (emphasizes leaving where you are).
additional_notes: Used with a destination or activity: irse a + place ("irse a casa" = to leave/go home) or irse a + infinitive ("irse a dormir" = to go to sleep). It’s the reflexive form of "ir" and highlights departure (often like “to head off”). Common forms: "me voy a", "te vas a", "se va a", "nos vamos a", "se van a".
target_language_example: Me voy a casa.
native_language_example: I’m going home (I’m leaving for home).

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb irse (“to leave/go away”) + a la cama (“to bed”). Very common for saying you’re going to sleep or calling it a night. Often used in the near future with ir a: "Me voy a ir a la cama" or more commonly "Me voy a la cama" (I’m going to bed). You can add a time: "Me voy a la cama a las diez" (I go to bed at 10).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado, me voy a la cama.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to bed.

meaning: to leave (a place); to go away from.
additional_notes: Used with a place/event after de. It’s the pronominal verb irse (“to leave/go away”), emphasizing departure. Common structures: irse de aquí/ahí (“leave here/there”), irse de la casa (“leave the house”), irse de fiesta (“go out partying”), irse de vacaciones (“go on vacation”). In the past: se fue de… (“he/she left…”).
target_language_example: Me voy de aquí porque es muy tarde.
native_language_example: I’m leaving here because it’s very late.

meaning: to get out of hand; to get out of control.
additional_notes: Used when a situation becomes uncontrolled or more extreme than expected. Often appears with "se" and an indirect object: "Se me fue de las manos" (It got out of hand on me / I lost control of it). Can refer to arguments, parties, projects, spending, etc.
target_language_example: La discusión se fue de las manos y terminaron gritando.
native_language_example: The argument got out of hand and they ended up shouting.

additional_notes: Used in chess when the opponent’s king is in check and has no legal move to escape. In everyday speech it can be used figuratively to mean someone has been completely defeated or left with no options.
target_language_example: ¡Jaque mate! La partida terminó.
native_language_example: Checkmate! The game is over.

additional_notes: Used for games where the outcome depends mainly on luck rather than skill (e.g., slots, roulette, lotteries). Often appears in rules, signs, and legal contexts (e.g., "prohibidos los juegos de azar"). Plural: "juegos de azar". Related terms: "apostar" (to bet), "apuesta" (bet), "lotería" (lottery).
target_language_example: En este país, los juegos de azar están regulados por ley.
native_language_example: In this country, games of chance are regulated by law.

additional_notes: Common everyday noun phrase for games you play on a table (often with a board, cards, pieces, or dice). Plural: juegos de mesa. Often used with verbs like jugar a (to play) and with gusta/n: Me gustan los juegos de mesa.
target_language_example: Los domingos jugamos a un juego de mesa en casa.
native_language_example: On Sundays we play a board game at home.

additional_notes: Used to say something is simple or effortless. It can be literal (a game for children) or idiomatic ("this is easy"). Often used with "Es" (Es juego de niños) or "Fue" (Fue juego de niños).
target_language_example: Para ella, resolver ese problema fue juego de niños.
native_language_example: For her, solving that problem was child’s play.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a joke or clever effect that depends on words (double meanings, similar sounds, etc.). Often appears with verbs like hacer (to make) or as part of an explanation: Es un juego de palabras (It’s a pun/wordplay).
target_language_example: Es un juego de palabras: "vino" puede significar la bebida o que alguien "vino" (came).
native_language_example: It’s a pun: “vino” can mean the drink or that someone “came.”

additional_notes: Used to talk about cheating or unfair behavior, especially in sports, games, or competition (and sometimes in politics or business). Literally means “dirty game/play.” You can also use it more generally: “Eso es juego sucio” = “That’s dirty/that’s unfair.”
target_language_example: Eso fue juego sucio; no se puede hacer trampa así.
native_language_example: That was dirty play; you can’t cheat like that.

meaning: “team player” (someone who works well with others).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who cooperates, shares responsibility, and prioritizes group success. Common in workplace or sports contexts. Gender can vary: jugador de equipo (male/neutral), jugadora de equipo (female). Often used with ser: “Ser un(a) jugador(a) de equipo”.
target_language_example: En el trabajo, María es una gran jugadora de equipo.
native_language_example: At work, María is a great team player.

additional_notes: Used for playing card games in general (póker, blackjack, etc.). You can also specify the game: “jugar al póker.” Note the structure “jugar a + el/la + [game/activity]”: “jugar al fútbol,” “jugar a los videojuegos.”
target_language_example: Los sábados jugamos a las cartas con mis amigos.
native_language_example: On Saturdays we play cards with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically near something else (location). It can also mean “together with” in more formal contexts (especially in writing), similar to “along with.” Often followed by a noun (junto a la casa) or a pronoun (junto a mí).
target_language_example: El banco está junto a la farmacia.
native_language_example: The bank is next to the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Used to add something/someone that accompanies or is included with something else. Very common in both everyday speech and writing. It can introduce a noun phrase ("junto con mi hermana") or an infinitive phrase ("junto con ayudarte"). Often interchangeable with "con" or "además de" depending on context.
target_language_example: Voy a la reunión junto con mis compañeros.
native_language_example: I’m going to the meeting together with my coworkers/classmates.

meaning: just in time; right on time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at the last possible moment, or exactly when needed. Often placed at the end of the sentence. Common with verbs like llegar (to arrive) and venir (to come).
target_language_example: Llegaste justo a tiempo para ver el inicio de la película.
native_language_example: You arrived just in time to see the start of the movie.

meaning: 'right now' / 'just now' (at this exact moment or very recently).
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to emphasize immediacy. Often interchangeable with "ahora mismo" (right now). Depending on context, it can mean (1) this exact moment: "Estoy ocupado justo ahora" or (2) a moment ago: "Justo ahora lo vi".
target_language_example: No puedo hablar justo ahora; te llamo en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’ll call you in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to point out a very specific location, often with emphasis. Common in everyday speech when giving directions or indicating where something is/should be. You can also hear it figuratively to mean “at that exact point/moment” in a story.
target_language_example: Pon la caja justo ahí, junto a la puerta.
native_language_example: Put the box right there, next to the door.

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning the musical instrument. It’s usually used literally (music class, instruments, bands). In Spain, “flauta” can also refer to a type of bread (like a baguette) in some contexts, but beginners will most often see it as the instrument.
target_language_example: Toco la flauta en la banda de la escuela.
native_language_example: I play the flute in the school band.

meaning: In Spain (slang/vulgar): “holy shit!” / “wow!” (strong surprise or emphasis). Literally: “the (Communion) host.”
additional_notes: Literally, *la hostia* is the consecrated wafer in Catholic Communion (formal/religious context). In everyday speech in Spain it’s a common but vulgar exclamation to show strong surprise, admiration, annoyance, etc.: *¡La hostia!* It can also appear as *una hostia* meaning “a slap/punch” or “a big hit/fall” (*Me di una hostia* = “I took a bad fall / got hit hard”). Avoid in polite or formal situations.
target_language_example: ¡La hostia, qué frío hace hoy!
native_language_example: Holy shit, it’s so cold today!

additional_notes: Literally means “the milk.” In Spain it’s also a very common informal intensifier: used to say something is great (“¡Es la leche!” = “It’s awesome!”) or to emphasize quantity/degree (“Habla la leche” = “He talks a lot”). Meaning depends heavily on context and tone.
target_language_example: ¡Este concierto es la leche!
native_language_example: This concert is awesome!

additional_notes: Spanish usually says "el mar" for "the sea," but "la mar" also exists. "La mar" is common in poetry, songs, and sailor speech, and it can sound more emotional or literary. You may also see it in set phrases like "la mar de" meaning "a lot of" (e.g., "la mar de cosas" = "a lot of things").
target_language_example: La mar estaba tranquila al amanecer.
native_language_example: The sea was calm at dawn.

la pelota está en el tejado

target_language_multi_word_term: la pelota está en el tejado
meaning: It’s up to you/them now; the ball is in your/their court.
additional_notes: An idiom used when you’ve done what you can and now the other person has to decide or take the next step. Often appears as “La pelota está en tu tejado” (it’s on you now). Not meant literally.
target_language_example: Ya te envié la propuesta; ahora la pelota está en tu tejado.
native_language_example: I already sent you the proposal; now the ball is in your court.

meaning: Vulgar: “absolutely nothing / not at all” (said sarcastically).
additional_notes: Very informal and offensive slang (common in Spain). Used as a blunt, sarcastic way to say that something didn’t happen or that you got no help/results—similar to “not a damn thing,” “yeah right,” or “my ass.” Avoid in polite/company settings. Literally means “the dick in vinegar,” but the real meaning isn’t literal.
target_language_example: —¿Te han ayudado en el trabajo? —La polla en vinagre.
native_language_example: —Have they helped you at work? —Not at all.

additional_notes: Feminine noun with the definite article: "la" + "vida". Often refers to life in general ("La vida es..." = "Life is...") or to someone’s lifestyle/way of living ("su vida" = "his/her life"). Common in set phrases like "la vida diaria" (daily life) and "toda la vida" (all my/your life).
target_language_example: La vida es corta.
native_language_example: Life is short.

additional_notes: A reflective phrase used to emphasize that time passes quickly, so you should enjoy life or take opportunities now. It can sound poetic or philosophical. You may also hear "La vida es corta" (more common in everyday speech) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Viaja si puedes; la vida es breve.
native_language_example: Travel if you can; life is short.

meaning: “the old woman”; sometimes “the wife” (informal, can sound rude).
additional_notes: Literally means “the old woman” (la + vieja). Depending on country and context, it can refer neutrally to an elderly woman, but it’s also used colloquially to mean “my wife / the wife.” In that sense it can sound disrespectful, so beginners may prefer safer options like “mi esposa” (my wife) or “mi mujer” (my wife/partner).
target_language_example: Mi viejo y yo vamos a cenar; la vieja eligió el restaurante.
native_language_example: My husband and I are going to dinner; the wife chose the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the positive part of a situation, often in the expression “ver el lado bueno (de algo)” (“to look on the bright side”). It can be followed by “de” + noun: “el lado bueno de la ciudad” (“the good side of the city”).
target_language_example: Intenta ver el lado bueno: al menos aprendimos algo.
native_language_example: Try to look on the bright side: at least we learned something.

meaning: the positive side (of something); the upside.
additional_notes: Used to focus on a good aspect of a situation, often with the set phrase "ver el lado positivo" (to look on the bright side). You can also say "el lado positivo de + noun" (the positive side of...).
target_language_example: Intento ver el lado positivo de la situación.
native_language_example: I try to look on the bright side of the situation.

additional_notes: Used when telling time. It normally appears after the verb: “Son las diez” (It’s ten o’clock). For times after 1:00, Spanish uses the plural feminine article “las” because it’s understood as “las horas” (the hours).
target_language_example: Son las diez y media.
native_language_example: It’s ten thirty.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to tell time: *Son las dos* = “It’s two o’clock.” It can also mean “the two” when referring to two feminine nouns (e.g., *las dos chicas* = “the two girls”). Note that the article changes with the number/gender: *la una* (1:00), *las dos* (2:00), and for masculine nouns you’d use *los dos* (“the two,” masculine/mixed group).
target_language_example: Son las dos; nos vemos a las dos y media.
native_language_example: It’s two o’clock; see you at two thirty.

additional_notes: Used after a time expression to mean “and something / and then some,” implying it’s late and the exact time isn’t important. Most often you’ll see it as “a las tantas” (“at some late hour”) or “a las tantas de la noche” (“late at night”). Common with verbs like llegar (to arrive), volver (to come back), and salir (to leave).
target_language_example: Llegó a casa a las tantas y estaba agotado.
native_language_example: He got home really late and was exhausted.

meaning: to wash your hands; (figuratively) to refuse responsibility.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: "lavarse" = "to wash oneself," so it usually needs a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se): "Me lavo las manos." Literal meaning is very common in daily situations (hygiene, before eating, after the bathroom). Figuratively, "lavarse las manos" means to 'wash your hands of' a problem—i.e., to say it's not your responsibility and not get involved.
target_language_example: Antes de comer, lávate las manos.
native_language_example: Before eating, wash your hands.

additional_notes: Used when shopping or ordering coffee to specify the type of milk. Common contrasts: "leche semidesnatada" (2%/reduced-fat) and "leche desnatada" (skim). "Entera" literally means "whole" and, for milk, implies it has its full fat content.
target_language_example: Quisiera un café con leche entera, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with whole milk, please.

additional_notes: In everyday Spanish, people more often say simply “leche” for regular milk. “Leche fresca” can be used to emphasize that it’s fresh (not powdered, not long-life/UHT). In some places you may also see “leche fresca” contrasted with “leche en polvo” (powdered milk) or “leche UHT / leche larga vida” (shelf-stable milk).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes leche fresca para el café?
native_language_example: Do you have fresh milk for the coffee?

meaning: to read between the lines (infer an implied meaning).
additional_notes: Used when the real message isn’t said directly and you have to infer it from context, tone, or hints. Often used with "hay que" (you have to) or in the command form "lee" (read).
target_language_example: Aunque no lo dijo, si lees entre líneas, está claro que no quiere venir.
native_language_example: Although he didn’t say it, if you read between the lines, it’s clear he doesn’t want to come.

additional_notes: Used when someone seems to know what you’re thinking or what you’re going to say, or as a joking way to say they guessed correctly. Often appears with indirect object pronouns: “leer la mente a alguien” or “leerle la mente (a alguien)”.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo lo supiste? ¡Me leíste la mente!
native_language_example: How did you know? You read my mind!

additional_notes: Used to indicate physical distance from a place (lejos de aquí = far from here). It can also mean 'far from' in the sense of 'not at all' or 'quite the opposite' when contrasting expectations (Lejos de ayudar, empeoró las cosas = Far from helping, he made things worse). Often used with estar/quedar: Está lejos de mi casa (It’s far from my house).
target_language_example: El restaurante queda lejos de aquí.
native_language_example: The restaurant is far from here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a language that is not your native language (or not spoken in your country). In everyday Spanish, people also say “idioma extranjero.” In schools you’ll hear it in contexts like “clase de lengua extranjera” (foreign-language class).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo inglés como lengua extranjera.
native_language_example: I’m learning English as a foreign language.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the first language you learned as a child. Also commonly said as "idioma materno". You’ll often see it in forms or school/work settings: "Mi lengua materna es..."
target_language_example: Mi lengua materna es el inglés, pero estoy aprendiendo español.
native_language_example: My native language is English, but I’m learning Spanish.

meaning: minority language (a language spoken by a smaller group within a country/region).
additional_notes: Used in discussions about culture, education, and language policy. It refers to a language that has fewer speakers or less official status than the dominant language in the area; it doesn’t necessarily mean the language is “small” globally. Common collocations: proteger una lengua minoritaria (to protect), hablar una lengua minoritaria (to speak), derechos de las lenguas minoritarias (rights).
target_language_example: En esta región se habla una lengua minoritaria además del español.
native_language_example: In this region, a minority language is spoken in addition to Spanish.

additional_notes: A common technical term for a computer language used to write code (e.g., Python, Java, C++). Often used with verbs like aprender (to learn), usar (to use), and estudiar (to study): “aprender un lenguaje de programación”. You may also hear “lenguaje de programación” shortened to “lenguaje” when the context is clearly about coding.
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo un lenguaje de programación para crear aplicaciones.
native_language_example: I’m learning a programming language to create apps.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: lentes de contacto (“contact lenses”). You can say llevar/usar lentes de contacto (“to wear contact lenses”). Also common: lentilla (Spain) for “contact lens.”
target_language_example: No puedo ver bien sin mis lentes de contacto.
native_language_example: I can’t see well without my contact lenses.

additional_notes:
This phrase is not standard Spanish because *escribido* is not the correct past participle of *escribir*.

Correct forms:
- **leído y escrito** = “read and written” (standard)
- As participles, **leído** (from *leer*) and **escrito** (from *escribir*) are used with **haber** to form the present perfect (e.g., *he leído*, *he escrito*) or as adjectives (e.g., *un texto escrito*).

Common mistake: Some verbs have **irregular past participles** (e.g., *escribir → escrito*, *ver → visto*, *poner → puesto*, *hacer → hecho*).
target_language_example: He leído y escrito muchos correos hoy.
native_language_example: I have read and written many emails today.

additional_notes: Used in legal/criminal-justice contexts for someone released from prison under conditions (rules) and supervision. The adjective "condicional" means "conditional" (depending on meeting certain conditions).
target_language_example: Le dieron libertad condicional después de cumplir dos años de condena.
native_language_example: He was granted parole after serving two years of his sentence.

additional_notes: A common formal phrase used in politics, law, news, and human rights contexts. It means the right to express opinions and ideas without censorship. Often appears with verbs like respetar (to respect), proteger (to protect), defender (to defend), and limitar (to limit).
target_language_example: La libertad de expresión es un derecho fundamental.
native_language_example: Freedom of expression is a fundamental right.

additional_notes: Common in economics and politics to talk about reducing tariffs/quotas and other barriers between countries. Often appears in phrases like “acuerdo de libre comercio” (free trade agreement) and “zona de libre comercio” (free trade zone).
target_language_example: El país firmó un acuerdo de libre comercio con sus vecinos.
native_language_example: The country signed a free trade agreement with its neighbors.

additional_notes: Used for a school or course book (for example, in a class). Often used with a possessive or article: "mi libro de texto", "el libro de texto". Plural: "libros de texto".
target_language_example: Tengo que comprar el libro de texto para la clase de español.
native_language_example: I have to buy the textbook for Spanish class.

additional_notes: Common term for the official document/permit that allows someone to drive. Also said as "permiso de conducir" in some countries (especially Spain). You’ll often see it in phrases like "tener/sacar/renovar la licencia de conducir" (to have/get/renew a driver’s license).
target_language_example: Necesito renovar mi licencia de conducir.
native_language_example: I need to renew my driver’s license.

meaning: blacklist; a list of people/things that are blocked or considered undesirable.
additional_notes: Used for people, companies, emails, phone numbers, etc. Common in everyday and business/tech contexts (e.g., being banned from an event, or an email address being blocked). Often appears with verbs like “estar en” (to be on) or “poner en” (to put on): “estar en la lista negra”, “poner a alguien en la lista negra”.
target_language_example: Su dirección de correo está en la lista negra.
native_language_example: His/Her email address is on the blacklist.

meaning: to attract attention; to call someone’s attention (tell them off).
additional_notes: Common expression with two main uses: (1) something “stands out” or “catches the eye” (often with “me/te/le llama la atención”): «Me llama la atención este vestido.» (2) to scold/reprimand someone: «El profesor le llamó la atención al alumno por llegar tarde.» In the reprimand sense, it can be close to “to tell someone off,” usually in a mild/official way.
target_language_example: Me llama la atención tu acento, ¿de dónde eres?
native_language_example: Your accent catches my attention—where are you from?

meaning: to arrive (at/to); to manage to / come to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with a destination: llegar a + place (often with a = “to”): Llegar a la estación, llegar a casa. Also used with an infinitive to mean “to manage to” or “to end up doing something”: llegar a + infinitive (e.g., llegar a entender = “to manage to understand”). In English you usually say “arrive in” a city/country and “arrive at” a specific place, so it won’t always translate word-for-word.
target_language_example: Llegamos a Madrid a las ocho.
native_language_example: We arrived in Madrid at eight.

meaning: 'to become' / 'to end up being' (often after a process).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a change over time or the result of a process/effort. Very close to "convertirse en" but often emphasizes the journey or eventual outcome. Common structure: "llegar a ser + noun/adjective" (e.g., llegar a ser médico, llegar a ser famoso).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, llegó a ser un gran líder.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a great leader.

meaning: to go far; to get far (achieve a lot).
additional_notes: Used both literally (traveling a long distance) and figuratively (making progress or becoming successful). In the figurative sense it often means “to make it” or “to get ahead.” You can also hear it in the negative: “No vas a llegar lejos” (“You won’t get far”).
target_language_example: Si sigues estudiando así, vas a llegar lejos.
native_language_example: If you keep studying like that, you’ll go far.

meaning: to arrive late; to be late.
additional_notes: Used to talk about arriving after the expected time. Common with a time expression (e.g., "llegar tarde a clase") or with a reason ("por el tráfico"). The opposite is "llegar temprano" (to arrive early).
target_language_example: Perdón, llegué tarde al trabajo por el tráfico.
native_language_example: Sorry, I arrived late to work because of traffic.

meaning: to carry out; to carry through; to conduct (a plan, project, task).
additional_notes: Used with an activity, plan, project, or action (not a physical object). Common in formal and everyday Spanish: llevar a cabo un proyecto/una tarea/una investigación/una reunión. Conjugate only "llevar": llevo a cabo, llevas a cabo, llevó a cabo, etc.
target_language_example: Vamos a llevar a cabo el proyecto la semana que viene.
native_language_example: We’re going to carry out the project next week.

meaning: to take a long time; to have been a long time (doing something).
additional_notes: Uses "llevar" to talk about duration. Common patterns: "Llevo mucho tiempo esperando" = "I’ve been waiting a long time" (present tense + gerund). Also "Lleva mucho tiempo" can mean "It takes a long time" or "It’s been a long time."
target_language_example: Llevo mucho tiempo viviendo aquí.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for a long time.

additional_notes: Used with clothing, shoes, accessories, etc. It describes what someone has on (more like “to have on” than “to carry”). Common in questions: “¿Qué llevas puesto/a?” = “What are you wearing?” Agreement sometimes appears with the person wearing it: “puesto” (masc.) / “puesta” (fem.).
target_language_example: Hoy llevo puesta una chaqueta azul.
native_language_example: Today I’m wearing a blue jacket.

meaning: to take time; to take a while.
additional_notes: Used to say that an activity or process requires a certain amount of time. It often appears as "llevar + amount of time" (e.g., "lleva dos horas") or "llevarle + time + a alguien" to show who it takes time for (e.g., "me lleva una hora"). In past tense, "llevó" means "it took".
target_language_example: Hacer la maleta lleva tiempo.
native_language_example: Packing takes time.

additional_notes: Used to say an action or process requires a short amount of time. It commonly appears as "Lleva unos minutos" (It takes a few minutes) or in questions like "¿Cuánto lleva?" (How long does it take?). You can swap in other time expressions: "lleva dos horas", "lleva un rato", "lleva un segundo".
target_language_example: Hacer el trámite lleva unos minutos.
native_language_example: Doing the paperwork takes a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used with a person: "llevarse bien con + [person]". The reflexive form "llevarse" means how people relate to each other; "bien" indicates they have a good relationship. In the present tense: "me llevo bien", "te llevas bien", "se lleva bien", "nos llevamos bien", "se llevan bien".
target_language_example: Me llevo bien con mis compañeros de trabajo.
native_language_example: I get along well with my coworkers.

meaning: to run over / knock down; (figuratively) to wipe out or take down.
additional_notes: Used for accidents or collisions (a car, bike, etc. knocks someone/something down), and also metaphorically for something that destroys or overwhelms people or plans (e.g., a crisis, a law, a mistake). Often appears as "se lo llevó por delante" (it took him/it out) or "me llevé por delante" (I knocked it over / ran into it).
target_language_example: El coche se llevó por delante una señal de tráfico.
native_language_example: The car knocked down a traffic sign.

meaning: to rain very heavily; to pour down (rain).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it’s raining a lot (a downpour). Often said as "Está lloviendo a cántaros". Literally "to rain in pitchers/buckets," but English doesn’t say it that way; common equivalents are "It’s pouring" or "It’s raining cats and dogs."
target_language_example: No salgas ahora: está lloviendo a cántaros.
native_language_example: Don’t go out now: it’s pouring rain.

additional_notes: A common environmental science term meaning rain made acidic by air pollution (often from factories, cars, etc.). It’s used in news, school, and discussions about pollution and the environment. Grammatically, it’s a noun phrase: "lluvia" (rain) + adjective "ácida" (acidic), with the adjective agreeing in gender and number (e.g., "lluvias ácidas" = acid rains).
target_language_example: La lluvia ácida puede dañar los bosques y los edificios.
native_language_example: Acid rain can damage forests and buildings.

additional_notes: Used to say you want something done at the earliest possible time. Very common in requests and instructions. Often follows verbs like hacerlo/enviarlo/venir/llamar: “Hazlo/Envíalo/Ven/Llámame lo antes posible.” You can also say “tan pronto como sea posible,” but “lo antes posible” is more everyday.
target_language_example: Envíame el documento lo antes posible, por favor.
native_language_example: Send me the document as soon as possible, please.

additional_notes: Uses the neuter article "lo" + an adjective to mean "that which is..." or "the ... thing". "Lo correcto" often refers to what is morally right or the proper/appropriate choice. It can stand alone (as a noun phrase) or after verbs like "hacer" (to do) or "ser" (to be).
target_language_example: Sé que es difícil, pero tienes que hacer lo correcto.
native_language_example: I know it’s difficult, but you have to do the right thing.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something surprising or unexpected. It’s a set phrase; literally it means “whether you believe it or not,” with the present subjunctive (creas). Often said as a standalone comment or followed by a full sentence.
target_language_example: Lo creas o no, nunca he probado el café.
native_language_example: Believe it or not, I’ve never tried coffee.

meaning: “the thing about … / …’s thing” (a situation, topic, or matter related to someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to refer vaguely to an issue or event without naming it directly. Common patterns: “lo de + person” = “what happened with + person / that person’s thing” (e.g., lo de Juan), and “lo de + noun” = “the matter of + noun” (e.g., lo de la reunión). Often used when both speakers already know the context.
target_language_example: ¿Supiste lo de Juan?
native_language_example: Did you hear about what happened with Juan?

additional_notes: Uses the neuter article “lo” to mean “the best (thing)” in general, not a specific masculine noun. Common in comparisons ("lo mejor de...") and in set phrases like “Lo mejor es...” (“The best thing is...”). Often followed by “que” in the pattern “Lo mejor que...” (“the best that...”).
target_language_example: Lo mejor es que mañana no trabajamos.
native_language_example: The best thing is that we don’t work tomorrow.

additional_notes: Literally refers to “the same thing.” Common in: “Es lo mismo” (“It’s the same”), “Da lo mismo” (“It’s the same / It doesn’t matter”), and “Me da lo mismo (X o Y)” (“I don’t care / Either is fine”). As a short reply, “Yo, lo mismo” means “Me too / Same here.”
target_language_example: Me da lo mismo si vamos en coche o en bus.
native_language_example: I don’t care whether we go by car or by bus.

additional_notes: Often used with negation (no, para nada) to emphasize that something is not true even a little: “No me interesa lo más mínimo” = “I don’t care in the slightest.” It can also appear with verbs like importar, interesar, preocupar, molestar. Less commonly, it can be used without negation to mean “the least/smallest thing” (e.g., “sin lo más mínimo de...” = “without the slightest...” ).
target_language_example: No me importa lo más mínimo lo que digan.
native_language_example: I don’t care in the slightest what they say.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an idea, fact, or thing (not a specific person). Very common in indirect questions and relative clauses: "No sé lo que pasó" = "I don’t know what happened." Often corresponds to English "what" meaning "the thing that".
target_language_example: Dime lo que necesitas.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need.

additional_notes: Used to mean “anything,” “whatever it is,” or “no matter what.” Common in casual speech: “Haz lo que sea” = “Do whatever (it takes).” It can also show indifference: “Me da igual, lo que sea” = “I don’t care, whatever.”
target_language_example: Podemos comer lo que sea; no tengo preferencia.
native_language_example: We can eat whatever; I don’t have a preference.

additional_notes: Used to apologize or to express sympathy (e.g., for bad news). It’s very common and polite. Often followed by “mucho” to emphasize: “Lo siento mucho” (“I’m very sorry”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, llegué tarde.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to mean “enough” in a general/neutral way (not tied to a specific noun). Often placed after a verb or adjective: “comer lo suficiente” (to eat enough), “es lo suficientemente grande” (it’s big enough). You may also see the related form “lo suficientemente + adjective/adverb” = “sufficiently / enough.”
target_language_example: No dormí lo suficiente anoche.
native_language_example: I didn’t sleep enough last night.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **lo + adjective** to mean “the (most) ___ thing” in a general/abstract sense. **Lo último** often means “the latest (news, fashion, update),” and can also mean “the last thing” in a sequence or the most recent thing that happened. Not to be confused with **por último** (“finally/lastly”).
target_language_example: ¿Has oído lo último?
native_language_example: Have you heard the latest?

meaning: "the most" (refers to a masculine plural group).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective (or sometimes a noun) to make the superlative for a masculine plural group: los más altos (the tallest), los más importantes (the most important). It can also mean “most people/the majority” when the adjective is omitted: Los más quieren ir (Most people want to go). Feminine plural is las más.
target_language_example: Ellos son los más altos de la clase.
native_language_example: They are the tallest in the class.

meaning: mine (my people: family, friends, teammates, etc.).
additional_notes: Uses the definite article + possessive to mean “my (ones/people).” It usually refers to a group you belong to or care about (often your family): *los míos* (my family/people), *los tuyos* (yours). It can stand alone (“mine”) or be followed by a noun for clarity: *los míos amigos* is not used; instead say *mis amigos* or *los míos* (implied “my people”).
target_language_example: Este fin de semana voy a ver a los míos.
native_language_example: This weekend I’m going to see my family/my people.

additional_notes: A preposition meaning “after” (time). It’s followed by a noun or an infinitive: luego de la cena (after dinner), luego de llegar (after arriving). Often interchangeable with “después de” (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Luego de la reunión, vamos a cenar.
native_language_example: After the meeting, we’re going to have dinner.

additional_notes: Used as a conjunction to introduce a clause that happens later in time than another action, similar to "después de que" or "después que". Common in some regions (especially Latin America). Often followed by a verb (e.g., "luego que llegues..."). Depending on meaning and region, it can sometimes be close to "as soon as" (immediate sequence).
target_language_example: Luego que terminó la reunión, nos fuimos a casa.
native_language_example: After the meeting ended, we went home.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for where someone works (office, shop, factory, etc.). Often used with prepositions like en (at/in) and from possessives: mi/tu/su lugar de trabajo. You may also hear centro de trabajo in more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Trabajo en un hospital; mi lugar de trabajo está cerca de mi casa.
native_language_example: I work in a hospital; my workplace is close to my house.

additional_notes: Used for the trip or period right after a wedding (often with irse de luna de miel = “to go on a honeymoon”). It can also be used figuratively for an early, happy phase of something (la luna de miel con el trabajo = “the honeymoon phase with the job”).
target_language_example: Después de la boda, nos fuimos de luna de miel a Cancún.
native_language_example: After the wedding, we went on our honeymoon to Cancún.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about the moon phase. Often appears with articles: "la luna llena" (the full moon) or "una luna llena" (a full moon).
target_language_example: Anoche hubo luna llena y el cielo estaba muy claro.
native_language_example: Last night there was a full moon and the sky was very bright.

additional_notes: Used literally for a green traffic light and figuratively to mean approval/authorization (often with verbs like "dar" or "tener": "dar luz verde" = to give the green light). In Spanish it’s usually a noun phrase; English often uses it as a verb ("to greenlight"), which Spanish typically expresses with "dar luz verde".
target_language_example: Nos dieron luz verde para empezar el proyecto.
native_language_example: They gave us the green light to start the project.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s negative or grumpy mood. Often appears with common verbs like "tener" (to be in a bad mood) and "estar de" (to be in a bad mood): "tener mal humor", "estar de mal humor". Also used as a noun phrase: "Su mal humor es evidente" (His/Her bad mood is obvious).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de mal humor, mejor hablamos mañana.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a bad mood; we’d better talk tomorrow.

meaning: “even if / although” (used to introduce a concession).
additional_notes: Used mainly in the fixed pattern “mal que + subjunctive,” meaning “even if it bothers/annoys (someone)” or “whether (someone) likes it or not.” It’s more literary/formal than “aunque.” Common set phrase: “mal que me pese” = “even if it pains me / whether I like it or not.”
target_language_example: Mal que le pese, tenemos que irnos ahora.
native_language_example: Whether he likes it or not, we have to leave now.

meaning: “whether you like it or not” / “even if it bothers you.”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something is true or will happen despite their dislike or disagreement. It can sound a bit confrontational or smug depending on tone. Often appears as “mal que le pese” (to him/her) or “mal que nos pese” (to us).
target_language_example: Mal que te pese, tengo razón.
native_language_example: Whether you like it or not, I’m right.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is known for negative reasons. Often appears with the verb "tener" (to have): "tener mala fama" = "to have a bad reputation". Also common with "ganarse" (to earn) or "dar" (to give someone a bad reputation).
target_language_example: Ese bar tiene mala fama en el barrio.
native_language_example: That bar has a bad reputation in the neighborhood.

meaning: weed; unwanted plant (often in a garden).
additional_notes: Literally “bad herb/plant.” Common in gardening and everyday speech for plants you don’t want growing. In plural: “malas hierbas” (weeds). Sometimes used figuratively in sayings like “Mala hierba nunca muere” (“Bad weeds never die”), meaning tough/undesirable people persist.
target_language_example: En mi jardín crece mucha mala hierba después de la lluvia.
native_language_example: In my garden, a lot of weeds grow after the rain.

meaning: bad mood; ill will (also: bad luck).
additional_notes: Common in Spain and parts of Latin America. Often means someone has a nasty attitude or is acting with ill intent: "Tiene mala leche" = "He/She has a mean streak." It can also mean "bad luck" in some contexts ("¡Qué mala leche!" = "What bad luck!/How unlucky!"). The literal meaning is "bad milk," but it’s usually idiomatic.
target_language_example: No le hagas caso; hoy tiene mala leche.
native_language_example: Don’t pay attention to him; he’s in a bad mood today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unlucky situation or outcome. You can say it as an exclamation when something goes wrong (¡Qué mala suerte!). It’s also common with verbs like tener (to have): Tengo mala suerte (I have bad luck).
target_language_example: ¡Qué mala suerte! Perdí las llaves otra vez.
native_language_example: What bad luck! I lost my keys again.

meaning: “Damn it!” / “For fuck’s sake!” (a strong exclamation of anger or frustration).
additional_notes: A common Spanish curse used when something goes wrong. Literally “may it be cursed,” but it’s usually just an exclamation. Often considered rude/vulgar depending on tone and setting; in more polite contexts you might use “¡Maldición!” or “¡Caray!”.
target_language_example: ¡Maldita sea! Se me olvidaron las llaves.
native_language_example: Damn it! I forgot my keys.

additional_notes: Can be literal (your physical right hand) or figurative to mean someone’s closest helper/supporter. Often used with "ser": "Ella es mi mano derecha" (She’s my right-hand person).
target_language_example: María es mi mano derecha en la oficina.
native_language_example: María is my right-hand person at the office.

meaning: left hand; (figuratively) tact/diplomacy (especially in “tener mano izquierda”).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “left hand.” Very commonly used in the expression “tener mano izquierda” = “to have tact / to handle people or a delicate situation diplomatically.” Often used when you need patience and a soft approach (e.g., with customers, children, or conflict).
target_language_example: Hay que tener mucha mano izquierda para hablar con él sin que se enfade.
native_language_example: You need a lot of tact to talk to him without him getting angry.

additional_notes: Common set phrase used to begin a task or project. Often said after planning or deciding something, to signal it’s time to start working. You can use it on its own or after “¡Bueno!” / “Entonces…”.
target_language_example: Ya tenemos el plan; manos a la obra.
native_language_example: We already have the plan; let’s get to work.

meaning: to stand firm; to hold your ground.
additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t give in under pressure, keeps their decision/opinion, or stays steady in a difficult situation. Often followed by “en” + a noun (mantenerse firme en su decisión) or used on its own. Literally “to keep oneself firm.”
target_language_example: A pesar de la presión, ella se mantuvo firme en su decisión.
native_language_example: Despite the pressure, she stood firm in her decision.

meaning: a rotten apple; (figuratively) a bad person who negatively affects a group (“bad apple”).
additional_notes: Literally means “rotten apple.” It’s often used figuratively like in English: “una manzana podrida” in a team, class, or organization. You may also hear the full saying: “Una manzana podrida echa a perder el cesto” (“One bad apple spoils the bunch”).
target_language_example: En el grupo hay una manzana podrida que siempre causa problemas.
native_language_example: In the group there’s a bad apple who always causes problems.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: adjective after the noun in Spanish (manzana + verde). Used literally to describe the color/type of apple; plural is "manzanas verdes."
target_language_example: Quiero una manzana verde, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a green apple, please.

additional_notes: Used especially for cars and other vehicles: "poner la marcha atrás" (to put the car in reverse) and "ir en marcha atrás" (to go in reverse). It can also mean 'to backtrack' or 'to reverse a decision' ("dar marcha atrás") in more general contexts.
target_language_example: Pon la marcha atrás y estaciona despacio.
native_language_example: Put it in reverse and park slowly.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time.
additional_notes: Used when you do something just to stay occupied while you wait or have nothing else to do. Very common and neutral in tone. Usually appears as a conjugated verb + the phrase: "Maté el tiempo...", "Estamos matando el tiempo...".
target_language_example: Estamos matando el tiempo en el café hasta que llegue el tren.
native_language_example: We’re killing time at the café until the train arrives.

additional_notes: Used for basic, unprocessed materials used to make products (wood, cotton, oil, etc.). Often appears in business, manufacturing, and economics contexts. It can be singular or plural in English depending on context; in Spanish it usually stays the same form (la materia prima / las materias primas).
target_language_example: Necesitamos materia prima para producir más zapatos.
native_language_example: We need raw materials to produce more shoes.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a headache. Structure: "me" = to me, "duele" = hurts (it hurts), "la cabeza" = the head. Spanish often phrases pain as "[body part] hurts (to me)": "Me duele + singular" (Me duele el brazo) or "Me duelen + plural" (Me duelen los ojos). You can add intensity: "Me duele mucho la cabeza" (My head hurts a lot).
target_language_example: Me duele la cabeza; creo que necesito descansar.
native_language_example: My head hurts; I think I need to rest.

additional_notes: From the verb "gustar". The grammar is different from English: it literally means “you are pleasing to me.” Use it when talking to one person (tú): "Me gustas". For more emphasis: "Me gustas mucho" (“I like you a lot”). Don’t confuse with "Me gusta" (“I like it”).
target_language_example: Me gustas mucho. ¿Quieres salir conmigo?
native_language_example: I like you a lot. Do you want to go out with me?

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself with your name. It comes from the verb "llamarse" (to be called), and it’s typically followed by a name: "Me llamo Ana." In questions, you’ll often hear: "¿Cómo te llamas?" (What’s your name?).
target_language_example: Hola, me llamo David. ¿Y tú?
native_language_example: Hi, my name is David. And you?

additional_notes: Very informal, playful rhyme based on the slang verb phrase “me piro” (from *pirarse* = to leave). Often used jokingly when you’re heading off, especially in Spain, typically among friends.
target_language_example: Bueno, gente, me piro vampiro, que ya es tarde.
native_language_example: Alright, guys, I’m out—it's already late.

additional_notes: Used in psychology and everyday speech to talk about unconscious or automatic ways people protect themselves from stress, anxiety, or uncomfortable feelings (e.g., denial, projection). In Spanish you’ll often hear it with verbs like "usar" (to use) or "tener" (to have).
target_language_example: Negar lo que pasó puede ser un mecanismo de defensa.
native_language_example: Denying what happened can be a defense mechanism.

additional_notes: Used for the prize awarded to first place (sports, competitions, awards). You can also say “ganar una medalla de oro” (to win a gold medal).
target_language_example: Ella ganó la medalla de oro en natación.
native_language_example: She won the gold medal in swimming.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration or waiting time. Common with expressions like “en media hora” (in half an hour) and “media hora más” (another half hour). It agrees as feminine because “hora” is feminine: “media hora” (not *medio hora*).
target_language_example: Espérame media hora, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for me half an hour, please.

meaning: half-turn; (in "dar/hacer media vuelta") to turn around / go back.
additional_notes: Often used with the verb "dar" or "hacer": "Dar/Hacer media vuelta" means to turn around (physically) and often implies returning the way you came. As an instruction: "¡Da media vuelta!" = "Turn around!"
target_language_example: Nos equivocamos de calle, así que dimos media vuelta.
native_language_example: We took the wrong street, so we turned around and went back.

additional_notes: Common in news, school, and official contexts when talking about nature, pollution, recycling, climate, and protecting the planet. Often used with verbs like proteger/cuidar (to protect/take care of) and with phrases like el cuidado del medio ambiente (care for the environment).
target_language_example: Tenemos que cuidar el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: We have to take care of the environment.

additional_notes: Often used in the singular to mean a type/channel of communication (e.g., internet, TV, radio). In the plural (medios de comunicación), it commonly refers to “the media” (news media).
target_language_example: Las redes sociales son un medio de comunicación muy importante hoy en día.
native_language_example: Social networks are a very important means of communication nowadays.

additional_notes: Used to say a place is very isolated or far from towns and people. Often appears with "en" ("en medio de la nada"), and you can also hear "en mitad de la nada" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en medio de la nada.
native_language_example: We ran out of gas in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Common in two contexts: (1) sports, meaning the break or midpoint of a game ("en el medio tiempo" = "at halftime"); (2) work/studies, meaning part-time ("trabajo de medio tiempo" = "a part-time job"). Also used as "a medias"/"not full" in some contexts (e.g., "a medio tiempo" can mean "partway").
target_language_example: Tengo un trabajo de medio tiempo y hoy veremos el partido hasta el medio tiempo.
native_language_example: I have a part-time job, and today we’ll watch the game until halftime.

additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to news media (TV, radio, newspapers, online news). Often appears as a plural subject: "Los medios de comunicación dicen..." It can also mean communication channels more generally, depending on context.
target_language_example: Los medios de comunicación informaron sobre el accidente.
native_language_example: The media reported on the accident.

additional_notes: Used to add an improved option or to correct/upgrade what you just said. Very common in conversation and writing. Often placed at the start of the new idea: “Mejor aún, …”. Also appears after a short pause: “Podemos ir mañana; mejor aún, el viernes.”
target_language_example: Podemos pedir pizza; mejor aún, vamos a cocinar en casa.
native_language_example: We can order pizza; better yet, let’s cook at home.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or suggest leaving (often because it’s late, unsafe, awkward, etc.). It commonly appears without a verb like "es" in casual speech: "Mejor irse" (= "It’s better to go/leave"). You can add time words like "ya" (now) or "antes" (before): "Mejor irse ya". "Irse" means "to leave/go away" (more like leaving a place), not just "to go" somewhere.
target_language_example: Mejor irse ya; está oscureciendo.
native_language_example: We’d better leave now; it’s getting dark.

meaning: a minor; underage (not legally an adult).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is under the legal age (often 18, depending on the country). Common in legal/official contexts (ID checks, alcohol, contracts). Often appears as "ser menor de edad" (to be underage) or "cuando era menor de edad" (when I was a minor).
target_language_example: No pueden vender alcohol a un menor de edad.
native_language_example: They can’t sell alcohol to a minor.

additional_notes: Used to express relief that something bad didn’t happen or that a situation turned out well. Very common in everyday speech. You can use it alone as an exclamation (“¡Menos mal!”) or before a clause (“Menos mal que…” = “Good thing that…”).
target_language_example: Menos mal que trajiste un paraguas.
native_language_example: Good thing you brought an umbrella.

additional_notes: Most commonly used for comparisons with numbers or quantities: "menos que + number" = "less than". It can also appear in the set phrase "a menos que" (often with subjunctive) meaning "unless"/"except if."
target_language_example: Cuesta menos que veinte euros.
native_language_example: It costs less than twenty euros.
