additional_notes: Common way to refer to an SMS. Often used with the verbs mandar/enviar (to send) and recibir (to receive): “mandar un mensaje de texto.” In many places you may also hear “SMS” or “un mensaje” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Te mando un mensaje de texto cuando llegue.
native_language_example: I’ll text you when I arrive.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is willing to consider new ideas or different opinions. Common with the verb "tener": "tener la mente abierta" (to be open-minded). It can also be used as an adjective phrase: "Es de mente abierta" (He/She is open-minded).
target_language_example: Hay que tener la mente abierta cuando viajas.
native_language_example: You have to keep an open mind when you travel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying or selling goods illegally, often because they are prohibited, scarce, or untaxed. It’s a neutral/serious term (not slang). You’ll often see it with verbs like "comprar" (to buy) or "vender" (to sell): "comprar en el mercado negro".
target_language_example: Dicen que venden esos boletos en el mercado negro.
native_language_example: They say they sell those tickets on the black market.

meaning: to mess up; to put your foot in it.
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning you made a mistake, often in a social situation (e.g., you said the wrong thing). It’s informal and often used with "lo siento" or "perdón" to apologize. Conjugates like a normal verb phrase: "metí la pata" (I messed up), "has metido la pata" (you’ve messed up).
target_language_example: Perdón, creo que metí la pata con ese comentario.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I put my foot in it with that comment.

meaning: to get into; to get involved in (often: to get into trouble).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean entering or becoming involved in something. Very common in phrases like: meterse en problemas/en líos (to get into trouble), meterse en una conversación (to jump into a conversation), or in advice/warnings: No te metas en eso (Don’t get involved in that).
target_language_example: No quiero meterme en problemas.
native_language_example: I don’t want to get into trouble.

meaning: "my soul"; also a very affectionate way to address someone (like "my dear").
additional_notes: Literally means "my soul." In everyday Spanish it can be used as a tender term of endearment, especially with family, partners, or close friends (often said to children). It can sound very warm/romantic, so use it with people you’re close to. You may also hear it in expressive phrases like "¡Ay, mi alma!" to show strong emotion.
target_language_example: Ven aquí, mi alma, que quiero hablar contigo.
native_language_example: Come here, my dear—I want to talk to you.

meaning: “my people” (my friends/group; people I identify with).
additional_notes: Used to refer affectionately to your crew, community, or the people you feel connected to. Often heard in greetings or shout-outs (especially in Latin music or on social media): “¡Mi gente!” = “My people!” / “My folks!” It can sound informal and warm; it doesn’t necessarily mean family.
target_language_example: ¡Mi gente, ya llegué! ¿Cómo están?
native_language_example: My people, I’m here! How are you all?

additional_notes: Use it to (1) contrast two ideas (“whereas”), often similar to “pero” but more formal/structured: "A..., mientras que B..."; or (2) indicate that two actions happen at the same time (“while”): "Hice X mientras que tú hacías Y." In everyday speech, "mientras" alone is also common for “while.”
target_language_example: Yo trabajo por la mañana, mientras que mi hermana trabaja por la tarde.
native_language_example: I work in the morning, whereas my sister works in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens during the time before another event. Often placed at the start of a sentence as a transition (Mientras tanto, ...) or used mid-sentence.
target_language_example: Voy a preparar la cena; mientras tanto, tú pon la mesa.
native_language_example: I’m going to make dinner; meanwhile, you set the table.

additional_notes: Used for large numbers, especially in news, finance, and population statistics. Spanish typically uses the long scale, so English “billion” = Spanish “mil millones” (literally “a thousand millions”). “Un billón” in Spanish usually means one trillion (1,000,000,000,000) in English.
target_language_example: La empresa vale mil millones de dólares.
native_language_example: The company is worth one billion dollars.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone to pay attention, often because they might break something, make a mistake, or hurt someone. It can sound like a quick warning or a mild scolding depending on tone. Often said when someone is being careless or moving without looking.
target_language_example: ¡Mira lo que haces! Vas a tirar el vaso.
native_language_example: Watch what you’re doing! You’re going to knock over the glass.

meaning: to look at; to face/turn toward.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object (often a person or thing): "Mira al profesor" = "Look at the teacher." It can also mean to face in a direction: "La casa mira al mar" = "The house faces the sea." Note the personal "a" before people: "mirar a Juan" often becomes "mirar a Juan" → "mirar a Juan" / "mirar al profesor" (a + el = al).
target_language_example: Mira al semáforo y luego cruza la calle.
native_language_example: Look at the traffic light and then cross the street.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to say you make eye contact with someone: “Mirar a alguien a los ojos”. It can be literal (eye contact) or figurative (to face something honestly or directly).
target_language_example: Mírame a los ojos cuando me hables.
native_language_example: Look me in the eyes when you talk to me.

additional_notes: Used when you turn your head/eyes to see what is around you (in a room, area, store, etc.). You can also hear the very similar phrase "mirar a tu alrededor" (to look around you). In Latin America, "mirar" is often used where Spain commonly uses "ver" (e.g., "ver alrededor" is less common).
target_language_example: Entré en la tienda y empecé a mirar alrededor.
native_language_example: I went into the store and started looking around.

meaning: to look up (toward something above you).
additional_notes: Used literally for directing your gaze upward (toward the ceiling, the sky, a sign, etc.). Often heard as a command: “¡Mira arriba!” For “look up” meaning “search for information,” Spanish usually uses “buscar” (e.g., “buscar en internet”), not “mirar arriba.”
target_language_example: Mira arriba: hay un pájaro en el árbol.
native_language_example: Look up: there’s a bird in the tree.

additional_notes: Used when you want to find out information about something: “mirar” here is like “to see” or “to check.” It’s very common after “vamos a” or “voy a”: “Vamos a mirar qué pasa” = “Let’s see what happens.”
target_language_example: Vamos a mirar qué opciones tenemos.
native_language_example: Let’s see what options we have.

additional_notes: Used to say that two people/things are in an identical location. Typically appears with an article ("el/este mismo lugar" = "this very same place") or after a noun ("en el lugar mismo" = "in the place itself"). Often used with prepositions like "en" (in/at) or "al" (to the).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el mismo lugar de siempre.
native_language_example: See you at the same place as always.

meaning: the indicative mood (used for stating facts).
additional_notes: A grammar term for the verb mood used to talk about real situations, facts, or things the speaker presents as true or certain. It contrasts with the subjunctive mood (modo subjuntivo), which is often used for doubts, wishes, or hypotheticals. You’ll see it in explanations like “Está en modo indicativo” or “Usa el modo indicativo aquí.”
target_language_example: En esta frase usamos el modo indicativo porque es un hecho.
native_language_example: In this sentence we use the indicative mood because it’s a fact.

meaning: the moment of truth (when you find out the real result).
additional_notes: Used when a decisive or revealing moment arrives—when something will finally be tested, decided, or confirmed (e.g., opening exam results, tasting a dish you cooked, giving a presentation). Often introduced with phrases like “Llegó/Ha llegado el momento de la verdad” (The moment of truth has arrived).
target_language_example: Bueno, llegó el momento de la verdad: vamos a ver si el coche arranca.
native_language_example: Well, the moment of truth has arrived: let’s see if the car starts.

meaning: to be starving; to be very hungry.
additional_notes: Literally “to die of hunger,” but it’s very often used as an exaggeration in everyday speech to mean you’re extremely hungry. You can use it with different subjects and tenses (e.g., “me muero de hambre” = “I’m starving”).
target_language_example: Me muero de hambre. ¿Vamos a comer algo?
native_language_example: I’m starving. Shall we go eat something?

meaning: "Break a leg" (good luck), especially in theatre; literally, "a lot of shit."
additional_notes: A common way to wish someone good luck in the performing arts (theatre, dance, etc.). It’s deliberately crude/vulgar, like English “break a leg,” and you usually say it before a performance instead of “buena suerte.” Outside that context, the literal meaning can sound insulting or offensive.
target_language_example: ¡Mucha mierda en el estreno!
native_language_example: Break a leg at the premiere!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck, especially before an exam, interview, trip, or performance. Often said as a standalone phrase: “¡Mucha suerte!” You can also add “con” to specify what: “Mucha suerte con el examen.”
target_language_example: ¡Mucha suerte mañana en tu entrevista!
native_language_example: Good luck tomorrow in your interview!

additional_notes: A common, polite way to express strong gratitude. Often used on its own, or with “por” + noun/infinitive: “Muchas gracias por tu ayuda” (Thanks a lot for your help). You can answer with “De nada” (You’re welcome).
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens repeatedly or frequently. It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence. Similar in meaning to "a menudo" (often) or "frecuentemente" (frequently).
target_language_example: Muchas veces voy al gimnasio después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I often go to the gym after work.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happened earlier than another time or event. Often followed by "de" + noun/phrase ("mucho antes de la clase" = much earlier than the class) or used on its own ("llegué mucho antes" = I arrived much earlier).
target_language_example: Llegamos mucho antes de que empezara la película.
native_language_example: We arrived long before the movie started.

additional_notes: A very common, polite greeting when you meet someone (often right after introductions). It literally means “much pleasure,” so you can also hear it as a response to “Encantado/a” or another “Mucho gusto.” Often said with “Hola” or “Soy…” during introductions.
target_language_example: —Hola, soy Ana. —Mucho gusto, Ana. Soy Mark.
native_language_example: “Hi, I’m Ana.” “Nice to meet you, Ana. I’m Mark.”

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that if the first thing isn’t true/possible, the second is even less true/possible. Common after a negative statement: "No tengo tiempo, mucho menos dinero". It can also mean "much less" in comparisons: "Cuanto más estudias, mucho menos te preocupa" (less common than the idiomatic "let alone" use).
target_language_example: No puedo pagar el alquiler, mucho menos comprar una casa.
native_language_example: I can’t pay the rent, let alone buy a house.

meaning: a long time; lots of time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about duration. Often appears in common phrases like "hace mucho tiempo" (a long time ago) and "desde hace mucho tiempo" (for a long time). Note the meaning is about time/duration, not the idea of "many times" (that would be "muchas veces").
target_language_example: No te veo desde hace mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in a long time.

additional_notes: A very strong, polite way to thank someone. "Muchísimas" is an emphatic form of "muchas" (“many/a lot of”), so it literally means something like “very many thanks.” Often used in customer service, emails, or when someone has helped you a lot.
target_language_example: Muchísimas gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

meaning: to change scenery; to get away for a while.
additional_notes: Often appears as “mudar de aires” (or “cambiar de aires”). It’s used when someone wants a break from their routine or a place that feels stressful, and they go somewhere else (a short trip or even moving) to feel better or start fresh.
target_language_example: Después de tantos problemas, necesito mudar de aires este fin de semana.
native_language_example: After so many problems, I need to change scenery this weekend.

additional_notes: Refers to the back molar that often comes in during the late teens or early twenties. Common in dental/medical contexts. Often used in the plural: "las muelas del juicio" (wisdom teeth).
target_language_example: Me duele la muela del juicio y necesito ir al dentista.
native_language_example: My wisdom tooth hurts and I need to go to the dentist.

additional_notes: Literally “dead from hunger,” but it’s usually used as an exaggeration to mean very hungry. It can also be used (more harshly) to insult someone as poor or miserable (“a nobody”), so be careful with tone and context. Often used with estar: “Estoy muerto/a de hambre.”
target_language_example: Estoy muerto de hambre. ¿Vamos a comer algo?
native_language_example: I’m starving. Shall we go eat something?

additional_notes: Used to contrast real life with a fictional/online world, ideas, or imagination. Often appears with the definite article: "en el mundo real" (in the real world).
target_language_example: En el mundo real, las cosas no siempre salen como en las películas.
native_language_example: In the real world, things don’t always turn out like in the movies.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to talk about frequency. It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence (or after the verb) to emphasize that something happens frequently. Similar to "con mucha frecuencia" and stronger than just "a menudo".
target_language_example: Muy a menudo voy al gimnasio después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Very often I go to the gym after work.

additional_notes: Common, versatile phrase. Use it to say you’re doing well ("Estoy muy bien"), to react positively ("¡Muy bien!" = “Great!”), or to show agreement/approval. It can also mean “very good” before nouns ("muy bien trabajo" is less common; usually you’d say "muy buen trabajo" with "buen" before a noun).
target_language_example: —¿Cómo estás? —Muy bien, gracias.
native_language_example: —How are you? —Very well, thanks.

additional_notes: Common, informal-sounding greeting used when arriving or starting a conversation, especially in Spain. It’s short for something like “muy buenas (tardes/días/noches)” and works at most times of day. Often said on its own: “¡Muy buenas!”
target_language_example: ¡Muy buenas! ¿Qué tal?
native_language_example: Hi! How’s it going?

additional_notes: A very common winter/holiday term. Literally means “doll/figure of snow,” but it refers to the snow figure people build outside. Plural: “muñecos de nieve.”
target_language_example: Los niños hicieron un muñeco de nieve en el patio.
native_language_example: The kids made a snowman in the yard.

additional_notes: Used for a machine that sews fabric. Often appears with the verb "coser" (to sew): "coser a máquina" = to sew by machine. You may also hear "máquina de coser doméstica" (home sewing machine) or "máquina de coser industrial" (industrial sewing machine).
target_language_example: Mi abuela tiene una máquina de coser en casa.
native_language_example: My grandma has a sewing machine at home.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the mechanical/electric device used to type on paper. It’s a common everyday phrase, though the object is less common today. Also used metaphorically in some contexts (e.g., the sound of keys like a typewriter).
target_language_example: Encontré una máquina de escribir antigua en el ático.
native_language_example: I found an old typewriter in the attic.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used for a (usually fictional) device that lets you travel through time. Use it with articles like "la/una": "la máquina del tiempo" (the time machine), "una máquina del tiempo" (a time machine). Plural: "máquinas del tiempo".
target_language_example: Si tuviera una máquina del tiempo, volvería al pasado.
native_language_example: If I had a time machine, I would go back to the past.

meaning: 'later' / 'later on' / 'further on' (in time or in a text).
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that will happen in the future (“later”) or that appears further along in a book, document, or conversation (“further on”). Common in planning: "Hablamos más adelante" = “We’ll talk later.” Similar idea: "más tarde" (later), but "más adelante" can also mean “further on” in a text or explanation.
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo; lo hablamos más adelante.
native_language_example: I can’t right now; we’ll talk later.

additional_notes: Commonly used to soften or correct what was just said: "No es caro, más bien es barato" (“It’s not expensive; rather, it’s cheap”). In questions/answers it often means “actually” or “more like”: "¿Quieres té?" — "Más bien café" (“Actually, coffee / I’d prefer coffee”). It can also introduce an alternative option (“rather/instead”) without sounding too blunt.
target_language_example: No estoy enojado; más bien estoy cansado.
native_language_example: I’m not angry; I’m rather tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something is excessive or beyond what’s appropriate/expected. Often follows a verb (hablar, beber, gastar, comer) or comes after the quantity being described. Similar to "demasiado" but a bit more idiomatic.
target_language_example: Gasté más de la cuenta en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I spent more than I should have at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase used to express an approximate amount (time, quantity, distance) or an uncertain/mediocre state. As an answer, it often means “so-so” or “kind of.” It can also soften a statement: “Más o menos entiendo” = “I understand, more or less.”
target_language_example: —¿Cómo estás? —Más o menos. Estoy un poco cansado.
native_language_example: —How are you? —So-so. I’m a little tired.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons: "más que + noun/adjective/adverb" (more … than …). With numbers it often means “more than/over”: "más que 100". It can also introduce a contrast: "Más que X, prefiero Y" (“Rather than X, I prefer Y”).
target_language_example: Esta casa es más grande que la otra.
native_language_example: This house is bigger than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to show that something is growing or happening to a greater degree over time. Common with verbs and adjectives (e.g., "me gusta más y más" / "está más y más cansado"). Often interchangeable with "cada vez más".
target_language_example: Cada día me gusta más y más vivir aquí.
native_language_example: Every day I like living here more and more.

additional_notes: A common genre label in Spanish. You’ll also hear it without "música" (just "pop"). Usually used with verbs like "escuchar" (to listen to) and "gustar" (to like).
target_language_example: Me gusta la música pop, sobre todo los años 90.
native_language_example: I like pop music, especially the 90s.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is going badly or you feel unwell. It’s a common intensifier: nada + adverb (bien/mal). Often used with estar (to be/feel): “No estoy nada bien.” Can also describe how something went: “Salió nada bien.”
target_language_example: Después de la comida, me sentí nada bien.
native_language_example: After the meal, I didn’t feel well at all.

additional_notes: Used to reject or deny something that was said, suggested, or implied. Common in conversation to correct someone or reassure them. Often appears with verbs like "no hay nada de eso" (there’s nothing like that) or "nada de eso" alone as a short reply meaning “not at all / no way.”
target_language_example: —¿Estás enojado conmigo? —Nada de eso, solo estoy cansado.
native_language_example: —Are you mad at me? —Not at all, I’m just tired.

additional_notes: An emphatic way to say there is zero of something (no money, no food, no news, etc.). It’s more informal and expressive than just "nada" and is common in spoken Spanish. Often used after a negative or in short replies.
target_language_example: ¿Te dijeron algo? Nada de nada.
native_language_example: Did they tell you anything? Nothing at all.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a number, person, or fact is impressive or surprising (“as many as / none other than”). Often appears as “nada menos que” before what’s being emphasized. Example: “nada menos que 20 personas” = “no less than 20 people.”
target_language_example: ¡Vinieron nada menos que veinte personas!
native_language_example: No less than twenty people came!

additional_notes: Common after a verb or at the end of a sentence to limit something: “only/just.” It can also mean “nothing else” in answers. In Spain you may hear “nada más” where Latin America often says “nada más” or “nomás” (more informal).
target_language_example: Quiero un café, nada más.
native_language_example: I just want a coffee, that’s all.

additional_notes: Used as a short answer when someone asks if there are updates, results, or if something has happened. “Todavía” implies you expect it might happen later (e.g., you’re still waiting). Often said on its own in conversation: “¿Alguna noticia?” — “Nada todavía.”
target_language_example: —¿Te han llamado del trabajo? —Nada todavía.
native_language_example: —Have they called you from the job? —Not yet.

additional_notes: Common phrase used to excuse a small mistake or remind someone not to judge too harshly. You can also hear it said on its own as a response after an error. Often used in a friendly, reassuring tone.
target_language_example: Perdón, me equivoqué… Bueno, nadie es perfecto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake… Well, nobody is perfect.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is not another person besides the one mentioned. Often appears after a noun/pronoun for emphasis (e.g., "yo y nadie más" = "me and no one else"). It can also be used with verbs like "ver" or "querer" to mean "(I) want/see no one else."
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con nadie más.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk to anyone else.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used in general statements about how people tend to think or behave. Often appears with articles: “la naturaleza humana” (human nature in general) or “nuestra naturaleza humana” (our human nature).
target_language_example: La naturaleza humana nos lleva a buscar compañía.
native_language_example: Human nature leads us to seek company.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people (or “you all,” depending on context) needs assistance. From necesitar (“to need”) + ayuda (“help”). It can refer to practical help or support in general. Often paired with clarifying details: “Necesitan ayuda con…” (“They need help with…”).
target_language_example: Los turistas necesitan ayuda para encontrar el hotel.
native_language_example: The tourists need help finding the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they need assistance or to check on them. It's informal in the sense that it uses the tú form (necesitas); for a more formal/polite version use “¿Necesita ayuda?” or “¿Necesita ayuda usted?” If you're asking as a question, add question marks: “¿Necesitas ayuda?”
target_language_example: ¿Necesitas ayuda con la tarea?
native_language_example: Do you need help with the homework?

additional_notes: Use this to ask for help in a respectful way, especially with strangers, older people, or in customer service. "Su" is the formal singular "your" (usted). With friends or family you’d usually say "necesito tu ayuda".
target_language_example: Disculpe, necesito su ayuda para encontrar la estación.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help to find the station.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone directly for assistance. From the verb “necesitar” (to need) + “tu ayuda” (your help). You can soften it by adding “por favor” (Necesito tu ayuda, por favor.) or make it more urgent with context (¡Necesito tu ayuda ahora!).
target_language_example: Necesito tu ayuda para encontrar mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: I need your help to find my passport.

additional_notes: Uses vosotros/vosotras (Spain) present tense of necesitar: necesitáis = “you all need.” It can be a question (with rising intonation or ¿…?) or a statement. For Latin America, the usual equivalent is ¿Necesitan ayuda? (ustedes).
target_language_example: ¿Necesitáis ayuda con las maletas?
native_language_example: Do you all need help with the suitcases?

additional_notes: Used to say something is far from true or far from a target/goal. Often followed by "de" + a number/amount or noun: "ni cerca de 100" (nowhere near 100). It can also be used alone as a short reply: "—¿Lo adivinaste? —Ni cerca."
target_language_example: No costó ni cerca de 100 dólares.
native_language_example: It didn’t cost anywhere near 100 dollars.

meaning: No way; not a chance; definitely not.
additional_notes: Commonly used to strongly refuse or reject something (similar to “not at all” or “forget it”). It can also respond to thanks to mean “don’t mention it,” but that meaning is less common than the refusal. Tone depends on context and can sound blunt.
target_language_example: —¿Me prestas tu coche? —Ni hablar.
native_language_example: —Can you lend me your car? —No way.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to say you don’t know or have no information. Often used alone as a short answer, or in the fuller form “No tengo ni idea” (“I have absolutely no idea”). You can also hear “Ni idea de…” (“No idea about…”).
target_language_example: —¿Dónde están las llaves? —Ni idea.
native_language_example: —Where are the keys? —No idea.

additional_notes: Strong refusal or rejection of an idea or request. Often used as a short standalone reply: “—¿Me prestas tu coche? —Ni pensarlo.” It comes from “(no) pensar” and implies “not even thinking about it,” so it can sound firm or a bit harsh depending on tone.
target_language_example: —¿Vas a copiar en el examen? —¡Ni pensarlo!
native_language_example: —Are you going to cheat on the exam? —No way!

meaning: "as if" / "like" (often to reject or mock an idea).
additional_notes: Used in informal speech, usually before a verb (often subjunctive) to say something is not true or not a big deal: "Ni que fuera..." = "It’s not like I were..." / "As if I were..." It can also appear as a reaction by itself: "¡Ni que!" = "Yeah, right!" / "As if!"
target_language_example: No te preocupes tanto, ni que fuera el fin del mundo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry so much—it’s not like it’s the end of the world.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something did not happen (or is not true) in the smallest or most expected case. It often comes before the word it highlights: "ni siquiera una vez" (not even once), "ni siquiera lo sé" (I don’t even know). It can also introduce a stronger negative point after another negative idea: "No llamó, ni siquiera mandó un mensaje" (He didn’t call, not even/texted). Usually used with a negative (no, nunca, nadie, etc.).
target_language_example: No tengo ni siquiera un dólar.
native_language_example: I don’t have even one dollar.

additional_notes: Used to add “you” to a negative statement, meaning “not you either.” It often appears after a negative phrase like “yo no…” or “a mí no…” and can be expanded to “ni tú tampoco.” In some contexts it can also be a sharp retort meaning “you’re no better.”
target_language_example: Yo no fui, ni tú tampoco.
native_language_example: I didn’t go, and you didn’t either.

meaning: not even one; not a single one.
additional_notes: Used for emphasis to mean “none at all,” often in negative sentences. It agrees in gender/number depending on what you’re referring to: ni uno (masculine), ni una (feminine). Common with words like “nadie”/“ninguno” style negatives or after “no”: “No tengo ni uno” = “I don’t have even one.”
target_language_example: No tengo ni uno de esos libros.
native_language_example: I don’t have a single one of those books.

additional_notes: Common polite reply meaning something is not an inconvenience (often after “gracias” or “perdón”). You can also say “no hay ningún problema.” The short form “ningún problema” is very common in conversation.
target_language_example: —Perdón por llegar tarde. —Ningún problema.
native_language_example: —Sorry for arriving late. —No problem.

additional_notes: Used in geography, weather, and travel to talk about altitude or elevation relative to the ocean’s surface. Often appears in phrases like “a nivel del mar” (at sea level) and “sobre el nivel del mar” (above sea level, abbreviated “s. n. m.”).
target_language_example: La ciudad está a 2.000 metros sobre el nivel del mar.
native_language_example: The city is 2,000 meters above sea level.

meaning: to not be able to take it anymore; to be unable to stand it any longer.
additional_notes: Used when someone has reached their limit emotionally, physically, or with a situation. It can refer to enduring pain, noise, stress, or someone’s behavior. Often followed by a noun or situation (e.g., el ruido, esta situación) or used on its own. Closely related to “¡No puedo más!” (I can’t take it anymore / I can’t go on).
target_language_example: No aguanto más este ruido; por favor, bájale la música.
native_language_example: I can’t take this noise anymore; please turn the music down.

meaning: “not like that / not that way”; “not so” (used to contrast).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is not done in a certain way, or to correct/contrast what was just said. It often appears after an explanation or instruction: “Hazlo así; no así” (“Do it like this; not like that”). It can also contrast two statements: “A él sí le gusta; a mí, no así” (“He likes it; I don’t, not like that”).
target_language_example: No se dice así; no así, sino así.
native_language_example: You don’t say it like that; not that way, but like this.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to mean something happens immediately after something else. Common patterns: "No bien + past tense (preterite) + ..., (ya)..." = "As soon as ..." and "No bien + had... (imperfect) + past (preterite), ..." = "No sooner had ... than ...". Often followed by "cuando" or "y" in the next clause.
target_language_example: No bien llegué a casa, te llamé.
native_language_example: As soon as I got home, I called you.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective to describe a person’s gender identity (e.g., "persona no binaria"). Often agrees in number: "no binaria" (feminine singular), "no binarios/no binarias" (plural). You may also see the inclusive form "no binarie" in some communities. In Spanish, it’s common to say "persona no binaria" rather than using it alone as a noun.
target_language_example: Alex es una persona no binaria.
native_language_example: Alex is a non-binary person.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand what someone said. It’s correct but a bit more formal; in everyday speech you’ll also hear “no entiendo.” Often followed by “¿Puede repetir?” (Can you repeat?) or “¿Qué significa…?” (What does … mean?).
target_language_example: Perdón, no comprendo. ¿Puede repetirlo más despacio?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand. Can you repeat it more slowly?

additional_notes: From the verb *creer* (“to believe/think”) in the present subjunctive, used as a negative command or as a quick response to disagree with something or correct an assumption. Often followed by *que*: *No creas que...* (“Don’t think that...”).
target_language_example: —¿Crees que va a llover? —No creas; el cielo se está despejando.
native_language_example: —Do you think it’s going to rain? —I don’t think so; the sky is clearing up.

meaning: to not say a word; to stay silent.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize complete silence (often meaning you shouldn’t reveal anything). Commonly appears with other verbs like "sin decir palabra" (without saying a word) or as a command: "¡No digas palabra!" = “Don’t say a word!” Literally “not to say (a) word.”
target_language_example: Durante la reunión, no dijo palabra.
native_language_example: During the meeting, he/she didn’t say a word.

additional_notes: Common phrase to say you don’t understand what someone said or what’s happening. Often followed by "..." + a noun or question word: "No entiendo la pregunta" (I don’t understand the question), "No entiendo por qué" (I don’t understand why). You can make it more polite/softer with "Lo siento, no entiendo" (Sorry, I don’t understand) or "No entiendo bien" (I don’t understand well).
target_language_example: Perdón, no entiendo. ¿Puedes repetirlo?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand. Can you repeat it?

additional_notes: Common polite reply after someone says “gracias” (like “you’re welcome” or “no problem”). It can also mean “It’s nothing” to minimize a problem or say something isn’t important. Often said as “No es nada.” or “No es nada, de verdad.”
target_language_example: —Gracias por tu ayuda. —No es nada.
native_language_example: —Thanks for your help. —Don’t mention it.

additional_notes: Informal negative command using the tú form of the verb fastidiar (“to bother/annoy”). Often said as a complaint or to tell someone to stop doing something irritating. You can add an object for clarity: “No me fastidies” = “Don’t bother me / Don’t bug me.”
target_language_example: No me fastidies, estoy tratando de trabajar.
native_language_example: Don’t bug me, I’m trying to work.

additional_notes: Common on signs and rules (e.g., in restaurants, public buildings, airplanes). It’s an impersonal instruction meaning smoking is not allowed. You may also see “Prohibido fumar” (Smoking prohibited).
target_language_example: Por favor, no fumar dentro del edificio.
native_language_example: Please, no smoking inside the building.

meaning: to have nothing more than; to only have to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean “there’s nothing to do but…” or “you only have to…”. Often appears as: “No hay más que + infinitive” (present) or “No había más que + infinitive” (past). Similar in meaning to “solo hay que / no hay más que”.
target_language_example: No hay más que esperar.
native_language_example: There’s nothing to do but wait.

additional_notes: Use this to say you don’t speak English. You can replace “inglés” with another language (e.g., “No hablo español”). If you want to be extra polite, you can add “lo siento” (No hablo inglés, lo siento) or “perdón” (Perdón, no hablo inglés). You may also hear the more general phrase “No hablo (mucho) español” = “I don’t speak (much) Spanish.”
target_language_example: Perdón, no hablo inglés. ¿Habla español?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak English. Do you speak Spanish?

meaning: to do nothing; not to do anything.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not doing any activity. You can use it as an infinitive after another verb (e.g., "Quiero no hacer nada" = "I want to do nothing") or in a conjugated form like "No hago nada" (I’m not doing anything). Commonly used to describe relaxing or being inactive.
target_language_example: Hoy no quiero hacer nada; solo descansar.
native_language_example: Today I don’t want to do anything; I just want to rest.

additional_notes: Uses the object pronoun "lo" ("it") attached to the infinitive "hacer" (to do/make). You’ll often see it after another verb (e.g., "prefiero no hacerlo" = "I’d rather not do it") or after "para" ("para no hacerlo" = "so as not to do it"). In a full sentence you can also separate it: "no lo hago" (I don’t do it).
target_language_example: Prefiero no hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: I'd rather not do it today.

additional_notes: Very common, friendly reply to accept a request, say something is okay, or reassure someone. Often used like “you’re welcome” after “gracias.” You may also hear the plural: “no hay problemas.”
target_language_example: —Perdón por llegar tarde. —No hay problema.
native_language_example: —Sorry for arriving late. —No problem.

meaning: “you don’t have to / there’s no need to …”
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is not necessary, often as gentle advice or reassurance. It can refer to a general situation (“no hay que preocuparse”) rather than a specific person. Similar in meaning to “no tienes que…,” but “no hay que…” sounds more general/impersonal.
target_language_example: No hay que correr; tenemos tiempo.
native_language_example: You don’t have to run; we have time.

meaning: "there’s no one who" / "no one can" (used to say something is impossible or unbearable).
additional_notes: Commonly used to complain or emphasize that a situation is too much: someone can’t do something, or something can’t be endured. It’s usually followed by a verb in the infinitive: "No hay quien + infinitive" (e.g., dormir, trabajar, estudiar). You’ll also see it in the pattern "No hay quien lo/la/los/las + verb" to refer to a person/thing ("No hay quien lo entienda" = no one can understand it).
target_language_example: Con tanto ruido, no hay quien duerma.
native_language_example: With so much noise, no one can sleep.

additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of **haber** (**haya**) and usually appears after **que** to express a wish, request, or requirement: **Que no haya más problemas** (“I hope there aren’t any more problems”). Common in set phrases like **Que no haya más preguntas** (“No more questions”).
target_language_example: Espero que no haya más retrasos.
native_language_example: I hope there aren’t any more delays.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t important or to reassure someone after a mistake or apology. It can also answer a “Does it matter?” question. Often heard as “No importa” or “No importa, está bien.” Similar in meaning to “No pasa nada.”
target_language_example: —Perdón, llegué tarde. —No importa, todavía tenemos tiempo.
native_language_example: —Sorry, I’m late. —It doesn’t matter; we still have time.

meaning: “You don’t really know (how much/how well).” / “You have no idea.”
additional_notes: Used for emphasis, often as a reply to someone who is underestimating something. It implies “if you knew, you’d agree” or “it’s more than you think.” The "lo" refers to whatever is being talked about (the situation, difficulty, amount, etc.). Commonly followed by an explanation.
target_language_example: —¿Es difícil el examen? —No lo sabes bien: estudié toda la semana y aun así me costó mucho.
native_language_example: —Is the exam hard? —You have no idea: I studied all week and it was still really hard.

additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Literally "I don't know it" (no + lo + sé). "Lo" refers to the thing you don’t know (the answer, the information). Often said as "No sé" as well; "No lo sé" can sound a bit more emphatic or specific ("I don't know it/that").
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora llega el tren? No lo sé.
native_language_example: What time does the train arrive? I don't know.

meaning: "I don't care" / "It doesn't matter to me."
additional_notes: In standard Spanish this is written "no me importa" ("m'importa" is not standard Spanish spelling and may be a typo or influence from another language). Used to say something doesn’t matter to you or you don’t mind. Often followed by "si...": "No me importa si llegas tarde" (I don’t care if you arrive late).
target_language_example: No me importa; elige tú.
native_language_example: I don't care; you choose.

meaning: “You don’t say!” / “No way!” (to show surprise or disbelief).
additional_notes: Literally means “don’t tell me,” but it’s most often used as a fixed expression reacting to news (similar to “Really?”). It can sound sarcastic depending on tone. In a literal sense, it can also be a direct request: “Don’t tell me (that).”
target_language_example: —Me ascendieron hoy. —¡No me digas! ¡Felicidades!
native_language_example: —I got promoted today. —No way! Congratulations!

meaning: “I don’t care” / “it doesn’t matter to me.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is not important to you, or that you have no preference. It can sound rude or dismissive depending on tone; softer options include “me da igual” (I don’t mind) or “no importa” (it doesn’t matter). Often followed by “si…” + a situation (e.g., “No me importa si llegas tarde”).
target_language_example: No me importa dónde comamos; tú eliges.
native_language_example: I don’t care where we eat; you choose.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “no more / no longer” when you’re stopping something or saying it doesn’t happen anymore: “No más.” = “No more.” It can also mean “only/just” (especially in Latin America) when placed after a quantity or time expression: “dos días no más” = “only two days.” Without context, beginners will most often use it as “no more.”
target_language_example: No más, por favor; ya no quiero comer.
native_language_example: No more, please; I don’t want to eat anymore.

meaning: to not stop; to keep going (constantly).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about doing something continuously. Very common pattern: "no parar de" + infinitive ("No paro de pensar" = "I can't stop thinking"). You can conjugate it like a normal verb: "no paro", "no paras", "no para", etc.
target_language_example: No paro de trabajar hoy.
native_language_example: I can’t stop working today.

additional_notes: Common, very natural phrase used to reassure someone, minimize a mistake, or respond to an apology or thanks. Often used like “It’s nothing.” Literal meaning is “nothing happens,” but it’s usually understood as “it’s not a big deal.”
target_language_example: Perdón por llegar tarde. —No pasa nada.
native_language_example: Sorry for arriving late. —No problem.

meaning: “They shall not pass” / “They will not get through.”
additional_notes: A strong slogan meaning the enemy/opponents won’t be allowed to advance or enter. Famous from the Spanish Civil War (“¡No pasarán!”) and still used in political/activist contexts (often anti-fascist). Grammatically, it’s the future tense: pasarán = “they will pass/get through,” so no pasarán = “they won’t.”
target_language_example: En la manifestación la gente gritaba: «¡No pasarán!»
native_language_example: At the protest people were shouting: “They shall not pass!”

meaning: to not be able to take it anymore; to be exhausted/fed up.
additional_notes: Used to express that you’ve reached your limit—physically (too tired), emotionally (overwhelmed), or mentally (can’t stand something anymore). Often followed by "con" + noun/pronoun: "No puedo más con este calor" (I can’t take this heat anymore).
target_language_example: No puedo más con este calor; estoy agotado.
native_language_example: I can’t take this heat anymore; I’m exhausted.

meaning: to not be able to stand (someone/something); to hate (someone/something).
additional_notes: Often used with a direct object (person/thing): “No lo/la puedo ver” = “I can’t stand him/her/it.” It’s stronger than “no me gusta” (I don’t like) and is common in everyday speech. In literal contexts it can also mean “to not be able to see,” but when talking about a person it usually means you can’t stand them.
target_language_example: No lo puedo ver desde que me mintió.
native_language_example: I can’t stand him since he lied to me.

additional_notes: Literally means “it can’t be,” used both to express disbelief/surprise (“No way!”) and to say something isn’t possible. Common in conversation; tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: ¡No puede ser! Se me olvidaron las llaves.
native_language_example: No way! I forgot my keys.

meaning: to be nothing; to be no big deal.
additional_notes: Used to downplay something or say it isn’t important. Often said in response to thanks or an apology (similar to “it’s nothing” / “no worries”), or to describe a problem as minor. Literally “to not be anything.”
target_language_example: —Gracias por ayudarme. —No es nada.
native_language_example: —Thanks for helping me. —It’s nothing.

additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Often used alone as a complete answer, or followed by an indirect question: "No sé dónde está" (I don’t know where it is). You can soften it with "No sé" + hesitation (e.g., "No sé…") or add "la verdad" (honestly) for emphasis: "No sé, la verdad."
target_language_example: No sé dónde está mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I don’t know where my phone is.

meaning: "I don’t know how many"; also "countless/so many" (when you don’t know the exact number).
additional_notes: Used when the exact number is unknown or not important. Often followed by a noun: "no sé cuántas veces" (I don’t know how many times). It can also emphasize that something happened many times or that there are many of something, similar to "umpteen" or "I don’t know how many."
target_language_example: He ido a ese restaurante no sé cuántas veces.
native_language_example: I’ve been to that restaurant countless times / I don’t know how many times.

meaning: a “something” you can’t quite name; a certain “je ne sais quoi.”
additional_notes: Used when you can’t explain exactly what it is about something/someone, but you feel there’s a special or strange quality. Often appears with verbs like tener: “Tiene un no sé qué.” It can also introduce an unclear or unknown detail: “No sé qué día viene” (“I don’t know what day they’re coming”).
target_language_example: Ese lugar tiene un no sé qué que me encanta.
native_language_example: That place has a certain something that I love.

meaning: “Don’t think so / Don’t believe it” (often: “Actually, no / not really”).
additional_notes: Literally “don’t you believe (it).” Used to correct someone’s assumption or to downplay what was just said. Very common in conversation. It can answer a question by meaning “Not really,” or it can introduce a correction (similar to “Actually…”).
target_language_example: —¿Estás enojado? —No te creas, solo estoy cansado.
native_language_example: —Are you mad? —Not really, I’m just tired.

additional_notes: Very common way to reassure someone. Literally “don’t you worry” (informal singular tú). Often used to respond to an apology or thanks (similar to “it’s okay” / “no problem”). You can also say “No se preocupe” for formal usted, and “No os preocupéis” in Spain for vosotros.
target_language_example: —Perdón por llegar tarde. —No te preocupes, no pasa nada.
native_language_example: —Sorry for arriving late. —Don’t worry, it’s no big deal.

meaning: to have no heart; to be heartless/cruel.
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone as cold or lacking empathy. Often said about a specific action: “No tienes corazón” (“You have no heart”). Not the same as “no tener corazón para…” (“not to have the heart to…”, meaning you can’t bring yourself to do something).
target_language_example: ¡No tienes corazón! ¿Cómo pudiste decirle eso?
native_language_example: You’re heartless! How could you say that to him/her?

meaning: to have no idea; to not know (at all).
additional_notes: Common way to say you don’t know something. Often used as: “No tengo idea” (I have no idea) or “No tenía idea” (I had no idea). You can also add “de + noun/verb” to specify what you don’t know: “No tengo idea de eso” (I have no idea about that) / “No tengo idea de cómo hacerlo” (I have no idea how to do it).
target_language_example: No tengo idea de dónde está mi llave.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my key is.

meaning: to have no idea; to not know at all.
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase to say you don’t know something. Used with a subject (often "yo") and can be followed by "de" + noun or by an indirect question: "No tengo ni idea de la dirección" / "No tengo ni idea de dónde está". Also common in the past: "No tenía ni idea" (I had no idea).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo ni idea de dónde está el baño.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have no idea where the bathroom is.

meaning: to be speechless (not know what to say).
additional_notes: Used when something surprises, shocks, impresses, or moves you so much that you can’t find words. Often followed by "para" + infinitive: "No tengo palabras para describirlo" (I have no words to describe it). You can use it in different tenses: "No tenía palabras" / "Me quedé sin palabras" (a common alternative).
target_language_example: No tengo palabras para agradecerte todo lo que hiciste.
native_language_example: I don’t have words to thank you for everything you did.

meaning: to have no solution; to be beyond help/repair (hopeless).
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation or problem can’t be fixed or avoided, or that someone won’t change. Often used with "esto" (this) or a person: "Esto no tiene remedio" / "Él no tiene remedio". Can also be used jokingly to mean someone is incorrigible.
target_language_example: Lo intentamos todo, pero la situación no tiene remedio.
native_language_example: We tried everything, but the situation has no solution.

additional_notes: Common way to say something isn’t worth doing because it won’t help or won’t change anything. Very common in Mexico and much of Latin America; in Spain you may hear "no tiene sentido" more. Often followed by an infinitive: "No tiene caso discutir" (There’s no point arguing).
target_language_example: No tiene caso esperar más; vámonos.
native_language_example: There’s no point waiting any longer; let’s go.

meaning: “you have no idea” / “it’s really (so)…”, used for emphasis.
additional_notes: Common colloquial expression (especially in Spain) used to intensify what you’re saying, often followed by a clause: “No veas lo + adjective” (e.g., “No veas lo caro que es”) or “No veas cómo…” (e.g., “No veas cómo llueve”). It can also be the literal command “don’t look/watch,” but the emphatic use is idiomatic.
target_language_example: No veas lo cansado que estoy hoy.
native_language_example: You have no idea how tired I am today.

meaning: to be irrelevant; to not apply (to the situation).
additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t relate to what’s being discussed or isn’t helpful to the current point. Often used with "eso" or "esto": "Eso no viene al caso" = "That’s not relevant." You can also say "no viene al caso" without "venir" in the infinitive. Register: neutral, common in conversation and writing.
target_language_example: Eso no viene al caso; estamos hablando de otra cosa.
native_language_example: That’s not relevant; we’re talking about something else.

additional_notes: A polite, common way to decline an offer or invitation. Often used in shops/restaurants when someone offers you something. You can soften it further with “No, gracias, estoy bien” (No thanks, I’m good) or “No, gracias. Tal vez después” (No thanks. Maybe later).
target_language_example: —¿Quiere una bolsa? —No, gracias.
native_language_example: —Would you like a bag? —No, thank you.

additional_notes: Refers to the night of a couple’s wedding (often the first night they spend together as a married couple, sometimes linked to the start of the honeymoon). Common in everyday conversation and in romantic contexts. Plural: “noches de bodas” (wedding nights).
target_language_example: Después de la boda, nos fuimos al hotel para nuestra noche de bodas.
native_language_example: After the wedding, we went to the hotel for our wedding night.

additional_notes: Used on forms and in official contexts to ask for or provide your full legal name (first name(s) + last name(s)). In many Spanish-speaking countries people may have two last names; you can still answer with your full name as you normally write it.
target_language_example: Por favor, escribe tu nombre completo aquí.
native_language_example: Please write your full name here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person’s given name, as opposed to their last name(s) (apellido/s). Common in forms and official contexts. In Spanish-speaking countries, people often have two last names, but only one (or sometimes two) given names; “nombre de pila” points specifically to the given name.
target_language_example: En el formulario escribe tu nombre de pila y tus apellidos.
native_language_example: On the form, write your first name and your last name(s).

additional_notes: In grammar, it means a proper noun: the name of a specific person, place, organization, etc., and it’s usually capitalized (e.g., Juan, Madrid, Google). In everyday forms and paperwork, it often refers specifically to your given/first name (as opposed to apellido(s) = last name(s)).
target_language_example: Escribe tu nombre propio y tus apellidos en este formulario.
native_language_example: Write your first name and your last name(s) on this form.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say that something is pleasing to us. The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so it often appears as: "Nos gusta + singular noun/infinitive" (e.g., "Nos gusta el café", "Nos gusta nadar"). For plural things, use "nos gustan" (e.g., "Nos gustan las películas").
target_language_example: Nos gusta este restaurante.
native_language_example: We like this restaurant.

additional_notes: From the verb irse (to leave/go away). Common in conversation to announce that you (and others) are leaving, or as a suggestion to go now. Often followed by a destination: “Nos vamos a casa.” You can add “ya” for emphasis: “Nos vamos ya” (“We’re leaving now”).
target_language_example: Nos vamos, que ya es tarde.
native_language_example: We’re leaving, because it’s already late.

additional_notes: A very common, informal goodbye. Literally means “we see each other,” but it’s used like English “see you.” You can extend it with time phrases: “Nos vemos mañana” (see you tomorrow), “Nos vemos luego” (see you later).
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Alright, I’m leaving. See you tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb "ver" (to see), in the future tense: "veremos" = "we will see." "Nos" indicates "each other". Common as a friendly goodbye, similar to "See you" or "We’ll see each other later." Often appears with time/place: "Nos veremos mañana" (We’ll see each other tomorrow).
target_language_example: Nos veremos mañana en el parque.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow at the park.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it’s specifically two people: you and I (or two people including the speaker). Often used for plans or relationships: “Nosotros dos vamos…” (the two of us are going…). You can also say “los dos” if the subject is already clear. Feminine equivalent: “nosotras dos” (two females speaking).
target_language_example: Nosotros dos vamos al cine esta noche.
native_language_example: The two of us are going to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: The Spanish number 95. Used for counting, prices, ages, years, temperatures, etc. In Spanish, numbers 31–99 are often formed as “[tens] y [ones]” (e.g., 90 = noventa; 5 = cinco).
target_language_example: Cuesta noventa y cinco dólares.
native_language_example: It costs ninety-five dollars.

additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened at any earlier time. Often placed at the start of a sentence for emphasis: “Nunca antes había…” (Never before had I…). It can be followed by a time reference: “nunca antes de hoy” (never before today).
target_language_example: Nunca antes había visto algo así.
native_language_example: I had never seen anything like that before.

additional_notes: A common saying used to suggest you shouldn’t rule something out completely, because circumstances can change and you might end up doing it anyway. Often said as advice or a mild warning after someone says they will never do something.
target_language_example: —Yo nunca voy a mudarme de ciudad. —Nunca digas nunca.
native_language_example: “I’m never going to move cities.” “Never say never.”

additional_notes: An emphatic way to say something will not happen or must not be done. Stronger than just "nunca" and common in spoken Spanish; often used for promises, refusals, or warnings.
target_language_example: Nunca jamás vuelvas a mentirme.
native_language_example: Never ever lie to me again.

meaning: never again; not anymore (from now on).
additional_notes: Used to say you will not do something again, or that something will not happen again. Often appears with the present tense for a decision from now on (e.g., “Nunca más vuelvo…” = “I’m never coming back again”). Can also be used alone as an emphatic response meaning “Never again.”
target_language_example: Nunca más voy a fumar.
native_language_example: I’m never going to smoke again.

additional_notes: Used to say something is uncertain, so it’s good to be prepared or consider a possibility. Literally “one never knows,” with an impersonal "se" (no specific person). Often followed by a possible outcome: "...nunca se sabe."
target_language_example: Lleva una chaqueta; nunca se sabe si va a hacer frío.
native_language_example: Bring a jacket; you never know if it’s going to get cold.

additional_notes: A common animal name. Even though it’s made of two words (“nutria” = otter, “marina” = marine/sea), Spanish uses the full phrase as the standard term for the sea otter.
target_language_example: La nutria marina flota boca arriba mientras come.
native_language_example: The sea otter floats on its back while it eats.

additional_notes: Used for a unique identification code on a product (electronics, appliances, documents, etc.). Often appears on labels or in manuals. Common question: “¿Cuál es el número de serie?” (What is the serial number?).
target_language_example: Necesito el número de serie de tu computadora para registrarla.
native_language_example: I need your computer’s serial number to register it.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, give, or talk about someone’s phone number. Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have), "dar" (to give), and "dejar" (to leave): "¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono?" / "Te doy mi número de teléfono". You can also say "número de celular/móvil" for a mobile number.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono?
native_language_example: What’s your phone number?

additional_notes: Literally “number two.” Used in lists/rankings (e.g., the second item). In informal, humorous context it can mean “poop” or “to go number two” (hacer número dos), especially with kids or to avoid being too direct.
target_language_example: En la lista, tú eres el número dos.
native_language_example: On the list, you are number two.

additional_notes: Used in math and everyday contexts to describe a number that is not divisible by 2 (1, 3, 5, etc.). Often contrasted with "número par" (even number). You may also hear it in expressions like "en número impar" (in an odd number/quantity).
target_language_example: Siete es un número impar.
native_language_example: Seven is an odd number.

additional_notes: Used in math and everyday contexts to describe numbers divisible by 2 (ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8). Opposite: "número impar" (odd number). Often used with "es" (is) or "son" (are), and in questions like "¿Es un número par?"
target_language_example: Ocho es un número par.
native_language_example: Eight is an even number.

additional_notes: Used in math to describe a whole number greater than 1 that has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. Plural: "números primos". Often used with verbs like "ser" (to be) and "encontrar" (to find).
target_language_example: El 7 es un número primo.
native_language_example: 7 is a prime number.

meaning: number one; the best; also: the toilet (#1).
additional_notes: Literally “number one.” Used to rank something/someone as the best (“He’s number one”). In some contexts (especially in spoken language), it can mean “pee/going to the bathroom,” often contrasted with “número dos” (poop).
target_language_example: Voy al baño: es número uno.
native_language_example: I’m going to the bathroom: it’s number one.

meaning: “I mean…,” “that is (to say)…,” or “so…” (used to clarify or rephrase).
additional_notes: Very common filler phrase in spoken Spanish. Use it to restate something in simpler words, correct yourself, or introduce an explanation. It can also show mild emphasis or disbelief depending on tone (similar to “I mean, come on…”). Often followed by a pause: “O sea, …”.
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy; o sea, tengo que trabajar hasta tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t go today; I mean, I have to work late.

o todos en el suelo, o todos en la cama

target_language_multi_word_term: o todos en el suelo, o todos en la cama
meaning: "Either all on the floor, or all in the bed" (either everyone shares it, or nobody does).
additional_notes: A colloquial saying used to insist on equal treatment: no special privileges for one person. It can mean “we’re all in this together”—either everyone gets the benefit, or everyone accepts the same restriction/penalty. Often used humorously or to pressure a group into fairness.
target_language_example: Si no nos dejan entrar a todos, entonces o todos en el suelo, o todos en la cama.
native_language_example: If they won’t let all of us in, then either everyone gets the same treatment or nobody does.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an artistic creation (a painting, sculpture, etc.). In everyday speech it can also be used figuratively to praise something as excellent or beautifully made (e.g., food, a plan, a design).
target_language_example: Ese cuadro es una obra de arte.
native_language_example: That painting is a work of art.

meaning: masterpiece (a great work of art or achievement).
additional_notes: Used for an outstanding work (a painting, book, film, piece of music, etc.). Often with an article: "una obra maestra" / "la obra maestra". Literally “master work,” but in English the natural translation is “masterpiece.”
target_language_example: Muchos consideran esta novela una obra maestra.
native_language_example: Many people consider this novel a masterpiece.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to the place where you send mail, buy stamps, or pick up packages. In some countries you may also hear “correo” (the postal service) or “el correo” used to mean mail/the post office depending on context.
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la oficina de correos para enviar este paquete.
native_language_example: I have to go to the post office to send this package.

meaning: "Watch out!" / "Be careful!" (said as a warning, often humorously).
additional_notes: Informal, playful way to warn someone that something could go wrong or that they should pay attention. It’s a non-standard/funny-sounding expression (you’re unlikely to see it in formal Spanish). Similar in function to "¡Ojo!" or "¡Ojo con...!".
target_language_example: Ojo a la funerala: esa escalera está suelta.
native_language_example: Watch out: that ladder is loose.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase (olvidarse + de + noun/infinitive). Often used when something slips your mind. It can take an indirect object pronoun to show who forgot: Se me olvidó (I forgot / It slipped my mind), Se te olvidó (You forgot). In Spain, "olvidarse de" is very common; in many contexts you’ll also hear non‑reflexive "olvidar" (to forget) without "de".
target_language_example: Se me olvidó llamarte.
native_language_example: I forgot to call you.

additional_notes: Refers to what most people in a society think about a topic (often politics, social issues, news). It’s commonly used with verbs like "influir en" (to influence), "formar" (to form), "cambiar" (to change), and "afectar" (to affect).
target_language_example: La opinión pública está dividida sobre la nueva ley.
native_language_example: Public opinion is divided about the new law.

meaning: “white gold”; (figuratively) something very valuable, often salt or cotton (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “white gold.” Used in news/history/business to talk about a product that brings a lot of wealth. Common references include salt (“oro blanco” in older contexts) and cotton (“oro blanco” in some regions); the exact meaning depends on the topic and place.
target_language_example: En esa época, la sal era considerada el oro blanco.
native_language_example: In that era, salt was considered “white gold.”

additional_notes: Used especially in news, economics, and politics to refer to oil as a valuable resource. It’s usually figurative (not actual gold). In some contexts it can also refer to coal, but most commonly it means oil.
target_language_example: Muchos países dependen del oro negro para su economía.
native_language_example: Many countries depend on black gold (oil) for their economy.

additional_notes: Common name for the animal that eats ants and termites (also called "tamandúa" in some regions). Literally "ant bear" ("oso" + "hormiguero"), but it refers to an anteater, not a bear.
target_language_example: En el zoológico vimos un oso hormiguero.
native_language_example: At the zoo we saw an anteater.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: **oso** (bear) + **polar** (polar/Arctic). Use with an article when talking about a specific one (**el oso polar**) or in general as a species (**Los osos polares viven en el Ártico**). Plural: **osos polares**.
target_language_example: El oso polar vive en el Ártico.
native_language_example: The polar bear lives in the Arctic.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens another time or is repeated. Very common in everyday Spanish. Similar options include "de nuevo" (again) and "una vez más" (one more time).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes repetirlo otra vez, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat it again, please?

additional_notes: Usually used with a possessive (mi/tu/su otro yo) to describe someone who is very similar to you, or a “second self”/persona you have in a different role or context. It can be literal (“another me”) or more figurative (“alter ego”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana es como mi otro yo.
native_language_example: My sister is like my other self.

meaning: the “black sheep” (the person who doesn’t fit in; the family outsider).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone seen as different, rebellious, or a source of embarrassment within a family or group. Often appears with the verb ser: “Él es la oveja negra de la familia.” It’s idiomatic but matches the English expression closely.
target_language_example: Siempre dijeron que yo era la oveja negra de la familia.
native_language_example: They always said I was the black sheep of the family.

meaning: to hear about; to have heard of.
additional_notes: Used when you’ve heard information or news about something/someone, or you know of their existence. Often followed by a noun or person: "He oído hablar de esa película" (I’ve heard about/of that movie). Common with the present perfect (he oído) for past experience, but can be used in other tenses too (oí, oigo). You can add an indirect object pronoun to say who you heard it from: "Le oí hablar de ti" = "I heard him/her talk about you."
target_language_example: He oído hablar de este restaurante, pero nunca he ido.
native_language_example: I’ve heard about this restaurant, but I’ve never gone.

additional_notes: Written abbreviation of “por ejemplo”. Common in lists, parentheses, or commas to introduce an example; it’s not usually said out loud (people say “por ejemplo” when speaking). Often appears as “p. ej.,” “p. ej.:” or in parentheses.
target_language_example: Necesitas frutas, p. ej., manzanas o plátanos.
native_language_example: You need fruit, e.g., apples or bananas.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to the Christian prayer that begins “Padre nuestro que estás en el cielo…”. Used in religious contexts (church, prayer) and also sometimes figuratively to refer to a very familiar or frequently repeated text.
target_language_example: En la misa rezamos el Padre Nuestro.
native_language_example: At Mass we pray the Our Father.

additional_notes: Used to describe something translated or repeated exactly, without changing wording. Common when talking about translations or quoting someone precisely. You can also say “traducir palabra por palabra” (to translate word for word).
target_language_example: Lo traduje palabra por palabra, pero suena raro en inglés.
native_language_example: I translated it word for word, but it sounds weird in English.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the device that converts sunlight into electricity (or heat). Often used in plural when talking about installations: "paneles solares". You’ll also hear related phrases like "energía solar" (solar energy) and "instalar paneles solares" (to install solar panels).
target_language_example: Vamos a instalar paneles solares en el techo.
native_language_example: We’re going to install solar panels on the roof.

additional_notes: More commonly used in the plural: **papas fritas** = “French fries.” In much of Latin America people say **papa** for “potato” (Spain often uses **patata**). You’ll see it as a side dish: *hamburguesa con papas fritas*.
target_language_example: Quiero una hamburguesa con papas fritas, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a hamburger with French fries, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward a lower place (often interchangeable with "hacia abajo"). It’s also used in some regions to mean "down there" (similar to "por ahí abajo"), and in expressions like "de arriba para abajo" (from top to bottom).
target_language_example: Baja las escaleras para abajo y gira a la derecha.
native_language_example: Go down the stairs and turn right.

meaning: in abundance; more than enough (to spare).
additional_notes: Colloquial expression used after a noun or verb to emphasize there’s a lot of something—so much it could even be “boring.” Often translated as “tons of,” “loads of,” or “plenty of.” Example patterns: “Hay + [noun] + para aburrir” (There are tons of…), “[Verb] + para aburrir” (…a lot / to spare).
target_language_example: En esa tienda hay zapatos para aburrir.
native_language_example: That store has tons of shoes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about moving forward physically (opposite of "para atrás") or progressing/continuing with something ("seguir para adelante" = to keep going). Often paired with verbs like "ir", "seguir", "mirar". In some contexts it can mean "in the future" (e.g., "de aquí para adelante" = from now on).
target_language_example: Vamos para adelante; no te rindas.
native_language_example: Let’s move forward; don’t give up.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward a place that is farther from the speaker (allá = there, farther away). Often follows verbs of movement like ir (to go), mirar (to look), caminar (to walk): "Ve para allá" = "Go that way." In many contexts you can also say "allá" alone; adding "para" emphasizes direction.
target_language_example: Vamos para allá después de comer.
native_language_example: We’re going over there after eating.

meaning: by the end of the year / for the year.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a deadline or time limit within the year (often understood as “by the end of the year”), or about something intended/planned for that year. Context and verb tense make it clear: with future plans it often means “by year’s end” (e.g., finish something), and with budgets/goals it can mean “for the year.”
target_language_example: Quiero terminar el proyecto para el año.
native_language_example: I want to finish the project by the end of the year.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point in an explanation, argument, or list (often like “first of all”). It can be followed by a noun or an infinitive: “Para empezar, …” / “Para empezar a hablar, …”. In more formal writing you may also see “para empezar” without a comma when it directly modifies what follows.
target_language_example: Para empezar, necesito tu nombre y tu número de teléfono.
native_language_example: To start, I need your name and your phone number.

additional_notes: Used to set a deadline or point in time relative to something already mentioned (a future or past reference point). Often implies that something will be finished or already true at that time. Similar to “para ese momento.”
target_language_example: Para entonces, ya habré terminado el trabajo.
native_language_example: By then, I’ll have already finished the work.

meaning: “To each their own.” / “Everyone has different tastes.”
additional_notes: A common Spanish saying used when people disagree about preferences (music, food, clothes, etc.). It means there’s no single “right” choice because tastes vary from person to person. Often said after giving your opinion or acknowledging someone else’s different opinion.
target_language_example: A mí me encanta esa camisa, pero si a ti no te gusta… para gustos, los colores.
native_language_example: I love that shirt, but if you don’t like it… to each their own.

additional_notes: Used when ordering food or drinks you will take with you rather than eat there. Common in restaurants and cafés: “¿Para aquí o para llevar?” = “For here or to go?” In many places you can also hear “para comer aquí” for “for here.”
target_language_example: Un café para llevar, por favor.
native_language_example: A coffee to go, please.

meaning: One example is enough to prove the point.
additional_notes: A common Spanish saying used to mean that you don’t need many examples or lots of evidence; a single small “sample” is enough. It’s often said after showing one clear example (sometimes with a slightly ironic tone).
target_language_example: Mira cómo llegó tarde otra vez; para muestra basta un botón.
native_language_example: Look, he arrived late again; one example is enough to prove the point.

meaning: not at all; not in the slightest.
additional_notes: Commonly used to strongly negate something (often as a reply). With a negative verb it can intensify the negation: "No me gusta para nada" = "I don’t like it at all." It can also be used alone: "—¿Te molesta? —Para nada."
target_language_example: —¿Te molestó lo que dije? —Para nada.
native_language_example: —Did what I said bother you? —Not at all.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose clause, usually followed by the subjunctive: "para que + subjunctive" (e.g., "para que puedas"). In questions it’s written with an accent: "¿para qué?" = "what for?/why?".
target_language_example: Te llamo para que me digas la dirección.
native_language_example: I’m calling you so that you can tell me the address.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the purpose or intended use of something. It’s written with an accent in questions and exclamations: ¿para qué…? / ¡para qué…! Often corresponds to English “what for?” or “why?” (meaning “to what end?”). Not the same as "por qué" (which asks for the reason/cause: “why?”).
target_language_example: ¿Para qué necesitas dinero?
native_language_example: What do you need money for?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that lasts indefinitely. Common in emotional statements (promises, love, goodbyes) and also in everyday contexts. It can be intensified as “para siempre jamás” (“forever and ever”).
target_language_example: Te amaré para siempre.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

meaning: for a change (often said ironically: “as usual”).
additional_notes: Used as a comment about something being different from the norm (“for a change”) or, very often, sarcastically to mean the opposite (“yeah, as usual / no surprise”). It commonly goes at the end of a sentence: “..., para variar.”
target_language_example: Se olvidó otra vez, para variar.
native_language_example: He forgot again, as usual (no surprise).

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you wait for a bus. In Spain you’ll also hear "parada de bus"; in some countries "paradero" is common. Often used with "en" (at) or "hasta" (to): "en la parada de autobús", "hasta la parada de autobús".
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la parada de autobús a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the bus stop at eight.

meaning: to seem to be (in a state/condition).
additional_notes: Used to describe an apparent temporary state or condition. It combines parecer (“to seem”) + estar (“to be,” for states/conditions). Very often you’ll see it followed by an adjective or a past participle: parecer estar cansado (to seem to be tired), parecer estar ocupado (to seem to be busy). In everyday Spanish, speakers also commonly say just parecer + adjective (e.g., Parece cansado) when the meaning is clear.
target_language_example: Parece estar cansado hoy.
native_language_example: He seems to be tired today.

additional_notes: A common term in Latin America for a place with rides and attractions. In Spain, you’ll often hear "parque de atracciones" instead. Plural: "parques de diversiones."
target_language_example: Vamos al parque de diversiones este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to the amusement park this weekend.

additional_notes: Used for protected natural areas managed by the government. Often appears on signs, maps, and travel information. Plural: "parques nacionales". You can also say "un parque nacional" (a national park) or "el Parque Nacional X" (the X National Park).
target_language_example: Vamos a visitar un parque nacional este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to visit a national park this weekend.

meaning: to burst out laughing; to laugh a lot.
additional_notes: Very common informal expression meaning you laugh so much you can’t stop (similar to “crack up”). Often used reflexively: "me parto de risa" (I’m cracking up), "nos partimos de risa" (we’re cracking up). You may also hear "partirse de la risa".
target_language_example: Me parto de risa con tus chistes.
native_language_example: I crack up at your jokes.

additional_notes: Used to say something is no longer fashionable or trendy. It agrees in gender and number with the noun: pasado de moda (masc. sing.), pasada de moda (fem. sing.), pasados/pasadas de moda (plural). Often used with clothing, hairstyles, designs, or ideas.
target_language_example: Ese vestido está pasado de moda.
native_language_example: That dress is out of fashion.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a day two days in the future. It’s a common time expression in everyday speech; you can also say “pasado mañana por la mañana/tarde/noche” to specify the time of day.
target_language_example: Pasado mañana tengo una cita con el médico.
native_language_example: The day after tomorrow I have a doctor’s appointment.
