additional_notes: A very common verb with several everyday uses: (1) physical movement: “to pass (by), to go past”; (2) events: “to happen” (often in the past: “¿Qué pasó?” = “What happened?”); (3) time: “to spend (time)” (“Pasé dos horas allí.” = “I spent two hours there.”); (4) “to stop by” with por (“Paso por tu casa.” = “I’ll stop by your house.”); (5) “to hand/pass (something)” in requests (“Pásame la sal.” = “Pass me the salt.”). It’s a regular -ar verb.
target_language_example: ¿Qué pasó?
native_language_example: What happened?

meaning: to have a good time; to enjoy yourself.
additional_notes: Usually used with a reflexive pronoun: "pasarlo bien" (I had a good time = "Lo pasé bien"). You can also use it as a wish/command: "Pásalo bien" = "Have a good time". In questions: "¿Lo pasaste bien?" = "Did you have a good time?"
target_language_example: Lo pasamos bien en la fiesta.
native_language_example: We had a good time at the party.

meaning: to ignore; to not care about; to not bother (doing something).
additional_notes: Common in casual speech. Used with a person/thing to mean “to ignore” (Pasa de mí. = He/She ignores me). Used with an infinitive to mean “I’m not going to / I can’t be bothered to” (Paso de estudiar. = I’m not going to study / I can’t be bothered studying). In more neutral contexts, pasar de can also literally mean “to go from ... to ...” (Pasamos de Madrid a Valencia), but the “ignore / not care” meaning is especially conversational.
target_language_example: Paso de ir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I’m not going to the party / I can’t be bothered to go to the party.

meaning: to keep going / to go past (without stopping).
additional_notes: Used when you pass a place or stop and don’t stop there (e.g., you miss your stop, or you decide not to stop). Often used with a direct object: “pasar de largo la parada/el pueblo”. Also common in the reflexive form “pasarse de largo” = to go past by mistake or unintentionally (e.g., missing your stop).
target_language_example: Me quedé dormido y me pasé de largo de mi parada.
native_language_example: I fell asleep and missed my stop (I went past it).

meaning: to pass the time; to hang out for a while.
additional_notes: Used for spending some time (often casually) while waiting or with no specific plan. Often appears as "pasar el rato" (no pronoun) or "pasar un rato" (spend a while). You can add "con" to say who you spend time with: "pasar el rato con amigos".
target_language_example: Vamos a pasar el rato en el parque.
native_language_example: Let’s hang out in the park for a while.

meaning: 'to have a bad time' / 'to go through something difficult' (usually: pasar mal / pasarlo mal).
additional_notes: “Pasar malam” isn’t standard Spanish; it’s almost certainly a misspelling of **pasar mal** or **pasarlo mal**. The most common form is **pasarlo mal** (“to have a hard time”), often in the past: **Lo pasé mal** = “I had a bad time.” It can refer to emotional difficulty, a rough experience, or feeling unwell. Related: **pasar mala noche** = “to have a bad night” (sleep badly).
target_language_example: Lo pasé mal durante el examen.
native_language_example: I had a hard time during the exam.

meaning: to overlook; to miss; to ignore (often unintentionally).
additional_notes: Used when something is not noticed or is skipped/ignored. It can mean accidental omission ("I overlooked it") or deliberate ignoring depending on context. Common with objects like details, mistakes, rules, or someone’s comment: "pasar por alto un detalle / un error / un comentario".
target_language_example: Perdón, pasé por alto tu mensaje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I overlooked your message.

meaning: to spend time (doing something / with someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used with "con" (with someone) or followed by an activity: "pasar tiempo con mi familia" / "pasar tiempo estudiando". You can also specify duration with "pasar + time period": "pasé dos horas..." (I spent two hours...).
target_language_example: Me gusta pasar tiempo con mis amigos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I like spending time with my friends on weekends.

meaning: to have a good time; to enjoy yourself.
additional_notes: Very common way to talk about having fun (at a party, on vacation, etc.). It’s formed with the verb "pasar" + the pronoun "lo" (referring to “it/time”) + "bien". You conjugate "pasar": "Lo paso bien" (I’m having a good time), "Lo pasamos bien" (We had a good time). Often used as a goodbye: "¡Pásalo bien!" = “Have a good time!” The opposite is "pasarlo mal" (to have a bad time).
target_language_example: Lo pasamos bien en la fiesta.
native_language_example: We had a good time at the party.

meaning: To have a blast; to have a great time.
additional_notes: Very common, informal/colloquial way to say you enjoyed yourself a lot. It’s usually used with an object pronoun: "lo" (most common) or "la" depending on what’s being referred to (e.g., "la tarde"), and it conjugates with the person: "me lo paso bomba", "nos lo pasamos bomba", "lo pasé bomba". Often followed by where/when: "en la fiesta", "con mis amigos".
target_language_example: Nos lo pasamos bomba en el concierto.
native_language_example: We had a blast at the concert.

meaning: to have a bad time; to suffer; to not enjoy oneself.
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "pasarlo" (from "pasarla" = to spend time / to have it) plus an adverb: "pasarlo mal" = to have a bad time. Very common to talk about difficult experiences (emotionally or physically): "Lo pasé mal" = "I had a rough time." You can also use other adverbs: "pasarlo bien" (have a good time), "pasarlo fatal" (have an awful time).
target_language_example: Lo pasé mal durante el examen porque estaba muy nervioso.
native_language_example: I had a rough time during the exam because I was very nervous.

meaning: To cross the line; to go too far.
additional_notes: Used when someone behaves in an unacceptable way or exceeds what’s reasonable (in a joke, comment, criticism, or action). Often said as a warning or reproach: "Te estás pasando de la raya" (You’re crossing the line). Similar to "pasarse" (to go overboard) and "pasarse de la línea" isn’t common—"de la raya" is the usual expression.
target_language_example: Oye, te estás pasando de la raya con esos comentarios.
native_language_example: Hey, you’re crossing the line with those comments.

additional_notes: Fixed expression used to say that something will be true or done regardless of the situation or outcome. It uses the present subjunctive (pase) to express uncertainty (“whatever may happen”). Often paired with a future action or commitment.
target_language_example: Pase lo que pase, voy a estar contigo.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I’m going to be with you.

meaning: step by step; little by little.
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something gradually and in order, one step at a time. Common in instructions, learning contexts, and reassuring someone not to rush (e.g., “Vamos paso a paso”).
target_language_example: Vamos a resolver el problema paso a paso.
native_language_example: We’re going to solve the problem step by step.

additional_notes: Literally means “step backward.” Used both physically (taking a step back) and figuratively (a retreat, setback, or reversing progress). Common in phrases like “dar un paso atrás” (to take a step back) and “dar marcha atrás” (to reverse/back up, especially with cars).
target_language_example: En este punto, es mejor dar un paso atrás y pensarlo bien.
native_language_example: At this point, it’s better to take a step back and think it through.

additional_notes: Common everyday item. Often used with the verbs "poner" (to put) and "usar" (to use): "ponte pasta de dientes" / "usa pasta de dientes". Also appears on labels and in stores (pharmacies, supermarkets).
target_language_example: Necesito comprar pasta de dientes.
native_language_example: I need to buy toothpaste.

additional_notes: A common dish made from minced/ground meat shaped into a loaf and baked. In some places it can also refer to a meat pie (a savory pastry with meat filling), so context matters. Literally “meat cake,” but it’s usually not a dessert.
target_language_example: Para la cena vamos a comer pastel de carne con puré de papas.
native_language_example: For dinner we’re going to eat meatloaf with mashed potatoes.

additional_notes: A common dessert. In Spain, you may also see "tarta de manzana" (often a tart/cake style) or "empanada de manzana" depending on the region. "De" means "of" here: a pie made with apples.
target_language_example: De postre, quiero un pastel de manzana.
native_language_example: For dessert, I want an apple pie.

additional_notes: Common way to name the dog breed. It’s a noun phrase: "pastor" (shepherd) + "alemán" (German). Usually used as "un/una pastor alemán" and the plural is "pastores alemanes".
target_language_example: Mi vecino tiene un pastor alemán muy grande.
native_language_example: My neighbor has a very large German Shepherd.

additional_notes: Common expression used with verbs like "estar" or "poner/dejar" to describe something physically flipped over or a place that’s very messy/disorganized. Often used about rooms/houses after searching for something: "Dejé el cuarto patas arriba".
target_language_example: La casa está patas arriba porque estábamos buscando las llaves.
native_language_example: The house is a mess because we were looking for the keys.

additional_notes: In Spain, "patatas" is the common word for potatoes (in much of Latin America you’ll often hear "papas"). "Patatas fritas" can mean fries (thin) or fried potato pieces more generally, depending on context. You’ll commonly see it on menus as a side dish or snack.
target_language_example: Quiero una hamburguesa con patatas fritas, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a hamburger with French fries, please.

additional_notes: In Spanish, "pavo" is a male turkey and "pava" is a female turkey. "Real" here is part of the common name for the animal (like “royal”); in everyday conversation people often just say "pavo"/"pava" or "pavo de Navidad" when talking about food.
target_language_example: En el campo vimos una pava real con sus crías.
native_language_example: In the countryside we saw a female turkey with her young.

additional_notes: A noun for the (male) peafowl. The female is often called "pava real" (peahen). Plural: "pavos reales". In Spanish, the adjective "real" here means “royal,” not “real” as in “not imaginary.”
target_language_example: En el zoológico vimos un pavo real con la cola abierta.
native_language_example: At the zoo we saw a peacock with its tail fanned out.

meaning: a mortal (very serious) sin; one of the seven deadly sins.
additional_notes: Used mainly in religious or moral contexts (Catholic/Christian tradition). In everyday speech it can be used figuratively to mean a major flaw or big mistake (e.g., in cooking, sports, work). Plural: "pecados capitales".
target_language_example: La gula es uno de los pecados capitales.
native_language_example: Gluttony is one of the deadly sins.

meaning: a very kind, gentle person (a “good soul”).
additional_notes: Commonly used with ser: "Es un pedazo de pan" to say someone is extremely sweet, harmless, or kind-hearted. Literally it means “piece of bread,” but in this idiomatic use it describes a person, not food.
target_language_example: No te preocupes por Juan: es un pedazo de pan y siempre quiere ayudar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about Juan: he’s a really kind person and always wants to help.

additional_notes: Used when you request assistance from someone. You can add “a” + a person: “Pedir ayuda a un amigo” (to ask a friend for help). Common polite ways to ask: “¿Puedes ayudarme?” or “¿Me puedes ayudar?”
target_language_example: Si no entiendes la tarea, puedes pedir ayuda al profesor.
native_language_example: If you don’t understand the homework, you can ask the teacher for help.

meaning: to apologize; to ask for forgiveness.
additional_notes: Literally “to ask for apologies,” but in everyday Spanish it means “to apologize.” Often used as “pedir disculpas (a alguien) por (algo)” = “to apologize (to someone) for (something).” Also common: “Te pido disculpas” (I apologize to you) and “Perdón”/“Lo siento” as shorter options.
target_language_example: Te pido disculpas por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I apologize for arriving late.

meaning: to shoot yourself (to kill yourself); also used hyperbolically: “I could die / I’d rather die.”
additional_notes: Reflexive expression (pegarse + un tiro). Literally it can mean suicide by gunshot, so use with care. In everyday speech it’s also used as dark exaggeration when someone feels extreme embarrassment, frustration, or regret (similar to “I could just die” or “I’d rather die” in English).
target_language_example: Como llegue tarde otra vez, me pego un tiro.
native_language_example: If I’m late again, I’ll just die (I’ll be mortified).

meaning: (to have) hair standing on end; to feel chills/goosebumps (often from fear).
additional_notes: Used in phrases like “poner(se) los pelos de punta” (“to make someone’s hair stand on end / to freak someone out”) and “tener los pelos de punta” (“to have your hair standing on end”). Commonly refers to fear, suspense, or something very creepy; sometimes it can also be used for strong emotion (e.g., being deeply moved).
target_language_example: Esa película de terror me puso los pelos de punta.
native_language_example: That horror movie made my hair stand on end.

additional_notes: Used to talk about movies in the horror genre. Often appears with verbs like ver (to watch) and nouns like género (genre): "Me gustan las películas de terror". You can pluralize it: "películas de terror". In Spanish you also hear "cine de terror" (horror cinema).
target_language_example: No quiero ver una película de terror esta noche.
native_language_example: I don’t want to watch a horror movie tonight.

additional_notes: Used mainly in legal, political, and news contexts to refer to the punishment of execution for a serious crime. Often appears with verbs like "aplicar" (to apply), "abolir" (to abolish), or "imponer" (to impose).
target_language_example: Muchos países han abolido la pena de muerte.
native_language_example: Many countries have abolished the death penalty.

meaning: to be hanging by a thread; to be in a very fragile situation.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a plan, relationship, someone’s health, a job, etc.) is in serious danger and could fail or end at any moment. Common structure: “Algo pende de un hilo.” You can also use it with “estar”: “Está pendiendo de un hilo.”
target_language_example: Después del accidente, su vida pendía de un hilo.
native_language_example: After the accident, his life was hanging by a thread.

meaning: to think of / about (to have an opinion about).
additional_notes: Used to ask for or express an opinion about a person, thing, or idea: “¿Qué piensas de…?” = “What do you think of…?” Often appears with a question word (qué) or with an opinion statement: “Pienso que…” is different (it means “I think that…” + clause). Don’t confuse with “pensar en” (“to think about” in the sense of “to think of/consider/think about doing something”).
target_language_example: ¿Qué piensas de esta película?
native_language_example: What do you think of this movie?

additional_notes: Used with a noun, pronoun, or infinitive to talk about what’s on your mind or what you are considering: pensar en alguien/algo (think about someone/something), pensar en + infinitive (consider doing something). It commonly needs the preposition en (not *pensar algo* in this meaning).
target_language_example: Estoy pensando en comprar un coche.
native_language_example: I’m thinking about buying a car.

additional_notes: Used when you can no longer see someone or something (physically), often because they moved away, you got separated in a crowd, or something disappeared from view. It can be used literally or figuratively ("stop paying attention to / lose track of"), but the most common beginner use is literal. Often appears as: "Perdí de vista a..." (I lost sight of...), "No lo pierdas de vista" (Don’t take your eyes off him/it).
target_language_example: En la estación, perdí de vista a mi amigo por un momento.
native_language_example: At the station, I lost sight of my friend for a moment.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning to spend time in a way that isn’t useful or productive (often because it won’t lead to the result you want). Can be used as a warning or complaint: “No pierdas el tiempo…” (“Don’t waste time…”). In Spanish you conjugate perder: pierdo, pierdes, pierde, perdemos, pierden.
target_language_example: No quiero perder el tiempo; vamos a empezar.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time; let’s start.

meaning: to miss the last train; (figuratively) to miss your last chance.
additional_notes: Literally means “to lose the last train,” but in English you normally say “miss the last train.” It can be used both for actually missing the final train of the day and more generally for missing an opportunity (your last chance). Often used with a time reference: “anoche,” “hoy,” etc.
target_language_example: Si no salimos ya, vamos a perder el último tren.
native_language_example: If we don’t leave now, we’re going to miss the last train.

meaning: to lose your head; to panic or act irrationally (also: to go crazy over something/someone).
additional_notes: Used when someone stops thinking clearly because of fear, stress, anger, or strong emotions. Common in advice like “No pierdas la cabeza” (“Don’t lose your head”). It can also mean being infatuated: “Perdió la cabeza por ella” (“He went crazy for her”).
target_language_example: No pierdas la cabeza; podemos resolverlo con calma.
native_language_example: Don’t lose your head; we can solve it calmly.

meaning: to lose your temper; to snap.
additional_notes: An idiom meaning to lose self-control, usually because of anger or frustration. Often used with "se" ("perderse los estribos") and with "con" to say who you snapped at: "Perdí los estribos con él". The literal words refer to losing the stirrups while riding (losing control), so the meaning isn’t obvious from the parts.
target_language_example: Perdí los estribos y le grité al conductor.
native_language_example: I lost my temper and yelled at the driver.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for weight loss. You can use it with a person as the subject ("Quiero perder peso") or to talk about someone else ("Ella está perdiendo peso"). In Spanish, "peso" can also mean "weight" in general, but in this phrase it usually refers to body weight. Not to be confused with "perder el peso" meaning losing a physical weight you’re carrying (less common).
target_language_example: Quiero perder peso antes del verano.
native_language_example: I want to lose weight before summer.

meaning: “low profile” (to keep a low profile; not draw attention).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person, attitude, or approach that avoids attention and stays discreet. Often appears with verbs like “mantener” or “tener”: “mantener un perfil bajo” = “to keep a low profile.” Can also describe a “low-profile” person (“una persona de perfil bajo”).
target_language_example: Después del escándalo, decidió mantener un perfil bajo.
native_language_example: After the scandal, he decided to keep a low profile.

meaning: “well, anyway…” / “oh well…” (often showing resignation or mild surprise).
additional_notes: Very common conversational filler. Use it to react to something unexpected, to change topic, or to wrap up a point. Tone depends on intonation: it can sound resigned (“oh well”), slightly annoyed (“come on / seriously”), or like you’re moving on (“anyway”).
target_language_example: Pero bueno, ya está; vamos a casa.
native_language_example: Oh well, it’s done; let’s go home.

additional_notes: A preposition meaning something happens or is true even though there is a difficulty or opposing fact. It’s typically followed by a noun or an infinitive (pese a la lluvia, pese a ser tarde). Often interchangeable with "a pesar de".
target_language_example: Pese a la lluvia, fuimos al parque.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, we went to the park.

meaning: heavyweight; a very important or influential person (a “big player”).
additional_notes: Literally “heavy weight.” Used both for boxing/weight classes (un peso pesado) and figuratively for someone with a lot of power, prestige, or influence in a field. Commonly used with the article: "un/una peso pesado" and often followed by "de" + area ("un peso pesado de la política").
target_language_example: Ella es un peso pesado en la industria tecnológica.
native_language_example: She is a heavyweight in the tech industry.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the common pet fish kept in a bowl or aquarium. Often used in the plural (peces de colores) to talk about several fish. Literally “fish of colors,” but in everyday Spanish it commonly means “goldfish” in the pet sense.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene dos peces de colores en una pecera.
native_language_example: My sister has two goldfish in a fishbowl.

meaning: a big shot; an important/influential person.
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone powerful or high-status (often in business, politics, or crime). It’s slightly informal and can sound critical or ironic. Often used with "ser" (to be) or "un" (a).
target_language_example: Dicen que él es un pez gordo en la empresa.
native_language_example: They say he’s a big shot at the company.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the large horizontal piano with a raised lid (often found in concert halls or larger rooms). Also commonly called simply "un piano" when context is clear. Not to be confused with "piano vertical" (upright piano).
target_language_example: En el teatro hay un piano de cola para el concierto.
native_language_example: In the theater there is a grand piano for the concert.

meaning: To do very hard, tedious work; to “pay your dues.”
additional_notes: An idiom used for difficult, often repetitive work that requires a lot of effort and patience (sometimes starting from the bottom or without much reward at first). It can describe physical labor or any tough grind (studying, working long hours, building experience).
target_language_example: Al principio me tocó picar piedra, pero con el tiempo conseguí un buen puesto.
native_language_example: At first I had to pay my dues, but over time I got a good position.

additional_notes: Used to talk about valuable minerals used in jewelry (like diamonds, rubies, emeralds). Plural: piedras preciosas. Note that "piedra" is feminine, so it’s "una piedra preciosa".
target_language_example: Este anillo tiene una piedra preciosa muy bonita.
native_language_example: This ring has a very pretty gemstone.

meaning: very cautiously; like walking on eggshells.
additional_notes: Idiom used to describe acting with extreme care to avoid upsetting someone, causing trouble, or making a mistake. Often used with verbs like andar/ir/estar: “Ando pisando huevos con mi jefe.”
target_language_example: Desde que hubo la pelea, ando pisando huevos en casa para no empeorar las cosas.
native_language_example: Ever since the fight, I’ve been walking on eggshells at home so I don’t make things worse.

additional_notes: Used for the floor at street level in a building. In many Spanish-speaking countries, "primer piso" can mean the floor above the ground floor (what Americans call the second floor). You’ll often see it in elevators, building directories, and real estate listings.
target_language_example: El apartamento está en la planta baja.
native_language_example: The apartment is on the ground floor.

meaning: main course; the main dish (often the most important part of a meal or menu).
additional_notes: Common in restaurants and at meals: after the starter/first course (entrada or primer plato) and before dessert (postre). In some contexts it can also mean the “main attraction” (the most important/interesting part) of an event or program.
target_language_example: De entrada pedí una ensalada y de plato fuerte, pollo con arroz.
native_language_example: For the starter I ordered a salad, and for the main course, chicken with rice.

additional_notes: This is a casual, colloquial way some speakers write or say “por favor,” often dropping the final -r sounds (por → po, favor → favó). Use it in friendly contexts (texts, joking tone), but avoid it in formal writing or with strangers—use “por favor” instead. It can also be used alone to show annoyance or disbelief (“Po favó…” = “Come on…”).
target_language_example: Po favó, ¿me pasas el agua?
native_language_example: Please, can you pass me the water?

meaning: not much; something of little importance/value.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is small, unimpressive, or not important. It can describe an object, an amount, a result, or even a person (sometimes sounding dismissive). Often used with "ser": "Es poca cosa" = "It’s no big deal / It’s not much."
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es poca cosa.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s no big deal.

additional_notes: An adverbial phrase meaning something happens infrequently. It often goes before the verb ("Pocas veces voy...") but can also appear after it for emphasis ("Voy pocas veces..."). It can be reinforced with "muy" ("muy pocas veces" = very rarely).
target_language_example: Pocas veces salgo entre semana.
native_language_example: I rarely go out on weekdays.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens slowly and step by step (progress, change, learning, recovery, etc.). It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence. You’ll also hear it as advice: “Poco a poco” = “Take it one step at a time.”
target_language_example: Poco a poco, estoy aprendiendo español.
native_language_example: Little by little, I’m learning Spanish.

meaning: little by little; bit by bit.
additional_notes: A very common, friendly way to say something happens gradually. It often implies patience and steady progress. You may also hear "poco a poco" (same meaning; slightly more neutral).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: vas a mejorar poco a poquito.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re going to improve little by little.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens a short time after another event. It’s common in stories, instructions, and everyday narration. It can refer to the recent past (Llegó y poco después se fue) or the near future (Salgo y poco después te llamo).
target_language_example: Llegué a casa y poco después me dormí.
native_language_example: I got home and shortly after I fell asleep.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as a verb meaning “can/to be able to,” followed by an infinitive: “Puedo + infinitive” (Puedo ayudarte = I can help you). It’s a stem-changing verb (o→ue) in many forms: puedo, puedes, puede, pueden (but: podía, pude). For polite requests, use “¿Puede…?” (formal) or “¿Puedes…?” (informal). As a noun, “el poder” means “power” (political power, ability to control, etc.).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go today.

meaning: to be able to change; can change.
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (to be able to/can) + an infinitive (cambiar). Common for talking about possibility/ability: present (puedo/puedes/puede...), past ability (pude/podía...), or polite requests (¿Puede cambiar...?). Often followed by what is being changed: cambiarlo/cambiarla (change it), cambiar de opinión (change your mind), cambiar de ropa (change clothes), cambiar dinero (exchange money).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo cambiar esta camiseta por una talla más grande?
native_language_example: Can I exchange this T-shirt for a bigger size?

meaning: to be able to handle (something); to cope with.
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing as the object (often a problem, task, or situation). In negatives it commonly means “can’t handle it / can’t take it anymore”: No puedo con esto. With people, it can mean “can’t beat/overcome” or “can’t deal with”: No puedo con él. (Different from just “poder” = “to be able to” do an action.)
target_language_example: No puedo con tanto trabajo esta semana.
native_language_example: I can’t handle so much work this week.

meaning: to be able to wait; can wait.
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (to be able to / can) + infinitive esperar (to wait). Often used to ask someone to wait politely (¿Puedes esperar…?) or to say whether it’s possible to keep waiting (No podemos esperar más = We can’t wait any longer). Depending on context, poder can express ability (“can”) or permission (“may”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes esperar un momento, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you wait a moment, please?

additional_notes: "Poder" means "to be able to" and is followed by an infinitive like "hablar". Use it to say you have the ability/permission to speak or to ask if someone can speak (a language). Common conjugations: "puedo hablar" (I can speak), "puedes hablar" (you can speak), "puede hablar" (you can/he/she can speak), "¿Puede hablar más despacio?" (Can you speak more slowly?).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar inglés?
native_language_example: Can you speak English?

additional_notes: Use a conjugated form of **poder** + infinitive **hacer** (or another verb) to talk about ability or possibility: *puedo hacer, puedes hacer, no puedo hacer...*. Often followed by a specific activity or by **lo** (“it”): *puedo hacerlo* = “I can do it.”
target_language_example: No puedo hacerlo hoy, pero puedo hacerlo mañana.
native_language_example: I can’t do it today, but I can do it tomorrow.

meaning: to be able to go; can go.
additional_notes: Used to talk about having permission, possibility, or ability to go somewhere. Conjugate only poder (puedo/puedes/puede/podemos/pueden) and keep ir in the infinitive: “No puedo ir hoy” (I can’t go today). Common in questions: “¿Puedes ir?” (Can you go?).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir mañana.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go tomorrow.

meaning: to be able to hear; can hear.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the ability to hear something (physically or because there’s enough volume/clarity). Often appears in questions and negatives: “¿Puedes oírme?” (Can you hear me?), “No puedo oírte bien.” (I can’t hear you well). In polite requests, Spanish often uses the conditional: “¿Podrías oír esto un momento?” (Could you listen to this for a moment?).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes oírme bien o hay mucho ruido?
native_language_example: Can you hear me well, or is there a lot of noise?

additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (to be able/can) + an infinitive. Conjugate poder to match the subject (puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden) and keep trabajar in the infinitive. Often used to talk about ability, permission, or possibility, depending on context.
target_language_example: Hoy no puedo trabajar porque estoy enfermo.
native_language_example: Today I can't work because I'm sick.

meaning: to be able to come; can (someone) come
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (can/to be able to) + an infinitive (venir). It’s common in questions and polite requests: “¿Puedes venir…?” (Can you come…?) or “¿Podrías venir…?” (Could you come…?). Conjugate poder for the subject (puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir mañana a las seis?
native_language_example: Can you come tomorrow at six?

meaning: to be able to see; can see.
additional_notes: Used to express ability/possibility to see something (because of distance, light, visibility, etc.). It’s often conjugated as two verbs: a form of "poder" + infinitive "ver" (e.g., "puedo ver", "podemos ver", "no puedo ver"). It can be literal (eyesight/visibility) or figurative (understanding: "No puedo ver la diferencia" = "I can’t see/understand the difference").
target_language_example: No puedo ver la pantalla con tanto sol.
native_language_example: I can’t see the screen with so much sun.

meaning: to be able to come back / return (again).
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "poder" (to be able to/can) + the infinitive "volver" (to return/come back). It often talks about having the possibility or permission to return to a place or situation. In some contexts, "volver" can also mean "to do again" (e.g., "volver a llamar" = to call again), but "poder volver" by itself usually means being able to come back/return.
target_language_example: No puedo volver mañana, pero puedo volver el viernes.
native_language_example: I can't come back tomorrow, but I can come back on Friday.

additional_notes: A common food term. In a restaurant you might see it on a menu or order it with: "Quiero pollo frito" (I want fried chicken) or "¿Tiene pollo frito?" (Do you have fried chicken?). "Frito" is the past participle of "freír" (to fry).
target_language_example: Voy a pedir pollo frito con papas.
native_language_example: I’m going to order fried chicken with fries.

meaning: to test; to put to the test.
additional_notes: Used for testing a person, thing, idea, or plan to see how well it works or how someone reacts. Often followed by a direct object: "poner a prueba + algo/a alguien". Common in everyday and formal contexts (e.g., products, skills, relationships).
target_language_example: Este trabajo va a poner a prueba tu paciencia.
native_language_example: This job is going to test your patience.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay heed.
additional_notes: Common in Latin America. In Spain you’ll also often hear "prestar atención" (same meaning). It’s followed by "a" + the thing/person: "poner atención a...". Also used as an imperative: "¡Pon atención!" = "Pay attention!".
target_language_example: Pon atención a lo que dice el profesor.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what the teacher is saying.

meaning: to get on someone’s nerves; to drive someone crazy (annoy/stress them a lot).
additional_notes: Usually used as: "poner a alguien de los nervios". It means someone/something is making you feel very irritated, stressed, or nervous. Common with object pronouns: "me/te/le/nos/les pone de los nervios". Similar idea: "poner nervioso/a", but "poner de los nervios" is more emphatic/idiomatic.
target_language_example: El ruido del tráfico me pone de los nervios.
native_language_example: The traffic noise gets on my nerves.

additional_notes: Often used literally (putting your finger somewhere). In some contexts it can also mean “to point out” an issue, especially in the common expression “poner el dedo en la llaga” (“to touch a sore spot” / “to hit a nerve”).
target_language_example: No pongas el dedo ahí; está sucio.
native_language_example: Don’t put your finger there; it’s dirty.

meaning: to start (a machine/process); to set in motion.
additional_notes: Used for starting something that begins operating (a car, a machine) or launching/implementing a plan, project, or initiative. Common in formal and everyday contexts. In many cases it’s similar to “arrancar/encender” for machines, but “poner en marcha” often emphasizes getting something up and running.
target_language_example: Vamos a poner en marcha el proyecto la semana que viene.
native_language_example: We’re going to get the project up and running next week.

meaning: to endanger; to put at risk.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase used when something/someone is made unsafe. It often takes a direct object (poner en peligro a alguien/algo). You can also use the reflexive form for yourself: ponerse en peligro (to put yourself in danger).
target_language_example: No pongas en peligro tu salud.
native_language_example: Don’t put your health at risk.

meaning: to put into practice; to apply (an idea/plan).
additional_notes: Used for implementing or applying something in real life (a plan, idea, technique, knowledge). Often followed by a noun or a clause: “poner en práctica un plan/una idea” or “poner en práctica lo que aprendiste.” Similar to “aplicar,” but a bit more focused on taking something from theory to action.
target_language_example: Es hora de poner en práctica lo que aprendimos en clase.
native_language_example: It’s time to put into practice what we learned in class.

additional_notes: Used for preparing the table before a meal (putting out plates, cutlery, glasses, etc.). Often used with commands or requests: “Pon la mesa” (Set the table). You can also specify for how many people: “poner la mesa para cuatro”.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner la mesa, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you set the table, please?

meaning: to cheat on (a partner); to be unfaithful.
additional_notes: A common idiom meaning to have sex or a romantic relationship with someone other than your partner (to ‘make someone a cuckold’). It’s often used in the pattern “ponerle los cuernos a alguien” (to cheat on someone). Also heard in the passive/received sense: “Me puso los cuernos” (He/She cheated on me). The word “cuernos” literally means “horns,” but the phrase is idiomatic and can sound blunt or gossipy, so use with care.
target_language_example: Me enteré de que le puso los cuernos a su novia.
native_language_example: I found out that he cheated on his girlfriend.

additional_notes: Used to show annoyance, impatience, disbelief, or sarcasm. It’s a common everyday expression and can be conjugated (e.g., "puso los ojos en blanco", "pones los ojos en blanco").
target_language_example: Cuando le dije que llegaría tarde otra vez, puso los ojos en blanco.
native_language_example: When I told her I’d be late again, she rolled her eyes.

meaning: to start (doing something); to begin to.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to …” form): “ponerse a + infinitive.” It often suggests a sudden or spontaneous start. Similar in meaning to “empezar a,” but “ponerse a” can feel more like “to suddenly start.” Conjugate “ponerse” to match the subject: me pongo a, se pone a, nos pusimos a, etc.
target_language_example: Se puso a llorar cuando escuchó la noticia.
native_language_example: He/She started crying when he/she heard the news.

meaning: to catch up; to get up to date.
additional_notes: Commonly used with work, emails, news, or tasks you’re behind on. Often followed by "con" + noun ("ponerse al día con el trabajo") or used as a reflexive verb ("me pongo al día"). It can also mean to get current on payments ("ponerse al día con los pagos").
target_language_example: Tengo muchos correos; esta tarde voy a ponerme al día.
native_language_example: I have a lot of emails; this afternoon I’m going to catch up.

meaning: to agree (with each other); to come to an agreement.
additional_notes: Used when two or more people reach the same decision or plan (often after discussing). It’s reflexive (ponerse), and it commonly appears as: “ponerse de acuerdo en + noun” (agree on something) or “ponerse de acuerdo para + infinitive” (agree to do something). You can add who: “ponerse de acuerdo con + person” (agree with someone / come to an agreement with someone).
target_language_example: Nos pusimos de acuerdo en la fecha de la reunión.
native_language_example: We agreed on the date of the meeting.

meaning: to stand up; to get to your feet.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase (ponerse + de pie). Common for changes of position: sitting/lying → standing. Often used as a command: «Ponte de pie» (informal), «Póngase de pie» (formal).
target_language_example: Cuando entró el profesor, todos se pusieron de pie.
native_language_example: When the teacher came in, everyone stood up.

meaning: to set off; to start a journey; to be on your way.
additional_notes: Common with the reflexive verb "ponerse" to mean beginning an action. Often used when leaving to go somewhere ("Nos ponemos en camino") or with "hacia" + destination ("ponerse en camino hacia Madrid"). Similar to "ponerse en marcha" (to get going).
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; vamos a ponernos en camino hacia el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: It’s already late; let’s set off for the airport.

meaning: little by little; bit by bit.
additional_notes: A very common way to say something happens gradually, step by step. It’s a slightly more emphatic, friendly version of "poco a poco." You can use it for progress, learning, recovery, or changes over time.
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo español poquito a poquito.
native_language_example: I’m learning Spanish little by little.

additional_notes: Common exclamation to show frustration, surprise, impatience, or to beg someone to do/stop something. Often used as part of longer phrases like “¡Por Dios, cálmate!” or “¡Por Dios!” on its own. It’s fairly strong and can sound dramatic; use with care in formal situations or with people who may be religiously sensitive.
target_language_example: ¡Por Dios, deja de gritar!
native_language_example: For God’s sake, stop yelling!

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally. Common with verbs like "romper" (to break), "borrar" (to delete), "cerrar" (to close), or "lastimar" (to hurt). Similar in meaning to "sin querer" (without meaning to).
target_language_example: Lo rompí por accidente.
native_language_example: I broke it by accident.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a nearby place or general area close to the speaker (or the group). It can also mean “over here” in casual directions. Often interchangeable with "por aquí," though "acá" can feel slightly more immediate/closer than "aquí" in some contexts.
target_language_example: El baño está por acá, sígueme.
native_language_example: The bathroom is around here—follow me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something temporary or true only up to the present. Common in endings like “Eso es todo por ahora” (“That’s all for now”). Often similar to “por el momento,” though “por ahora” can also imply “until further notice.”
target_language_example: Por ahora, vamos a esperar aquí.
native_language_example: For now, we’re going to wait here.

additional_notes: Very common phrase used to be intentionally vague about place, time, or quantity. For location, it means “around there / somewhere around.” With time it can mean “around then / sometime.” It can also mean “about/roughly” with numbers: “por ahí de las tres” = “around three o’clock.” Often used after verbs like estar, vivir, andar, pasar: “Estoy por ahí” = “I’m around / I’m out and about.”
target_language_example: Creo que mi móvil está por ahí, en la sala o en la cocina.
native_language_example: I think my phone is somewhere around there, in the living room or in the kitchen.

meaning: for a reason; not for nothing.
additional_notes: Used to say there is a reason behind something (often implying the reason is important or makes sense). Common in the expression “No es por algo, pero…” (“Not to be rude/Not for nothing, but…”) to soften a comment.
target_language_example: Por algo te lo digo: confía en mí.
native_language_example: I’m telling you for a reason: trust me.

meaning: 'over there' / 'around there' (in that general direction or area).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a place that’s not here and is often vague or approximate (not a precise location). Common with verbs of movement (ir, andar, pasar): "Voy por allá" = "I’m going over there / around that area." It can also refer to an approximate time: "por allá en 2010" = "around 2010." Similar idea to "por aquí" (around here).
target_language_example: Vamos a comer por allá, cerca del parque.
native_language_example: Let’s eat over there, near the park.

additional_notes: Used to indicate an imprecise location or area, often meaning you’re not specifying exactly where. It can also mean “around” a place (passing through or in the vicinity). Similar to "por ahí"; "allí" sounds a bit more specific/distant than "ahí".
target_language_example: Creo que mi móvil está por allí, cerca de la mesa.
native_language_example: I think my phone is over there, near the table.

meaning: 'for the love of God' (used to beg, emphasize, or show frustration).
additional_notes: Common exclamation in Spanish. It can express pleading (“please!”), urgency, disbelief, or annoyance, depending on tone. It’s strong but widely used in everyday speech; in more formal situations you may prefer a softer option like “por favor.”
target_language_example: Por amor de Dios, baja la música que tengo que dormir.
native_language_example: For the love of God, turn the music down—I have to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific period in the past, often already mentioned or understood from context. It’s a more narrative/literary way to say "en aquel tiempo" or "en esa época". Common in storytelling and biographies.
target_language_example: Por aquel entonces, vivíamos en Madrid y yo estudiaba en la universidad.
native_language_example: Back then, we lived in Madrid and I was studying at the university.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a general location nearby (“around here”) or to point/guide someone (“this way”). Often appears with movement verbs like venir/pasar/ir: “Ven por aquí” (come this way), “Pasa por aquí” (come through here).
target_language_example: ¿Hay un cajero por aquí?
native_language_example: Is there an ATM around here?

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or movement from a higher place: "por arriba" = "from above/overhead." It can also mean "on top (of something)" or "over" in a spatial sense: "por arriba de" + noun = "above/over." In directions, you may hear it as a casual way to say "go up" or "go via the upper/top side" depending on context.
target_language_example: Pasa por arriba del puente y sigue recto.
native_language_example: Go over the bridge and keep going straight.

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you’re saying when it’s not meant literally, or when you’re using an unusual comparison or expression. It often comes after the phrase it comments on, and is common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es el jefe, por así decirlo, del proyecto.
native_language_example: He’s the boss, so to speak, of the project.

meaning: nicely; willingly; without force (often contrasted with “por malas”).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the set phrase “por las buenas” (“the nice/peaceful way”), meaning someone does something calmly, by agreement, persuasion, or good manners—rather than by threats or force. It’s commonly paired with “por malas” / “por las malas” (“the hard way”).
target_language_example: Lo vas a hacer por buenas o por malas.
native_language_example: You’re going to do it the nice way or the hard way.

additional_notes: Often used to ask politely if someone happens to know or have something: “¿Por casualidad…?” It can also describe something that happened accidentally or as a coincidence. Similar to “de casualidad,” though “por casualidad” is very common in questions.
target_language_example: ¿Por casualidad sabes dónde está la estación?
native_language_example: By any chance do you know where the station is?

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, followed by a noun, pronoun, or an infinitive phrase (e.g., "por causa de la lluvia" / "por causa de no estudiar"). It’s similar to "a causa de" and is fairly formal; in everyday speech, people often use "por" ("Lo hice por ti") or "porque" + clause ("porque llovía").
target_language_example: Cancelaron el partido por causa de la lluvia.
native_language_example: They canceled the game because of the rain.

additional_notes: Used after a number to express a percentage. It’s very common in prices, discounts, and statistics. Often written with the symbol “%” (e.g., 20%).
target_language_example: El descuento es del veinte por ciento.
native_language_example: The discount is twenty percent.

meaning: by the hundreds; in the hundreds (hundreds at a time).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a large quantity, meaning something happens or exists in groups of hundreds. Often used with verbs like "llegar" (to arrive), "contar" (to count), or "venir" (to come).
target_language_example: Los turistas llegan por cientos en verano.
native_language_example: Tourists arrive by the hundreds in summer.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an extra comment, a new but related topic, or something you just remembered. It can also mean “certainly/indeed” in some contexts, but beginners will most often see it as “by the way.”
target_language_example: Por cierto, ¿a qué hora empieza la reunión?
native_language_example: By the way, what time does the meeting start?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is finished or done 100%. Often goes with verbs like "terminar" (to finish), "cambiar" (to change), "destruir" (to destroy), or "olvidar" (to forget). Similar to "completamente" and "del todo".
target_language_example: Lo entendí por completo.
native_language_example: I understood it completely.

meaning: because of; on behalf of; at the expense of (charged to).
additional_notes: Common meanings depend on context: (1) **because of / due to**: *Por cuenta del tráfico, llegué tarde.* (2) **on behalf of** (acting for someone): *Lo hice por cuenta de mi jefe.* (3) **charged to / at the expense of** (cost paid by someone or put on their account): *Ponlo por cuenta de la empresa.* Often followed by **de + noun/person**.
target_language_example: Pusieron la cena por cuenta de la empresa.
native_language_example: They charged the dinner to the company.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without help or for their own benefit/responsibility. Common with verbs like hacer, trabajar, vivir, or aprender. Also used for self-employment (trabajar por cuenta propia = to be self-employed / to work freelance).
target_language_example: Aprendí español por cuenta propia.
native_language_example: I learned Spanish on my own.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened because someone/something caused it in a negative way, placing blame. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: por culpa de él/ella, por culpa del tráfico, por culpa de la lluvia. If you just mean “because of” without blame, beginners often use neutral alternatives like “por” or “debido a”.
target_language_example: Llegué tarde por culpa del tráfico.
native_language_example: I arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position or level that is lower than something else. Common with measurements, temperatures, prices, and rankings. It can be physical (under something) or figurative (below a limit/standard). Often followed by a number or noun: "por debajo de 10 grados", "por debajo del precio normal".
target_language_example: La temperatura está por debajo de cero.
native_language_example: The temperature is below zero.

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you just said, often to show it’s not meant literally or it’s an approximate description. It can go at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Es, por decirlo así, el jefe del equipo.
native_language_example: He’s, so to speak, the boss of the team.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position or movement: "por delante de" = "in front of" (location) or "ahead of" (in a race or line). It can also mean having something ahead of you in time or remaining work: "todavía queda mucho por delante" = "there’s still a lot ahead / a lot left to do."
target_language_example: El coche rojo va por delante del azul.
native_language_example: The red car is ahead of the blue one.

meaning: from behind; in the back; behind (something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position or movement at the back of something/someone (similar to "por delante" = in front). It can also describe an entrance/area at the back: "la puerta de por detrás" (the back door). With verbs of entering/exiting or going, it often means "through the back": "entrar por detrás" (to come in through the back).
target_language_example: Entró por detrás para que nadie lo viera.
native_language_example: He came in through the back so that nobody would see him.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an example. Very common in both spoken and written Spanish; often followed by a noun or a full clause. In speech it’s also common to shorten it to “por ej.” in writing.
target_language_example: Me gustan muchas frutas, por ejemplo, las fresas y los plátanos.
native_language_example: I like many fruits, for example, strawberries and bananas.

meaning: "for the love of God!" (a strong plea: "please!", "for heaven’s sake!")
additional_notes: Used to beg someone to do (or stop doing) something, often showing frustration, urgency, or impatience. It can be dramatic but is common in everyday speech. You can also hear variants like "por el amor de Dios, no..." or "por Dios" (shorter).
target_language_example: Por el amor de Dios, baja la música.
native_language_example: For the love of God, turn the music down.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast with what was just said. Common in both speech and writing. Often followed by a full clause ("Por el contrario, ..."). Similar to "al contrario" (slightly more direct), and close in meaning to "en cambio" ("instead/by contrast").
target_language_example: Pensé que iba a llover; por el contrario, salió el sol.
native_language_example: I thought it was going to rain; on the contrary, the sun came out.

additional_notes: Used after giving an example to mean “and similar things” or “and so on.” Common in conversation. It can refer to things, situations, or approximate descriptions (similar to “or the like” / “or something along those lines”).
target_language_example: Podemos ir al cine, a cenar o por el estilo.
native_language_example: We can go to the movies, go out to dinner, or something like that.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or will be done temporarily, with the idea that it may change later. Common in everyday speech. Similar to “por ahora” and “de momento.”
target_language_example: Por el momento, no tengo trabajo, pero estoy buscando.
native_language_example: For the moment, I don’t have a job, but I’m looking.

meaning: on the ground; (figurative) very low / ruined.
additional_notes: Literally means “on/along the ground.” Used for things that are lying on the floor/ground (e.g., papers, clothes), or figuratively to say something like morale, energy, or prices are very low (“estar por el suelo”). Often follows verbs like estar, caer, tirar, dejar.
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, había vasos y servilletas por el suelo.
native_language_example: After the party, there were cups and napkins on the ground.

additional_notes: Used to say something is made specially because a person or client requested it (not mass-produced). Common in shops and services: "hacer + [producto] + por encargo" (to make something to order) or "trabajo por encargo" (commissioned work).
target_language_example: Hacemos pasteles por encargo.
native_language_example: We make cakes to order.

meaning: above; on top of; over (in comparison: “more than”).
additional_notes: Often used with “de” (por encima de) to mean “above/over” in a physical sense (higher than) or figuratively (beyond/over). Also used to compare amounts or levels: “por encima de 100” = “over 100,” and “por encima de la media” = “above average.”
target_language_example: El avión voló por encima de las nubes.
native_language_example: The plane flew above the clouds.

additional_notes: Used to say something should be provided as a written document/message (email, letter, form), often in formal or work/administrative contexts. Common with verbs like "poner" (to put), "dejar" (to leave), "enviar" (to send), and "confirmar" (to confirm): "ponlo por escrito", "confírmalo por escrito".
target_language_example: ¿Me lo puedes confirmar por escrito, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you confirm it in writing for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to give a reason or explanation, often referring to something just mentioned. Common at the start of a sentence (“Por eso, …”) or after a statement. Similar to “por eso” = “for that,” but in English it’s usually “that’s why/so.”
target_language_example: No tengo dinero; por eso no voy al cine.
native_language_example: I don’t have money; that’s why I’m not going to the movies.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to make a polite request (“Please…”). It can also be used to politely get someone’s attention (“Por favor,” at the start of a sentence). In some countries/situations, “por favor” can be used to respond to “gracias” meaning “you’re welcome,” though “de nada” is often more common.
target_language_example: Por favor, ¿me puede ayudar?
native_language_example: Please, can you help me?

meaning: by force; necessarily (whether you want to or not).
additional_notes: Used to express that something happens compulsorily or inevitably. Often appears as “a la fuerza” (by force) in very similar situations. Can be used with “tener que” or in phrases like “por fuerza mayor” (due to force majeure).
target_language_example: Tuvo que aceptar por fuerza, aunque no quería.
native_language_example: He had to accept by force, even though he didn’t want to.

meaning: for pleasure; just because; (often) for no good reason.
additional_notes: Used to say you do something because you enjoy it or simply because you feel like it ("just because"). Very often used in negative sentences to mean "for no reason / for nothing" (e.g., "No lo hagas por gusto" = don’t do it just to do it / for no good reason). Also appears in expressions like "por gusto" = "willingly" in some contexts.
target_language_example: No lo hice por gusto; lo hice porque era necesario.
native_language_example: I didn’t do it for fun; I did it because it was necessary.

additional_notes: Used to talk about rates (pay, fees, prices) or something calculated hourly. Common with money and units: "10 euros por hora" (10 euros per hour). It can also describe hourly work/charging: "cobramos por hora" (we charge by the hour).
target_language_example: Me pagan 15 dólares por hora.
native_language_example: They pay me 15 dollars per hour.

meaning: “for today” / “for now (today)” (i.e., that’s enough for today).
additional_notes: Used to say something is limited to today or that you’re stopping for the day. Common in phrases like “Eso es todo por hoy” (That’s all for today) or “Por hoy ya terminé” (I’m done for today). It refers specifically to today, unlike “por ahora” (for now) which is more general.
target_language_example: Eso es todo por hoy; continuamos mañana.
native_language_example: That’s all for today; we’ll continue tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say someone acts based on intuition or natural impulse rather than careful thinking or planning. Often follows a verb of action (e.g., reaccionar, actuar, saber).
target_language_example: Reaccioné por instinto cuando vi que se caía.
native_language_example: I reacted by instinct when I saw he was falling.

additional_notes: Very formal phrase used in letters, emails, contracts, and official notices to refer to the current document (“this letter,” “this notice”). Often followed by a verb in the present tense: “Por la presente, le informo…” It’s not used in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Por la presente, le informo que su solicitud ha sido aprobada.
native_language_example: I hereby inform you that your application has been approved.

por las buenas o por las malas

target_language_multi_word_term: por las buenas o por las malas
meaning: One way or another (willingly or by force).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say something will happen whether someone agrees or not. It often sounds like an ultimatum or threat, especially with verbs like "hacer" or "conseguir": "Lo harás por las buenas o por las malas."
target_language_example: Vas a venir por las buenas o por las malas.
native_language_example: You’re going to come one way or another (willingly or by force).

additional_notes: Used to add a general comment after mentioning details, or to contrast with what was just said (similar to “apart from that / other than that”). Often appears at the start of a sentence. Can also mean “in other respects.”
target_language_example: Por lo demás, todo está bien.
native_language_example: Otherwise, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Common phrase for talking about what happens most of the time (a general tendency). It often appears at the beginning of a sentence to set the tone: “Por lo general, …”. Similar in meaning to “generalmente” or “normalmente”.
target_language_example: Por lo general, voy al trabajo en autobús.
native_language_example: I usually go to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a minimum amount/number, or to soften a statement by mentioning a minimum expectation. Common in everyday speech; also appears as "por lo menos" or "por lo menos" within a longer sentence. Similar in meaning to "al menos".
target_language_example: Necesito por lo menos diez minutos.
native_language_example: I need at least ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a result or consequence of what was just mentioned. Often follows an explanation: “..., por lo que ...” = “..., so/therefore ...”. It can also mean “which,” when referring back to a whole idea (similar to “por lo cual”).
target_language_example: No tengo coche, por lo que voy a ir en autobús.
native_language_example: I don’t have a car, so I’m going to go by bus.

meaning: as far as I know (to my knowledge).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is true according to the information you currently have, without claiming complete certainty. It uses the present subjunctive of saber (sepa) and is common before giving an opinion or fact you’re not 100% sure about. Similar expressions: "que yo sepa" and "hasta donde yo sé".
target_language_example: Por lo que sepa, la tienda cierra a las ocho.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the store closes at eight.

meaning: 'as far as I know' / 'from what I know.'
additional_notes: Used to qualify what you’re saying and show it’s based on your knowledge, which may be incomplete. It often introduces information you believe is true: "Por lo que sé, ..." It’s similar to "que yo sepa" and can also appear mid-sentence.
target_language_example: Por lo que sé, la reunión es mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting is tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Common connector used in more formal speech and writing to introduce a conclusion or result. Often follows a cause statement: "..., por lo tanto, ...". Similar to "así que" (more common in conversation).
target_language_example: No tengo dinero; por lo tanto, no puedo salir esta noche.
native_language_example: I don’t have money; therefore, I can’t go out tonight.

meaning: around the time of; back around (a certain year/period).
additional_notes: Used to place something approximately in time, often with a year or a decade: "por los años de 2010" = around 2010; "por los años 80" = in/around the 80s. It suggests an approximate time period, not an exact date.
target_language_example: Por los años de 2010 vivía en Madrid.
native_language_example: Around 2010, I was living in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to say you almost didn’t make it or something almost happened, but you succeeded/avoided it at the last moment. Very common in spoken Spanish. Often used with verbs like "llegar" (to arrive), "ganar" (to win), "salvarse" (to be saved), or "aprobar" (to pass an exam).
target_language_example: Llegué al tren por los pelos.
native_language_example: I caught the train by a hair / I barely made the train.

meaning: very low; on the floor (often: doing very badly).
additional_notes: Often used with "estar" to describe prices, moods, energy, confidence, sales, etc. being extremely low or in a terrible state ("Las ventas están por los suelos"). It can also be literal (something is lying on the ground/floor), but it’s very common as an idiom meaning "rock bottom."
target_language_example: Después del examen, mi autoestima estaba por los suelos.
native_language_example: After the exam, my self-esteem was rock bottom.

meaning: the hard way; by force (often short for “por las malas”).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish as a shortened version of “por las malas,” meaning doing something through pressure, threats, or force instead of calmly (“por las buenas”). Often used with verbs like convencer, obligar, entrar, conseguir, etc.
target_language_example: Si no lo aceptas por las buenas, lo aceptarás por malas.
native_language_example: If you won’t accept it the easy way, you’ll accept it the hard way.

additional_notes: Used to express the method or channel used to do something (similar to “via” or “through”). Common with communication and procedures: por medio de internet/correo electrónico/una llamada. In many contexts it’s interchangeable with “a través de” or “mediante,” and it’s followed by a noun or noun phrase.
target_language_example: Te enviaré los documentos por medio de correo electrónico.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the documents by email.

meaning: for my part; as for me.
additional_notes: Used to give your own perspective, contribution, or intention—often to contrast with what others think or will do. Common in polite conversation and in work/school contexts. It can also introduce what you personally will do next: “Por mi parte, ya terminé.”
target_language_example: Por mi parte, estoy de acuerdo, pero prefiero hablarlo mañana.
native_language_example: As for me, I agree, but I’d rather talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you’re telling the truth or making a serious promise. It’s a dramatic/emotional expression (literally “by my life”), common in speech. Similar in tone to “I swear (on my life).”
target_language_example: Por mi vida, yo no fui.
native_language_example: I swear, it wasn’t me.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens off and on, in certain moments rather than continuously. Often similar to "a ratos" or "a veces" depending on context. It can also emphasize that something changes or intensifies in particular moments (e.g., emotions, weather).
target_language_example: Me sentí mejor por momentos, pero luego volvió el dolor.
native_language_example: I felt better at times, but then the pain came back.

additional_notes: A prepositional phrase used to give the reason for something. It’s fairly formal/literary; in everyday speech you’ll more often hear "por" or "a causa de". It’s followed by a noun, pronoun, or an infinitive phrase (e.g., "por mor de + noun/infinitive").
target_language_example: Cancelaron el viaje por mor de la tormenta.
native_language_example: They canceled the trip because of the storm.

meaning: by far; by a lot (the most).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a big difference, often in comparisons and superlatives. Very common pattern: “por mucho, el/la/los/las + superlative” (e.g., “por mucho, la mejor”). It can also appear after a comparison: “más … por mucho” (“much more, by far”).
target_language_example: Por mucho, este es el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.
native_language_example: By far, this is the best restaurant in the city.

additional_notes: Used to express that something doesn’t change even if you try hard or to introduce a contrast. Common patterns: (1) + subjunctive for “no matter how much”: Por más que estudie, no aprendo. (2) + indicative for “even though”: Por más que lo intentó, no pudo abrir la puerta.
target_language_example: Por más que corras, no vas a llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: No matter how much you run, you won’t arrive on time.

additional_notes: Often used to give your opinion or permission. Common patterns: "Por mí, ..." (As far as I’m concerned, ...), and "Por mí, bien" / "Por mí, no hay problema" (For me, it’s fine / no problem). Not the same as "para mí" (for me, intended for me / in my opinion); "por mí" often implies "on my part" or "from my side" (approval, willingness).
target_language_example: Por mí, podemos ir mañana.
native_language_example: As far as I’m concerned, we can go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common, informal-sounding reply after someone says “gracias.” It literally means “for nothing,” and can also be used to mean “(it was) nothing” or “no problem.” Often heard as “De nada,” which is very similar and sometimes more common.
target_language_example: —Gracias por tu ayuda. —Por nada.
native_language_example: —Thanks for your help. —You’re welcome.

meaning: because of; by the work/agency of.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is the cause of an event, often with a formal tone. It commonly appears as "por obra de + noun" (e.g., a person, an organization, a force), and in the set phrase "por obra y gracia de" (“by the work and grace of”), sometimes used ironically.
target_language_example: El cambio se produjo por obra de un nuevo equipo de ingenieros.
native_language_example: The change happened because of a new team of engineers.

meaning: by default (if nothing else is specified).
additional_notes: Used when something happens automatically because no other option was chosen or stated. Common in forms, instructions, and tech settings. Often appears as "valor/opción por omisión" (= default value/option). Similar in meaning to "por defecto".
target_language_example: Si no eliges un idioma, se usará el español por omisión.
native_language_example: If you don’t choose a language, Spanish will be used by default.

additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting idea or to introduce an additional consideration. It’s common in both spoken and written Spanish; often followed by a comma. Similar to "por un lado ... por otro lado" ("on the one hand ... on the other hand").
target_language_example: Me gusta vivir aquí; por otra parte, es un poco caro.
native_language_example: I like living here; on the other hand, it’s a bit expensive.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting idea or a different aspect of the same topic. Common in both speech and writing. It can be used without a strong contrast, more like 'also' or 'besides' when adding another consideration.
target_language_example: Me gusta vivir aquí; por otro lado, es un poco caro.
native_language_example: I like living here; on the other hand, it’s a bit expensive.

meaning: “from (the side of)”, “on the part of” (from a person/group).
additional_notes: Used to say who does something or where something comes from (a comment, request, decision, support, etc.). Often follows a noun: “una llamada por parte de…”, “una queja por parte de…”. In many cases you can translate it as simply “from” or “by” in English.
target_language_example: Recibimos una queja por parte de un cliente.
native_language_example: We received a complaint from a customer.

additional_notes: Used to suggest doing or explaining something little by little, one section at a time. Common in conversation when someone wants to go more slowly or break a problem down. Often used with verbs like "hacer" (to do) or "explicar" (to explain): "Vamos por partes" = "Let’s take it step by step."
target_language_example: No te preocupes: vamos por partes y lo resolvemos juntos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll take it step by step and solve it together.

additional_notes: Used to say something almost happened but didn’t, often with a sense of “just barely.” Common in the pattern “Por poco + (verb in past)” or “Por poco + (present) + …” meaning “I/you/etc. almost …”. Example: “Por poco me caigo” = “I almost fell.”
target_language_example: Por poco pierdo el tren.
native_language_example: I almost miss the train.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening/happened for the first time. Often placed at the start or end of the sentence. You can also use it with time expressions: "por primera vez en mi vida" (for the first time in my life) or "por primera vez desde..." (for the first time since...).
target_language_example: Visité Madrid por primera vez el año pasado.
native_language_example: I visited Madrid for the first time last year.

additional_notes: Literal phrase made of por (“through/by/per”) + puertas (“doors”). It’s not a very fixed/common expression on its own; in everyday Spanish you’ll more often see specific forms like por la puerta (“through the door”) or de puerta en puerta / puerta a puerta (“door to door”). You might see por puertas in pricing/counting contexts to mean “per door/entrance.”
target_language_example: El presupuesto es de 50 euros por puertas.
native_language_example: The quote is 50 euros per door.

additional_notes: Used in direct and indirect questions. In Spanish, it’s written as two words and has an accent (qué). Compare: “porque” (one word) = “because,” “porqué” (one word, with accent) = “the reason,” and “por que” (two words, no accent) used in more specific structures (e.g., “por que” = “so that/for which”).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué estás triste?
native_language_example: Why are you sad?

additional_notes: Used to say people or things are not together, or that you should do something one by one/individually. Common with verbs like "hacer" (to do), "pagar" (to pay), "hablar" (to speak), and "ir" (to go): "hacerlo por separado" = do it separately.
target_language_example: Vamos a pagar por separado.
native_language_example: We’re going to pay separately.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something as a precaution or preparing for a possible situation. Often appears as "por si + (present tense)" (e.g., "por si llueve" = in case it rains) or "por si acaso" = just in case. It can also be used before an infinitive in some contexts (e.g., "por si venir" in more formal/less common constructions), but beginners will most often see it with a present-tense verb.
target_language_example: Lleva un paraguas por si llueve.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella in case it rains.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something as a precaution because something might happen. It’s very common with carrying/bringing something or doing something extra: “Llévate un paraguas, por si acaso.” Also used alone to mean “just in case” / “to be safe.”
target_language_example: Llévate una chaqueta, por si acaso hace frío.
native_language_example: Take a jacket, just in case it gets cold.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that lasts indefinitely (often in romantic, poetic, or emphatic contexts). It’s similar to “para siempre” (very common), but “por siempre” can sound a bit more literary or emotional depending on the context. Placement is flexible: often at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Te amaré por siempre.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without help or without being accompanied. It often implies independence (doing it yourself) and sometimes being alone. You can change the possessive to match the person: por mi cuenta (on my own), por tu cuenta (on your own), por nuestra cuenta (on our own), por su cuenta (on his/her/their own).
target_language_example: Prefiero ir por mi cuenta.
native_language_example: I prefer to go on my own.

additional_notes: Used in formal or polite contexts to emphasize that someone must appear or act themselves (not through a representative). Often seen in instructions, invitations, or legal/administrative language. Similar in meaning to “en persona” or “personalmente.”
target_language_example: Para recoger el paquete, debe presentarse por su persona con una identificación.
native_language_example: To pick up the package, you must show up in person with an ID.

additional_notes: Used to express relief that something turned out well. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence ("Por suerte, ..."), but it can also appear later ("... , por suerte"). Similar in meaning to "afortunadamente" (more formal).
target_language_example: Por suerte, encontramos un taxi a tiempo.
native_language_example: Luckily, we found a taxi in time.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree, confirm, or say something is obvious/expected. Very common in conversation and generally polite (though tone can sound impatient if stressed). Often used alone as a full answer: “—¿Vienes? —Por supuesto.”
target_language_example: —¿Me puedes ayudar? —Por supuesto.
native_language_example: —Can you help me? —Of course.

meaning: by himself; on his own (by itself / on its own).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone or without help. It agrees with the subject: por sí mismo (he/it), por sí misma (she/it), por sí mismos (they, masc./mixed), por sí mismas (they, fem.). Often used with verbs like hacer, resolver, aprender, or quedar: hacerlo por sí mismo = do it by himself; quedar por sí solo = stand on its own.
target_language_example: Él lo hizo por sí mismo, sin ayuda.
native_language_example: He did it by himself, without help.

meaning: by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something acts, works, or exists independently. It often refers to a thing (“El aparato funciona por sí solo”), and for people you commonly use the gender/number forms: “por sí sola” (she/it feminine), “por sí solos/solas” (they). Close in meaning to “solo/solamente,” but “por sí solo” emphasizes independence rather than “only.”
target_language_example: Este aparato funciona por sí solo.
native_language_example: This device works by itself.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or result from what was just said. Common in more formal speech and writing; in casual conversation you might also hear "así que" or "entonces." Often followed by a comma in writing: "Por tanto, ..."
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo; por tanto, no puedo ir.
native_language_example: I don’t have time; therefore, I can’t go.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in many places or spread around. You can use it for location (people/things are everywhere) or movement (to go/walk around everywhere). Common with verbs like "estar," "haber," "ver," "ir," and "buscar."
target_language_example: Hay gente por todas partes en el centro.
native_language_example: There are people everywhere downtown.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "gracias" and "perdón": "Gracias por todo" = "Thanks for everything." It can also mean "all over/throughout" when talking about location or distribution, often with a noun: "por todo el jardín" (all over the garden).
target_language_example: Gracias por todo.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything.

meaning: everywhere; on all sides; all over the place.
additional_notes: Used to say something is in many places or in every direction. Very common in everyday speech. Similar to "por todas partes". With verbs like "haber" or "estar" it often means "there are/it’s ... everywhere" (e.g., "Hay gente por todos lados").
target_language_example: Había gente por todos lados en el concierto.
native_language_example: There were people everywhere at the concert.

meaning: by all means; by any means possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something no matter what, using every possible way or resource. Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Often appears with verbs like "hacer", "intentar", "buscar", or "evitar" (e.g., "hacer todo lo posible por todos los medios"). Not the same as English "by all means" meaning “certainly/please do” (that idea is usually "claro", "por supuesto", or "desde luego").
