target_language_example: Lo intenté por todos los medios, pero no pude resolver el problema.
native_language_example: I tried by all means, but I couldn’t solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening a single time, often contrasting with what usually happens. It can express a wish/complaint (“for once!”) or a limited exception (“just this once”). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Por una vez, llega a tiempo.
native_language_example: For once, show up on time.

meaning: per time; each time; at a time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how many times something happens or how much is allowed/charged each occasion. It often appears with a number or quantity (e.g., “dos por vez”) and is common in signs/instructions meaning “at a time.” In many everyday contexts Spanish also uses “cada vez” (each time) or “a la vez” (at the same time).
target_language_example: Solo pueden entrar dos personas por vez.
native_language_example: Only two people can enter at a time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you won’t repeat something again (often sounds impatient, annoyed, or very firm). Common in warnings, instructions, or arguments. You can also say "te lo digo por última vez" (“I’m telling you for the last time”).
target_language_example: Te lo digo por última vez: no toques eso.
native_language_example: I’m telling you for the last time: don’t touch that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the last point in a list, explanation, or sequence (similar to “lastly” or “to finish”). Often paired with other connectors like “primero…” (first) and “por último…” (finally). You can also say “y por último…” for “and finally…”.
target_language_example: Primero vamos a cenar, luego iremos al cine y por último volveremos a casa.
native_language_example: First we’re going to have dinner, then we’ll go to the movies, and finally we’ll go back home.

meaning: to behave well; to be good.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s behavior (often children, but also adults) and can be a request or instruction. The verb is reflexive: "portarse" (yo me porto, tú te portas, etc.). You can also use it in the negative: "portarse mal" = "to behave badly."
target_language_example: Los niños tienen que portarse bien en la escuela.
native_language_example: The kids have to behave well at school.

meaning: to catch fire; to set (something) on fire.
additional_notes: Used both intransitively (something catches fire) and transitively (someone sets something on fire). Intransitive: "La casa prendió fuego" / "El coche prendió fuego". Transitive: "Prendieron fuego al coche" (= They set the car on fire). Often appears with "a" before the thing that starts burning ("prender fuego a algo"), especially in Spain.
target_language_example: El motor prendió fuego y llamaron a los bomberos.
native_language_example: The engine caught fire and they called the firefighters.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay close attention to.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to tell someone to focus or notice something. It’s often followed by "a" + noun/thing ("presta atención a las instrucciones") or "a" + person ("presta atención a tu profesor"). In commands: "Presta atención" (informal tú), "Preste atención" (formal usted).
target_language_example: Presta atención a lo que te estoy diciendo.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what I’m telling you.

additional_notes: Refers to the first person someone falls in love with (often used nostalgically). You can also say "mi primer amor" (my first love). Sometimes used to mean the first serious romance rather than just a childhood crush.
target_language_example: Nunca olvidaré a mi primer amor.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget my first love.

additional_notes: Used mainly in countries with a parliamentary system. In Spain, it refers to the head of government (often also called "el presidente del Gobierno"). It’s a job title, so it’s often preceded by the definite article: "el/la primer(a) ministro(a)".
target_language_example: El primer ministro anunció nuevas medidas económicas.
native_language_example: The prime minister announced new economic measures.

meaning: first class (top category/quality; also first-class travel).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the highest category of service (especially on planes, trains, or buses) or something of excellent quality. As a noun phrase it’s often used with "en" (e.g., "viajar en primera clase"); as an adjective it can describe something as high-quality ("un servicio de primera clase").
target_language_example: Viajamos en primera clase porque era una oferta.
native_language_example: We traveled first class because it was a deal.

additional_notes: Used for a woman who is the head of government in a parliamentary system. Spanish uses gendered titles: "primer ministro" (male) and "primera ministra" (female). It’s usually preceded by the definite article: "la primera ministra".
target_language_example: La primera ministra dio un discurso anoche.
native_language_example: The prime minister gave a speech last night.

additional_notes: Used in grammar to talk about verbs/pronouns for the speaker: first person singular = "yo" (I) and first person plural = "nosotros/nosotras" (we). Also used in storytelling: "narrar en primera persona" = to tell a story from the "I" point of view.
target_language_example: Está escrito en primera persona: "Yo fui al mercado".
native_language_example: It’s written in the first person: “I went to the market.”

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something for the first time. Often appears with “por” (por primera vez = “for the first time”) or with “la” (la primera vez que… = “the first time that…”). You can also use it in questions like “¿Es tu primera vez?” (“Is it your first time?”).
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que vengo a Madrid.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to refer to basic emergency care given to someone who is injured or suddenly ill before professional help arrives. Common in signs (e.g., “Botiquín de primeros auxilios” = first-aid kit) and in phrases like “saber primeros auxilios” (to know first aid) or “dar primeros auxilios” (to give first aid).
target_language_example: ¿Hay un botiquín de primeros auxilios en la oficina?
native_language_example: Is there a first-aid kit in the office?

additional_notes: Used for software/apps used to write and format documents (e.g., Microsoft Word, Google Docs). In Spanish you’ll also hear “procesador de texto” (singular) for the same idea. Often appears with verbs like “usar” (to use), “abrir” (to open), or “escribir en” (to write in).
target_language_example: Necesito un procesador de textos para escribir mi currículum.
native_language_example: I need a word processor to write my résumé.

additional_notes: Used to refer to foods made from milk, such as milk, cheese, yogurt, and butter. Common on food labels, grocery signs, and in dietary contexts (e.g., “sin lácteos” = dairy-free; “intolerancia a la lactosa” is related but different). Singular: producto lácteo; plural: productos lácteos.
target_language_example: Soy alérgico a los productos lácteos, así que no como queso ni yogur.
native_language_example: I’m allergic to dairy products, so I don’t eat cheese or yogurt.

additional_notes: Used for forecasts you see on TV, apps, or websites. Also commonly phrased as “el pronóstico del tiempo” (the weather forecast). “Tiempo” here means “weather,” not “time.”
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el pronóstico del tiempo para mañana?
native_language_example: What is the weather forecast for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used in politics/government to refer to a draft law being discussed before it becomes a ley (law). If it passes/gets approved, it can become a ley. Common verbs: presentar (to introduce), debatir (to debate), aprobar (to approve), rechazar (to reject).
target_language_example: El Congreso aprobó el proyecto de ley.
native_language_example: Congress approved the bill.

additional_notes: Used in holiday greetings, especially around New Year’s. Most commonly appears as part of the fixed phrase “Feliz y próspero año nuevo” (“Happy and prosperous New Year”). Also written without accents in casual contexts: “prospero año nuevo,” though the correct spelling is “próspero.”
target_language_example: ¡Feliz y próspero año nuevo para ti y tu familia!
native_language_example: Happy and prosperous New Year to you and your family!

additional_notes: Uses the formal “usted” form (puede). Literally “(you) can help me.” Common when asking a stranger, staff, or someone you want to address politely. You can add “por favor” to be extra polite: “¿Puede ayudarme, por favor?”
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿puede ayudarme a encontrar la estación?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you help me find the station?

additional_notes: Used to express possibility/uncertainty. Very commonly followed by the subjunctive: “puede que + subjunctive” (e.g., “Puede que llueva”). Similar in meaning to “quizá(s)” and “tal vez.”
target_language_example: Puede que mañana tengamos clase.
native_language_example: Maybe we’ll have class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses tú (informal “you”) and literally means “you can help me.” Often used as a polite request; you can add “por favor” for extra politeness. For a more formal version (usted), say “¿Puede ayudarme?”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ayudarme, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

additional_notes: Used for the door at the back/rear of a house, building, or vehicle. In tech contexts it can also mean a “backdoor” (a hidden way into a system), but the everyday meaning is the physical door. Often used with location phrases like “por la puerta trasera” (through the back door).
target_language_example: Entra por la puerta trasera, por favor.
native_language_example: Come in through the back door, please.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about the time when the sun goes down. Often used with verbs like "ver" (to watch) or "disfrutar" (to enjoy): "ver la puesta de sol". Also heard as "puesta del sol"; "puesta de sol" is very common in travel/nature contexts.
target_language_example: Vamos a la playa para ver la puesta de sol.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the beach to watch the sunset.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the time/event when the sun goes down. It’s often used with verbs like ver (to see), disfrutar (to enjoy), and with prepositions like al atardecer / durante la puesta del sol (“at/around sunset” / “during sunset”). Also used in set phrases like "la puesta del sol" (the sunset).
target_language_example: Vamos a ver la puesta del sol en la playa.
native_language_example: Let’s go watch the sunset at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to name a specific place where people agree to meet (in a city, at an event, for tours, etc.). You’ll often see it on signs or in messages with a location: "El punto de encuentro es..."
target_language_example: Quedamos en el punto de encuentro a las seis.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the meeting point at six.

additional_notes: Used to express someone’s opinion or perspective. Common patterns: "desde mi punto de vista" (from my point of view), "punto de vista de + person" (someone’s point of view), and "cambiar de punto de vista" (to change your mind/your perspective).
target_language_example: Desde mi punto de vista, esta idea es mejor.
native_language_example: From my point of view, this idea is better.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a person’s or thing’s main weakness or vulnerability. Common in everyday speech and can be literal (a weak spot in a plan/argument) or personal (someone’s weakness for sweets). Often appears with "mi/tu/su" (my/your/his/her/their) or "el punto débil de..." (the weak point of...).
target_language_example: El punto débil de este plan es que cuesta mucho dinero.
native_language_example: The weak point of this plan is that it costs a lot of money.

additional_notes: Most commonly means the punctuation mark “.” at the end of a sentence. Figuratively, it can mean “the end” or “that’s final,” often used to close a discussion or make a firm decision (e.g., “y punto final”).
target_language_example: Pon un punto final al final de la frase.
native_language_example: Put a period at the end of the sentence.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone or something is especially good at (a skill, advantage, or best feature). Often appears with ser: "Mi punto fuerte es..." You can also use the plural for multiple strengths: "puntos fuertes".
target_language_example: Mi punto fuerte es la comunicación.
native_language_example: My strong point is communication.

meaning: A very vulgar exclamation used like “F***!” or “Damn!” (depending on tone).
additional_notes: Strong profanity. On its own (often as “¡Puta madre!”) it expresses anger, frustration, or surprise. It can also appear in insults (e.g., “hijo de puta madre”), and related phrases like “de puta madre” can mean “really great,” but the term itself is still very crude—avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: ¡Puta madre! Se me olvidó la cartera.
native_language_example: F***! I forgot my wallet.

additional_notes: Literally “web page.” In everyday Spanish it can refer to a single page or to an entire website, depending on context. Often used with verbs like “visitar” (to visit) or “entrar en” (to go to/access): “visitar una página web,” “entrar en la página web.”
target_language_example: Puedes visitar nuestra página web para más información.
native_language_example: You can visit our website for more information.

additional_notes: A common religious/heartfelt good-wish said to someone (often after they help you, when saying goodbye, or when expressing care). It’s polite and warm; you’ll also hear the shortened version “Dios te bendiga.” Uses the subjunctive “bendiga” to express a wish (“may…”).
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por tu ayuda; que Dios te bendiga.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help; may God bless you.

additional_notes: Used as a polite phrase before someone starts eating or when serving food. It can be said to one person or a group (also common: “¡Que aproveche!” or “¡Buen provecho!”).
target_language_example: Aquí tienes tu comida; que aproveche.
native_language_example: Here’s your food; enjoy your meal.

meaning: “just so it’s clear / for the record.”
additional_notes: Used to clarify your position or add a note (often a correction or disclaimer). Common in speech and writing. Often followed by “que…”: “Que conste que…” = “Just so it’s clear that…”.
target_language_example: Que conste que yo no dije eso.
native_language_example: Just so it’s clear, I didn’t say that.

additional_notes: Common Caribbean Spanish slang (especially Dominican Spanish). It’s a shortened form of “¿Qué es lo que…?” and is used like a quick “What’s up?” when you see someone. Often written with accents as “¿Qué lo qué?” in casual texting, but spelling varies.
target_language_example: —¿Qué lo que, manito? —Todo bien, ¿y tú?
native_language_example: —What’s up, bro? —All good, and you?

additional_notes: Literally, it’s like “(let) them kill me” (subjunctive: maten). In everyday speech it’s often an exaggerated way to show frustration, embarrassment, or that something is very hard/annoying, similar to “just kill me now.” It can also appear in longer sentences meaning “even if they kill me” or “before they kill me,” depending on context.
target_language_example: ¡Con todo el trabajo que tengo hoy, que me maten!
native_language_example: With all the work I have today, just kill me!

meaning: “(about) whether… / if…” (introduces a doubt, discussion, or hypothetical).
additional_notes: Often used to introduce or refer to a question or debate: *que si viene o no* (“whether he’s coming or not”). It can also appear in informal speech as part of a back-and-forth story/argument: *que si esto, que si lo otro* (“this and that; one thing and another”), implying lots of reasons/excuses or talking around the point.
target_language_example: No sé que si va a llover mañana o no.
native_language_example: I don’t know whether it’s going to rain tomorrow or not.

additional_notes: Used to insist or reassure that something is true or will happen. Common after someone doubts you or asks again (like “Yes, I did!”). It can also appear in longer phrases like “¡Que sí, hombre!” (“Yes, really!”). Depending on tone, it can sound a bit impatient.
target_language_example: —¿De verdad vienes mañana? —Que sí, que te lo prometo.
native_language_example: —Are you really coming tomorrow? —Yes, I am—I promise you.

meaning: “Screw you,” “get lost,” or “go to hell.” (very rude)
additional_notes: A highly offensive way to dismiss someone or show anger. Literally it means something like “may they give you (something),” but it’s used idiomatically as an insult. Often said on its own as an exclamation (e.g., “¡Que te den!”) and can be intensified with vulgar additions (avoid). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Si vas a seguir gritándome, ¡que te den!
native_language_example: If you’re going to keep yelling at me, screw you!

meaning: 'as far as I know' / 'to my knowledge'.
additional_notes: Used to limit what you’re saying to what you currently know (you’re not 100% sure). Often appears at the start of a sentence or after a negation: “Que yo sepa, no…” = “Not that I know of…”. It uses the subjunctive (sepa) because it refers to uncertain/limited knowledge.
target_language_example: Que yo sepa, la tienda abre a las nueve.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the store opens at nine.

meaning: to be located; to stay/remain; to agree to meet; to fit (clothes).
additional_notes: Very common verb with several everyday uses. (1) Location: “¿Dónde queda…?” = “Where is…?” (literally: where does it remain/where is it located). (2) Arranging plans: “quedar con alguien” = to meet up with someone / to have plans with someone (“Quedamos a las 8” = We’re meeting at 8). (3) Clothes fit: “Me queda bien/mal” = It fits me well/badly. Also common as “quedarse” (reflexive) meaning “to stay” or “to end up” (e.g., “Me quedo en casa” = I’m staying home).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde queda el baño?
native_language_example: Where is the bathroom?

meaning: to arrange to meet (someone); to meet up with (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a person to talk about making plans or having an agreed meeting. Very common in Spain. Conjugate "quedar" and keep "con" + person: "Quedo con Ana" (I’m meeting Ana / I’ve arranged to meet Ana). You can add a time/place: "Quedamos a las seis" (Let’s meet at six), "Quedamos en el café" (Let’s meet at the café). Also appears as "quedar en" (to agree on a place/plan), but "quedar con" specifically highlights who you’re meeting.
target_language_example: He quedado con Luis mañana a las siete.
native_language_example: I’m meeting up with Luis tomorrow at seven.

meaning: to agree on; to arrange (a plan, time, or place).
additional_notes: Used to say what people decided or agreed to do. Common patterns: “quedar en + infinitive” (agree to do something): "Quedamos en llamarte." and “quedar en + noun/time/place” (agree on something): "Quedamos en el café" / "Quedamos en las seis." Often used with the plural: "Quedamos en..." (= We agreed/We arranged...).
target_language_example: Quedamos en vernos mañana a las seis.
native_language_example: We agreed to meet tomorrow at six.

meaning: to be free/available (not busy); to be left open.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "quedar" + adjective "libre" to talk about time, a place, or a resource that is available: "Me queda libre la tarde" (my afternoon is free) or "Queda libre esta silla" (this chair is free). In some countries (especially Argentina/Uruguay), in an academic context "quedar libre" can also mean to lose the right to take the class/exam as a regular student (often due to absences).
target_language_example: Me queda libre la tarde, así que podemos vernos.
native_language_example: My afternoon is free, so we can meet up.

meaning: to look bad; to make a bad impression; to let someone down (by not showing up or not doing what you said).
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about social reputation or failing to meet expectations. Often appears as "quedar mal con alguien" (to look bad with someone / to let someone down) and "quedar mal" by itself (to look bad). In some contexts it can also mean something doesn’t fit or sit well (e.g., clothes: "me queda mal" = it looks bad on me / doesn’t fit me well).
target_language_example: No quiero quedar mal con ellos, así que voy a llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to make a bad impression with them, so I’m going to arrive on time.

meaning: to stay; to remain (to end up in a state/place).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb, so it’s used with a reflexive pronoun: me/te/se/nos/os/se (e.g., me quedo = I stay). Very common patterns: quedarse en + place (to stay in/at), quedarse con + thing (to keep something for yourself), quedarse sin + thing (to be left without), and quedarse + adjective (to end up/become: quedarse dormido = to fall asleep; quedarse callado = to go quiet).
target_language_example: Me voy a quedar en casa hoy.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay home today.

meaning: to keep; to take/accept (responsibility, etc.); to be left with.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. Common uses: (1) Physical possession: "Me quedo con esto" = "I’ll keep this." (2) Responsibility/task: "¿Te quedas con esto?" = "Will you take/handle this?" (3) Result/leftover: "Me quedé con la cuenta" = "I was left with the bill." It uses the reflexive verb "quedarse" + "con" + noun/pronoun.
target_language_example: Yo me quedo con las llaves.
native_language_example: I’ll keep the keys.

meaning: to fall asleep; to fall asleep accidentally (doze off).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se): "Me quedé dormido/a" = "I fell asleep." Often implies it wasn’t planned (e.g., you dozed off or fell asleep without meaning to). Agreement: dormido (male) / dormida (female).
target_language_example: Me quedé dormido en el sofá viendo la tele.
native_language_example: I fell asleep on the couch watching TV.

meaning: to run out of; to be left without.
additional_notes: Used to say you no longer have something (often because it was used up, lost, or taken away). It’s followed by a noun: "quedarse sin + [thing]". Common in everyday situations like running out of money, battery, food, or time.
target_language_example: Me quedé sin dinero y sin batería en el teléfono.
native_language_example: I ran out of money and my phone battery died (I was left without battery).

additional_notes: A very common verb. Most often it means “to want” + a noun or + an infinitive: Quiero agua. / Quiero comer. With people, “querer a + person” often means “to love/care about” in a family/friendly way (less intense than amar). In polite requests you can use the conditional: Quisiera… (“I would like…”). Also common: querer decir = “to mean” (Eso quiere decir…).
target_language_example: Quiero un café.
native_language_example: I want a coffee.

additional_notes: Used with a person (or pet) as the direct object: "Quiero a mi mamá" = "I love my mom." It’s different from "querer" meaning "to want" ("Quiero un café" = "I want a coffee"). The "a" is the personal "a" used before a person/pet who receives the action.
target_language_example: Quiero mucho a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: I love my grandparents a lot.

meaning: to love someone; to care about someone.
additional_notes: Uses the personal “a” before a person: querer a mi madre. In this meaning, “querer” is about affection/caring (family, friends, partners), not about wanting something. For romantic love, Spanish also often uses “amar,” but “querer a” is very common in everyday speech. Compare: “Quiero a Ana” (I love/care about Ana) vs. “Quiero un café” (I want a coffee).
target_language_example: Quiero mucho a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: I love my grandparents a lot.

meaning: to mean; to intend to say.
additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of something or to clarify what someone intended. Often appears in questions like “¿Qué quiere decir…?” (What does … mean?) or to correct yourself: “Lo que quiero decir es…” (What I mean is…). Conjugate only “querer” (quiero, quieres, quiere, etc.); “decir” stays in the infinitive.
target_language_example: ¿Qué quiere decir esta palabra?
native_language_example: What does this word mean?

meaning: to want to talk (to want to speak).
additional_notes: Uses the verb querer (“to want”) + an infinitive (hablar). Often followed by con + person (“querer hablar con alguien” = “to want to talk to someone”). In questions, it can be a polite way to ask if someone wants to talk: “¿Quieres hablar?”
target_language_example: Quiero hablar contigo.
native_language_example: I want to talk to you.

additional_notes: A somewhat formal, old-fashioned way to express hope that something will happen, literally meaning “may God want it.” Used like an interjection, often at the start or end of a sentence (similar to “God willing,” “hopefully,” or “I hope so”).
target_language_example: Llegaremos a tiempo, quiera Dios.
native_language_example: We’ll arrive on time, God willing.

meaning: "whether you want it or not" / "like it or not."
additional_notes: Fixed expression used to say something is true or will happen regardless of someone’s wishes. It often appears as a parenthetical at the start or in the middle of a sentence: "Quiera que no, ..." You may also see the very similar variant "quiera o no" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Quiera que no, vas a tener que hablar con él.
native_language_example: Whether you like it or not, you’re going to have to talk to him.

meaning: "whether you like it or not" / "like it or not."
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to emphasize that something is true or will happen regardless of your opinion or preferences. Often appears as "quieras que no, ..." or "quieras o no" and is followed by a statement.
target_language_example: Quieras que no, vas a tener que hablar con ella.
native_language_example: Whether you like it or not, you’re going to have to talk to her.

meaning: "I mean" / "that is to say" (used to clarify).
additional_notes: Literally "I want to say," but most often used like English "I mean" to correct yourself, add clarification, or rephrase. Commonly followed by a noun, an infinitive, or a full clause. In questions, it can also mean "Do you mean…?" (e.g., "¿Quieres decir que…?").
target_language_example: Llegaré el lunes, quiero decir, el martes.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive on Monday—I mean, on Tuesday.

meaning: to take your hat off; (figuratively) to show admiration or respect.
additional_notes: Literally means removing your hat. Very common as an idiom to praise someone: “Me quito el sombrero (ante/por ti)” = “I take my hat off to you.” Often used in the reflexive form (quitarse) and can be followed by “ante” (before) or “por” (for) the person/thing you admire.
target_language_example: Me quito el sombrero ante ustedes por el gran trabajo que hicieron.
native_language_example: I take my hat off to you for the great job you did.

meaning: to take one’s own life; to commit suicide.
additional_notes: A serious, formal/neutral expression often used in news reports or official statements. It’s a reflexive verb phrase: "quitarse" + "la vida" (e.g., "se quitó la vida" = "he/she took his/her own life"). You may also hear "suicidarse" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: La policía informó que el hombre se quitó la vida.
native_language_example: The police reported that the man took his own life.

meaning: to feel relieved; to get a weight off your shoulders.
additional_notes: An idiom used when a worry, responsibility, or stressful situation is removed or resolved, and you feel relief afterward. Often used with forms of "quitarse" (me/te/se quitó) and sometimes followed by "cuando" to explain why you felt relieved.
target_language_example: Cuando me dijeron que todo estaba bien, me quité un peso de encima.
native_language_example: When they told me everything was fine, I felt a weight off my shoulders.

additional_notes: Common adverb used to express uncertainty or possibility. Often interchangeable with "tal vez". It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence. You may also see the plural form "quizás" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Quizá mañana llueva.
native_language_example: Maybe it will rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or possibility. It can start a sentence or appear before/after the verb. With a possible-but-uncertain future meaning, it’s often followed by the subjunctive (Quizás venga), though the indicative is also common (Quizás viene), especially when the speaker feels it’s more likely.
target_language_example: Quizás mañana llueva, así que lleva un paraguas.
native_language_example: Maybe it will rain tomorrow, so bring an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise that something happened or turned out true. Often said after learning unexpected news or seeing an unexpected outcome. Literally “who would say it?”, but it’s used like English “who would’ve thought?”.
target_language_example: ¡Quién lo diría! Al final, a Juan le encantó la comida picante.
native_language_example: Who would have thought! In the end, Juan loved spicy food.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or that nobody knows the answer. Often said as a standalone response to a question. It can also mean "maybe" depending on tone and context. It literally means "who knows" (quién = who, sabe = knows).
target_language_example: —¿Va a llover mañana? —Quién sabe.
native_language_example: —Is it going to rain tomorrow? —Who knows.

additional_notes: Used to ask who is approaching or who is at the door/entrance, often as a challenge or when you can’t see the person (e.g., in the dark, in a hallway). It’s usually said as a question: “¿Quién va?” In everyday situations you may also hear “¿Quién es?” or “¿Quién anda ahí?”
target_language_example: —¿Quién va? —Soy yo, Ana.
native_language_example: —Who’s there? —It’s me, Ana.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to react to good news, something you like, or something that went well. Often said on its own (“¡Qué bien!”) or with a follow-up clause (“¡Qué bien que…!” = “How great that…!”). It’s neutral and common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: —Aprobé el examen. —¡Qué bien!
native_language_example: —I passed the exam. —That’s great!

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation in reaction to good news or something you like. Often followed by “que…” + a clause: “¡Qué bueno que…!” (“How great that…!”). Also commonly used on its own as a quick positive response.
target_language_example: —Voy a poder ir al viaje. —¡Qué bueno!
native_language_example: —I’m going to be able to go on the trip. —That’s great!

additional_notes: A very informal and often vulgar way to show surprise, anger, or frustration. Common in many Latin American countries. You’ll also hear it in questions like “¿Qué carajo haces?” (“What the hell are you doing?”). Avoid in formal situations or with people you don’t know well.
target_language_example: ¿Qué carajo estás haciendo aquí?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here?

meaning: “what a thing!” / “what!” (expression of surprise, annoyance, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Often used as an exclamation reacting to something unexpected: Qué cosa más rara. It can also mean “what thing?” in questions (less common than “¿qué cosa?” or simply “¿qué?”). Very similar to “qué cosa más…” = “what a …!”; in many contexts English would use “wow,” “geez,” or “what the heck.”
target_language_example: ¡Qué cosa! Otra vez se fue la luz.
native_language_example: What a thing! The power went out again.

additional_notes: An emphatic way to ask “what?” showing surprise, annoyance, or frustration. It’s informal and can sound rude depending on tone and context; use with friends or in strong situations, not in polite/formal settings. Often appears in questions like “¿Qué demonios estás haciendo?”
target_language_example: ¿Qué demonios estás haciendo aquí?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here?

additional_notes: Used to ask what something is, usually pointing to or referring to an object, sound, situation, or something you don’t recognize. Often said with surprise or curiosity. More natural for “that (over there)” than “this (here)” (which would be “¿qué es esto?”).
target_language_example: ¿Qué es eso? No lo entiendo.
native_language_example: What is that? I don’t understand it.

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or situation: ¿Qué fue (lo) que pasó? = “What happened?” In several Latin American countries (especially in casual speech), ¿Qué fue? can also work like “What’s up?” or “So, what happened?” The literal word-for-word sense is “what was,” but the usual meaning depends on context.
target_language_example:
—¿Qué fue? Te vi salir corriendo.
—Nada, se me hizo tarde.
native_language_example:
—What happened? I saw you run out.
—Nothing, I was running late.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness or pleasure. Common in greetings like “¡Qué gusto verte/conocerte!” (“Nice to see/meet you!”). You can also use it to react to good news: “¡Qué gusto!” (“That’s great!”). Often appears with exclamation marks (¡Qué gusto!).
target_language_example: ¡Qué gusto verte otra vez!
native_language_example: Nice to see you again!

additional_notes: Used in questions like "¿Qué hay?" or "¿Qué hay de nuevo?" to ask what’s happening or what news there is. Often used as a casual greeting similar to "What’s up?" In other contexts it can be more literal, meaning "what is there" (e.g., asking what food is available).
target_language_example: —Hola, ¿qué hay? —Nada, todo bien.
native_language_example: —Hi, what’s up? —Nothing, all good.

additional_notes: Common way to ask for the current time. Often used as a full question by itself. You can make it more polite by adding “Perdón,” or “Disculpe,” at the beginning (e.g., “Perdón, ¿qué hora es?”). In Spanish you normally include the opening and closing question marks: “¿Qué hora es?”
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿qué hora es?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Used to express sympathy, disappointment, or regret about a situation (yours or someone else’s). It can be said alone as a reaction (¡Qué lástima!) or followed by a clause (Qué lástima que… / Qué lástima que no…). Often interchangeable with “qué pena.”
target_language_example: —No puedo ir a la fiesta. —Qué lástima, quería verte.
native_language_example: —I can’t go to the party. —That’s too bad, I wanted to see you.

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening, or as a casual greeting similar to “What’s up?”. In questions it often appears as “¿Qué pasa?”; you may also hear “¿Qué pasa?” to react when something seems wrong (“What’s the matter?”).
target_language_example: —Hola, ¿qué pasa? ¿Todo bien?
native_language_example: —Hi, what’s up? Everything good?

additional_notes: Used to ask what happened or what the problem is. Often said on its own as a quick question when something seems off. In speech you may also hear it as "¿Qué pasó?" (neutral) or with pronouns: "¿Qué te pasó?" (What happened to you?) and "¿Qué pasó con…?" (What happened with…?).
target_language_example: ¿Qué pasó? Te ves preocupado.
native_language_example: What’s wrong? You look worried.

meaning: “I feel sorry for you” (often said in a pitying or condescending way).
additional_notes: Used to express pity toward someone, sometimes genuinely, but very often sarcastically or to put someone down (similar to “How pathetic” / “I pity you”). It’s directed at a person (tú). More neutral options are “Qué pena” (“What a shame”) or “Me da pena” (“It makes me feel sorry”).
target_language_example: ¿Sigues diciendo eso? Qué pena me das.
native_language_example: You’re still saying that? I feel sorry for you.

additional_notes: Usually heard as part of the expression “yo qué sé”, used to show you don’t know or don’t have an opinion, similar to “I have no idea” or “beats me.” It can also sound like “what do I know?” Often used in casual speech; tone depends on context and can sound a bit dismissive.
target_language_example: —¿A qué hora llega? —Qué sé, pregúntale a ella.
native_language_example: —What time is he arriving? —I don’t know, ask her.

additional_notes: Common, informal greeting. Often used on its own (“¿Qué tal?”) or with a follow-up like “¿Qué tal estás?” (How are you?). You can also use it to ask how something was or went: “¿Qué tal la película?” (How was the movie?).
target_language_example: —Hola, ¿qué tal? —Muy bien, ¿y tú?
native_language_example: —Hi, how’s it going? —Very well, and you?

additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion or propose a possibility, often followed by a verb in the present tense: "¿Qué tal si vamos...?" It’s common in conversation and can sound polite depending on tone. Similar to "¿Y si...?".
target_language_example: ¿Qué tal si cenamos en casa esta noche?
native_language_example: How about we have dinner at home tonight?

meaning: "how" + adjective/adverb ("how ...?" / "how ..."), especially for degree or extent.
additional_notes: Used to ask about or express the degree/intensity of something, usually before an adjective or adverb: "¿Qué tan + adj/adv ...?" or in indirect questions: "No sé qué tan...". Often interchangeable with "cuán" (more formal) and sometimes "qué tan" can be rephrased as "¿Qué tan + adj ... es/está ...?".
target_language_example: ¿Qué tan lejos está el hotel?
native_language_example: How far is the hotel?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask about degree or quantity. Often followed by a verb: “¿Qué tanto te gusta…?” = “How much do you like…?” It can also mean “how often” depending on context: “¿Qué tanto vienes por aquí?” = “How often do you come around here?” Similar in meaning to “cuánto,” but “qué tanto” emphasizes degree/extent.
target_language_example: ¿Qué tanto te gusta la comida mexicana?
native_language_example: How much do you like Mexican food?

meaning: "what can I say" (used as a filler to react or comment).
additional_notes: Common in casual conversation to express resignation, uncertainty, or that you don’t have much to add (similar to “what can I say?” / “you know…”). It often appears alone or followed by a comment: “Qué te digo… es complicado.” Literally it’s “what do I tell you?”, but it’s usually not a real question asking for an answer.
target_language_example: ¿Te gustó la película? —Qué te digo… estuvo rara.
native_language_example: Did you like the movie? —What can I say… it was weird.

additional_notes: Most often used as a short question when you’re concerned about someone/something: ¿Qué tiene? = “What’s wrong (with him/her)?” You can specify who with an indirect object: ¿Qué le tiene? (less common) or more naturally: ¿Qué le pasa? (“What’s wrong with him/her?”). It can also be literal about possession/condition, especially with a noun: ¿Qué tiene tu coche? (“What’s wrong with your car?” / “What does your car have?”).
target_language_example: ¿Qué tiene Ana? Se ve preocupada.
native_language_example: What’s wrong with Ana? She looks worried.

additional_notes: Literally means “what do you have?” but very commonly used to ask what’s wrong or what’s the matter, depending on context and tone. Often followed by a clarification like “¿Qué tienes? ¿Estás bien?” (What’s wrong? Are you okay?). You can also use it neutrally to ask what someone has (food, items, a condition): “¿Qué tienes en la mochila?” (What do you have in your backpack?).
target_language_example: ¿Qué tienes? Te veo preocupado.
native_language_example: What’s wrong? You look worried.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a category, style, or variety, usually followed by "de" + noun ("¿Qué tipo de música te gusta?"). Often interchangeable with "¿Qué clase de …?". Note: "tipo" can also mean "guy/dude" in some countries, but in the question "¿Qué tipo de …?" it means "type/kind".
target_language_example: ¿Qué tipo de comida te gusta?
native_language_example: What kind of food do you like?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to strongly disagree, deny something, or reject a suggestion. Often said on its own as a quick response, or followed by a clarification (e.g., “Qué va, no tengo tiempo.”). Very common in Spain; informal tone. Similar in meaning to “para nada” (“not at all”) and sometimes to the sarcastic “yeah right.”
target_language_example: —¿Te gusta el café? —Qué va, no me gusta nada.
native_language_example: —Do you like coffee? —No way, I don’t like it at all.

additional_notes: A common, regional name for an opossum in parts of Latin America (often also written as one word: “rabipelado”). Literally means “hairless tail,” referring to the animal’s tail.
target_language_example: Anoche vi un rabo pelado en el jardín.
native_language_example: Last night I saw an opossum in the garden.

additional_notes: An adverbial phrase meaning something happens not often. Commonly placed before the verb ("Rara vez voy...") or at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Rara vez salgo..."). Similar to "casi nunca" (almost never) but less extreme.
target_language_example: Rara vez comemos fuera entre semana.
native_language_example: We rarely eat out during the week.

meaning: a bookworm (someone who reads a lot).
additional_notes: A common, mostly playful expression for a person who spends a lot of time reading or in libraries. Often used with "ser" (to be): "Soy un/una ratón/ratona de biblioteca." You can also say "un ratón de biblioteca" as a noun phrase. It’s not rude, but it can be teasing depending on tone.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es un ratón de biblioteca: siempre está leyendo.
native_language_example: My sister is a bookworm: she’s always reading.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all humans as a group (often in formal or philosophical contexts). In many modern contexts, especially in social science, people may prefer terms like "la humanidad" (humanity) to avoid implications associated with "race."
target_language_example: Debemos proteger el planeta por el bien de la raza humana.
native_language_example: We must protect the planet for the good of the human race.

additional_notes: Feminine form. Use for a baby girl or for a female person/animal that has just been born. Masculine: "recién nacido". Often used with "bebé" ("bebé recién nacida") or as a noun: "la recién nacida" = "the newborn baby girl". "Recién" means "just/recently" and is commonly used before past participles (e.g., "recién hecho" = "just made").
target_language_example: La bebé es una recién nacida.
native_language_example: The baby is a newborn (girl).

additional_notes: Used for online services/apps where people connect and share content. Commonly used with verbs like "usar" (to use), "seguir" (to follow), and "publicar" (to post): "usar una red social", "seguirme en una red social", "publicar en una red social". Plural: "redes sociales".
target_language_example: No uso muchas redes sociales, pero tengo Instagram.
native_language_example: I don't use many social networks, but I have Instagram.

additional_notes: A formal/neutral phrase used in medical, legal, or educational contexts to refer to sex. In everyday conversation, people often say "tener sexo" or "acostarse con alguien" (more informal). It’s usually used with verbs like "tener" (to have) or "mantener" (to maintain).
target_language_example: Es importante usar protección durante una relación sexual.
native_language_example: It’s important to use protection during sexual intercourse.

additional_notes: A common way to specify a watch you wear on your wrist (as opposed to a wall clock, "reloj de pared," or an alarm clock, "reloj despertador"). Often shortened to just "reloj" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un reloj de pulsera para la excursión?
native_language_example: Do you have a wristwatch for the trip?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about (similar to “as for…”). Common in formal and neutral contexts, especially in writing and emails. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: "respecto a tu pregunta" (regarding your question), "respecto a eso" (regarding that).
target_language_example: Respecto a tu solicitud, te responderé mañana.
native_language_example: Regarding your request, I’ll reply to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: A finance term for the risk that the value of an investment (or a company/portfolio) changes because of broad market movements (e.g., interest rates, exchange rates, stock prices). Common in news, banking, investing, and risk-management contexts.
target_language_example: Antes de invertir, es importante entender el riesgo de mercado.
native_language_example: Before investing, it’s important to understand market risk.

meaning: to burst into tears; to start crying suddenly.
additional_notes: Common structure: "romper a" + infinitive to mean "to suddenly start doing" something (often with emotion), e.g., "romper a reír" (to burst out laughing). It implies an abrupt, uncontrollable start.
target_language_example: Al escuchar la noticia, rompió a llorar.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she burst into tears.

meaning: to break up with; to break off (relations) with.
additional_notes: Commonly used for ending a romantic relationship: "romper con alguien" (to break up with someone). It can also mean ending ties/relations with a person, group, habit, or tradition: "romper con la tradición" (to break with tradition). The "con" introduces who/what you are ending the connection with.
target_language_example: Decidí romper con mi novio porque no éramos felices.
native_language_example: I decided to break up with my boyfriend because we weren’t happy.

additional_notes: Literally “white clothes,” but it commonly means household linen and laundry, especially sheets, pillowcases, towels, etc. In many Latin American contexts, “lavar la ropa blanca” means to wash the whites (white laundry).
target_language_example: Tengo que lavar la ropa blanca hoy.
native_language_example: I have to do the laundry (wash the whites) today.

meaning: underwear; underwear/clothes worn under your clothes.
additional_notes: Common everyday term. Often used as a singular collective (“la ropa interior”), but it can also be plural (“las ropas interiores,” less common). You can specify items with “de”: “ropa interior de mujer/hombre” (women’s/men’s underwear).
target_language_example: Necesito comprar ropa interior nueva.
native_language_example: I need to buy new underwear.

meaning: “ropa vieja”: a shredded beef stew (traditional dish); literally “old clothes.”
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a specific Latin/Cuban/Spanish-style dish made with shredded beef (often in a tomato-based sauce) served with rice, beans, or plantains. In context, it’s usually food, not actual clothing. As a literal phrase, it can also mean “old clothes,” but that’s less common as a fixed expression and is typically clarified by context (e.g., “Tengo ropa vieja para donar”).
target_language_example: Voy a pedir ropa vieja con arroz y frijoles.
native_language_example: I’m going to order ropa vieja with rice and beans.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or location in the direction the river flows (toward the mouth). Common with verbs like ir, bajar, nadar, remar, and with locations: más río abajo (further downstream).
target_language_example: Vamos a remar río abajo hasta el puente.
native_language_example: We’re going to paddle downstream to the bridge.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or location in the direction the river comes from (opposite the current). Often used with verbs like ir (to go), subir (to go up), and navegar (to sail). Contrast: "río abajo" = downstream.
target_language_example: Caminamos río arriba hasta el puente.
native_language_example: We walked upstream to the bridge.

meaning: "God knows" / "who knows?" (used to say something is unknown).
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or that nobody really knows the answer. Often appears in phrases like "Sabe Dios cuándo/dónde/cómo..." (= "God knows when/where/how..."). In everyday speech it can mean "who knows" without being strongly religious.
target_language_example: Sabe Dios cuándo volverá a llamar.
native_language_example: God knows when he’ll call again.

meaning: to know (a fact/information); to know how to (do something).
additional_notes: Used for knowledge of facts and information: "saber algo" (to know something) and with question words: "saber dónde/cuándo/por qué...". Also used with an infinitive to mean "to know how to": "saber nadar" (to know how to swim). Contrast with "conocer", which is used for being familiar with people/places or having met someone ("conocer a alguien").
target_language_example: ¿Sabes dónde está el baño?
native_language_example: Do you know where the bathroom is?

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about having the ability/knowledge to do something: "saber cómo + infinitive" (e.g., "saber cómo llegar"). Often also appears in questions like "¿Sabes cómo...?" = "Do you know how...?". Note: "saber" is about knowing facts/skills; for being familiar with a person/place, Spanish uses "conocer" instead.
target_language_example: No sé cómo hacerlo, ¿me ayudas?
native_language_example: I don’t know how to do it; can you help me?

meaning: to know about; to be familiar with; to have knowledge of.
additional_notes: Used to talk about knowing about a topic, situation, or field (not knowing a fact). Often followed by a noun or infinitive: "saber de historia" (know about history), "saber de cocina" (know about cooking). In some contexts it can also mean "to find out about" something: "¿Supiste de lo que pasó?" (Did you hear/find out about what happened?).
target_language_example: No sé mucho de fútbol, pero me gusta verlo.
native_language_example: I don’t know much about soccer, but I like watching it.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about practical skills learned through experience or training. You may also see it as a noun: "el saber hacer" = "the know-how." Similar to "saber + infinitive" (to know how to do something), but "saber hacer" is commonly used as a set phrase meaning know-how.
target_language_example: En esta empresa valoramos el saber hacer de nuestro equipo.
native_language_example: In this company we value our team’s know-how.

additional_notes: Common colloquial expression used to say something is unknown or impossible to know. It often carries a tone of uncertainty, resignation, or mild frustration. You can also hear it as "¡Sabrá Dios!" as a standalone reply meaning “Who knows!”
target_language_example: ¿Cuándo va a llegar? Sabrá Dios.
native_language_example: When is he going to arrive? God knows.

meaning: to drive someone crazy; to make someone lose their temper.
additional_notes: Used when someone or something irritates you so much that you feel you’re losing patience or self-control. Often appears as “Me saca de quicio” (It drives me crazy) or “Me saca de quicio que…” (It drives me crazy that…). The literal image is “to take someone out of their hinges,” so it’s not usually translated word-for-word.
target_language_example: Me saca de quicio que siempre llegue tarde.
native_language_example: It drives me crazy that he always arrives late.

meaning: to bring out the best in (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, situation, or activity makes someone show their best qualities or produces the best result. It’s often followed by a person or pronoun (de mí, de ti, de él/ella, de nosotros).
target_language_example: Este trabajo saca lo mejor de mí.
native_language_example: This job brings out the best in me.

meaning: to take advantage of; to make the most of (something).
additional_notes: Used to say you benefit from a situation or use something well. Often followed by "de": "sacar provecho de" + noun/verb (e.g., "sacar provecho de la oportunidad"). Can be positive (make good use of time/resources) or negative (take advantage of someone), depending on context.
target_language_example: Tenemos que sacar provecho de esta oportunidad.
native_language_example: We have to make the most of this opportunity.

meaning: to get something off your chest; to let it all out (emotionally).
additional_notes: Used when someone expresses feelings or thoughts they’ve been holding in, often to feel relief. It’s common with a direct object like “todo”, “la bronca”, “lo que siento/tenía”, etc. Literal words are “to take out from inside,” but it’s usually meant figuratively.
target_language_example: Necesitaba sacarme de adentro todo lo que sentía.
native_language_example: I needed to get off my chest everything I was feeling.

additional_notes: Used for the place where you wait before an appointment or service (doctor’s office, hospital, airport, etc.). Often appears with the verb "esperar" (to wait): "Esperamos en la sala de espera."
target_language_example: Por favor, espere en la sala de espera.
native_language_example: Please wait in the waiting room.

additional_notes: A common term for the main room in a home where people relax, sit, watch TV, or receive guests. Often used with the article: "la sala de estar". In many places you may also hear "la sala" for short, or "el salón" (Spain).
target_language_example: Estamos en la sala de estar viendo la tele.
native_language_example: We’re in the living room watching TV.

meaning: to come up (in conversation); to be brought up.
additional_notes: Used when a topic or detail is mentioned during a conversation, often unexpectedly. Common patterns: "salió a colación el tema de..." (the topic of... came up) or "cuando salió a colación..." (when ... came up). Similar meaning: "salir en la conversación"; related expression: "sacar a colación" = to bring up (a topic).
target_language_example: En la cena salió a colación el tema de las vacaciones.
native_language_example: At dinner, the topic of vacations came up.

meaning: to come to light; to be revealed (become known).
additional_notes: Used when information, a secret, or the truth becomes public or is discovered. Often appears in news or formal contexts: "salió a la luz" (it came to light). Can also be used with "que": "Salió a la luz que..." (It came to light that...).
target_language_example: Salió a la luz la verdad sobre el accidente.
native_language_example: The truth about the accident came to light.

meaning: to get by; to pull through; to move forward (despite difficulties).
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about overcoming problems, especially financial, personal, or work-related ones. It can mean “to manage” (economically or in daily life) or “to recover/come out okay” after a hard situation. Often used with verbs like poder, querer, or lograr: "Vamos a salir adelante."
target_language_example: Aunque no tenemos mucho dinero, vamos a salir adelante.
native_language_example: Even though we don’t have much money, we’re going to get by.

meaning: to step in to address/stop something (often criticism, rumors, a problem).
additional_notes: Commonly used with "de": "salir al paso de + algo" = to respond quickly in order to counter or defuse something (e.g., accusations, doubts, rumors). It can also be literal: "salir al paso a alguien" = to go out to meet someone on their way.
target_language_example: El portavoz salió al paso de las críticas y aclaró lo ocurrido.
native_language_example: The spokesperson stepped in to address the criticism and clarified what happened.

meaning: to go out with; to date.
additional_notes: Used to talk about spending time/socializing with someone (friends or family) or dating someone romantically—context makes it clear. For romantic dating, it’s very common in the present continuous: “Estoy saliendo con…” (I’m dating/seeing…). With plans, it can mean simply “to go out with”: “Voy a salir con mis amigos.”
target_language_example: Estoy saliendo con Ana desde hace dos meses.
native_language_example: I’ve been dating/seeing Ana for two months.

meaning: to leave / to go out of / to get out of (a place or situation).
additional_notes: Used with "de" to show where you are leaving from or what you are getting out of. Common with places: "salir de casa" (leave the house), "salir de la oficina" (leave the office). It can also be used for escaping a situation: "salir de un problema" (get out of a problem). In schedules/transportation it can mean "to depart from": "El tren sale de Madrid" (The train leaves from Madrid).
target_language_example: Salgo de casa a las ocho.
native_language_example: I leave the house at eight.

additional_notes: Used when a situation becomes chaotic or no longer manageable. Often appears as "se salió de control" (it got out of control) or "esto se está saliendo de control" (this is getting out of control).
target_language_example: La fiesta se salió de control y llegaron los vecinos a quejarse.
native_language_example: The party got out of control and the neighbors came to complain.

meaning: (very vulgar) ‘to do something just because I feel like it.’
additional_notes: A highly offensive, very vulgar Spanish (especially Spain) expression. Most commonly used as "me sale de la polla" or "no me sale de la polla" to mean “because I feel like it / because I want to” or “I don’t feel like it / I can’t be bothered.” It expresses defiance or refusal and should be avoided in polite or neutral situations.
target_language_example: Lo hago porque me sale de la polla.
native_language_example: I’m doing it because I feel like it.

meaning: to go badly; to turn out badly.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an event, plan, situation, or result that ends badly or doesn’t work. Common with things like a trip, a project, a test, or a conversation: “La reunión salió mal” (The meeting went badly).
target_language_example: El plan salió mal y tuvimos que cambiarlo.
native_language_example: The plan went badly and we had to change it.

meaning: to get your way; to get away with it.
additional_notes: Used when someone succeeds in doing what they wanted (often against other people’s wishes) or avoids consequences. The phrase literally refers to “ending up with one’s own (thing/way),” but it’s best learned as an idiom. Common structure: "(Alguien) se sale con la suya". Often implies the person was stubborn, pushy, or a bit sneaky.
target_language_example: Aunque nadie estaba de acuerdo, Juan se salió con la suya y eligieron su plan.
native_language_example: Even though nobody agreed, Juan got his way and they chose his plan.

additional_notes: Common food item used in cooking (pasta, pizza, etc.). You may also see it as "salsa de tomate" (general) or "salsa de tomates" depending on region; in some places, "salsa de tomate" can refer to a cooked tomato sauce, while "puré de tomate" (tomato purée) and "kétchup" (ketchup) are different products.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes salsa de tomate para la pasta?
native_language_example: Do you have tomato sauce for the pasta?

meaning: to jump out of bed; to get out of bed quickly.
additional_notes: Used when you get up suddenly/quickly, often because you’re surprised, late, or excited. It’s a literal image (to “jump” from the bed), but in everyday speech it often just means getting up fast. Common with time pressure: “Tuve que saltar de la cama” (I had to jump out of bed).
target_language_example: Cuando sonó la alarma, salté de la cama porque iba tarde.
native_language_example: When the alarm rang, I jumped out of bed because I was late.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone from the aristocracy or a royal family. It’s usually figurative (not literal blood) and can be neutral or slightly ironic depending on tone.
target_language_example: Dicen que tiene sangre azul porque su familia es de la nobleza.
native_language_example: They say he has blue blood because his family is noble.

meaning: calmness and self-control (especially in a stressful situation).
additional_notes: Most often used in the phrase "mantener la sangre fría" = "to keep your cool" or "stay calm". It can describe someone’s personality (someone who doesn’t panic) or how you should react in an emergency. Literally "cold blood," but in English you normally say "keep your cool" rather than "keep cold blood."
target_language_example: Cuando empezó el incendio, Marta mantuvo la sangre fría y llamó a los bomberos.
native_language_example: When the fire started, Marta kept her cool and called the firefighters.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived or is okay after a trip, accident, scare, etc. Common with verbs like "llegar" (to arrive) and "estar" (to be): "Llegamos sanos y salvos" / "Está sano y salvo." It agrees with the person: "sana y salva" (one woman), "sanos y salvos" (mixed/men plural), "sanas y salvas" (women plural).
target_language_example: Me llamaron para decirme que llegaron sanos y salvos a casa.
native_language_example: They called me to tell me they got home safe and sound.

meaning: “good heavens!” / “oh my God!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, or frustration).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection to react strongly to something you just saw or heard. It’s fairly common and generally not vulgar; it can sound a bit old-fashioned or emphatic depending on tone. Often said alone, or followed by a comment: “¡Santo cielo, qué calor!”
target_language_example: ¡Santo cielo! No puedo creer lo que pasó.
native_language_example: Good heavens! I can’t believe what happened.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how something is typically eaten, without saying who eats it. Very common in recipes, menus, and general statements about food. Often followed by an adjective or phrase describing how it’s served (e.g., frío, caliente, con pan). Note: "come" is from "comer" (to eat) and is a false friend with English "come."
target_language_example: Este plato se come frío.
native_language_example: This dish is eaten cold / People eat this dish cold.

additional_notes: Common sign or phrase to indicate that Spanish is spoken in a place (store, office, website). It uses the impersonal/passive "se" construction, so it doesn’t specify who speaks Spanish. You’ll also see it with other languages: "Se habla inglés" (English is spoken).
target_language_example: En esta tienda se habla español.
native_language_example: Spanish is spoken in this store.

additional_notes: Common sign or service phrase meaning that English is spoken in a place (hotel, store, restaurant). Uses the impersonal/passive "se" (no specific subject). You can turn it into a question: "¿Se habla inglés aquí?" = "Is English spoken here?"
target_language_example: ¿Se habla inglés aquí?
native_language_example: Is English spoken here?

meaning: “you can / it’s possible” (it can be done).
additional_notes: Impersonal expression with "se" that talks about what is possible or allowed in general (not a specific person). Often used to ask permission or check feasibility: "¿Se puede...?" = “May I…?/Is it possible to…?” Also used to say something is doable: "Se puede hacer" = “It can be done.”
target_language_example: ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?
native_language_example: Can you pay by card? / Is it possible to pay by card?

additional_notes: Used to say what is expected (obligation/plan) or what people assume is true. Often appears as “Se supone que + clause” (Supposedly…, It’s assumed that…), or “Se supone que + verb” meaning “is supposed to + verb.” Common in conversation and can imply doubt or mild complaint depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Se supone que el autobús llega a las ocho, pero siempre llega tarde.
native_language_example: The bus is supposed to arrive at eight, but it always arrives late.

additional_notes: Used to move on from a detail that doesn’t change the main point, similar to “in any case” or “anyway.” It’s relatively formal and common in writing or careful speech. You may also hear the shorter version “sea como sea” (“either way”).
target_language_example: Sea como fuere, tenemos que terminar hoy.
native_language_example: Be that as it may, we have to finish today.

additional_notes: Used to show that the exact thing doesn’t matter or isn’t known, and you’ll accept it anyway. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence. From the subjunctive of ser (“sea”) + “lo que sea” (“whatever it may be”).
target_language_example: Sea lo que sea, te voy a ayudar.
native_language_example: Whatever it is, I’m going to help you.

meaning: to keep going; to move forward; to continue.
additional_notes: Often used to encourage someone to continue despite difficulty (like “keep going”). It can refer to continuing an activity, a plan, or progress in life. In everyday speech you may also hear it as “Sigue adelante” (you, keep going) or “Vamos a seguir adelante” (we’re going to move forward).
target_language_example: Aunque sea difícil, vamos a seguir adelante.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, we’re going to keep going.

meaning: to keep going like this; to continue this way.
additional_notes: Used to say that something should continue in the same manner as it has been. Often used as advice or encouragement (e.g., 'Don’t stop; keep doing it this way'). It can describe either a person’s behavior or how a situation is unfolding. With the same idea, you may also hear: "Sigue así" (Keep it up / Keep going like that).
target_language_example: Vas muy bien; ¡sigue así!
native_language_example: You’re doing really well; keep it up!

additional_notes: Used with a noun or an infinitive to say you continue an activity, task, or situation. Common patterns: "seguir con + noun" (seguir con el trabajo = keep working on the job) and "seguir + gerund" is another option ("sigo estudiando" = I keep studying), but "seguir con" is especially common before a noun or to emphasize 'continue with it'.
target_language_example: Voy a seguir con la tarea después de cenar.
native_language_example: I’m going to continue with the homework after dinner.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used for an insurance policy that pays money to beneficiaries when the insured person dies. Often used with verbs like tener (to have), contratar (to take out), or pagar (to pay): “Tengo un seguro de vida.”
target_language_example: Mi papá tiene un seguro de vida.
native_language_example: My dad has life insurance.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 6,000, often with a noun: "seis mil dólares" (six thousand dollars). With masculine plural nouns you may see "seis mil" + noun: "seis mil libros" (six thousand books).
target_language_example: El coche cuesta seis mil euros.
native_language_example: The car costs six thousand euros.

meaning: to suit (someone); to agree with (someone), e.g., a food or a color.
additional_notes: Used to say that something looks good on someone (clothes, colors, hairstyles) or that something agrees with someone physically (food/drink doesn’t make you feel sick). Often appears as: “(algo) le sienta bien a (alguien)” or “me/te/le sienta bien”. For the opposite, you’ll hear “sentar mal” (to not agree with / to look bad on).
target_language_example: Esa chaqueta te sienta muy bien, y la sopa me sienta bien cuando estoy enfermo.
native_language_example: That jacket suits you very well, and soup agrees with me when I’m sick.

meaning: to settle down; to become more responsible/mature.
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone stops acting impulsively (partying a lot, changing jobs/partners constantly, being irresponsible) and starts living more seriously. It often implies a lasting change in attitude or lifestyle. You’ll also hear it in the reflexive form: "sentarse la cabeza" (less common).
target_language_example: Después de tantos años de fiesta, por fin sentó cabeza y empezó a ahorrar dinero.
native_language_example: After so many years of partying, he finally settled down and started saving money.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb (used with reflexive pronouns: me/te/se/nos/os/se). Often used as a polite command: “Siéntate” (sit down) or “Siéntense” (you all sit down). In some contexts, “sentar” (without -se) means “to seat someone” (e.g., “Voy a sentar al niño”).
target_language_example: Siéntate, por favor.
native_language_example: Sit down, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical, reasonable judgment that most people are expected to have. Often appears with verbs like “tener” (to have) and “usar” (to use): “tener sentido común,” “usar el sentido común.”
target_language_example: Hay que usar el sentido común en esta situación.
native_language_example: We need to use common sense in this situation.

additional_notes: Used in philosophical or personal conversations about what gives life meaning. It can also be used more casually or humorously (e.g., someone finds something very satisfying). Often appears with verbs like "buscar" (to look for), "encontrar" (to find), or "preguntarse" (to wonder).
target_language_example: A veces me pregunto cuál es el sentido de la vida.
native_language_example: Sometimes I wonder what the meaning of life is.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability to find things funny or to joke. Often used with tener (to have): "tener sentido del humor". You can also say "buen/mal sentido del humor" (good/bad sense of humor).
target_language_example: Mi jefe tiene muy buen sentido del humor.
native_language_example: My boss has a very good sense of humor.

meaning: 'to be' (for identity, inherent characteristics, origin, etc.).
additional_notes: Spanish has two common verbs for 'to be': ser and estar. Use ser for things that are seen as essential or defining (who someone is, what something is, where someone is from, what something is like in general), and for time and dates. Common uses: identity/profession (Soy médico.), origin (Somos de México.), characteristics (Es interesante.), time/date (Son las tres. / Hoy es lunes.).
target_language_example: Soy de Canadá, pero mi hermana es de México.
native_language_example: I’m from Canada, but my sister is from Mexico.

meaning: to be friends with; to be a friend of.
additional_notes: Used with a person or group: "Soy amigo de Ana" (I’m friends with Ana). In Spanish you normally use "de" here (not "con"), even though English says "with". You can also use it more broadly to mean being a supporter/fan of something: "Soy amigo del buen vino" (I’m a fan of good wine).
target_language_example: ¿Eres amigo de Marta?
native_language_example: Are you friends with Marta?

meaning: to be good (by nature/character); to be a good person.
additional_notes: Uses **ser** (not *estar*) to describe a more permanent quality (personality, character, what something is generally like). **Bueno** changes to match gender/number: *bueno, buena, buenos, buenas*. It can also mean “to be good at” something with **en**: *Soy bueno en matemáticas* (“I’m good at math”). For temporary states like food tasting good, Spanish usually uses **estar**: *La sopa está buena* (“The soup is good”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano es bueno y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: My brother is good and always helps others.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (to be) to describe a lasting relationship (friendship), not a temporary state. Often appears in different forms depending on the subject and tense: somos buenos amigos (we’re good friends), éramos buenos amigos (we were good friends). You can also say ser muy buenos amigos (to be very good friends).
target_language_example: Desde la universidad, Ana y yo somos buenos amigos.
native_language_example: Since university, Ana and I have been good friends.

meaning: to be from; to belong to; to be made of.
additional_notes: Used mainly with (1) origin: "Soy de México" (I’m from Mexico); (2) possession/ownership: "Es de Ana" (It’s Ana’s / It belongs to Ana); and (3) material: "Es de madera" (It’s made of wood). You’ll often see the contraction "de + el" → "del" ("Soy del Perú").
target_language_example: ¿De quién es este libro? Es de Juan.
native_language_example: Whose book is this? It’s Juan’s.

meaning: to be history; to be in the past/over.
additional_notes: Often used to say that something (a relationship, plan, problem, trend, etc.) is finished and no longer matters or is no longer current. In the past tense it’s very common: “Eso ya es historia” = “That’s all in the past / That’s history now.” In a more literal sense, it can also mean “to be history” as an academic subject (e.g., “Mi materia es historia”), but as a phrase it most often means “to be in the past.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: eso ya es historia.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: that’s all in the past.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning a member of the human species. It’s more formal or neutral than "persona" and is common in general statements, science, ethics, or human-rights contexts. Plural: "seres humanos".
target_language_example: Todos los seres humanos merecen respeto.
native_language_example: All human beings deserve respect.

meaning: to be a battle; to be very difficult/chaotic.
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation is like a war (hard, stressful, full of conflict), often in a figurative or joking way. Common with "esto es la guerra" or "¡es la guerra!" to mean "that’s how it is" when something is tough or unfair. Usually refers to a situation, not a literal war.
target_language_example: Trabajar con niños pequeños es la guerra.
native_language_example: Working with little kids is a battle (it’s chaotic and exhausting).

meaning: to be the first to arrive (female speaker).
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives before everyone else. The adjective and article agree with the person: "ser el primero en llegar" (male), "ser la primera en llegar" (female). Often followed by "pero" to contrast with what happened next: "Fui la primera en llegar, pero...".
target_language_example: Ayer fui la primera en llegar a la oficina.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was the first to arrive at the office.

meaning: to be (a certain time), used in telling the time (e.g., “It’s two o’clock”).
additional_notes: Used when giving the time with hours other than 1: you normally say **Son las + [hour]** (e.g., *Son las dos*). For 1 o’clock, Spanish uses singular: **Es la una** (not *Son las una*). You can add minutes: *Son las tres y diez* (3:10), or use *menos* for “to”: *Son las cinco menos diez* (4:50).
target_language_example: Son las ocho.
native_language_example: It’s eight o’clock.

meaning: a loved one; someone dear to you.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a noun phrase: "un ser querido" / "mis seres queridos". It literally means “a dear/liked being,” but in real use it refers to a person you love (family member, partner, close friend). Often heard in emotional contexts (health, loss, caring for someone).
target_language_example: Quiero pasar más tiempo con mis seres queridos.
native_language_example: I want to spend more time with my loved ones.

meaning: to be all ears; to listen attentively.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re ready to listen carefully to what someone is going to say. It’s most common as "Soy todo oídos" (masculine speaker) or "Soy toda oídos" (feminine speaker). You can also say "Estamos todo oídos" / "Estamos toda oídos". Note that "oídos" stays plural even though you say "todo/toda".
target_language_example: Cuéntame, soy todo oídos.
native_language_example: Tell me—I'm all ears.

meaning: to be all ears (to listen very attentively).
additional_notes: Used when you’re ready to listen closely and with full attention, often as a response to someone who is about to explain something: “Cuéntame, soy todo oídos.” It’s a fixed expression with the verb ser (soy/eres/es/somos/son todo oídos).
target_language_example: Cuéntame qué pasó; soy todo oídos.
native_language_example: Tell me what happened; I’m all ears.

meaning: a living being; (informal) a clever/sly person.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a noun: “un ser vivo” (a living thing/being), especially in science or nature contexts (plants, animals, humans). In some contexts it can also describe someone who’s “too clever” or a bit sneaky (street-smart). Plural: “seres vivos”.
target_language_example: Todos los seres vivos necesitan agua.
native_language_example: All living beings need water.

additional_notes: A cardinal number used for counting, ages, prices, dates, etc. Often used with a noun: "setenta y cinco euros" (75 euros). In Spanish, numbers from 31–99 are commonly written with "y" between tens and ones: "setenta y cinco".
target_language_example: Tengo setenta y cinco años.
native_language_example: I am seventy-five years old.

additional_notes: A direct, explicit term for a sexual activity. It’s understood by most Spanish speakers but can sound blunt; in medical/educational contexts it’s neutral, while in casual conversation you may want to use more tact depending on the setting.
target_language_example: Hablaron sobre sexo anal en una clase de educación sexual.
native_language_example: They talked about anal sex in a sex education class.

additional_notes: A direct, explicit term used in sexual/medical contexts. In everyday conversation it can sound blunt, so use with care depending on the situation. You’ll also see it in health information or consent-related discussions.
target_language_example: En la clase de educación sexual hablaron del sexo oral y de cómo practicarlo de forma segura.
native_language_example: In sex education class they talked about oral sex and how to practice it safely.

meaning: “if so/if that’s the case”; also “if anything / or something (like that)” in casual speech.
additional_notes: Used in conversation to refer back to what was just said (“if that’s true”) or to soften a suggestion/estimate, similar to “if anything” or “or something.” Often appears at the end of a sentence: “...si eso.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las ocho, si eso.
native_language_example: See you at eight, or something (like that).

meaning: “if there are any” / “if ever there were any” (used for emphasis).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to emphasize it as a strong or classic example: “a true X, if ever there was one.” It often follows expressions like “uno de los mejores” (“one of the best”) or “el mejor …, si los hay” (“the best …, if there are any”). The pronoun “los” refers back to the plural noun already mentioned.
target_language_example: Es uno de los mejores restaurantes de la ciudad, si los hay.
native_language_example: It’s one of the best restaurants in the city, if ever there were any.

additional_notes: Written as two words, it’s usually the opposite/alternative in a conditional: "si no" = "if not" or "otherwise". Often appears after a clause starting with "si" (if): "Si no + verb...". Don’t confuse with "sino" (one word), which means "but rather/except" after a negative: "No quiero té, sino café."
target_language_example: Si no estudias, no vas a aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: If you don’t study, you’re not going to pass the exam.

meaning: “Yeah, I know / OK, already.” (often written “sí, ya”).
