additional_notes: In conversation, people often say “sí, ya” to show they understand, agree, or want to end the topic: “OK, I get it.” It’s very common with object pronouns: “Sí, ya lo sé” (Yeah, I know). Note: without the accent ("si"), it can also literally mean “if … already” in other sentences, but as a standalone reply it’s usually “sí, ya.”
target_language_example: —Te lo dije ayer. —Sí, ya, perdón.
native_language_example: —I told you yesterday. —Yeah, I know, sorry.

additional_notes: Used to complain (or joke) that something keeps repeating and never changes. Often said about routines, repeated problems, or someone’s behavior. You can also use it as a short comment: “¡Siempre lo mismo!” = “Same old thing!”
target_language_example: Cada lunes hay una reunión a primera hora: siempre lo mismo.
native_language_example: Every Monday there’s a meeting first thing: same old thing.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition: "Siempre que + present subjunctive" (common in Spain and Latin America), meaning "as long as / provided that." Example: "Te ayudo siempre que me lo pidas". It can also mean "whenever" with the indicative when talking about repeated situations: "Siempre que voy, está cerrado". Distinct from "siempre" (always) + "que" in other contexts, but in this phrase it works like a conjunction meaning "as long as/provided that".
target_language_example: Puedes usar mi coche siempre que lo devuelvas hoy.
native_language_example: You can use my car as long as you return it today.

additional_notes: Used to state a condition that must be met. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive when referring to a possible or future condition: “Siempre y cuando + subjunctive…”. Similar to “con tal de que.”
target_language_example: Puedes salir siempre y cuando termines tu tarea.
native_language_example: You can go out as long as you finish your homework.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 7,000 (people, years, euros, etc.). In Spanish, thousands are written with a period or a space (7.000 or 7 000), and the comma is used for decimals (7,5 = 7.5).
target_language_example: El coche cuesta siete mil euros.
native_language_example: The car costs seven thousand euros.

additional_notes: A set of seven major sins in Christian tradition (often listed as pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath, and sloth). Used in religious, cultural, and everyday contexts (e.g., books, movies, moral discussions). Usually appears with the definite article: “los siete pecados capitales”.
target_language_example: En la clase hablamos de los siete pecados capitales.
native_language_example: In class we talked about the seven deadly sins.

additional_notes: Medical term for basic body measurements used to check a person’s condition (e.g., pulse, blood pressure, temperature, breathing rate). Common in hospitals/clinics and emergencies; often used with verbs like tomar/medir/revisar (to take/measure/check).
target_language_example: La enfermera va a tomar tus signos vitales.
native_language_example: The nurse is going to take your vital signs.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase: *silla* (chair) + *de* (of/for) + *ruedas* (wheels). Used for a chair that moves on wheels for someone who has difficulty walking. Often appears with the verb *estar/ir en* (to be/go in): *Está en silla de ruedas.*
target_language_example: Mi abuelo usa silla de ruedas.
native_language_example: My grandfather uses a wheelchair.

additional_notes: Used when ordering food or drinks or describing products. Often paired with items like café, té, jugo, or yogurt (e.g., “café sin azúcar”). You can also hear “sin azúcar añadido” (“no added sugar”) on labels.
target_language_example: Quiero un café sin azúcar, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a coffee with no sugar, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe an action that continues continuously/constantly. Common with verbs like hablar (to talk), llover (to rain), trabajar (to work), or sonar (to ring). Similar to “sin parar” and “sin descanso.”
target_language_example: Ha estado lloviendo sin cesar toda la semana.
native_language_example: It’s been raining nonstop all week.

additional_notes: Common phrase to express strong certainty. It often comes at the beginning of a sentence as a comment on what follows ("Sin duda, ..."), but it can also appear later ("... sin duda").
target_language_example: Sin duda, es la mejor opción.
native_language_example: Without a doubt, it’s the best option.

additional_notes: An emphatic way to say you’re certain about something. It’s slightly stronger than just “sin duda.” Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Often placed at the start of a sentence, but it can also appear mid-sentence.
target_language_example: Sin duda alguna, fue la mejor decisión.
native_language_example: Without a doubt, it was the best decision.

additional_notes: Common in check-ins, reports, or when someone asks how things are going. It often implies that there are no problems or changes (similar to “all quiet” or “nothing to report”). You may hear it in work, travel, or even police/military-style contexts.
target_language_example: —¿Cómo va todo? —Sin novedad, todo en orden.
native_language_example: —How’s everything going? —No news, everything’s fine.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know what to say because you’re surprised, shocked, very impressed, or emotional. Often used as a short reaction on its own ("¡Sin palabras!") or with "me quedo" ("Me quedo sin palabras" = "I’m left speechless").
target_language_example: Cuando vi el regalo, me quedé sin palabras.
native_language_example: When I saw the gift, I was left speechless.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something immediately, without stopping to reflect. Often follows a verb: “lo dije sin pensar” (I said it without thinking). Can also describe acting impulsively: “actuar sin pensar.”
target_language_example: Lo dije sin pensar y después me arrepentí.
native_language_example: I said it without thinking, and then I regretted it.

additional_notes: Common, informal-friendly phrase meaning something is not an issue. Often used as a response to a request (like “Sure” / “No problem”) or to reassure someone (“Don’t worry”). Also heard as "sin problemas" (plural) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: —¿Me puedes ayudar un momento? —Sí, sin problema.
native_language_example: —Can you help me for a moment? —Yes, no problem.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened without meaning to. Often goes with verbs like "hacer" (to do), "decir" (to say), "romper" (to break), or "golpear" (to hit): "Lo hice sin querer" = "I did it by accident." Similar to "sin querer queriendo" (jokingly: 'accidentally on purpose'), but "sin querer" itself is neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Perdón, te golpeé sin querer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I hit you by accident.

meaning: homeless; without a place to live.
additional_notes: Literally “without a roof.” Commonly used in news and formal contexts (e.g., "personas sin techo"). You may also hear "sin hogar" (without a home). It can sound impersonal, so in some contexts "persona sin hogar" is preferred.
target_language_example: Hay un programa para ayudar a las personas sin techo.
native_language_example: There’s a program to help homeless people.

additional_notes: A common medical/biology term for the body system made up of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Often used with verbs like afectar (to affect) or dañar (to damage): “afecta el sistema nervioso.”
target_language_example: Esta enfermedad afecta el sistema nervioso.
native_language_example: This illness affects the nervous system.

additional_notes: Used for computer and phone software like Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, or iOS. Often appears with the verb "tener" (to have) or "usar" (to use): "Mi computadora tiene..." / "Uso...". Plural: "sistemas operativos".
target_language_example: ¿Qué sistema operativo usas en tu computadora?
native_language_example: What operating system do you use on your computer?

additional_notes: Very common term for a website. Also heard as "página web" (web page/website). Usually used with "un/una": "un sitio web".
target_language_example: Nuestro sitio web tiene toda la información.
native_language_example: Our website has all the information.

meaning: "under the pretext of" / "on the grounds of".
additional_notes: Very formal and often legal or administrative. It means someone uses an excuse or stated reason to justify an action, sometimes suggesting the real motive is different. It’s often followed by a noun or an infinitive clause: “so color de la ley” (under the color of the law), “so color de ayudar” (under the pretext of helping).
target_language_example: Entró en la casa so color de ayudar con la mudanza, pero en realidad quería espiar.
native_language_example: He went into the house under the pretext of helping with the move, but in reality he wanted to spy.

additional_notes: Common idiom used after verbs like ir/salir/marchar to say something is going very well or without problems: “Todo va sobre ruedas.” Literally “on wheels,” but it usually means “smoothly” rather than talking about actual wheels. You can also use it to mean “accessible for wheelchairs” in contexts like “acceso/entrada sobre ruedas,” but the idiomatic “going well” meaning is most common.
target_language_example: La reunión salió sobre ruedas.
native_language_example: The meeting went smoothly.

additional_notes: Used to highlight the most important point or the main thing in a group. Often placed before what you want to emphasize ("sobre todo + noun/phrase") or after a clause (", sobre todo,"). Note: as one word ("sobretodo") it means "overcoat," but "sobre todo" (two words) is the common phrase meaning "especially."
target_language_example: Me gusta la comida mexicana, sobre todo los tacos.
native_language_example: I like Mexican food, especially tacos.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning a group/organization whose members and activities are kept hidden. Often used in stories, history, conspiracies, or mystery contexts. You can also say "una sociedad secreta" (a secret society) or plural "sociedades secretas" (secret societies).
target_language_example: Dicen que existe una sociedad secreta en esa ciudad.
native_language_example: They say there is a secret society in that city.

meaning: to usually do (something); to tend to.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about habitual actions: "soler + infinitive" (e.g., "suelo ir"). It’s common in the present (suelo, sueles, suele, solemos, soléis, suelen) and imperfect (solía, solías, etc.); it’s rarely used in other tenses.
target_language_example: Suelo levantarme temprano.
native_language_example: I usually get up early.

meaning: to usually do; to tend to do.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "soler" + an infinitive to talk about habitual actions (similar to "usually" or "tend to" in English). "Soler" is irregular: suelo, sueles, suele, solemos, soléis, suelen. It’s mostly used in the present or imperfect (solía) and not commonly used in the future or in compound tenses. Example: "Suelo hacer" = "I usually do / I tend to do."
target_language_example: Suelo hacer ejercicio por la mañana.
native_language_example: I usually exercise in the morning.

meaning: to usually live; to tend to live (somewhere/in some way).
additional_notes: Uses the verb **soler** + infinitive to talk about a usual habit or typical situation: **Suelo vivir…** = “I usually live…”. **Soler** is commonly used in the **present** (*suelo, sueles, suele…*) and **imperfect** (*solía, solías, solía…*). It’s followed by an infinitive (here, **vivir**), not a gerund.
target_language_example: Suelo vivir cerca del trabajo.
native_language_example: I usually live near work.

additional_notes: Used to minimize what you’re doing/saying or to introduce a short comment. Very common in polite phrases like “Solo quería decir…” (I just wanted to say…). Note that “solo” can also be written “sólo” in older spelling; both are understood.
target_language_example: Solo quería decirte gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: I just wanted to say thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to compare how something seems or sounds, often giving an impression or guess. Conjugate the verb sonar: "Suena como..." (It sounds like...), "Sonó como..." (It sounded like...). Can be literal (a noise) or figurative (an idea/plan).
target_language_example: Eso suena como una buena idea.
native_language_example: That sounds like a good idea.

meaning: to blow out the candle (usually on a birthday cake).
additional_notes: Used especially in birthday contexts when someone blows out the candle(s) after making a wish. In real life you’ll often hear the plural: “soplar las velas” (to blow out the candles). You can also say “apagar la vela/las velas” (to put out the candle(s)).
target_language_example: Pide un deseo y sopla las velas.
native_language_example: Make a wish and blow out the candles.

additional_notes: Used to say your nationality or where you’re from. Use "soy inglés" if you’re a man. "Soy" is the "I am" form of "ser" (to be), and "inglesa" agrees with the speaker’s gender.
target_language_example: Hola, soy inglesa, pero vivo en Madrid.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m English, but I live in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to state your nationality or origin. Use it when the speaker is male; a woman would say "soy inglesa". Often appears with more context, e.g., "Soy inglés, pero vivo en España" (I’m English, but I live in Spain).
target_language_example: Hola, soy inglés y vivo en Londres.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m English and I live in London.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ser" ("soy" = "I am") to state identity/religion. "Musulmán" changes with gender: a woman would say "soy musulmana". You can also use the plural: "somos musulmanes/musulmanas" (we are Muslim).
target_language_example: Hola, soy musulmán.
native_language_example: Hi, I am Muslim.

meaning: to dream about; to long for.
additional_notes: Most commonly means “to dream about” something (often in sleep): *Soñé con mi perro.* It can also mean “to dream of / long for” in the sense of wanting something strongly: *Sueño con viajar por el mundo.* In the past, the preposition usually changes to **con**: **soñé con**, **soñaba con**. Don’t confuse **soñar con** (to dream about) with **soñar que** (to dream that + a clause).
target_language_example: Anoche soñé con mi abuela.
native_language_example: Last night I dreamed about my grandmother.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about imagining things or letting your mind wander while you’re awake. It can be used neutrally or as a mild criticism (not paying attention). You can conjugate the verb: "Sueño despierto" (I daydream), "Estaba soñando despierto" (I was daydreaming).
target_language_example: Perdón, estaba soñando despierto y no escuché la pregunta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was daydreaming and I didn’t hear the question.

meaning: “Your Honor” (a formal way to address a judge).
additional_notes: Used mainly in legal/court settings when speaking to or referring to a judge. It’s very formal and typically capitalized in writing (Su Señoría). Often used with verbs in the third person: “Su Señoría tiene razón.”
target_language_example: Con la venia, Su Señoría, quisiera hacer una pregunta al testigo.
native_language_example: With the court’s permission, Your Honor, I would like to ask the witness a question.

additional_notes: Common noun for the playground toy that goes up and down. Literally “up and down,” and it’s often used with the verb jugar (to play) or montar (to ride).
target_language_example: Los niños juegan en el sube y baja del parque.
native_language_example: The kids play on the seesaw at the park.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption or a premise before giving a conclusion. Often followed by a clause in the indicative when it means “since/given that” (treating it as a fact): “Supuesto que ya llegaste…”. It can also be used like “assuming (that)” to set a condition or hypothesis. Similar in meaning to “ya que,” “dado que,” or “puesto que,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Supuesto que ya terminaste, podemos irnos.
native_language_example: Given that you’ve already finished, we can leave.

additional_notes: Reflexive emphasis meaning “(one)self,” used after a subject pronoun or noun to stress that the person did it personally. It agrees in gender/number: sí mismo (he/himself), sí misma (she/herself), sí mismos / sí mismas (they/themselves). Often appears after prepositions: para sí mismo (for himself), por sí mismo (by himself), en sí mismo (in itself). Don’t confuse with “si” (if) without an accent.
target_language_example: Lo hizo por sí mismo.
native_language_example: He did it by himself.

additional_notes: Used to address a man respectfully (or someone you’re treating formally). Often a warm, emphatic way to agree or confirm. For a woman, say “sí, señora”; for a more neutral/polite option, you can also say “sí, señor(a)”.
target_language_example: —¿Entendiste las instrucciones? —Sí, señor.
native_language_example: —Did you understand the instructions? —Yes, sir.

additional_notes: Used to compare or describe something in the same way as something else. Often followed by a clause (tal como dijiste) or a noun phrase (tal como estaba). Similar to "igual que" and "así como" in many contexts. Can also introduce an example meaning “such as,” especially in more formal writing.
target_language_example: Hazlo tal como te lo expliqué.
native_language_example: Do it just as I explained it to you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unchanged or should be kept/accepted exactly the same. Often follows a noun or pronoun: "as is" (e.g., selling something without repairs) or confirms that something is exactly correct: "Exactly."
target_language_example: Lo quiero tal cual, sin cambiar nada.
native_language_example: I want it just as it is, without changing anything.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the same way, in the same condition, or follows the same instructions as something else. Often appears before a clause: “tal y como dijiste…” (just as you said…). Similar to “igual que” or “como”.
target_language_example: Hazlo tal y como te lo expliqué.
native_language_example: Do it just as I explained it to you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize distance (physical or figurative). Often followed by "de" + noun/pronoun: "tan cerca de la estación" (so close to the station), "tan cerca de mí" (so close to me). You can also use it without "de" when the context is clear: "Está tan cerca" (It’s so close).
target_language_example: Estamos tan cerca de la estación que podemos ir caminando.
native_language_example: We’re so close to the station that we can walk there.

meaning: 'as soon' / 'as soon as' (as early/quickly as possible).
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase "tan pronto como" = "as soon as" followed by a verb: "Tan pronto como llegues..." It can also be used without "como" to mean "as soon as possible": "Llámame tan pronto puedas."
target_language_example: Tan pronto como termine, te llamo.
native_language_example: As soon as I finish, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening immediately after another event. It’s often followed by a verb (usually in the present tense when referring to the future): "Te llamo tan pronto como llegue" (I’ll call you as soon as I arrive). Also common with "posible" to mean “as soon as possible”: "tan pronto como sea posible."
target_language_example: Llámame tan pronto como puedas.
native_language_example: Call me as soon as you can.

additional_notes: Used to ask for something quickly or to say you will do something without delay. Often shortened in speech to "tan pronto como puedas/pueda" (as soon as you can) depending on who you’re speaking to. "Sea" is the present subjunctive of "ser" and is used here in a fixed expression meaning “as ... as possible.”
target_language_example: Envíame los documentos tan pronto como sea posible, por favor.
native_language_example: Send me the documents as soon as possible, please.

additional_notes: Used to express cause-and-result: something happens to such a degree that it leads to a consequence. Common with the imperfect: "Era/estaba tan + adjective + que..." or "Hacía tanto + noun + que...". Often you’ll see the shorter form "tan ... que" (e.g., "tan cansado que..."); "tanto que" is used especially after verbs/adverbs or with quantities.
target_language_example: Me reí tanto que me dolía el estómago.
native_language_example: I laughed so much that my stomach hurt.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen at some point in the future, even if you don’t know when. It’s common in advice, warnings, or predictions. Literally “late or early,” but the natural English meaning is “sooner or later.”
target_language_example: Tarde o temprano vas a tener que hablar con ella.
native_language_example: Sooner or later you’re going to have to talk to her.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a card you use to pay and borrow money from a bank or company. Common in shops, restaurants, hotels, and online payments. You may also hear the plural: "tarjetas de crédito".
target_language_example: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta de crédito?
native_language_example: Can I pay with a credit card?

additional_notes: Used for a card you send by mail, usually with a photo or picture on one side and space for a message and address on the other. Also commonly said as "postal" on its own in some contexts. The plural is "tarjetas postales".
target_language_example: Te envío una tarjeta postal desde Barcelona.
native_language_example: I’m sending you a postcard from Barcelona.

additional_notes: A common dessert; in Spain, "tarta" often refers to a cake or tart, while in many Latin American countries "pastel" is more common for cake. You may also hear "pay de manzana" in Mexico/US Spanish for "apple pie."
target_language_example: De postre, quiero una porción de tarta de manzana.
native_language_example: For dessert, I want a slice of apple pie.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "amar" and usually expresses deep/romantic love. Common with partners or in very emotional contexts. For many everyday situations (friends/family), Spanish speakers often use "te quiero" instead, which can feel softer.
target_language_example: Te amo con todo mi corazón.
native_language_example: I love you with all my heart.

additional_notes: Common way to say you miss someone. Literally it’s like “I throw you less,” but it just means “I miss you.” You can change the person: “Te echo de menos” (I miss you), “Lo/La echo de menos” (I miss him/her/it), “Los/Las echo de menos” (I miss them). You can also intensify it: “Te echo mucho de menos” (I miss you a lot).
target_language_example: Te echo de menos desde que te fuiste.
native_language_example: I miss you since you left.

meaning: "I love you" / "I care about you" (to someone you’re close to).
additional_notes: Literally "I want you," but in everyday Spanish it usually means affectionate love (often less intense than "te amo"). Common with partners, family, and close friends. Use "te quiero mucho" for "I love you a lot."
target_language_example: Te quiero mucho, mamá.
native_language_example: I love you a lot, Mom.

additional_notes: Common goodbye among friends and family. Literally means “I see you,” but it’s usually used to mean you’ll see the person later. You can add a time: “Te veo mañana” (See you tomorrow).
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. ¡Te veo mañana!
native_language_example: Okay, I’m leaving. See you tomorrow!

meaning: "fabric/cloth made of" (used to name the material).
additional_notes: Used before a material to describe what something is made of or what kind of fabric it is: "tela de algodón" (cotton fabric), "tela de lino" (linen fabric). You’ll often see it in shopping, clothing, or sewing contexts. On its own, "tela de" usually needs a word after it.
target_language_example: Busco tela de algodón para hacer una camiseta.
native_language_example: I’m looking for cotton fabric to make a T-shirt.

additional_notes: Common in Latin America. In Spain, people often say "móvil" (or "teléfono móvil"). You can also just say "celular" in many contexts. Not the same as "teléfono fijo" (landline).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes tu teléfono celular a mano?
native_language_example: Do you have your cell phone handy?

additional_notes: Common term in Spain for a mobile phone. Often shortened to "móvil" when the context is clear. In many Latin American countries, "celular" is more common.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes tu teléfono móvil contigo?
native_language_example: Do you have your cell phone with you?

additional_notes: Refers to a phone available for public use (often on the street or in stations), typically requiring coins or a card. The plural is “teléfonos públicos.”
target_language_example: No tengo batería; voy a llamar desde un teléfono público.
native_language_example: I don’t have battery; I’m going to call from a payphone.

additional_notes: Used to say you have an object available nearby and ready to use. Common with items like a phone, keys, a pen, documents, etc. It can also mean having something “at hand” in a more general sense (easy to access), not necessarily physically in your hand.
target_language_example: Ten el teléfono a mano por si te llamo.
native_language_example: Keep your phone handy in case I call you.

meaning: to look down on; to disdain; to think less of.
additional_notes: Means treating someone or something as inferior or not worthy of respect (similar to “despise” or “belittle”). It’s somewhat formal/literary; in everyday Spanish you may also hear/see the very common variant “tener en menos.” It’s used with a direct object (person/thing): “No me tengas a menos” = “Don’t look down on me.”
target_language_example: No tengas a menos a tus compañeros; todos pueden aportar algo.
native_language_example: Don’t look down on your classmates; everyone can contribute something.

meaning: to have something to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Used to say that one thing is connected or relevant to another. Often appears in questions and negatives: “¿Qué tiene que ver eso con…?” (What does that have to do with…?) and “No tiene nada que ver con…” (It has nothing to do with…). You can change “algo” to “mucho/poco/nada” depending on how strong the connection is.
target_language_example: Esto tiene algo que ver con tu trabajo.
native_language_example: This has something to do with your job.

additional_notes: Spanish uses "tener" (to have) to talk about age. It’s usually used with a number: "Tengo 20 años" (I’m 20). In questions: "¿Cuántos años tienes?" (How old are you?). Often "años" can be omitted when it’s obvious: "Tengo 20".
target_language_example: ¿Cuántos años tienes? Tengo 25 años.
native_language_example: How old are you? I’m 25 (years old).

meaning: to have enough; to have had enough.
additional_notes: Uses the verb tener + bastante (“enough/quite a lot”). Often followed by de + noun (tener bastante de algo = to have enough of something) or used alone to mean you’ve had enough (¡Ya tengo bastante! = That’s enough!/I’ve had enough!). In many contexts English uses “enough” rather than a literal “have.”
target_language_example: Ya tengo bastante de tus excusas.
native_language_example: I’ve had enough of your excuses.

meaning: to have a good heart; to be kind-hearted.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character as kind, caring, and well-intentioned. You can say it in any tense (e.g., "tiene," "tenía"). A common variant is "tener un buen corazón" (with "un").
target_language_example: Aunque es muy serio, tiene buen corazón y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: Even though he’s very serious, he has a good heart and always helps others.

meaning: to have a good eye (good judgment; be good at noticing/choosing things).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is good at spotting details, judging quality, or making good choices (often about art, clothes, people, opportunities, etc.). It’s commonly followed by “para” + noun/verb: “tener buen ojo para la moda / para elegir.” Literal translation is possible, but in English it often corresponds to “have a good eye” or “have good instincts.”
target_language_example: Tienes buen ojo para elegir ropa; esa chaqueta te queda genial.
native_language_example: You have a good eye for choosing clothes; that jacket looks great on you.

meaning: to have brains; to use common sense.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is smart or should think before acting. Often appears in negative or in commands (e.g., "no tiene cerebro", "¡ten cerebro!"). It’s a bit blunt/colloquial, so be careful using it directly about a person.
target_language_example: ¡Ten cerebro y mira antes de cruzar la calle!
native_language_example: Use your brain and look before crossing the street!

meaning: to be clear about (something); to be sure/understand clearly.
additional_notes: Used to say you clearly understand something or have made a firm decision. Often followed by a noun or a clause: “tener claro el plan” (be clear about the plan), “tener claro que…” (be clear that…). Similar to “tener muy claro” = “to be very clear about.”
target_language_example: Tengo claro que no quiero cambiar de trabajo ahora.
native_language_example: I’m sure that I don’t want to change jobs right now.

meaning: to have class; to be classy/elegant.
additional_notes: Often used in two ways: (1) literally, to mean you have a class/lesson scheduled ("Tengo clase a las 9"). (2) figuratively, to describe someone as classy or having good taste ("Ella tiene mucha clase"). The figurative meaning is common and is about style and manners, not social class.
target_language_example: No puedo ir; tengo clase esta tarde.
native_language_example: I can't go; I have class this afternoon.

meaning: to have company; to not be alone (to be with someone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is accompanied (at home, on a trip, etc.) or that you’d like someone to be with you. Often appears as "¿Tienes compañía?" (Are you with someone?) or "No quiero estar sola; quiero tener compañía" (I don’t want to be alone; I want company).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir? Me gustaría tener compañía esta noche.
native_language_example: Do you want to come? I’d like to have company tonight.

additional_notes: Common warning or reminder. Often used with "con" + noun ("Ten cuidado con el coche" = Be careful with the car) or "al" + infinitive for actions ("Ten cuidado al cruzar" = Be careful when crossing). In the tú imperative, it’s "ten cuidado"; you may also hear "¡Cuidado!" as a shorter warning.
target_language_example: Ten cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: to be in pain; to have pain.
additional_notes: Used to talk about feeling pain in general or in a specific body part. Often used with a body part: “tener dolor de cabeza” (to have a headache) or “tener dolor en la espalda” (to have pain in your back). In everyday Spanish, “me duele…” is also very common for specific pain (“Me duele la cabeza.”).
target_language_example: Tengo dolor en la rodilla.
native_language_example: I have pain in my knee.

meaning: to take into account; to keep in mind.
additional_notes: Used to say you will consider something when making a decision or planning. Often followed by a noun or by “que” + clause: “Ten en cuenta el precio” / “Ten en cuenta que mañana es festivo.” In informal speech you may also hear “tenlo en cuenta” (“keep it in mind”).
target_language_example: Ten en cuenta que el museo cierra a las cinco.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that the museum closes at five.

meaning: to keep in mind; to have in mind.
additional_notes: Used to say you are considering or remembering something while making a decision or talking. Common with a direct object or a clause: “Ten esto en mente” (Keep this in mind), “Ten en mente que…” (Keep in mind that…).
target_language_example: Ten en mente que mañana es feriado.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that tomorrow is a holiday.

additional_notes: Used to describe how you feel (temperature), not the weather. Spanish commonly uses “tener” (to have) for sensations: tener frío/calor/hambre/sed/sueño. For the weather, you usually say “Hace frío” (It’s cold).
target_language_example: Tengo frío. ¿Puedes cerrar la ventana?
native_language_example: I’m cold. Can you close the window?

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to want to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express desire or motivation. It’s usually followed by "de" + infinitive: "tener ganas de comer" (to feel like eating). In the negative, it means you don’t feel like doing something: "no tengo ganas". You can also use it with a noun: "tener ganas de chocolate" (to feel like chocolate).
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de salir esta noche.
native_language_example: I feel like going out tonight.

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to want to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express desire/motivation to do an action. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: "tener ganas de + infinitive" (e.g., "Tengo ganas de comer"). You can also use it with a noun when the desire is for a thing: "Tengo ganas de pizza" (I feel like pizza). Conjugate "tener" to match the subject (tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, etc.). Common negatives/questions: "No tengo ganas de..." (I don’t feel like...), "¿Tienes ganas de...?" (Do you feel like...?).
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de salir esta noche.
native_language_example: I feel like going out tonight.

meaning: to be lucky (Spain); to have nerve/guts (depending on context).
additional_notes: In Spain, **tener leche** is a common informal expression. Most often it means **to have (good/bad) luck**: *¡Qué leche!* / *Tiene mucha leche* (he/she has a lot of luck) or sometimes bad luck depending on tone/context. It can also be used to mean someone has **nerve/a lot of cheek** (often with a negative tone): *Tienes leche* = “You’ve got some nerve.” It’s not about literal milk in these idiomatic uses.
target_language_example: ¡Tienes leche! Justo hoy que no traje paraguas, se pone a llover.
native_language_example: You’ve got (bad) luck! The one day I didn’t bring an umbrella, it starts raining.

meaning: to take place; to happen (of events).
additional_notes: Used to talk about events (meetings, concerts, ceremonies, accidents, etc.) happening, often in a formal or written style. Commonly used with a place and/or time: "La reunión tendrá lugar mañana en la oficina." In everyday speech, "pasar" or "ocurrir" are also common for "to happen."
target_language_example: La conferencia tendrá lugar el viernes a las 10 en el auditorio.
native_language_example: The conference will take place on Friday at 10 in the auditorium.

additional_notes: Literally “to have fear,” but in Spanish the common way to express fear is with tener + noun (tener miedo). Often followed by de + noun/infinitive: tener miedo de las arañas (to be afraid of spiders), tener miedo de volar (to be afraid of flying). You can also add que + clause: Tengo miedo de que lleguemos tarde (I’m afraid we’ll be late).
target_language_example: Tengo miedo de hablar en público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Almost always used in the negative: “no tener nada en contra (de…)”. It means you don’t dislike someone or you don’t object to something. It’s commonly followed by “de” + person/thing/verb: “No tengo nada en contra de ti / de eso / de que vengas.”
target_language_example: No tengo nada en contra de tu idea, pero creo que es muy cara.
native_language_example: I have nothing against your idea, but I think it’s very expensive.

meaning: to be (noticeably) effeminate; to have “gay mannerisms”.
additional_notes: Informal and often stereotypical; it can sound mocking or offensive depending on tone and context. It’s most commonly said about men (often implying they are gay), but it can be used more broadly. Literally it means “to have a feather,” but the real meaning is idiomatic. A more neutral way to talk about this idea is “ser afeminado” (more formal) or simply describing specific behaviors without labels.
target_language_example: No me gusta cómo habla de Juan diciendo que “tiene pluma”.
native_language_example: I don’t like how he talks about Juan saying he’s “effeminate.”

additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or judgment about someone/something: “tener a alguien/algo por + adjective/noun.” It’s fairly formal and common in writing. Often similar to “considerar” or “tomar por.” Example patterns: “Lo tengo por amigo” (I consider him a friend), “La tienen por inteligente” (They regard her as intelligent).
target_language_example: Lo tengo por una persona honesta.
native_language_example: I consider him an honest person.

meaning: 'to keep in mind'; 'to bear in mind'.
additional_notes: Used to remind someone (or yourself) not to forget an important fact or condition. Common in advice, instructions, and planning. It’s slightly formal/neutral. Often followed by "que" + a clause: "Ten presente que..." or by a noun: "Ten presente la fecha". Conjugates like "tener": "ten presente" (tú), "tenga presente" (usted), "tened presente" (vosotros).
target_language_example: Ten presente que mañana es feriado, así que la oficina estará cerrada.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that tomorrow is a holiday, so the office will be closed.

meaning: to have (something) on; to be wearing.
additional_notes: Used mainly with clothing, accessories, or items you wear/carry (glasses, coat, shoes, perfume). It often describes a state (what someone is wearing) rather than the action of putting it on (which is usually "ponerse"). Common pattern: "tener + [clothing/item] + puesto/a/os/as" to agree with the item: "tener puesta la chaqueta", "tener puestos los zapatos". Can also refer to having something placed/installed: "tener puesto un anuncio/una alarma".
target_language_example: Hoy tengo puesta una chaqueta porque hace frío.
native_language_example: Today I’m wearing a jacket because it’s cold.

meaning: "to have to" / "must" (to need to do something).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. Conjugate **tener** and follow it with **que + infinitive**: *tengo que estudiar* (I have to study), *tienes que ir* (you have to go). In the negative: *no tengo que...* (I don’t have to...). Often sounds like an external requirement (rules, circumstances); **deber** can sound more like "should/ought to".
target_language_example: Tengo que trabajar mañana.
native_language_example: I have to work tomorrow.

meaning: to have to go; to need to leave.
additional_notes: Uses the structure "tener que + infinitive" to express obligation/necessity. Here the infinitive is "ir" (to go). Commonly used to politely end a conversation: "Tengo que ir." You can add a destination with "a": "Tengo que ir a casa" (I have to go home). Conjugate "tener" to match the subject: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que ir; es tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go; it’s late.

meaning: to have to leave; to need to go (away).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re obligated to leave. Conjugate both verbs: (yo) tengo que irme, (tú) tienes que irte, (él/ella) tiene que irse, etc. The pronoun changes with the subject (irme/irte/irse/nos/vos/irse). Often followed by a reason: “porque…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que irme ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to leave now.

meaning: to be right; to be correct.
additional_notes: Used to agree that someone’s opinion or statement is correct. It literally means “to have reason,” and is often used with pronouns: “tienes razón” (you’re right), “tengo razón” (I’m right). Common reply: “Sí, tienes razón.”
target_language_example: Tienes razón: ese restaurante está cerrado.
native_language_example: You’re right: that restaurant is closed.

meaning: to make sense; to be logical/meaningful.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is logical or understandable. Common in questions/negatives: “¿Tiene sentido…?” (Does it make sense…?), “No tiene sentido” (It doesn’t make sense). In past: “tenía sentido” (made sense).
target_language_example: No tiene sentido pagar tanto por eso.
native_language_example: It doesn’t make sense to pay so much for that.

additional_notes: Neutral-to-direct way to talk about sex; in everyday Spanish, many people more often say "tener relaciones (sexuales)" (a bit more formal/less blunt). Conjugates with "tener": "tuve sexo" (I had sex), "tiene sexo" (he/she has sex). Often used with "con" (with): "tener sexo con alguien".
target_language_example: No quiero tener sexo sin protección.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have sex without protection.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Common way to talk about luck in general or in a specific situation. Often used with "¡Qué suerte!" (What luck!) or "Tuve suerte" (I was lucky). You can also add "con" to specify what you were lucky with: "Tuve suerte con el examen" (I got lucky with the exam).
target_language_example: Tuviste suerte de encontrar entradas.
native_language_example: You were lucky to find tickets.

meaning: to be sleepy; to feel like sleeping.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "tener" (to have) with the noun "sueño" (sleepiness) to talk about feeling sleepy right now. Common in everyday speech. You can add intensity: "Tengo mucho sueño" (I’m very sleepy).
target_language_example: Tengo sueño, así que me voy a dormir temprano.
native_language_example: I’m sleepy, so I’m going to sleep early.

meaning: To be a big deal; to be intense/complicated (often: pretty tough or shocking).
additional_notes: Very common colloquial expression (especially in Spain). Used as “tiene tela” to comment that something is more serious, difficult, surprising, or extreme than expected (similar to “that’s something else,” “it’s no joke,” “it’s a lot”). Not literal: it doesn’t mean “to have fabric.”
target_language_example: El examen de mañana tiene tela.
native_language_example: Tomorrow’s exam is no joke (it’s pretty tough).

meaning: to have a job; to be employed.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has employment (a job). Very common in everyday conversation. You can also use it more generally to mean you have work/tasks to do: "Tengo mucho trabajo" = "I have a lot of work." For the opposite, say "no tener trabajo" (to not have a job / be unemployed).
target_language_example: Ahora tengo trabajo, así que no puedo salir esta noche.
native_language_example: Now I have a job, so I can’t go out tonight.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about achieving a good result in general (in life, at work, in a project). It’s often followed by “en” + area (“tener éxito en los negocios”) or “con” + thing (“tener éxito con el plan”). In Spanish you can also say “tener mucho éxito” (to be very successful) or “no tener éxito” (to not succeed).
target_language_example: Espero tener éxito en mi nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: I hope to be successful in my new job.

meaning: to have guts / to have balls (to be very brave or bold).
additional_notes: Very informal and somewhat vulgar: “los” usually refers to testicles. Used to praise someone’s courage or nerve, especially for saying/doing something risky or standing up to someone. You may also hear variations like “tenerlos bien puestos” or “tener bien puestos los…”. Use with caution, as it can sound crude.
target_language_example: Para decirle eso al jefe, tienes que tenerlos bien puestos.
native_language_example: To say that to the boss, you’ve got to have balls.

meaning: to have guts / to have balls (to be brave).
additional_notes: Very informal and somewhat vulgar: “los” usually refers to testicles. Used to praise courage or to challenge someone to prove they’re brave. Often appears as “Hay que tenerlos puestos (para…)” = “You have to have guts (to…).”
target_language_example: Hay que tenerlos puestos para decirle eso al jefe.
native_language_example: You have to have guts to say that to the boss.

additional_notes: In Spanish you usually say you “have” heat/cold: tengo calor (I’m hot) / tengo frío (I’m cold). Not used to mean “hot/sexy” (that would be “estoy bueno/a” in some countries, or “está muy atractivo/a”). You can intensify it: “tengo mucho calor” (I’m very hot).
target_language_example: Tengo calor. ¿Puedes abrir la ventana?
native_language_example: I’m hot. Can you open the window?

additional_notes: Literally “I have hunger,” but the natural English meaning is “I’m hungry.” Use it to talk about your current state. You can change the subject: “tienes hambre” (you’re hungry), “tiene hambre” (he/she/you formal is hungry), “tenemos hambre” (we’re hungry).
target_language_example: Tengo hambre. ¿Dónde podemos comer?
native_language_example: I’m hungry. Where can we eat?

additional_notes: Common, polite way to get someone’s attention before asking something (in class, at work, in a store, etc.). Often followed by a question: “Tengo una pregunta: ¿…?” You can also say “Tengo una duda” (“I have a doubt / I’m not sure”) when you’re confused about something.
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo una pregunta: ¿a qué hora empieza la clase?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: what time does the class start?

additional_notes: Literally “third degree.” In everyday Spanish, it often refers to being questioned very intensely (like being grilled), especially in casual speech: “hacerle a alguien el tercer grado” = to give someone the third degree. It can also be used more literally for “third grade” (school level) depending on the country/context.
target_language_example: Mi mamá me hizo el tercer grado cuando llegué tarde.
native_language_example: My mom gave me the third degree when I got home late.

meaning: “a long time ago” / “it’s been a while.”
additional_notes: An old-fashioned/literary way to say that something happened a long time ago. You’ll most often see it in writing (stories, news, formal narration), sometimes with a specific time amount: “dos años ha” = “two years ago.” In everyday conversation, speakers usually say “hace tiempo” or “hace mucho (tiempo)” instead.
target_language_example: Tiempo ha que no nos vemos.
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about time when you’re not working, studying, or busy with obligations. Common with verbs like tener (to have) and expressions like en mi tu tiempo libre (in my/your free time).
target_language_example: En mi tiempo libre, me gusta leer y salir a caminar.
native_language_example: In my free time, I like to read and go for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to describe a job, schedule, or contract with fewer hours than full-time. Common in job ads: "trabajo a tiempo parcial" (a part-time job) or "contrato a tiempo parcial" (a part-time contract).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un trabajo a tiempo parcial porque estudio por las mañanas.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a part-time job because I study in the mornings.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a man who seems strong, intimidating, or tries to act macho. It can be neutral or slightly critical/ironic depending on tone (like someone "acting tough"). Common in Spain; in Latin America you may also hear similar ideas expressed with other words (e.g., "tipo rudo").
target_language_example: No te preocupes, solo parece un tipo duro.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he just looks like a tough guy.

meaning: to give up; to throw in the towel.
additional_notes: Common idiom (from boxing): it means to stop trying because you think you can’t continue or succeed. Often used with "no" to encourage someone ("No tires la toalla") or in past tense ("tiré la toalla").
target_language_example: Después de varios intentos, tiré la toalla.
native_language_example: After several attempts, I gave up.

additional_notes: Very informal/vulgar everyday phrase. Literally “to throw oneself a fart,” but it just means “to fart.” You can also hear “tirarse un gas” (a bit softer) or simply “peerse” (more direct).
target_language_example: Perdón, me tiré un pedo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I farted.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "tocar" for playing musical instruments (not *jugar*). You can swap in other instruments: "tocar la guitarra", "tocar el piano". Conjugate "tocar" as needed ("toco", "tocas", "toca", etc.).
target_language_example: Mi hermana sabe tocar el violín.
native_language_example: My sister knows how to play the violin.

meaning: to annoy someone; to piss someone off (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar expression, common in Spain. It means someone is bothering you or being a nuisance. You can use it as "Me estás tocando las pelotas" (You’re really annoying me) or "No me toques las pelotas" (Don’t mess with me / Don’t annoy me). Avoid in polite situations; use a softer option like "molestar" or "fastidiar".
target_language_example: Deja de tocarme las pelotas y ponte a trabajar.
native_language_example: Stop annoying me and get to work.

additional_notes: Common in two main senses: (1) duration up to now: “all my/your life” (Toda mi vida he vivido aquí.) and (2) “always/ever since I can remember” as an emphasis (Es así de toda la vida.). It can also mean “forever” in romantic or dramatic contexts (Te amaré toda la vida.). Often used with possessives: toda mi/tu/su vida.
target_language_example: He querido ser médico toda la vida.
native_language_example: I’ve wanted to be a doctor my whole life.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that has been true for your entire life up to now. Often appears with the present perfect (he + participle) for life experiences ("He vivido aquí toda mi vida") or with the present tense for long-term situations ("Trabajo aquí toda mi vida"—common in some regions, though many learners will hear "He trabajado aquí toda mi vida").
target_language_example: He vivido en esta ciudad toda mi vida.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city my whole life.

additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t happened up to now, but may happen later. Common in short answers and with the present perfect or simple present. Similar to “aún no.”
target_language_example: Todavía no he terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: I haven’t finished the homework yet.

additional_notes: Common, casual response to “¿Cómo estás?” or “¿Qué tal?”; can also be used to reassure someone (“Está todo bien”). Often heard as “Todo bien, ¿y tú?”
target_language_example: —¿Cómo estás? —Todo bien, ¿y tú?
native_language_example: —How are you? —All good, and you?

additional_notes: Common in directions, especially in Latin America. It means to continue forward without turning (sometimes for a long distance: “keep going straight”). You may also hear “sigue todo derecho” or “vete todo derecho.”
target_language_example: Sigue todo derecho y la farmacia está a la izquierda.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and the pharmacy is on the left.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or lasts for the entire day (from morning to night). Don’t confuse it with **todos los días** (“every day”). It can also emphasize how long something took: *¡Me llamó todo el día!* (“He/She called me all day!”).
target_language_example: He estado estudiando todo el día.
native_language_example: I’ve been studying all day.

additional_notes: Literally “all the world,” but it’s most commonly used to mean “everyone/everybody.” It often takes a singular verb in Spanish (e.g., “Todo el mundo sabe…”). In some contexts it can also mean “the whole world” literally.
target_language_example: Todo el mundo sabe que mañana es feriado.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that tomorrow is a holiday.

additional_notes: Common in everyday Spanish to mean something happens repeatedly or continuously. Similar to "todo el tiempo". Often used to complain or emphasize frequency (e.g., someone talking, calling, or doing something nonstop).
target_language_example: Está todo el rato mirando el móvil.
native_language_example: He’s on his phone all the time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very often or continuously. It can also mean “the whole time” in a specific situation (e.g., during a trip). Similar to “siempre,” but “todo el tiempo” often emphasizes frequency/continuity. Word order usually stays the same; you can place it at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Estoy cansado todo el tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m tired all the time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the entire period up to now or up to a point being discussed. It often implies “for the whole time” or “the entire time” (sometimes with surprise or emphasis: “all this time, and I didn’t know”).
target_language_example: No sabía que vivías aquí todo este tiempo.
native_language_example: I didn’t know you lived here all this time.

additional_notes: Often used for grouping things (people, objects) in one place or doing something as a group. Very commonly used when talking about spelling or formatting: “todo junto” means the word(s) should be written as one unit (no spaces). Contrast with “todo separado” (“all separate”).
target_language_example: Escribe "por favor" todo junto: "porfavor".
native_language_example: Write “por favor” all together: “porfavor”.

additional_notes: Used to strongly contradict what was just said or assumed. Often follows a negative statement: "No estoy cansado, todo lo contrario" (“I’m not tired—quite the opposite”). You can also use it after "al": "al todo lo contrario" is not used; instead say "al contrario" or "todo lo contrario".
target_language_example: Pensé que ibas a enojarte, pero fue todo lo contrario.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to get angry, but it was quite the opposite.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all the other things/people not already mentioned. Common in lists or contrasts (e.g., “this and everything else”). It agrees in gender/number if needed: “toda la demás” is not used; instead you say “todo lo demás” (neutral) or “toda la demás gente” is incorrect—say “toda la gente demás” is also incorrect; better: “el resto de la gente”.
target_language_example: Yo me encargo de la comida y tú de todo lo demás.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of the food and you take care of everything else.

additional_notes: Used to mark an upper limit (a maximum), often with time, numbers, or quantities. It commonly appears after a pause/comma: "..., todo lo más." Similar to "como mucho" or "a lo sumo."
target_language_example: Tardamos una hora, todo lo más.
native_language_example: We’ll take an hour, at most.

additional_notes: Used to say you will do your best or that you’ll do whatever you can. Very common after verbs like hacer (to do/make), intentar (to try), or ayudar (to help): “Haceré todo lo posible.” It can also refer to taking every possible step to achieve something.
target_language_example: Haré todo lo posible para llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains what “everything” refers to: todo lo que + verb. It often means “all the things that…”. Because it uses neuter lo, it’s a set phrase for “everything that…”. For people, you usually use todos/todas los/las que (“everyone who…”), not todo lo que.
target_language_example: Haz todo lo que puedas.
native_language_example: Do everything you can.

additional_notes: Common (especially in Latin America) as a shorter, more casual version of “todo el mundo” (“everyone”). Literally “all (the) world,” but it’s used to mean “everyone.”
target_language_example: Todo mundo quiere ir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: Everyone wants to go to the party.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific group of people/things already mentioned. “Ellos” is masculine plural, and it’s also used for mixed-gender groups; for an all-female group you’d usually say “todas ellas.” You can also use it after a noun for emphasis: “Los conocí a todos ellos” = “I met all of them.”
target_language_example: Invité a varios amigos y todos ellos vinieron a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I invited several friends and all of them came to the party.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group that includes the speaker (“we”) and everyone in that group. It agrees in gender/number: mixed/masculine default is “todos nosotros”; feminine group is “todas nosotras”. Often used for emphasis compared to just “nosotros” (we).
target_language_example: Todos nosotros queremos aprender español.
native_language_example: All of us want to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to address a group with the formal pronoun “ustedes” (“you” plural). Common in Latin America, where “ustedes” is used for most plural “you” situations; in Spain, “ustedes” is mainly formal (otherwise “vosotros” is used). Often used for emphasis (e.g., “all of you”).
target_language_example: Quiero agradecerles a todos ustedes por venir hoy.
native_language_example: I want to thank all of you for coming today.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to mean the entire group without exception. It often appears with "de" + plural noun or pronoun: "todos y cada uno de los/las...", "todos y cada uno de ustedes". It agrees in gender/number when referring only to women: "todas y cada una".
target_language_example: Quiero agradecer a todos y cada uno de ustedes por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I want to thank each and every one of you for your help.

additional_notes: This is a proper name, not a Spanish phrase. In Spanish it’s usually kept as-is to refer to the constructed language called “Toki Pona.” It often appears in italics or with capitalization (Toki Pona), but many people also write it in lowercase (toki pona), following the language’s own style.
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo toki pona.
native_language_example: I’m learning Toki Pona.

meaning: to get some fresh air; to take a breath.
additional_notes: Used for stepping outside or pausing to breathe, often to relax, recover, or calm down. Common in phrases like "salir a tomar aire" (go out for some fresh air) and "necesito tomar aire" (I need to catch my breath / take a moment).
target_language_example: Voy a salir a tomar aire un momento.
native_language_example: I’m going to go out and get some fresh air for a moment.

meaning: to have/take something (often food, a drink, or medicine).
additional_notes: Very common with meals and drinks: "tomar un café" (have a coffee), "tomar agua" (drink water). It’s also used for medicine: "tomar una pastilla" (take a pill). Depending on the country and context, "tomar" can overlap with "beber" (to drink) and "comer" (to eat), but "tomar" is a general, natural choice in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Voy a tomar algo antes de la reunión.
native_language_example: I’m going to have something (to drink/eat) before the meeting.

meaning: to have a seat; to sit down (polite).
additional_notes: A polite way to invite someone to sit, common in restaurants, offices, waiting rooms, etc. Often used as an imperative: “Tome asiento” (formal usted) or “Toma asiento” (informal tú). Also heard as “Tomen asiento” (plural ustedes) and “Tomen asiento, por favor.”
target_language_example: Por favor, tome asiento y espere un momento.
native_language_example: Please have a seat and wait a moment.

meaning: to get some fresh air; to go outside for a bit.
additional_notes: Commonly used when you step outside briefly to breathe fresh air, take a short break, or go for a walk. Very natural with verbs like “salir” (to go out): “Voy a salir a tomar el aire.” It’s usually not about “taking” air literally, but about being outdoors for a moment.
target_language_example: Voy a salir a tomar el aire un momento.
native_language_example: I'm going to go out and get some fresh air for a moment.

meaning: to tease someone; to pull someone’s leg.
additional_notes: Common colloquial expression meaning to joke with someone or trick them in a playful way. Often used with an object pronoun: “Me estás tomando el pelo” (You’re pulling my leg). It can sound annoyed depending on tone/context, like “Are you kidding me?”
target_language_example: ¡No me tomes el pelo! Sé que eso no es verdad.
native_language_example: Don’t pull my leg! I know that isn’t true.

meaning: to take into account; to consider.
additional_notes: Used to say you will consider information, a factor, or someone’s opinion before deciding or acting. Very common in both formal and everyday Spanish. Often followed by what you’re considering: “tomar en cuenta + noun/phrase” (e.g., “Toma en cuenta el tiempo”). Similar expressions: “tener en cuenta” (also very common).
target_language_example: Toma en cuenta lo que te dije antes de decidir.
native_language_example: Take into account what I told you before deciding.

meaning: to speak; to take the floor.
additional_notes: Used in meetings, classes, or discussions when someone begins speaking (often after being invited) or asks for permission to speak. It can also mean to interrupt politely to add a point. Common with verbs like “dejar” or “dar”: “¿Me dejas tomar la palabra?” / “Le doy la palabra a Ana.”
target_language_example: Si no les importa, voy a tomar la palabra un momento.
native_language_example: If you don’t mind, I’m going to speak for a moment.

meaning: to take note; to write something down.
additional_notes: Common in class, meetings, and instructions. Often used with “de” for what you’re noting: “tomar nota de algo” (to take note of something). You can also say “Toma nota” as an imperative meaning “Take note / Write it down.”
target_language_example: Toma nota de la dirección, por favor.
native_language_example: Write down the address, please.

meaning: to take (someone) by surprise; to catch (someone) off guard.
additional_notes: Used when something unexpected happens and surprises someone. Often appears as "me/te/le/nos/les tomó por sorpresa" (it took me/you/him/her/us/them by surprise). You can also use it with a noun: "La noticia tomó por sorpresa a todos". Similar idea: "sorprender" (to surprise).
target_language_example: La noticia me tomó por sorpresa.
native_language_example: The news took me by surprise.

additional_notes: Used to say that something requires a certain amount of time: “Va a tomar tiempo.” Often appears as “tomar (mucho/poco) tiempo” or with an estimate: “tomar dos horas”. With an article, “tomar el tiempo (a alguien)” can also mean “to time someone” (measure how long they take).
target_language_example: Arreglar la computadora va a tomar tiempo.
native_language_example: Fixing the computer is going to take time.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase. Literally “to take a siesta,” but in Spanish you use tomar (or sometimes echarse) with siesta. Often used for a short rest in the afternoon.
target_language_example: Después de comer, voy a tomar una siesta.
native_language_example: After eating, I'm going to take a nap.

meaning: to take a vacation; to go on holiday.
additional_notes: Common way to talk about taking time off work or school to rest or travel. You’ll also hear: “ir de vacaciones” (to go on vacation). Use it with a time or place: “tomar vacaciones en julio / en México.”
target_language_example: Voy a tomar vacaciones en agosto.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a vacation in August.

meaning: curfew (a time when people must be off the streets / stay at home).
additional_notes: Used for official restrictions (often by the government or police), especially during emergencies, protests, or security situations. Commonly appears with the verb "imponer" (to impose): "imponer un toque de queda". It can be general (for everyone) or specific (for certain areas or times).
target_language_example: Debido a la emergencia, el gobierno impuso un toque de queda a partir de las diez de la noche.
native_language_example: Because of the emergency, the government imposed a curfew starting at 10 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s profession or role: trabajar como + noun (often without an article), e.g., “trabajo como profesor/a”. You can also use it for a temporary role: “trabajo como voluntario/a”. To say where you work, use “trabajar en” (trabajo en un hospital).
target_language_example: Trabajo como ingeniera en una empresa de software.
native_language_example: I work as an engineer at a software company.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about putting in a lot of effort at work, school, or a project. You can also hear "trabajar mucho" (to work a lot). It’s straightforward: trabajar = to work, duro = hard.
target_language_example: Estoy trabajando duro para aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: I'm working hard to pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people cooperate or collaborate on the same task or project. "Trabajar" is "to work" and "juntos" is "together" (masc./mixed plural; you may also hear "trabajar juntas" for a group of all women).
target_language_example: Tenemos que trabajar juntos para terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: We have to work together to finish the project on time.

additional_notes: Common term for swimwear. In Spain you may also hear "bañador" (especially for men) and "bikini" (two-piece). Often used with "ponerse" (to put on) or "llevar" (to wear).
target_language_example: No olvides tu traje de baño para ir a la piscina.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your swimsuit to go to the pool.

meaning: to deal with; to treat (someone) in a certain way.
additional_notes: Used with people, organizations, or situations. With a person/organization, it often means to interact or do business with them ("deal with"). With "bien/mal", it means to treat someone well/badly. In some contexts it can also mean to handle a problem ("deal with" a situation).
target_language_example: No me gusta tratar con gente grosera; prefiero tratar bien a todos.
native_language_example: I don’t like dealing with rude people; I prefer to treat everyone well.

meaning: 'to try to' (with an infinitive); also 'to be about' (a topic).
additional_notes:
Two very common patterns:
1) **tratar de + infinitive** = “to try to …” (often like “make an effort to”). Example: *Trato de estudiar*.
2) **(algo) trata de + noun/topic** = “(something) is about …” (used for movies, books, stories, conversations). Example: *La película trata de amor y amistad*.
Be careful: it usually does **not** mean “to treat (someone)” in the English sense.
target_language_example: Voy a tratar de llegar temprano.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to arrive early.

meaning: to be about; to be a matter of.
additional_notes: Used mostly as an impersonal expression: "Se trata de + noun/infinitive" to explain what something is or what the real issue is. Common in more neutral/formal explanations. Often appears in contrasts like "No se trata de..., sino de..." ("It’s not about..., but about...").
target_language_example: Se trata de un problema serio, no de una simple discusión.
native_language_example: It’s a serious problem, not just a simple argument.

additional_notes: Used to accept an offer or agree on a plan, like shaking hands on an agreement. Often said on its own as a quick confirmation. Related phrase: “¡Trato!” (Deal!).
target_language_example: —Te lo dejo en 20 euros. —Trato hecho.
native_language_example: —I’ll leave it at 20 euros. —Deal.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 35 for age, prices, dates, quantities, etc. In Spanish numbers 31–39 are formed as: treinta y + number (e.g., treinta y uno, treinta y dos, etc.).
target_language_example: Tengo treinta y cinco años.
native_language_example: I am thirty-five years old.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 31 when counting, giving a date, an age, a quantity, or a price. In everyday writing it’s often written as one word: “treinta y uno,” but before a masculine noun it shortens to “treinta y un” (e.g., “treinta y un días”).
target_language_example: El mes tiene treinta y un días.
native_language_example: The month has thirty-one days.

additional_notes: This is the shortened form of "treinta y uno" when it comes directly before a masculine singular noun: "treinta y un días". Use "treinta y uno" when the number stands alone: "Tengo treinta y uno". Before a feminine singular noun, use "treinta y una": "treinta y una personas". Note: it’s spelled "un" (no accent), not "ún".
target_language_example: Hay treinta y un días en enero.
native_language_example: There are thirty-one days in January.

additional_notes: Used for the number 3,000 when counting, giving prices, quantities, years, etc. Spanish writes thousands with a space or a period (3 000 / 3.000) and uses a comma for decimals (3.000,50). Before a noun, it stays the same: "tres mil personas" (not *tres miles*).
target_language_example: El coche cuesta tres mil euros.
native_language_example: The car costs three thousand euros.

additional_notes: Used for an illusion or stunt performed by a magician. You can also hear "un truco" (a trick) when the context is already clear. Related: "hacer un truco de magia" (to do/perform a magic trick).
target_language_example: El mago hizo un truco de magia increíble.
native_language_example: The magician did an incredible magic trick.

additional_notes: Literally the possessive phrase “your mother” (tú + madre). It’s normal and neutral in sentences like questions about someone’s family. However, said on its own (or in phrases like “¡Tu madre!”), it can be used as a rude comeback/insult in some contexts, so be careful with tone and situation.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo está tu madre?
native_language_example: How is your mother?

additional_notes: Very common informal spoken contraction of “está bien” (often written “’ta bien” or “ta bien”). Used to agree, accept a plan, or say something is fine/acceptable. In more formal situations, use “está bien”.
target_language_example: —¿Nos vemos a las ocho? —Tá bien.
native_language_example: “Shall we meet at eight?” “Okay.”

additional_notes: A common type of tea. In cafés or at home you might hear it when ordering or describing a drink. It can be served solo (plain) or con leche (with milk), and you can add azúcar (sugar) or limón (lemon).
target_language_example: Quiero un té negro con un poco de leche, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a black tea with a little milk, please.

additional_notes: A common drink name. Use it when ordering or talking about beverages. With drinks, Spanish often uses the article: "un té verde" (a green tea), "el té verde" (green tea/the green tea).
target_language_example: Quisiera un té verde, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a green tea, please.

meaning: “You’ve got to be kidding!” / “No way!” (very vulgar).
additional_notes: Very vulgar Spanish (especially common in Spain). Used as an exclamation to show disbelief, annoyance, or outrage—similar in force to “You’re kidding me” / “For f***’s sake.” Literally it means “touch your balls,” but it’s normally not meant literally. Often said as: “¡Tócate los cojones!”
target_language_example: ¡Tócate los cojones! Otra vez han cancelado el tren.
native_language_example: You’ve got to be kidding! They’ve cancelled the train again.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis or to say someone should do/experience something personally: "Hazlo tú mismo" (do it yourself), "Lo viste tú mismo" (you saw it yourself). It agrees in gender/number: "tú misma" (to a female), "vosotros mismos/mismas" (you all yourselves). Often placed after the pronoun or at the end of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Hazlo tú mismo.
native_language_example: Do it yourself.

additional_notes: Used to include the other person in something that was just said. It can be a friendly reply to a wish or greeting (e.g., “Gracias.” → “Tú también.”). Often written without the accent in casual texting (“tu también”), but the correct form is “tú” (with accent) when it means “you.”
target_language_example: ¡Que tengas un buen día! — Tú también.
native_language_example: Have a good day! — You too.

additional_notes: Common in phrases like "no + verb + un carajo" to emphasize that you don’t know/understand/have/care about anything: "No entiendo un carajo" = "I don’t understand a damn thing." It’s strong, rude language; avoid in polite or professional situations. It can also be used as an angry rejection: "¡Un carajo!" ≈ "Hell no!" / "No way!"
target_language_example: No entiendo un carajo de esta clase.
native_language_example: I don’t understand a damn thing in this class.

meaning: one of these days; sometime soon.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you expect or plan to do in the near future, without giving an exact date. It can be used for promises, plans, or warnings (often with a slightly vague tone): “Un día de estos voy a…”
target_language_example: Un día de estos vamos a cenar juntos.
native_language_example: One of these days we’ll have dinner together.

meaning: “a pleasure” (as in “nice to meet you” / “glad to”).
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used when meeting someone or after an introduction: “Mucho gusto” (“Nice to meet you”), “Un gusto (conocerte)” (“A pleasure (to meet you)”). You can also use it when you’re happy to do something: “Un gusto ayudarte” (“Glad to help”).
target_language_example: —Hola, soy Ana. —Un gusto, Ana.
native_language_example: —Hi, I’m Ana. —Nice to meet you, Ana.

meaning: an egg; (informal) a lot / a long time.
additional_notes: Literally means “an egg.” In many places it’s also informal slang meaning “a lot” (quantity) or “a long time,” often after verbs like tener (“to have”) or with time expressions: “Hace un huevo (que no…)” = “It’s been ages (since…).”
target_language_example: Hace un huevo que no te veo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you in ages.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to wait briefly (in person, on the phone, or in customer service). It can also mean “a moment” in general when talking about time (e.g., “for a moment”). Often said alone as a quick request: “Un momento.”
target_language_example: Un momento, por favor; ahora te ayudo.
native_language_example: Just a moment, please; I’ll help you now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small amount or degree. It can modify adjectives/adverbs ("Estoy un poco cansado" = "I’m a little tired"), or follow a verb to mean "for a little while" ("Espera un poco" = "Wait a bit"). With "de" it means "a little (of)": "un poco de agua" = "a little water". You may also hear the diminutive "un poquito" (same meaning, often softer).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar un poco más despacio?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate a small additional amount of something (food, time, volume, distance, etc.). Often follows what you want more of: “un poco más de + noun” (a little more of…). You can also use it alone as a polite request: “¿Un poco más, por favor?”
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un poco más de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more water, please?

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify an adjective or statement, similar to “a little” or “kind of.” Often appears before adjectives (e.g., “un tanto difícil”) or in the phrase “un tanto así” (“something like that”). It sounds fairly formal/literary compared to “un poco.”
target_language_example: Estoy un tanto cansado hoy.
native_language_example: I’m somewhat tired today.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group. It’s followed by a plural noun or by “las/unas” (e.g., “una de las chicas” = “one of the girls”). Use “uno de” with masculine nouns (“uno de los chicos”).
target_language_example: Ella es una de las mejores estudiantes de la clase.
native_language_example: She is one of the best students in the class.

meaning: “one of two”; used to say there are only two possibilities (“either…or…”).
additional_notes: Common when you’re reasoning out loud or giving someone a choice: “una de dos: o X, o Y.” It often introduces an ultimatum or a simple decision between two options. The verb is implied (“it’s one of two possibilities”).
target_language_example: Una de dos: o llegamos temprano o nos vamos sin cenar.
native_language_example: It’s one of two: either we arrive early or we leave without dinner.

additional_notes: A vulgar insult or blunt way to say something is awful, worthless, or that you strongly dislike it (about a thing, situation, plan, etc.). Also used in phrases like “¡Es una mierda!” (It sucks) and “No vale una mierda” (It’s worth nothing / It’s worthless). Not appropriate in polite situations.
target_language_example: Este trabajo es una mierda.
native_language_example: This job sucks.

additional_notes: Common in Spain. Used as an exclamation or comment about something very good: “¡Es una pasada!” = “It’s amazing!” It can also mean something is excessive or over the top: “El precio es una pasada” = “The price is ridiculous/way too high.” Literally it can mean “a pass” or “a time (something happened),” but in this slang sense it means “incredible.”
target_language_example: ¡Tu casa es una pasada, me encanta!
native_language_example: Your house is amazing—I love it!

additional_notes: Used to say how many times something happened: "una vez" = "once". It can also mean "one time" when telling a past experience ("Una vez, conocí a un actor..."). In "una vez que + verb", it means "once/after" ("Una vez que llegues, llámame" = "Once/After you arrive, call me").
target_language_example: Solo fui a Madrid una vez.
native_language_example: I only went to Madrid once.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening again or to repeat something (a request, action, explanation, etc.). Common in everyday speech. Often used at the start or end of a sentence: “Una vez más, gracias” (Once again, thank you).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes repetirlo una vez más, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat it one more time, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly, often with an implied feeling of annoyance, frustration, or emphasis. Very common in everyday speech. You can also say “otra vez y otra vez.”
target_language_example: Te lo he dicho una y otra vez: no dejes la puerta abierta.
native_language_example: I’ve told you over and over: don’t leave the door open.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an alternate or hypothetical reality (often in science fiction), or metaphorically about someone living in a very different “world” from yours. As a noun phrase, it can take articles (el/un universo paralelo) and plural (universos paralelos).
target_language_example: A veces siento que vivo en un universo paralelo.
native_language_example: Sometimes I feel like I live in a parallel universe.

meaning: one of these days; sometime soon (or eventually).
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something at an unspecified time in the near future (and sometimes it implies it keeps getting postponed). Often followed by a future tense or ir + a + infinitive. You can also hear it as an informal warning/threat: “¡Uno de estos días…!”
