target_language_example: Uno de estos días voy a visitar a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: One of these days I’m going to visit my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the subject and object are the same person (“by oneself” / “for oneself”). It agrees in gender and number: uno mismo (m.), una misma (f.), uno mismo/una misma can also mean “the same person”; plural: nosotros mismos / nosotras mismas, ustedes mismos / ustedes mismas, ellos mismos / ellas mismas.
target_language_example: Lo hice yo mismo.
native_language_example: I did it myself.

meaning: one by one; one at a time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing or checking things individually (not all together). Common in instructions and procedures. Also used for counting/distributing items individually.
target_language_example: Vamos a revisar los documentos uno por uno.
native_language_example: We’re going to review the documents one by one.

meaning: one after another; one behind the other.
additional_notes: Used to describe things happening or appearing in sequence, often repeatedly. Common with verbs like pasar (to happen), venir (to come), salir (to come out), and entrar (to go in). Similar to "uno detrás de otro" (more literal: "one behind another").
target_language_example: Los autobuses llegaron uno tras otro.
native_language_example: The buses arrived one after another.

meaning: a few; quite a few; several.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified small number (sometimes it can imply “quite a few” depending on context). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: unos cuantos (masc. plural), unas cuantas (fem. plural). Often followed by a noun: unos cuantos días (a few days), unas cuantas personas (a few people).
target_language_example: Me voy a quedar unos cuantos días más.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay a few more days.

additional_notes: Used before a number to mean an approximate amount (like “about” or “roughly”). It agrees in gender/number with the implied noun: most commonly "unos" with masculine or mixed groups ("unos dos minutos"), and "unas" with feminine nouns ("unas dos horas"). Often appears in phrases like "unos dos" + noun (time, people, blocks, etc.).
target_language_example: Llego en unos dos minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in about two minutes.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “a few” (some, but not many). For feminine plural nouns, use “unas pocas” (e.g., unas pocas cosas). You can also use it on its own if the noun is understood: “Solo tengo unos pocos.”
target_language_example: Tengo unos pocos amigos aquí.
native_language_example: I have a few friends here.

additional_notes: Used before a number to mean “approximately” or “around.” It commonly introduces an estimate (time, quantity, distance, etc.). "Unos" agrees with the noun you’re estimating (e.g., "unas tres horas" = about three hours).
target_language_example: Tardaré unos tres minutos en llegar.
native_language_example: It’ll take me about three minutes to get there.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis or to say someone should do/see something personally, addressing one person with the formal pronoun "usted." It agrees in gender/number: "usted misma" (female), "ustedes mismos/mismas" (plural). Often used after the pronoun: "usted mismo".
target_language_example: Puede verlo usted mismo en la página web.
native_language_example: You can see it yourself on the website.

additional_notes: Used to address exactly two people (not just one). In most of Latin America, "ustedes" is the normal word for plural “you” (both formal and informal), so "ustedes dos" is a common way to say “you two.” In Spain, everyday “you two” is often "vosotros dos" (informal) and "ustedes dos" is more formal/less common.
target_language_example: ¿Ustedes dos van a venir mañana?
native_language_example: Are you two going to come tomorrow?

meaning: “One, coming up!” / “That’s one!” (as you count or announce orders).
additional_notes: Used when counting items or calling out/confirming orders, especially in restaurants, bars, or busy situations. It’s like saying “one!” or “one for you!” after someone requests something. Often heard as part of a sequence: “Va uno, van dos, van tres…” (one, two, three…).
target_language_example: ¿Dos cafés? Perfecto: va uno para aquí y va otro para llevar.
native_language_example: Two coffees? Perfect: one is for here and the other is to go.

meaning: to be worth; to be valid; to matter.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to talk about value (money or usefulness): "¿Cuánto vale?" (How much is it worth?). It can also mean "to be valid" for tickets/coupons/documents: "Este cupón no vale" (This coupon isn’t valid). In some contexts it means "to be good for" or "to serve": "Esto no me vale" (This doesn’t work for me / This isn’t good enough for me).
target_language_example: ¿Cuánto vale esta chaqueta?
native_language_example: How much is this jacket worth?

meaning: to be worth it; to be worthwhile.
additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, cost, or trouble. Often appears in questions and negatives: "¿Vale la pena...?" (Is it worth it?), "No vale la pena" (It’s not worth it). You can add "que + verb" to say it’s worth doing something: "Vale la pena estudiar" / "Vale la pena que estudies".
target_language_example: Vale la pena visitar este museo.
native_language_example: It’s worth visiting this museum.

additional_notes: Often used to introduce what you’re going to check, think about, or explain next (“Let’s see…”). It can also mean “we’ll see” when you’re not sure yet or don’t want to commit. Very common filler in conversation; typically followed by a pause. Literal meaning is “we’re going to see,” but the idiomatic use is usually “let’s see.”
target_language_example: Vamos a ver si hay mesa para dos.
native_language_example: Let’s see if there’s a table for two.

meaning: “We’ll talk” / “Let’s stay in touch” (we’ll talk later).
additional_notes: Used when saying goodbye or ending a conversation to suggest you’ll continue the conversation later. It’s friendly and common in everyday speech, often implying no fixed time: “we’ll catch up.” Literally it’s “we go on talking,” but in practice it’s a farewell/keep-in-touch phrase.
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. Vamos hablando, ¿vale?
native_language_example: Alright, I’m heading out. We’ll talk, okay?

additional_notes: Used to say something happened repeatedly, but not an exact number. Often placed after the verb (Lo vi varias veces) or at the beginning for emphasis (Varias veces te lo dije). You can also use it in questions: ¿Cuántas veces? (How many times?) / ¿Varias veces? (Several times?).
target_language_example: He ido a México varias veces.
native_language_example: I’ve been to Mexico several times.

meaning: “Go with God” / “God be with you” (a farewell).
additional_notes: A traditional, often formal-sounding goodbye that invokes God’s protection. Commonly used when someone is leaving (especially for a long trip) or as a respectful farewell; you may also hear it as “vaya usted con Dios” (more formal) or “vayan con Dios” (plural).
target_language_example: Que tenga un buen viaje. Vaya con Dios.
native_language_example: Have a good trip. God be with you.

additional_notes: A scientific expression meaning how fast light travels (often used in physics, astronomy, and sci‑fi). In everyday speech it can also be used figuratively to mean "extremely fast."
target_language_example: El mensaje llegó a la velocidad de la luz.
native_language_example: The message arrived at the speed of light.

additional_notes: Informal command using the tú form of venir (“to come”). Use it with friends, family, kids, or someone you address as tú. For a more polite/formal version, say “venga acá” (usted) or “ven aquí” (similar meaning). Often used to call someone over or get their attention.
target_language_example: Ven acá un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, please.

meaning: 'to come to'; 'to end up' (doing); 'to amount to/about'.
additional_notes: Often used as a periphrasis with an infinitive ("venir a + infinitive") to express the final result or outcome of a process (similar to "to end up" / "to come to" in English). It’s also common to express an approximate value or conclusion, especially in "venir a ser" = "to come to / to turn out to be" (often meaning "roughly" or "more or less").
target_language_example: Eso viene a costar unos 20 euros.
native_language_example: That ends up costing about 20 euros.

meaning: to be relevant; to apply (to the situation).
additional_notes: Used to say something is (or isn’t) related to what you’re talking about. Very common in the negative: “No viene al caso” = “That’s not relevant / That doesn’t apply here.” Often followed by “que…” when introducing a point: “Viene al caso que…” = “It’s relevant that…”.
target_language_example: Eso no viene al caso ahora.
native_language_example: That’s not relevant right now.

meaning: to be convenient / to come in handy; to suit (someone).
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les viene bien (or viene muy bien). It means something is a good fit or is convenient for you (time, plan, object, etc.). Common with times: “El lunes me viene bien” = “Monday works for me.”
target_language_example: ¿Te viene bien si quedamos a las seis?
native_language_example: Does it work for you if we meet at six?

meaning: to come with; to include (come with).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone accompanies you ("Vengo con mi amigo") or that something is included as part of a purchase/feature ("Viene con cargador"). In the past, use "vino con"; for a question, "¿Viene con...?".
target_language_example: ¿Este teléfono viene con cargador?
native_language_example: Does this phone come with a charger?

additional_notes: Used to invite or tell someone to accompany you. It’s the infinitive "venir" (to come) + "conmigo" (with me). In polite requests, you’ll often hear "¿Puedes venir conmigo?" or "¿Quiere venir conmigo?"
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir conmigo al supermercado?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me to the supermarket?

additional_notes: Used as a near-past construction: **venir de + infinitive** to say something happened very recently. Conjugate **venir** to match the subject (vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, vienen) and keep the next verb in the infinitive. Often translates as “just” in English; the literal “to come from” meaning is different and takes a noun/place (e.g., *vengo de México*).
target_language_example: Acabo de llegar; vengo de hablar con el jefe.
native_language_example: I just arrived; I just spoke with the boss.

meaning: to run in the family; to be a family trait.
additional_notes: Used to say a characteristic, talent, habit, or even an illness is common in someone’s family. Often said as “Eso viene de familia” (“It runs in the family”). It can also refer more generally to someone’s family background (similar to “come from a good family”), depending on context.
target_language_example: En mi casa todos somos músicos; eso viene de familia.
native_language_example: In my family we’re all musicians; it runs in the family.

meaning: "to come for" / "to come pick up" (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used when someone arrives to get a person or thing (often to pick them up and take them somewhere). It’s commonly followed by a person or object: "Vengo por ti" (I’m coming for you / to pick you up), "Vengo por el paquete" (I’m here for the package). In many situations, English would naturally say “pick up” or “come by for.”
target_language_example: Paso a las ocho y vengo por ti.
native_language_example: I’ll stop by at eight and pick you up.

additional_notes: Common verb used for seeing something (“ver algo”) and watching something like a movie or TV (“ver una película / la tele”). Also used in set phrases like “A ver…” (“Let’s see…”). Conjugation is irregular: yo veo, tú ves, él/ella ve, nosotros vemos, ellos ven; preterite: vi.
target_language_example: Quiero ver la película esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to watch the movie tonight.

additional_notes: Used when someone sees two images of a single object (double vision), often due to dizziness, illness, eye problems, or being drunk/tired. Common with verbs like "empezar a" (to start to) or "estar" (to be): "Estoy viendo doble."
target_language_example: Después de dos copas, empecé a ver doble.
native_language_example: After two drinks, I started seeing double.

meaning: “to see/watch the …” (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (ver = “to see/to watch”) plus the feminine singular definite article la (“the”). It must be followed by a feminine singular noun: ver la película (watch the movie), ver la tele (watch TV), ver la ciudad (see the city). Unlike al/del, there is no contraction with la.
target_language_example: Quiero ver la película esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to watch the movie tonight.

meaning: to see (someone) in person; literally, “to see (someone’s) face.”
additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object to mean you actually see the person: “No le he visto la cara” = “I haven’t seen him/her (in a while).” You can also say “verle la cara a alguien” (to see someone’s face / to see someone in person).
target_language_example: Hace semanas que no le veo la cara.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him in weeks.

additional_notes: Often used in apps, menus, and websites as a button/link to show the full list of items (e.g., products, photos, messages). In everyday speech it can also mean to watch/view something completely (for example, finishing a series).
target_language_example: Haz clic en "Ver todo" para mostrar todos los resultados.
native_language_example: Click "View all" to show all the results.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a truthful explanation, clarification, or slight correction, often after a pause (like “well, actually…”). In everyday Spanish you’ll very often hear it as “La verdad es que…”. You can omit “que” if no clause follows: “La verdad es…”
target_language_example: La verdad es que no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: The truth is that I don’t have time today.

meaning: secondhand embarrassment; embarrassment for someone else.
additional_notes: Used when you feel embarrassed because of what someone else did or said (even if they aren’t embarrassed). Very common in everyday Spanish. Often appears with verbs like “dar” (to cause): “Me da vergüenza ajena…”. Literally “someone else’s shame/embarrassment,” but the natural English meaning is “secondhand embarrassment.”
target_language_example: Me dio vergüenza ajena cuando empezó a gritar en el restaurante.
native_language_example: I felt secondhand embarrassment when he started yelling in the restaurant.

meaning: to see oneself; to look/seem (also used for “see you” / “see each other”).
additional_notes: Reflexive form of "ver" (to see). Very common for appearance: "Te ves bien" = "You look good." It’s also used for meeting/parting: "Nos vemos" = "See you" / "We’ll see each other." Not related to English "verse" (poetry).
target_language_example: Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow.

meaning: “Go to hell,” “fuck off.” (a very rude way to tell someone to go away)
additional_notes: Very strong, offensive insult. Use only if you intend to be rude; not appropriate in polite conversation. Often used in anger. Grammar: vete = informal tú command of irse (“leave/go away”); a la mierda literally means “to the shit.” Variants: ¡Vete a la mierda! / ¡Vayan(se) a la mierda! (you all) / ¡Váyase a la mierda! (formal, still rude).
target_language_example: ¡Vete a la mierda y déjame en paz!
native_language_example: Fuck off and leave me alone.

meaning: “Who knows?” / “Your guess is as good as mine.”
additional_notes: Idiomatic way to say you don’t know (or it’s impossible to know) the answer. Often expresses uncertainty, resignation, or mild annoyance. Usually used on its own or after a statement: “No me llamó; vete a saber por qué.”
target_language_example: No me contestó el mensaje; vete a saber qué le pasó.
native_language_example: He didn’t reply to my message; who knows what happened to him.

meaning: “go with God” (a religious way to say goodbye, like “God go with you”).
additional_notes: Used to wish someone well as they leave; common in religious contexts and among older speakers. It can sound formal/solemn, similar to “God bless you” or “go in peace.” Often said as an imperative: “Vete con Dios.” You may also hear “Vaya con Dios” (more formal/polite) or “Id con Dios” (Spain; plural).
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; vete con Dios.
native_language_example: It’s late; go with God (God bless you as you go).

meaning: to time travel; to travel through time.
additional_notes: Used for science fiction or hypotheticals about going to the past or the future. The most common verb is "viajar" (to travel), and you can specify direction with "al pasado" (to the past) or "al futuro" (to the future).
target_language_example: Si pudieras viajar en el tiempo, ¿irías al pasado o al futuro?
native_language_example: If you could time travel, would you go to the past or the future?

additional_notes: Used to say you are traveling for work (meetings, conferences, clients), not for vacation. Often appears with verbs like "ir" (to go) or "estar" (to be): "Estoy de viaje de negocios". You can also say "viajar por negocios" (to travel for business).
target_language_example: La próxima semana tengo un viaje de negocios a Madrid.
native_language_example: Next week I have a business trip to Madrid.

meaning: public life; life in the public eye.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s activities, career, or role that is visible to society (often politics, government, media, or being a public figure). Common contrast: "vida privada" (private life).
target_language_example: Desde que es alcaldesa, su vida pública es muy intensa.
native_language_example: Since she became mayor, her public life is very intense.

meaning: real life; the real world (as opposed to online, movies, games, etc.).
additional_notes: Often used to contrast everyday reality with fiction, social media, or virtual settings. Common in phrases like "en la vida real" (in real life) and "en la vida real, no es así" (in real life, it’s not like that).
target_language_example: En la vida real, las cosas no siempre salen como en las películas.
native_language_example: In real life, things don’t always turn out like in the movies.

meaning: “old school”; traditional, from an earlier style.
additional_notes: Used to describe people, methods, or tastes that follow traditional ways (often with a positive tone: “classic,” “authentic,” “the way it used to be”). Can also be mildly critical, depending on context, meaning “outdated.” You’ll often hear it with ser: “Es de la vieja escuela.”
target_language_example: Mi abuelo es de la vieja escuela y prefiere pagar en efectivo.
native_language_example: My grandfather is old school and prefers to pay in cash.

additional_notes: Commonly used when ordering drinks or talking about wine. In Spanish it’s a straightforward noun phrase: vino (wine) + blanco (white). You may also hear it with an article: "un vino blanco" (a white wine) or "el vino blanco" (the white wine).
target_language_example: Para mí, un vaso de vino blanco, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of white wine, please.

additional_notes: A sweet wine served with (or after) dessert. In restaurants you might see it on a drink menu or hear it when ordering dessert. Literally “wine of dessert.”
target_language_example: ¿Tienen vino de postre para acompañar el pastel?
native_language_example: Do you have dessert wine to go with the cake?

additional_notes: A common way to order or talk about red wine. In Spain, “vino tinto” is the standard term; in some Latin American countries you may also hear “vino rojo.”
target_language_example: Para mí, una copa de vino tinto, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of red wine, please.

meaning: the spitting image; an exact look-alike.
additional_notes: Usually used in the fixed expression "ser la viva imagen de + (person)" to say someone looks extremely similar to someone else (often a family member). It literally means “living image,” but in English you’d normally say “the spitting image” or “a carbon copy.”
target_language_example: Ana es la viva imagen de su madre.
native_language_example: Ana is the spitting image of her mother.

meaning: to live with; to cope with / live with (a situation).
additional_notes: Often followed by a person or pet (cohabitation): "Vivo con mi hermana." It can also mean accepting/coping with something difficult: "Tengo que vivir con este dolor." In this second sense, English also uses “live with” similarly.
target_language_example: No puedo vivir con tanto ruido.
native_language_example: I can't live with so much noise.

meaning: to do again; to go/come back to.
additional_notes: Common patterns: (1) "volver a" + infinitive = “to do (something) again”: "volver a intentar" (try again), "volver a llamar" (call again). Conjugate "volver" and keep "a" + infinitive: "Vuelvo a empezar", "Volvimos a verlo". (2) "volver a" + place/thing = “to return to”: "volver a casa" (go back home), "volver al trabajo" (go back to work).
target_language_example: Voy a volver a llamar más tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to call again later.

meaning: to regain consciousness; to come to one’s senses.
additional_notes: Used when someone wakes up after fainting/being unconscious, or when someone recovers mentally/emotionally and starts thinking clearly again. Common with verbs like "hacer" in the past ("volvió en sí") and can be followed by "después de" + noun/infinitive ("después del golpe").
target_language_example: Después de desmayarse, volvió en sí a los pocos minutos.
native_language_example: After fainting, she regained consciousness a few minutes later.

meaning: a dissenting opinion (in a court decision).
additional_notes: Used mainly in legal/judicial contexts in Spain (and sometimes in other Spanish-speaking contexts) to refer to the written opinion of a judge who disagrees with the majority decision. It’s often introduced with verbs like "emitir" (to issue) or "formular" (to file/express): "emitir/formular un voto particular". Not the same as a regular "voto" in an election.
target_language_example: El juez emitió un voto particular en contra de la sentencia.
native_language_example: The judge issued a dissenting opinion against the ruling.

meaning: “I’ll be right back” / “I’m coming and going (quickly).”
additional_notes: Commonly said when you’re leaving for a short moment and expect to return soon (e.g., to the bathroom, to grab something nearby). It’s informal and idiomatic; often used alone as a quick heads-up. You may also hear: “Voy y vuelvo.”
target_language_example: Espera un momento: voy y vengo.
native_language_example: Wait a moment: I’ll be right back.

meaning: 'and so', 'and like that' (continuing in the same way).
additional_notes: Used to show continuation, result, or that something keeps going in the same way. Often appears in lists or explanations (sometimes repeated as "y así" or expanded to "y así sucesivamente" = "and so on"). It can also refer back to a previously mentioned action: "Hice esto y así" = "I did this and (then) like that."
target_language_example: Fuimos al mercado, compramos pan y así seguimos con el día.
native_language_example: We went to the market, bought bread, and then we continued with the day.

meaning: “and well…” / “anyway…” (a conversational filler to continue or wrap up).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Spanish to transition to a new point, restart after a pause, or gently conclude what you were saying. Often used at the beginning of a sentence (and can be followed by a pause): “Y bueno, …”. Tone depends on context; it can sound casual, reflective, or like you’re moving on.
target_language_example: Y bueno, ¿qué hacemos ahora?
native_language_example: Anyway, what do we do now?

additional_notes: Used at the end of a request to be polite, similar to “and thanks.” Often implies “thanks in advance.” You can also hear it as “y, gracias” after a short pause. Common in casual speech and messages (e.g., when ordering or asking for help).
target_language_example: ¿Me traes la cuenta, y gracias?
native_language_example: Can you bring me the bill, and thanks?

additional_notes: Used after a number to add half a unit. Very common with time: “a las dos y media” = 2:30. With age, money, distance, etc., it means “and a half”: “dos años y medio” = two and a half years. Note agreement: “y medio” (masculine singular), “y media” (feminine singular), “y medios / y medias” (plural), depending on the noun (e.g., “un kilo y medio,” “una hora y media,” “dos kilos y medio”).
target_language_example: Quedamos a las seis y media.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at six thirty.

additional_notes: Used to end a discussion firmly, meaning “no more debate” or “I won’t change my mind.” Often follows a statement or decision. Can sound blunt or a bit rude depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: No voy a ir, y punto.
native_language_example: I’m not going, period.

meaning: "and what not / and so on" (and other similar things).
additional_notes: Used informally at the end of a list to mean “and other things like that / etc.” In writing you’ll often see it with accents and punctuation: “y qué no” or “y qué sé yo”.
target_language_example: Compré fruta, pan, queso y qué no para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I bought fruit, bread, cheese, and what not for the party.

additional_notes: Used as a short reply to show you don’t think something matters, or to challenge what someone just said. Often sounds dismissive or confrontational depending on tone. Also appears in questions like “¿Y qué pasó?” (“And what happened?”).
target_language_example: —Llegué tarde. —¿Y qué?
native_language_example: —I arrived late. —So what?

meaning: 'and stuff / and so on' (and that kind of thing).
additional_notes: Casual filler used at the end of a list or description when you don’t want to name every detail. Similar to "y eso", "y todo eso", or "y demás". Very common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Fuimos al cine, cenamos y tal, y luego nos fuimos a casa.
native_language_example: We went to the movies, had dinner and stuff, and then we went home.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is included as part of a set, often with a nuance of surprise or emphasis. Common in spoken Spanish after a noun or phrase: "con la ropa y todo" (with the clothes and everything), "fue y todo" (he/she even went). It’s basically "y" + "todo" and can often be translated literally as "and everything/and all".
target_language_example: Llegó con el traje y todo.
native_language_example: He/She showed up with the suit and everything.

additional_notes: Very informal and rude/vulgar. Used to strongly disagree with or reject what someone just said, often as a standalone exclamation: “¡Y una mierda!”. You’ll also hear it after repeating the claim you reject: “¿Que no pasó nada? ¡Y una mierda!”. Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: —Dice que no te va a pagar. —¿Que no me va a pagar? ¡Y una mierda!
native_language_example: “He says he’s not going to pay you.” “He’s not going to pay me? Yeah, right!”

additional_notes: Used to end a statement and emphasize that nothing else is needed or will happen. Common in spoken Spanish and can sound firm or a bit abrupt depending on tone. Often follows an instruction or conclusion: “Haces esto y ya.”
target_language_example: Solo tienes que firmar aquí y ya.
native_language_example: You just have to sign here, and that’s it.

additional_notes: Used to express impatience or relief that something has happened after taking longer than expected. Often said as a comment on a situation (it can sound slightly complaining, depending on tone). Also commonly heard as: "¡Ya era hora de que...!" + verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "¡Ya era hora de que llegaras!").
target_language_example: ¡Ya era hora! Llevábamos una hora esperándote.
native_language_example: About time! We’d been waiting for you for an hour.

additional_notes: Very common phrase used to say something is finished or settled. It can mean (1) a task is completed: "Ya está" = "It’s done"; (2) something is enough or you want someone to stop: "¡Ya está!" = "That’s enough!"; (3) to wrap up or conclude a point: "Ya está" = "That’s it." Tone depends a lot on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Ya está, terminé la tarea.
native_language_example: All set, I finished the homework.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree with what someone just said, often like “Of course!” or “Absolutely!” It can also add emphasis to a statement (“…and you can be sure of that”). Very common in conversation. Literally it’s like “I already believe it,” but it’s usually not translated word-for-word.
target_language_example: —Hace mucho frío hoy. —¡Ya lo creo!
native_language_example: —It’s really cold today. —You bet!/Definitely!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a situation has changed: before there were people, but now there aren’t. Very often appears as “ya no” + verb + “nadie” (e.g., “Ya no viene nadie”). On its own, “ya nadie” is usually followed by a verb (e.g., “ya nadie sabe…”).
target_language_example: Ya nadie quiere salir tan tarde.
native_language_example: No one wants to go out that late anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say something that was true before is now no longer true. It often goes right before the verb: “ya no + verb” (e.g., “ya no vivo aquí” = “I don’t live here anymore”). You can also use it with “ser/estar”: “ya no es…” / “ya no está…”. Common contrast: “ya” = “already,” but “ya no” = “no longer.”
target_language_example: Ya no tengo tiempo para ir al gimnasio.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to go to the gym anymore.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a statement by saying that if something is true for a smaller/easier case, it’s even more true for a bigger/harder one. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., “ya no digamos + noun/verb”). Similar to “ya no hablemos de…,” and may appear as “ya ni digamos” (more informal/colloquial).
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo para salir; ya no digamos para irme de vacaciones.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to go out, let alone go on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason or explanation. It’s a common connector in more neutral/formal speech and writing (similar to “puesto que” or “porque”). It can also mean “given that” when the reason is treated as already known or obvious.
target_language_example: Ya que estás aquí, ¿puedes ayudarme con esto?
native_language_example: Since you’re here, can you help me with this?

meaning: “since we’re at it” / “while we’re at it.”
additional_notes: Used to add an extra request, comment, or action that makes sense to do now because you’re already doing something related. Very common in conversation. Often followed by another clause: “Ya que estamos, …”
target_language_example: Ya que estamos, ¿me puedes mandar el enlace también?
native_language_example: Since we’re at it, can you send me the link too?

meaning: “Yeah, exactly” / “I’m telling you” (used to strongly agree or emphasize).
additional_notes: Common in casual spoken Spanish. Often used to show strong agreement with what the other person just said (“Exactly!”) or to emphasize your point (“I’m telling you”). Similar to “ya” = “already/now” + “te digo” = “I tell you,” but the real meaning is idiomatic. You may also hear it repeated: “Ya te digo, ya.”
target_language_example: —Este trabajo es agotador. —Ya te digo, no paro en todo el día.
native_language_example: —This job is exhausting. —Tell me about it / Exactly, I don’t stop all day.

additional_notes: Used to postpone a decision or to say something is uncertain until more information is available. It can sound neutral (“we’ll see”) or mildly doubtful/avoidant depending on tone and context. Often refers to the future: “later we’ll see.”
target_language_example: —¿Vas a venir mañana? —Ya veremos.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —We’ll see.

additional_notes: Common in conversation to show you understand or to acknowledge what someone is saying. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral and polite (“OK, OK”) or impatient/dismissive (“Yeah, yeah”). Written with a comma and repeated for emphasis; often said quickly.
target_language_example: Ya, ya, lo entiendo. No hace falta que lo repitas.
native_language_example: Yeah, yeah, I understand. You don’t need to repeat it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you personally did something or experienced something. It can also mean “by myself / on my own” in context. For gender/number agreement: a man typically says “yo mismo,” a woman “yo misma.” Plural: “nosotros mismos / nosotras mismas.”
target_language_example: Lo hice yo mismo.
native_language_example: I did it myself.

additional_notes: Intentionally incorrect Spanish (the correct form is “yo no sé”). Often used jokingly or to imitate a childlike/limited way of speaking; it can sound uneducated or mocking, so avoid it in formal situations and with strangers.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se dice “receipt” en español? — Yo no sabo.
native_language_example: How do you say “receipt” in Spanish? — I don’t know.

meaning: "I’ll know" / "I’ll figure it out" (i.e., it’s up to me).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll handle it yourself or that it’s your decision/business. It can sound firm or a bit defensive, especially if someone is questioning you. Often appears as a standalone reply: “—¿Por qué lo haces? —Yo sabré.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: yo sabré qué hacer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll know what to do / I’ll figure out what to do.

additional_notes: Used to agree or add that the same thing is true for you. Also common as just “también” (“me too”) when “yo” is already clear from context. Often used as a short reply.
target_language_example: —Me gusta el chocolate. —Yo también.
native_language_example: —I like chocolate. —Me too.

meaning: “I know you” (I’m familiar with you / I recognize you).
additional_notes: Uses the verb “conocer” for knowing a person, place, or being familiar with something (not “saber,” which is for facts/skills). “Yo” is often optional because the verb ending already shows the subject; it can be included for emphasis (“I know you”). “Te” is the informal singular “you” (tú).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, yo te conozco: eres el hermano de Marta.
native_language_example: Relax, I know you: you’re Marta’s brother.

additional_notes: Used to talk about staying in what feels easy and familiar, or encouraging someone to try new things (“salir de la zona de confort” = “to step out of your comfort zone”). Often used in self-improvement, work, and lifestyle contexts.
target_language_example: Quiero salir de mi zona de confort y probar algo nuevo.
native_language_example: I want to step out of my comfort zone and try something new.

additional_notes: A common holiday phrase. Capitalization varies: “árbol de Navidad” is common in general writing; “Navidad” is often capitalized because it refers to Christmas. The indefinite article is usually “un”: “un árbol de Navidad”.
target_language_example: Vamos a comprar un árbol de Navidad para la sala.
native_language_example: We’re going to buy a Christmas tree for the living room.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a grassy or planted public space in a city (like a park, garden area, or green space). Common on signs and in city planning contexts. Plural: “áreas verdes.”
target_language_example: Hay un área verde cerca de mi casa donde puedo caminar.
native_language_example: There’s a green area near my house where I can go for a walk.

additional_notes: Reflexive/intensifier phrase used to emphasize that it was the man/boy personally (and not someone else), or to mean “himself” with a reflexive verb. Often used after the subject (“Él mismo lo hizo”) or after a noun (“el rey mismo”). Feminine: “ella misma”; plural: “ellos mismos / ellas mismas”.
target_language_example: Él mismo preparó la cena.
native_language_example: He himself made dinner.

additional_notes: A very common story-opening phrase (especially fairy tales). "Érase" is an old-fashioned form meaning roughly "it was," so it sounds literary/old-timey rather than everyday speech.
target_language_example: Érase una vez una princesa que vivía en un castillo.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a princess who lived in a castle.

meaning: the last straw (the final thing that makes you lose patience).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the fixed expression “la última gota” or “la gota que colmó el vaso” (“the drop that overflowed the glass”). Used when something small happens after many problems, and it’s the final trigger.
target_language_example: Cuando cancelaron el vuelo otra vez, fue la última gota y me fui.
native_language_example: When they canceled the flight again, it was the last straw and I left.

meaning: “breaking news”; “last minute” (at the last possible moment).
additional_notes: Common in news contexts: "a última hora" = "at the last minute / at the last moment" and "noticias de última hora" = "breaking news." Also used for sudden, recent updates: "información de última hora". Literal meaning is "last hour," but it usually refers to something very recent or done at the last moment, not exactly 60 minutes.
target_language_example: Cancelaron el vuelo a última hora por el mal tiempo.
native_language_example: They canceled the flight at the last minute because of bad weather.

meaning: the last word; the final say/decision.
additional_notes: Often used literally (the last word spoken in a conversation) or figuratively to mean the final authority in a discussion or decision. Common in expressions like "tener la última palabra" (to have the final say) and "decir la última palabra" (to get the last word in).
target_language_example: En esta casa, mi mamá tiene la última palabra.
native_language_example: In this house, my mom has the final say.

meaning: the last minute; the last moment.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something done or decided very late, right before a deadline or event. Often appears in phrases like “a último momento” (at the last minute) or “de último momento” (last-minute, sudden).
target_language_example: No lo dejes para el último momento.
native_language_example: Don’t leave it until the last minute.

additional_notes: Used when there are no better choices left. Often appears with phrases like "como último recurso" (as a last resort) or "ser el último recurso" (to be the last resort).
target_language_example: Como último recurso, llamamos a la policía.
native_language_example: As a last resort, we called the police.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small final detail or adjustment that completes something (a project, decoration, outfit, makeup, etc.). Often appears with verbs like "dar" (to give) or "poner" (to put): "dar el último toque" / "poner el último toque".
target_language_example: Solo falta dar el último toque a la presentación.
native_language_example: We just need to put the finishing touch on the presentation.
